News.title: When do the clocks change? Date the UK clocks go forward and back, and what time it happens
News.content:
THE CLOCKS are set to go back in the coming weeks, giving us an extra hour in bed – but darker evenings and shorter days.

The UK switches to Greenwich Mean Time in October – here’s everything you need to know about exactly when it happens.



When do the clocks go back in 2026?

The clocks go back on Sunday, October 25, 2026, at 2am, when the time jumps to 1am.

It happens on the last Sunday in October each year and marks the end of British Summer Time (BST).



Phones, computers and most smart devices update on their own, but older watches, stereos, clocks in cars, and some kitchen appliances may need changing manually.

But not everyone gets an extra hour in bed; people working a night shift when the clocks change could end up working an extra hour.



When do the clocks go forward in 2027?

British Summer Time returns on Sunday, March 28, 2027, when the clocks jump forward from 1am to 2am, meaning we effectively lose an hour of sleep.

The yearly schedule is fixed, with clocks moving forward an hour at 1am on the last Sunday in March every year, and then back an hour at 2am on the last Sunday in October.

If you can’t remember which way the clocks go, there’s a simple phrase to help you remember – “spring forward, fall back.”

Why do the clocks change?

The weekend changeover was chosen because moving the clocks overnight on a Saturday into Sunday causes less disruption to schools and businesses.



The idea of making better use of daylight goes back hundreds of years.

Benjamin Franklin discussed the benefits of getting up earlier to make use of morning sunlight in a satirical essay written in 1784.

But the campaign to change Britain’s clocks was led more than a century later by builder William Willett.

In 1907, he published a pamphlet called The Waste of Daylight, arguing that clocks should be moved forward during the summer so people could make better use of daylight.

His original proposal was more complicated than the system that was eventually adopted.



He called for clocks to move forward by a total of 80 minutes in four separate 20-minute steps.

Attempts to introduce daylight saving legislation were rejected by Parliament several times between 1908 and 1916.

But that changed during World War I, when The Summer Time Act received Royal Assent on May 17, 1916, with the clocks going forward for the first time on May 21 of that year.

The wartime measure was intended partly to boost productivity and reduce fuel use.

Britain later went even further during World War II, when Double Summer Time put clocks two hours ahead of GMT during parts of the year.



The system was dropped after the war but was briefly brought back during the fuel crisis of 1947.

Britain has also experimented with keeping the clocks permanently an hour ahead.

British Standard Time was introduced on October 27, 1968, meaning the UK remained on GMT+1 through the winter instead of putting the clocks back.

The trial ended on October 31, 1971, after Parliament voted against making it permanent.

Opposition was particularly strong in Scotland and other northern areas, where the change meant much darker winter mornings, and also among groups including farmers and industrial workers.



The debate over changing the clocks has never completely gone away.

Around 70 countries use some form of daylight saving time.

The European Commission proposed ending seasonal clock changes across the EU in 2018, and the European Parliament backed the move the following year.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

But the proposal has not taken effect and no final decision has been agreed.

Until that happens, EU countries continue to change their clocks twice a year on the same Sundays as the UK.

News.title: Brit man rescued almost week after Nepal flood disaster as death toll passes grim 1,000 milestone & 4,500 remain missing
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

MIRACLE RESCUE Brit man rescued almost week after Nepal flood disaster as death toll passes grim 1,000 milestone & 4,500 remain missing

A BRITISH man has miraculously been pulled alive from rubble nearly a week after the devastating flash floods which killed over 1000 people.

The survivor – who has not yet been identified – was one of 33 nationals unaccounted for.

A search and rescue spokesperson said: “We have rescued 118 Nepalese people… 44 are female and 74 are male.

“We have also rescued one British male during this search and rescue operation.”





It comes as a rapid deployment team from the UK arrived in Nepal, China on Saturday to provide support for Brits and their families.

The team, comprising specially trained crisis response staff, will work alongside the British embassy and local authorities.

Over 4,500 people remain missing after after catastrophic flash floods ravaged the region and neighbouring Tibet.

The staggering death toll is expected to climb further as rescuers continue the desperate search for those still unaccounted for, who include 48 Brits – 33 in Nepal and 15 in Tibet.



Only 20 people killed in the horror floods have been reunited with their families as desperate loved ones continue to search overflowing hospitals and mortuaries.

News.title: Huge fire erupts near homes as smoke billows for miles & residents warned to close windows after ‘explosions’ heard
News.content:
BLAZE BATTLE Huge fire erupts near homes as smoke billows for miles & residents warned to close windows after ‘explosions’ heard

A HUGE inferno has broken out on a busy industrial estate near homes, with plumes of black smoke seen for miles and explosions heard.

Nine fire crews and sixteen fire engines were scrambled to the scene in Brislington, Bristol, after the blaze ignited in a disused building earlier today.



Members of the public heard loud “explosions” at the industrial estate as the fire ripped through the building, Bristol Live reports.

Firefighters from nearby Hicks Gate, Temple, Kingswood, Avonmouth, Yate, Bath, Patchway, Bedminster and Nailsea are all currently at the scene of the huge inferno.



Avon Fire and Rescue have urged residents to avoid the area as crews attempt to bring the flames under control.

People have been told to keep their doors and windows closed as smoke pours from the fire and into the surrounding area.

Roads have been closed nearby with a police cordon in place around the site of the fire.

A spokesperson for Avon Fire and Rescue said: “Fire crews were called at 2:27 pm, and firefighters from Hicks Gate, Temple, Kingswood, Avonmouth, Yate, Bath, Patchway, Bedminster and Nailsea are currently on the scene tackling the fire.



“We are asking residents and local businesses to keep their windows and doors closed and avoid the area where possible.”

Police said enquiries into the fire remain ongoing at this time.

Images from the scene show pillars of orange fire jetting through the roof of the disused building.

A thick plume of smoke can be seen rising over the industrial estate as emergency services work to extinguish the fire.

People can be seen watching on in horror as the blaze tears through the abandoned building.



There have been no reported injuries.

Police have asked drivers to keep their distance from the fire amid rush hour.

Queues of traffic have begun to build on nearby roads as drivers face delays.

Inrix said: “Emery Road in both directions closed, queuing traffic due to building fire from A4 Bath Road to Bonville Road.”

Avon and Somerset Police said in a statement online: “Officers are on the scene supporting the fire service who are responding to an ongoing warehouse fire off Emery Road, in Bristol, today (Monday 1 September).



“A 200m cordon is in place, and officers are currently evacuating the area around warehouse. Enquiries are ongoing.”

News.title: Two killed and one seriously hurt after boat ploughs into inflatable ride in horror crash off coast of France
News.content:
SEA HORROR Two killed and one seriously hurt after boat ploughs into inflatable ride in horror crash off coast of France

TWO people have been killed as a boat ploughed into an inflatable ride off the coast of southern France, it has been reported.

The incident happened off Saint-Cyprien, in the Pyrénées-Orientales, this afternoon after the pilot of the vessel, which was tugging the buoy, was ejected.

One of those killed was the pilot, who was reportedly struck by a propeller as the boat went “haywire”.



The vessel then reversed and struck several passengers on the inflatable.



A woman also died, while a man suffered serious injuries to his arm and leg and was flown to a nearby hospital via a helicopter.

A source close to the investigation said: “The pilot was hit by the boat’s propeller and sank immediately.

“Initially, he was reported missing, before his body was found.”

Four others sustained minor injuries. In total, seven people were involved in the incident.

“It would appear that the boat was unbalanced by the waves generated and the pilot was ejected,” said public prosecutor of Perpignan, Jérôme Bourrier, according to Le Parisien.

“The boat went haywire, circling, passing over the buoy and hitting the victims. All these elements must for the moment be taken with caution.”

He added: “For the moment, the investigation is open for manslaughter, but we have little information about the facts at this stage.”



Designed for recreational riding, inflatable buoys are pulled behind a motorboat, normally at high speeds.

So far, it remains unconfirmed how the pilot was ejected from the vessel.

Around 20 firefighters have since been dispatched to the beach, as well as water rescue specialists.

News.title: Three injured after bus ploughs into 12 vehicles in train station car park as road closed & services axed
News.content:
BUS SMASH Three injured after bus ploughs into 12 vehicles in train station car park as road closed & services axed

THREE people have been injured after a bus ploughed into cars outside a train station – forcing the road to close and rail services to be cancelled.

Travel chaos has erupted following the horror smash at the station in Portslade, East Sussex, this afternoon.



A woman was rushed to hospital and two men were treated by paramedics after the crash, which occurred at around 2pm.

Pictures showed severe damage to the front of the bus, while wrecked cars could be seen lined up near the level crossing.



Boundary Road, which stretches either side of the busy tracks, has ground to a halt while emergency crews deal continue recovery work.

Eyewitnesses described seeing the number 46 bus “going into the back” of two cars, before piling into several more.

Lisa Putman told Brighton and Hove News: “The gates were down. The 46 bus turned at the station and went into the back of two cars…

“[It] then swerved and hit seven cars in the station car park.”



The bus is understood to have struck one car, before ploughing into 11 stationary cars in the cark park, Sussex Police said.

But nobody on board the bus was injured, the force added.

A spokesperson said: “Emergency services responded to a report of a collision involving a bus and 12 stationary cars.

“Three motorists were injured. A woman was taken to hospital to be treated while two men were treated at the scene.

“The bus is believed to have collided with a car before colliding with parked cars in Portslade railway station car park.



“Police are appealing for witnesses, and anyone with dashcam footage, to email collision.appeal@sussex.police.uk, quoting serial 697 of 1/9.”

Portslade has now reopened after the station and level crossing were closed to allow emergency services access.

Matt Ashton, managing director for Brighton and Hove Buses, confirmed an “incident occurred today at Portslade Station”.

Govia Thameslink Railway had said: “Portslade Station is closed while emergency services deal with an incident at the front of the station.

“We’re sorry to Southern customers who are affected.”



Southern Rail previously warned passengers disruption could continue until 4.30pm.

Issuing a statement on X, it said: “No trains can stop at Portslade Until further notice.

“You will need to use an alternative route to reach your destination.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“You should allow at least an additional 45 minutes to complete your journey today.

“If you are travelling to/from Portslade you will need to use an alternative route. Disruption is expected until 16:30.”

News.title: Age you can legally leave a child home alone after school in England
News.content:
SCHOOLS are officially back in session, but what does that mean for childcare?

With many parents working late into the evening, hours after the final bell, families have been left at a loss for after-school plans.

So the question is – at what age can you legally leave children at home on their own in England?



There is currently no law that outlines a specific age for leaving a child unsupervised at home.



However, parents are reminded that it is a criminal offence if youngsters are put at risk.

You can face fines or even jail if your child suffers harm due to being left alone.

Child protection laws prohibit leaving a minor “in a manner likely to cause unnecessary suffering or injury to health”.

The government advises parents to use common sense when determining if a child is mature enough to be left at home alone.

The National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC) offers a comprehensive guide for this topic.

“Every child matures differently, so it would be almost impossible to have a ‘one size fits all’ law,” it says on its website.

The NSPCC recommends children under the age of 12 are rarely mature enough to be left alone for a long period of time.



Kids aged under 16 should not be left home alone overnight, no matter how responsible they seem.

And babies, toddlers, and very young children must never be left alone, even for a moment.

The NPCC’s Helen Westerman said parents need to consider a couple of critical factors, including how both they and their child feels about the latter playing outside unsupervised.

“Lots of parents will be thinking about whether it’s safe to leave their children at home safely, and if they’re old enough to leave the house unsupervised,” she told the Liverpool Echo.

“As well as determining if a child is ready to be left alone, many parents will also find balancing work with the school break quite challenging, especially considering the rising child costs and the cost of living crisis, which is placing additional strain on families.”



Helen added: “As children get older, it’s common for them to want more freedom and learn to be independent.

“As every child is different, we recommend building up their independence at their pace and checking in with them to make sure they feel safe.”

And if the first step towards independence is letting them walk home alone from school, experts have also shared advice on this.

News.title: ‘Serious threat’ as killer Asian hornets are spotted in UK county for first time ever with Brits told to ‘be vigilant’
News.content:
INVASIVE Asian hornets have been spotted in a UK county for the first time.

A sting from the critters, which have distinctive yellow legs, can be painful or fatal in rare cases with Brits urged “to be vigilant”.

The National Bee Unit was called in to help after one of the insects was spotted by a beekeeper in Ashcott last week.



Further hornets were tracked to a nest, which is due to be destroyed this week.



The hornets are an invasive predator and prey on honeybees, bumblebees, hoverflies and other insects.

Its venom causes an intense burning sensation, which many have compared to being jabbed with a red hot needle.

Lynne Ingram, master beekeeper and organiser of the Somerset Beekeepers Association’s yellow-legged hornets teams, said: “This is the first time yellow‑legged Asian hornets have ever been found in Somerset, and early reporting made all the difference.”

Lynne added: “We want Somerset to remain a yellow‑legged hornet‑free zone, and the public’s vigilance is absolutely essential.”

The hornets were first detected in the UK in 2016, and are believed to have arrived from mainland Europe.

Sightings ever since have skyrocketed, rising to a staggering 544 confirmed reports in 2025 – an increase of 871 per cent compared to 2023.

The species first arrived in France in 2004.



They are believed to have nested in a shipment of pottery from China.

Five people died from Asian hornet stings in France in 2015.

News.title: Thug kept homeless slave he called ‘Scrapyard Dog’ in squalid shed for 3 YEARS to steal £63k for lavish holidays
News.content:
SLAVERY HORROR Thug kept homeless slave he called ‘Scrapyard Dog’ in squalid shed for 3 YEARS to steal £63k for lavish holidays

A THUG kept a homeless slave he called his “Scrapyard Dog” in a squalid shed for three years while stealing £63,000 from him to fund holidays.

James Dean Harrison, 51, from Coventry, forced his victim to do manual labour and stole his universal credit and pension.



Between November 2022 and February 2026 Harrison kept the man in his garden shed after he became homeless and approached Harrison for help.

The victim, in his 60s, shared the shed with his partner, a woman in her 50s, and Harrison’s dog.



A court heard that vile Harrison took the man’s bank cards and refused to return them.

He initially gave his victim £30 a day from his own account before reducing it to £20.

A total of £63,625.44 was missing from the pensioner’s account, which police said came from his pension and universal credit.

It is believed this money was used by Harrison to fund holidays for himself.

Harrison’s victim was forced to work in a scrapyard, painting skips, unloading skips and cleaning lorry cabs.

The man was regularly subjected to verbal and physical abuse, police said, with Harrison referring to him as his “Scrapyard Dog.”



Police launched a probe into the harrowing situation after the victim met with a local councillor regarding emergency housing and the councillor raised concerns.

Harrison was then taken into custody in February before appearing in court and pleading guilty to requiring a person to perform forced labour.

He has now been jailed for six and a half years for his sick crime and has been served with a Slavery and Trafficking Reparation Order.

This forces him to pay compensation of £10,000.

Investigating officer DC Hutt of the Trafficking and Exploitation Team said “The treatment that James Dean Harrison subjected the victim to – stripping him of his dignity, his finances, and seriously impacting his health – was appalling in every way.



“He had approached Harrison as a friend in need of help, and Harrison chose to exploit him for labour and to defraud him of his money.

“We might never have heard about this had it not been for the local community and their councillor – we thank them for calling this to our attention, and allowing us to work to put Harrison in prison for his actions.”

News.title: Andy Burnham LIVE: PM blasts Brexit and austerity for '10 years of stalled growth'
News.content:
Starmer's resignation statement in full

In a statement issued on X, Sir Keir Starmer said it was the right time to “hand the baton over to a successor”.

He said: “Over the summer, I have had time to reflect and consider my future. I have decided that now is the right time to step down as MP for Holborn and St Pancras and hand the baton over to a successor.

“It’s been an honour and privilege to represent the best constituency in the country since taking over from the great Frank Dobson 11 years ago. But it is now time to step aside and focus on other issues: international affairs including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast changing world. I will also continue working with others as I have done over many decades to tackle violence against women and girls.

“As I do that, I will always remain immensely proud to have represented the place Vic, the kids and I call home.

“I look back with pride on what my constituency team and I have delivered in Holborn and St Pancras since 2015 and I thank all those who I was privileged to work with on so many issues of local concern: affordable housing projects, delivering first class education and tackling youth violence through our Camden Youth Safety Taskforce.

“I want to thank my CLP team who have always stood firmly by me, and given me the support I needed as I stood for leader of the Labour Party and then as I took my party from political, moral and financial ruin to an historic landslide election win in 2024 and two years as prime minister when we stabilised the economy, rebuilt our public services, invested record amounts in our defence and security, began lifting hundreds of thousands of children out of poverty and transformed Britain’s reputation with international partners.

“I want to thank my constituency staff who, throughout all those 11 years, have worked tirelessly on casework and helped me do my utmost to serve the people of Holborn and St Pancras. I could not have done this job without them.

“There will now be a process to appoint my successor ahead of a by-election. Whoever is lucky enough to become the Labour candidate here will have my full support and backing and I will continue to give my full support to the Prime Minister and this Labour government.

“Keir Starmer.”

News.title: BBC axe 'truly iconic' sports programme after nearly 50 years leaving presenter devastated
News.content:
BBC axe 'truly iconic' sports programme after nearly 50 years leaving presenter devastated

The BBC has continued its drastic cutbacks to its sports broadcasting offering by axing winter sports show Ski Sunday, which has been on our screens since 1978

View 3 Images The BBC has axed another sports show (Image: James Gill - Danehouse/Getty Images)

The BBC has axed Ski Sunday after nearly 50 years on air. The winter sports show has been on our screens since 1978, but will not return.

‌



It was last broadcast in February ahead of the Winter Olympic Games and has been presented by Chemmy Alcott and Ed Leigh in recent years.

‌



Explaining the decision, the BBC said: “Changing audience behaviours and the tough financial decisions needed to meet savings requirements. BBC Sport must continually review how it delivers value for licence fee payers and serves audiences across all platforms. This decision forms part of that process.”

‌



Four-time Winter Olympian skier Alcott joined the presenting team on Ski Sunday in 2021 and was shocked by the decision. "As you can imagine this has devastated me," she wrote on Instagram. "Full response coming soon."

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

BBC axes another football show as broadcaster continues cull on terrestrial channels READ MORE :

Philip Bernie, head of BBC Sport events, said Ski Sunday "has been a truly iconic programme".

‌



He added: "Generations of viewers have enjoyed its coverage of the best in winter sports. We are enormously proud of the role it has played in bringing these moments to audiences across the UK, and extremely grateful to the brilliant people who have delivered them, not least the current outstanding team.

View 3 Images Chemmy Alcott is devastated by the decision (Image: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Getty Images)

"These decisions are never easy, but as audience viewing habits evolve and we work to deliver value for licence fee payers, we have to make tough choices. We remain committed to bringing audiences the very best of winter sport, above all at the Winter Olympics, across BBC Sport's platforms."

‌



Ski Sunday is the latest in a growing number of programmes to be axed by the BBC amid budget cuts. The terrestrial broadcaster also announced on Tuesday that The Women's Football Show had been discontinued.

View 3 Images Ed Leigh and Graham Bell both presented Ski Sunday (Image: Julian Finney/Getty Images)

Football Focus was also axed earlier in 2026, ending 52 years on our screens. The decisions have been taken as part of huge cuts across the corporation, with the new director general of the BBC, Matt Brittin, recently announcing plans to cut £80million from programming on TV, radio and news.

Article continues below

The BBC is expected to cut around 2,000 jobs in order to deliver £160m of £500m in savings by the 2028-29 financial year. "On the financial side, I knew that cuts had been announced and that savings had been announced, but I hadn't really understood the severity," Brittin said last week at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival.

Ski Sunday began in the 1970s by only covering skiing, but later expanded to cover other winter sports like snowboarding. As well as Leigh and Alcott, it has been presented by former Team GB skier Graham Bell.

News.title: Mass burials carried out across flood-hit Nepal as search for missing Brits continues
News.content:
Mass burials carried out across flood-hit Nepal as search for missing Brits continues

Among the 48 Brits still unaccounted for across Nepal and China is Hindu priest Nabhi Nandan Das, 64, who was leading a pilgrimage tour when the floods hit on August 26

View 5 Images Across Nepal, the authorities have been forced to dig mass graves after 900 people were killed in devastating flash floods (Image: Getty Images)

Mass burials are being carried out across flood-hit Nepal as the death toll reached more than 1,000 people.

‌



Desperate efforts to trace thousands of people were continuing as Nepal's disaster agency said 1,003 deaths had been counted there, with 3,916 people missing, including 583 foreign nationals. Among the 48 Brits still unaccounted for across Nepal and China is a Hindu priest from south London who was leading a pilgrimage.

‌



Nabhi Nandan Das, 64, who runs the Sanatan Mandir and Community Centre in Coulsdon, was leading a pilgrimage tour, which included 11 British nationals, for Alpine Eco Trek when a glacier collapse triggered devastating the floods hit on August 26. The tour group was on a nine-day tour to Mount Kailash in Nepal and had just crossed into China.

‌



View 5 Images Nabhi Das, from south London, had been leading a tour group at the time of the floods (Image: Facebook)

Nepal flood disaster survivor shares details of miraculous escape READ MORE :

Final happy photo of Brits on Nepal tour - then they were gone READ MORE :

Mr Das' family have not heard from him since he sent them a message the day before the disaster. Dee Shah said the priest, who is her mother's cousin, has been leading pilgrimages in the area for more than 20 years. She said: "He went out there with 16 others and on the day it happened they had crossed the Nepal border into China.

"I think they think they're now just going to get a body - but they want to find the body as it's been too long not having a body. I think they just want to get closure."

‌



She said Mr Das' wife and son are now in Nepal, but have not yet got permission to cross the border into China. They have provided DNA to assist with identification, she added. Ms Shah has launched a GoFundMe fundraiser, which has raised more than £10,000 and will be used to help with the family's travel costs and assist search and rescue teams.

View 5 Images Surrounded by razor wire, mass burials have taken place in a jungle on the outskirts of Kathmandu (Image: Sanjit Pariyar/NurPhoto/Shutterstock)

She said money may also be used towards funerals of those missing on the tour group and any remaining will be donated to the Red Cross in Nepal. "The reason I started the fundraiser was because of a lack of communication from the Foreign Office," Ms Shah said.

‌



"Every time we've been ringing them they just say they don't know anything further - we've been ringing every few hours but being told there is no further information."

Rescue teams with search dogs continued to search through mud, rocks and debris on the border with Nepal and China for thousands of people still missing following the catastrophic floods.

View 5 Images Trenches were also dug in Chitwan, Nepal, so the authorities can bury those killed in the tragedy (Image: AP Photo/Nisha Shrestha)

‌



In Kathmandu, police worked in heavy rain to begin burying dozens of bodies in multiple trenches next to a forested area. Barbed wire was erected around the site, while blue numbered markers identified the graves of people whose names were not yet known.

Authorities in Nepal have been burying bodies in temporary graves until they can be identified. They are preserving DNA samples, photographing distinguishing facial features and recording other identifying details. Each body is assigned a reference number to help families identify and claim the remains later.

Rescue teams are also working to assist survivors in areas where roads and other transportation routes have been damaged or cut off. The immediate priority remains finding at least 900 workers who are missing from 12 hydropower projects damaged by the flash floods, about 500 of whom are believed to be trapped inside tunnels.

‌



View 5 Images Massive rescue efforts have been launched to recover trapped tunnel workers (Image: Prime Minister Secretariat, Nepal/AFP via Getty Images)

Brigadier General Raja Ram Basnet, Nepal's army spokesperson, said teams assisted by foreign experts were working at several hydropower projects to reach people trapped in blocked tunnels. Visuals released by the army showed rescue teams entering dark, debris-filled tunnels, wading through mud and water and climbing over rocks as they searched for signs of life.

At the Upper Trishuli 3A site, rescuers broke through into the upper part of a mud-swamped tunnel, pumping air inside, then using drilling and excavator machines to dig down. A spokesperson said: "When members of the team descended using ropes and called out to those inside, there was no response."

‌



Sita Pandey, whose husband Jiblal was working in one of the tunnels, told local media: "I still have a 50 per cent hope that he is alive because there is an oxygen system inside." She revealed that she last spoke to him on Wednesday morning, hours before the flood hit.

Desperately hoping that he is found quickly, she added: "We can understand that the rescue operation is technically complex. But we cannot accept delays. Our people are inside there. For us, every second counts."

Bimal Sharma, a helicopter pilot who has been flying rescue missions since the disaster began, said he was shocked to see the devastation in Timure, a border town close to Tibet that he has known for years.

Article continues below

He said: "It felt like I was flying over an entirely different landscape." At least 11,814 people have been rescued so far, according to Nepalese authorities.

News.title: Audi driver yawns and falls into 'microsleep' moments before causing fatal crash
News.content:
Audi driver yawns and falls into 'microsleep' moments before causing fatal crash

Kolawole Erunkulu, 45, spent 53 hours driving in the three days leading up to the fatal crash and took a maximum break of seven hours - building up a "sleep debt"

Surrey: Moment driver veers off the road and causes a fatal crash while having a 'microsleep'

This is the shocking moment an Audi driver, 45, yawned and fell into a "microsleep" before causing a fatal crash.

‌



Kolawole Erunkulu, 45, veered off the A23 in Merstham, Surrey, and struck Philip Dray in August last year. Police said the taxi driver had spent 53 hours driving in the three days leading up to the crash with a maximum break of seven hours - building up a "sleep debt."

‌



Dashcam footage from Erunkulu's Audi show him yawning at the wheel before he shut his eyes. Surrey Police said Erunkulu, from Bexleyheath, in southeast London, fell into a "microsleep:" a very brief episode of sleep lasting just seconds during which the brain is not processing information.

‌



View 4 Images Erunkulu was seen yawning at the wheel before he shut his eyes (Image: Surrey Police / SWNS)

A66 crash investigators to bring in National Crime Agency experts to hunt gang bosses behind tragedy READ MORE :

During one such episode his vehicle was seen to veer across the carriageway and collide with Mr Dray, who was standing within a layby at the side of the road. Mr Dray, 59, had parked up to take a break and was opening the driver's door to climb back into his Volkswagen when he was struck.

He died at the scene. Erunkulu, who has joint British and Nigerian nationality, was charged with causing death by dangerous driving in March 2026.

‌



He pleaded guilty when appearing at court in June and was last week sentenced for six years at Guildford Crown Court. He pleaded guilty when appearing at court in June and, last week at Guildford Crown Court, he was jailed for six years.

Officers said that, had Erunkulu been convicted after a trial, the sentence would have been nine years. He has also been disqualified from driving for eight years which runs concurrently, and will be subject to an extended retest if he reapplies for his licence.

View 4 Images Erunkulu had a microsleep, causing his vehicle to veer across the carriageway (Image: Surrey Police / SWNS)

‌



Her Honour Judge Lees said: “The footage shows the defendant was extremely tired and, in my view, has continued to drive when he must have known that.

"He was driving commercially. Even though he didn’t have a passenger, he could have done and has driven in that state. All of this could have been stopped had he have slept.”

Acting Det Insp Rob Baldwin said: “This case sadly highlights the very real dangers of driving while fatigued. Mr Erunkulu had worked long hours with insufficient rest over the preceding days, accumulating a sleep debt.

‌



“Fatigue can seriously impair a driver’s ability to remain alert and react safely, particularly during the early hours of the morning when the natural drive to sleep is at its strongest.

"Anyone who feels tired should not continue driving, as the consequences can be devastating.” Paying tribute to him, Mr Dray's family described him as "an amazing partner and man."

View 4 Images Erunkulu has accumulated a sleep debt (Image: Surrey Police / SWNS)

‌



His sister said he was dependable and steady: the sort of person people could rely on without hesitation. “He never sought attention and lived his life quietly, but he cared deeply about others and treated people with respect and decency. He was simply a good man," she said.

“Philip spent his life as a careful and conscientious driver, ensuring the safety of his passengers and other road users. The fact that he, someone who worked every day to keep others safe, had his life taken in such a way makes this loss even more incomprehensible and tragic.”

Mr Dray's partner described him as a "sweet, gentle, and caring man." She said they were each other’s “cheerleader, advisor, partner, and best friend”, and he was “the one who was always there to give me a hug.”

‌



View 4 Images Erunkulu was jailed for six weeks (Image: Surrey Police / SWNS)

She added: “Phil was my partner and my soulmate” and described “an enormous emotional and physical void” without him. “He would ring me several times a day whenever he was waiting for a client or at lunch, just to see how my day was going. I miss those calls very much.”

To highlight the dangers of driving whilst fatigued, the family have agreed to the release of video footage of the driver falling asleep at the wheel. Police analysed data from Erunkulu's employer that showed he had been driving for around 53 hours over the three days leading up to the collision.

Article continues below

His longest rest period between drives was three days beforehand for just seven hours. Other breaks included one of approximately four hours and two of around two hours. In the period immediately before the collision, he had been working as a taxi driver for around 12 hours, with only minor breaks.

News.title: Meghan Markle 'had been planning return to acting for quite some time' before UK return
News.content:
Meghan Markle 'had been planning return to acting for quite some time' before UK return

A source close to the Duchess of Sussex has revealed that Meghan has been discussing her potential return to acting for a while, despite previously speaking of having no desire to be an actress again

View 4 Images Meghan Markle's longtime makeup artist Daniel Martin is allegedly a fan of the Augustinus Bader The Cream (Image: Getty)

Meghan Markle has been planning her return to acting for ‘quite some time’, according to a source close to the Duchess of Sussex.

‌



With Harry and Meghan now settling into their new life back in the UK for an ‘extended period’, it has emerged that the Duchess is reportedly ‘in talks’ to resurrect her acting career. Meghan is believed to be discussing a potential return to acting with a role in the Netflix show The Gentlemen, which is filmed in the Cotswolds and has been confirmed for a third season.

‌



The Guy Ritchie crime show, which stars Theo James in the lead role, is about a British Duke who unexpectedly inherits his father’s country estate and discovers it is home to a cannabis empire run by notorious criminals.

‌



Marius Borg Høiby leaves house arrest to join procession for late King Harald with Norwegian Royal Family READ MORE :

View 4 Images Meghan Markle is believed to be eyeing up a return to acting (Image: GETTY)

The role would be Meghan’s first major acting job since leaving the legal drama Suits, in which she played paralegal Rachel Zane for seven seasons, only to leave the show as her relationship with Prince Harry progressed. After the Duke and Duchess quit their royal roles in 2020 and moved to California, Meghan seemed to have no interest in returning to acting, as she told Variety in 2022: “I guess never say never, but my intention is to absolutely not.”

However, a source close to Meghan has now told People magazine that she has been planning her potential return to acting for ‘quite some time’. Meghan has made a few on-screen appearances in recent years, from her Netflix lifestyle series With Love, Meghan, as well as a cameo as herself in the film Close Personal Friends, which has yet to be released.

‌



Meghan was spotted on the set of the film in November 2025, with a source telling People she appeared “very relaxed and happy”, as they added: “She introduced herself to everyone and was very sweet and down-to-earth.”

View 4 Images Meghan starred in the legal drama Suits for seven seasons (Image: USA NETWORK)

While Meghan’s potential role in The Gentlemen has yet to be confirmed, Netflix’s scripted chief in the UK Manda Levin, gave a cryptic answer when asked about Meghan’s rumoured casting at the Edinburgh TV Festival last week, as she said: “All bets are off.”

‌



The idea of the Duchess returning to acting has many royal watchers intrigued about her potential next move, as PR expert Mayah Riaz has encouraged the career change for Meghan, as she told the Mirror she has the chance to build a profile outside the Royal Family if she chooses the right project.

Mayah said: “A return to acting could actually be quite interesting for Meghan because it would take her back to an identity that existed before the Royal Family."

View 4 Images The Duchess is 'in talks' for a role in The Gentlemen (Image: Getty Images)

‌



She added: "There can be something quite powerful about returning to an old profession rather than constantly trying to invent a new one. It could allow people to see Meghan as an actress again, rather than exclusively as the Duchess of Sussex.”

However, the PR expert said the main issue is how her potential return to acting will be framed, and if she relies on her royal connections, or decides to rehash any grievances about her time as a working royal, to promote any upcoming projects.

Article continues below

Mayah said: “The bigger issue would be the publicity surrounding the comeback. If every interview, premiere or casting announcement becomes another opportunity to discuss Harry, the Royal Family or their past experiences, then the old narrative immediately follows her into the new career. If she genuinely wants a fresh chapter, she has to be prepared to talk about the work rather than the feud.”

News.title: Brits taking more business trips than pre-pandemic - but it's not all bad
News.content:
Brits taking more business trips than pre-pandemic - but it's not all bad

A new study suggests one in four workers are travelling more for business than before the pandemic, with many embracing the new 'bleisure' trend.

View 2 Images Business travel is back on the rise (Image: Getty Images)

A quarter of workers are now travelling more for business than they did before the pandemic, research has revealed. A study of 2,000 adults who have previously travelled for work discovered 18% have undertaken 12 or more business trips in the past year.

‌



During that period, the busiest months for travel were May, September and April, with the average employer willing to splash out £165 for accommodation. Meanwhile, £68 was the average daily allowance for meals and transport.

‌



The research was commissioned by Hotels.com, which has introduced a new business travel experience through its app to make work trips quicker and simpler to arrange.

‌



The app allows business travellers to save work-trip preferences, locate business-ready hotels, rebook favoured stays and earn rewards on corporate trip.

View 2 Images Workers are now embracing having to travel and visit cities like New York and London (Image: Getty Images)

The study also forms part of the global marketplace's Booked for Business report, which discovered 48% of workers believe the finest business travel destinations combine work and leisure, reflecting what it describes as "the growing importance of 'bleisure' travel".

‌



According to those surveyed, cities London, New York and Paris epitomise this 'bleisure' travel trend the most, making them the optimal destinations for work-related travel.

Business travellers are also placing greater emphasis on the benefits they receive when travelling for their jobs – with 26% revealing they make a hotel stay "great."

These include a complimentary breakfast (51%), room upgrades (32%) and flexible check-in (26%).

Article continues below

But when it comes to completing the job, 57% said access to high-speed Wi-Fi is a crucial priority.

Melanie Fish, travel expert and spokesperson for Hotels.com, said : "Business travel is no longer just about getting from one meeting to the next. Travellers want a hotel and destination that can keep up with both sides of their personality.

From high-speed Wi-Fi and an early breakfast before a big presentation to a great location and a comfortable place to unwind afterwards."

News.title: BBC axes another football show as broadcaster continues cull on terrestrial channels
News.content:
BBC axes another football show as broadcaster continues cull on terrestrial channels

The BBC have put another football programme on the chopping block as the broadcaster continues a major shake-up

View 3 Images The BBC are making further cutbacks (Image: 2024 James Gill - Danehouse)

The BBC has discontinued The Women’s Football Show with the new Women’s Super League season kicking off on Friday, August 4. The move continues a recent trend for the broadcaster of axing sports-related programming, while it has also surrendered its licence to show several major events.

‌



The BBC have claimed that they are “fully committed to women’s football and the WSL” despite cancelling its flagship BBC One highlights programme for the women's game.

‌



According to The Guardian, the Beeb is set to channel its focus toward digital platforms, particularly its newly launched YouTube women’s football channel for highlights.

‌



The broadcaster also plans to launch a YouTube chat show about women’s football, presented by former Arsenal star Alex Scott. Multiple sources informed The Guardian that the show is aiming to be in the “style of the Overlap”, Gary Neville’s hugely successful football show on Sky Sports.

The dramatic culling of The Women’s Football Show comes after the BBC lost the broadcast rights for the Women’s FA Cup to Channel 4 and TNT Sports last year.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



Alan Shearer confirms real reason he is scaling back BBC Match of the Day appearances READ MORE :

Match of the Day commentator fires back at Richard Keys in row over BBC programme READ MORE :

Earlier in 2026, the BBC also stopped airing Football Focus after 52 years on our screens. The beloved lunchtime broadcast is making way for The Football Interview, which is fronted by Kelly Somers.

The new director general of the BBC, Matt Brittin, has announced plans to cut £80 million from programming on TV, radio and news, as part of huge cuts across the corporation. BBC Sport has also cut Ski Sunday from its schedule, with its axing ending a five-decade run for the show.

View 3 Images Chloe Kelly is a big draw in the WSL (Image: Photo by Alex Burstow/Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

‌



BBC sources were adamant that the broadcaster was not cutting back on its women’s football coverage, however. A BBC spokesperson told the Guardian: “BBC Sport remains fully committed to women’s football and the WSL.

"As we build towards the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup, audiences will be able to watch highlights from every WSL match across BBC platforms, including iPlayer, YouTube and the BBC Sport website and app.

“In addition, BBC Sport will broadcast 25 live WSL matches, alongside live UEFA Women’s Champions League coverage, ensuring fans can follow the biggest stories and moments from the women’s game on free-to-air platforms.”

‌



Follow the latest updates, rumours and done deals with our Deadline Day Live Blog

The BBC and Sky Sports are heading into the second season of a five-year domestic broadcast rights deal. Every WSL match is shown live, with the vast majority by Sky Sports.

The Guardian claimed that the drastic call to shelve the women’s football show has disappointed several BBC Sport insiders and has come as a complete surprise to many. Those who worked on the show last season told the publication that they first learned of its cancellation when the Cutback reported it in August.

‌



View 3 Images Alex Scott will front a YouTube chat show for the BBC (Image: James Baylis - AMA, Getty Images)

Rumours that the BBC’s director of sport, Alex Kay-Jelski, was solely behind the decision to discontinue the show have been quashed, with some sources at the BBC insisting this was not the case.

The WSL is believed to be comfortable with the BBC's assurances that it will be enhancing its coverage across its platforms. The show was co-funded by the BBC and the league while its production was reportedly supported by WSL Football.

Article continues below

Prior to 2024, the Football Association backed the programme, while the BBC picked up the bill for on-screen costs. The new Women's Super League season gets underway on Friday when London City Lionesses host Manchester United.

News.title: Gen Z makes paddleboards the new seaside must-do – but still rates one classic
News.content:
Gen Z makes paddleboards the new seaside must-do – but still rates one classic

Young Brits are swapping traditional beach-day pastimes for paddleboards, surfing and a dip in the sea – but they still love one thing

View 3 Images Gen Z beachgoers are doing things differently (Image: PinPep)

Gen Z is redefining the great British day at the seaside, replacing traditional favourites like arcade games and crazy golf with paddleboarding and surfing. A poll of 2,000 adults found 11% of Gen Z consider paddleboarding to be essential to the perfect day by the sea, compared to just 7% of Millennials and 3% of Boomers. They were also far more likely to take a dip, with 38% saying swimming in the sea is a beach day priority.

‌



Classic seaside pastimes appear to be losing their appeal among younger adults as 74% would skip arcade games, and 87% would happily avoid a round of crazy golf.

‌



But seaside traditions such as tucking into fish and chips, a picnic and coastal walks were still among the most treasured experiences across all those surveyed.

‌



Bryony Walker from Walker's Shortbread, which brought its newly launched Wee Chunkies bites to a seaside pop-up on Brighton beach, said: "While the research shows beachgoers still crave the classic seaside experiences, it's interesting to see what now makes up the ideal day at the beach.

"Activities like paddleboarding are becoming more popular with younger generations, but what remains constant is a dip in the sea.

‌



"The coast holds special appeal, combining nostalgia, quality family time and the simple joys of a well-packed picnic, fresh air and time outdoors."

View 3 Images Brits love a dip in the sea followed by a tasty treat (Image: PinPep)

The study, conducted through OnePoll, revealed that 15 minutes is considered the perfect amount of time to spend in the water.

‌



Following the dip, beachgoers enjoy wrapping themselves in a toasty towel (49%) or tucking into a warm sweet snack to restore energy levels (18%) - a tradition the Scots refer to as a 'Shivery Bite' - something only 9% of Brits are familiar with.

Due to the unfamiliarity with this Scottish phrase, Walker's Shortbread decided to introduce the Shivery Bite concept to Bank Holiday beachgoers and swimmers along Brighton's bustling seafront.

View 3 Images Walker's Shortbread brought its newly launched Wee Chunkies to Brighton Beach (Image: PinPep)

Article continues below

Bryony Walker added: "The insights have revealed the nation's ideal beach day, with fresh sea air, sunshine, blue skies and that essential paddle in the water. "After a summer of intense heat, beachgoers are craving a moment of relief, whether it's a colder coastal breeze or cosy comfort food.

"Few things beat wrapping up after a swim or enjoying a warm treat, something in Scotland we call a 'Shivery Bite', and our new shortbread offering is exactly for this moment, best served warm, to help make the most of the post-dip feeling."

News.title: Keir Starmer announces he is standing down as MP
News.content:
Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer has announced he is to stand down as an MP to focus on a role in international affairs.

The move will trigger a by-election in the London seat of Holborn and St Pancras, long a Labour stronghold, which he has represented since 2015.

Sir Keir, who left Downing Street in July, had previously said he would stay on as an MP until the next UK general election, which is not due until 2029.

But in a surprise statement hours before his successor Andy Burnham made his debut in the House of Commons, he said he was resigning to work on issues such as international affairs and violence against women and girls.

Paying tribute to his predecessor, Burnham highlighted Sir Keir's work with Ukraine and the Hillsborough Law drawn up under his government to improve the accountability of public officials, which is going through Parliament.

"He has given this country an lifetime of public service, particularly for those fighting for justice," he added.

"His leadership took our party from one of its worst defeats to its best victories and created a platform to change this country for the better. We will use it well, and we wish his family the very best for the future."

Announcing his resignation, Sir Keir told the Camden New Journal, external it had been a "huge honour and privilege" to represent the London constituency for 11 years, ending weeks of speculation about whether he would remain an MP.

He added he was ready to "pass the baton to a successor", telling the newspaper it was the "right time" for him to leave Parliament.

He said: "I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world.

"I will also continue, as I have done for a long time now with others, to work on combating violence against women and girls; that is an issue that matters to me hugely.

"It's work I started before I became an MP and it's work I'm keen to continue after I'm an MP. So international affairs on the one hand, and continuing my work on violence against women and girls on the other."

Sir Keir became prime minister after winning a landslide majority at the 2024 election, but quit No 10 after pressure from Labour MPs to stand aside.

News.title: Summer 2026 was UK's hottest on record, Met Office says
News.content:
In a rapid attribution study - which looks at how much of a role climate change plays - the Met Office say the average temperature was made around 130 times more likely due to human-induced climate change.

And step back from this summer and there is clue to our changing climate in the temperature record itself.

In a climate that isn't changing, new records should become progressively rarer, because every time a record falls, it raises the bar for the next one.

Think about the 100m race. Each time someone sets a new record, it becomes harder to beat. And there's another thing. Typically records are only ever broken by a few fractions of a second â often just a millisecond or two.

In June 1991, for example, Leroy Burrell ran 9.90 seconds, beating Carl Lewis's 1988 world record of 9.92 seconds by just two hundredths of a second.

Now look at the UK summer temperature record. Until last year, the four hottest summers on record were separated by just five hundredths of a degree.

Then 2025 beat the previous record by 0.34C. And this summer has beaten that new record by another 0.40C.

So after years when the record moved by tiny fractions, in just two summers the bar has been raised by 0.74C.

Head of Climate Attribution at the Met Office, Dr Mark McCarthy said that summer 2026 was "remarkable" and we can expect to see extremes occurring more frequently in the future because of climate change.

So why is this happening so quickly here? The UK sits on the western edge of Europe, the fastest-warming continent on Earth - warming at roughly twice the global rate.

There are a few reasons for that. Land heats up faster than the oceans, parts of Europe stretch into the rapidly warming Arctic, and changes in weather patterns have favoured more frequent and intense summer heatwaves.

Scientists are still working out exactly how much each factor contributes, but the result is clear: the background climate in which British weather happens is getting warmer.

None of this means the UK will break its summer record every year. Weather will always give us cooler summers as well as hotter ones. But the pattern is becoming unmistakable: records that once marked the extreme edge of the UK's climate are being overtaken with remarkable speed.

So the question is not whether the UK will experience summers hotter than this one. It is how often they will come - and how much hotter they might be.

News.title: The final minutes before floodwater crashed through Nepal-China border
News.content:
When a 21-member Chinese rescue team reached Gyirong on 28 August, one rescuer told Chinese state media: "As far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins."

The crossing had only recently recovered from another major flood. In July 2025, flooding shut Rasuwagadhi for nearly six months. It reopened on 1 January after China built a temporary bridge.

Traffic had since returned. Chinese border authorities say more than 100,000 people had passed through Gyirong by June, while Nepali immigration records show 53,742 arrivals and departures at Rasuwagadhi in the year to mid-July. The two figures are based on different reporting periods and counting systems, making a direct comparison difficult.

Indians were the largest group recorded at the Nepali immigration point, followed by Nepalis and Chinese.

Gyirong had also become one of the main arteries linking Nepal and China.

Posh Raj Pandey, chairman emeritus of the Kathmandu-based South Asia Watch on Trade, Economics and Environment, says Rasuwagadhi is one of Nepal's two main trading points with China, alongside Tatopani, and accounts for about a third of Nepal's $2.95bn trade with its northern neighbour.

Around 60 to 70 trucks passed through the gorge each day, carrying electronics, machinery, vehicles, fruit, clothing and other goods towards Kathmandu. Pandey says the route also handled about 80% of Nepal's electric-vehicle imports from China.

Its closure has left Nepal increasingly dependent on Tatopani - which Chinese authorities have also temporarily closed, external because of landslide risks on the Nepali side, the Kathmandu Post reports.

The crossing also lies along the proposed route of the railway connecting the region to Kathmandu, part of plans by Nepal and China to develop a trans-Himalayan rail network.

"Nepal should develop an alternative China trade route and reconsider its wider development strategy, including its heavy concentration of hydropower projects along the same river system," Pandey says.

"We have put all eggs here. We need to develop an alternative border port."

Across the border, Pokharel was left thinking about conversations he had with the colleagues who were now missing.

The previous year's flood had made staff at the Rasuwagadhi immigration office acutely aware of the danger. At night, he says, they sometimes "felt vibrations" and went outside to check the river. They had even discussed among themselves about escaping uphill if another flood struck.

"But my friends could not get that chance," he said.

News.title: Watch: Norway's new king takes oath as mourners pay respects to his late father
News.content:
Norway's Haakon VIII has sworn an oath before parliament in Oslo in the first major step of his reign as King.

During Tuesday's ceremony, parliament also held a minute's silence for Haakon's father, the late King Harald V, who died on Friday.

Haakon's wife, Queen Mette-Marit, was absent from the formalities as she continues to recover from a lung transplant.

Following the ceremony, mourners began paying their respects at the late King's coffin, which is lying in state at the Royal Palace until 8 September.

News.title: UK long-term borrowing costs highest since 1998 ahead of October Budget
News.content:
Long-term government borrowing costs have risen to a 28-year high, putting further pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham ahead of his first Budget next month.

The yield on a 30-year gilt â a loan to the British government â rose to 5.89%, the highest since 1998.

The effective cost of borrowing for governments across the globe has continued to rise this morning with new multi-decade highs in market interest rates.

The moves reflect concerns about inflation arising from the ongoing Iran war, competition from major tech firms for long-term borrowing, and concerns about state borrowing levels.

All of those factors will make the Budget process trickier for Burnham, who on Tuesday addressed MPs for the first time as prime minister, and his Chancellor John Healey.

Burnham told the House of Commons his government's "bedrock" as it seeks to tackle the cost-of-living crisis will be "fiscal responsibility".

He said the economy and the cost of living were "the biggest issues facing the country".

Higher borrowing costs will reduce the amount of headroom the government has against its self-imposed fiscal rules, limiting the amount Healey can spend on consumer-friendly measures to ease the cost of living.

Despite the squeezed public finances, Burnham said said he would bring about "more substantial change" to ease living costs.

"Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be," he added.

The yield on the benchmark 10-year gilt rose to its highest rate since June 2008, at the height of the global financial crisis.

Gilt yields move counter to the value of the bonds, meaning their prices fall when yields rise.

Borrowing costs in the US, Japan and Europe have hit similar highs in recent days.

The chancellor has previously said he will stick to a set of fiscal rules imposed by his predecessor Rachel Reeves that restrict borrowing. These rules are designed to help markets have clarity about the path of borrowing.

The more that is forecast to be spent on interest costs, the more likely that there will be a squeeze on spending or some form of tax rise to meet these rules.

The moves in interest rates could already wipe out half of the room for manoeuvre to meet these rules forecast at the last set of official numbers last March.

On top of that, higher government rates can feed through to higher business and household borrowing costs, and so weigh on the economy.

The tax and spend balance in act was already tricky due to extra spending pressures on defence and the cost of living. These moves make these balancing acts trickier still.

Global markets reacted in particular after suggestions in the US that its central bank could raise rates. The UK market was closed for the bank holiday yesterday. Japan is also facing pressure to raise rates.

The Chancellor is in the USA attending a meeting of global finance ministers and central bankers. He told the G20 that the UK had the fastest growth in the G7 in 2026 so far, that productivity was improving and that the UK was cutting its borrowing at the fastest rate of the major economies.

News.title: Man in court charged with murder after deaths of woman and girl in Teesside fire
News.content:
A 23-year-old man has appeared in court charged with murdering a woman and her seven-year-old niece who died in a house fire.

Natalie McDonald, 34, died in the blaze in Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, in the early hours of 26 August, along with Valentina Foster.

Jaden Wright appeared at Teesside Magistrates' Court charged with two counts of murder as well as multiple grievous bodily harm offences.

Wright, of no fixed address, was remanded in custody during the hearing that lasted less than two minutes, and is next due to appear at Teesside Crown Court on Thursday.

He is also accused of two counts of grievous bodily harm with intent and two charges of attempted grievous bodily harm with intent.

These charges relate to the six people in the house at the time of the blaze.

No pleas were entered during the hearing on Tuesday morning.

News.title: It's taken me a long time to process Olympics breaking experience, says Raygun
News.content:
Just hours before representing Australia at the Paris 2024 opening ceremony, Rachael Gunn had a panic attack in the middle of the Olympic village.

Thrust into an environment full of experienced athletes, it dawned on Gunn, whose professional background is as a university lecturer, what she had got herself into.

Known as Raygun when competing, she was about to take part in the breakdancing event - or breaking - which was making its Olympic debut.

"I felt like an imposter," said the 38-year-old breaker, during a new Netflix documentary about her experience at the Games.

She describes how she reacted when she saw someone she recognised from the Olympic team.

"I just could not stop crying... I had a panic attack. 'What am I doing? What have I done? Should I be doing this?'" she said.

Just a few hours later, she was sailing down the River Seine alongside the rest of the Australian cohort, waving to onlookers.

Less than a fortnight after that, her Olympic journey was over. Gunn failed to win any of her three round-robin battles at the Games, but walked away pleased with how she had acquitted herself.

"Finishing my last round, the world champion Nicka [Dominika Banevic] gave me props for my moves, the MC celebrated my stuff and the vibe was just generally good," Gunn told BBC Sport.

What she hadn't anticipated was that one of her performances, in which she debuted some unconventional moves including a sprinkler and a kangaroo hop, had gone viral.

There were memes. There was a sketch on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon. Adele referenced the performance in one of her concerts. Chris Hemsworth defended Gunn in an interview with Jimmy Kimmel. At one point in August 2024, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese even felt moved to speak out, praising Gunn for having "a crack".

"It was pretty wild the way I became a topic of conversation in spaces I never thought I would be," said Gunn.

Alongside the teasing, there were more sinister forces brewing, including conspiracy theories about nepotism - for instance that Gunn's husband and trainer, Samuel Free, had been on the selection committee when she qualified to represent her country at the Games, when he hadn't been.

"It was really tough when mine and Sammy's credibility, ethics and motivations were being called into question," Gunn said.

"You could just spend 30 seconds researching and find plenty of sources to debunk these conspiracies, but that's not how people use the internet anymore."

That new-found scrutiny took a toll on Gunn's mental health.

"I felt like my whole life was just kind of crumbling before me.. .and I was just trying to get through the day," she says in the documentary.

In the process of making a film about that time, however, she feels that she's been able to regain some agency.

"It's taken a long time for me to process what happened," Gunn told BBC Sport.

"It's really exciting for me to finally have a voice again."

News.title: Could Tupac verdict inspire new efforts to also find killer of his rap rival?
News.content:
The breakthrough in finally solving the Shakur case largely came down to one thing: Davis' own words.

Through documentaries with the media, his own memoir, podcasts and even a secret police interview, he acknowledged his role in Shakur's death. Davis said he tossed a firearm in the backseat and his nephew, Orlando Anderson, used the gun to fatally shoot Shakur as they pulled up alongside his vehicle in Las Vegas on 7 September, 1996.

Anderson was shot dead in 1998, having denied killing Shakur.

During the trial, there were no eye-witnesses to place Davis as being in the car, no murder weapon presented, no video or photo evidence. His defence team went as far as to argue there wasn't even proof that he was in Las Vegas that night.

Rahmani said it was a difficult case to prosecute. He noted the rumours and speculation surrounding Davis were nothing new and had been around for decades - but the decision to charge him and go to trial was an "uphill climb" - a gutsy move - for prosecutors.

"Look, when you're a prosecutor, you're expected to win every time. They made a difficult decision to charge a case that a lot of people thought might be a loser," he explained. "And they got justice, where other people didn't even bother trying."

Davis' attorney Michael Sanft asked the jury to consider "what facts do you have?" He urged the panel, before they decided their guilty verdict, to discredit his client as a liar who told tales to sell books and make money.

"There's no proof," he argued to the jury.

The moment the guilty verdict was read in court, there was an outpouring of emotion among Shakur's family. Some cried and wiped tears with tissues. Others hugged and held hands - one family member even embraced one of the prosecutors in the case.

News.title: Laundry rooms to be turned into cells to tackle prison overcrowding
News.content:
The government is to create more cells in existing prisons in England and Wales as part of its plans to tackle overcrowding.

An investment of Â£110m, which will come from existing budgets, will be used to convert unused office space, laundry rooms and storage space into cells, the Ministry of Justice said.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris is also due to give more details in the Commons later on changes to the early release scheme, which aims to free up space in prisons as they near maximum capacity.

He told the BBC prisoners being released early did not mean "freedom" and victims would have a say in restrictions placed on those criminals.

Asked where clothes would be washed if laundry rooms were converted into cells, Norris told BBC Breakfast: "Of course we're going to make sure that the prisons can still function properly.

"This is a creative look, as I say, around our estate and being able to use some space that we can re-prioritise."

Norris said he suspected the number of extra prison spaces created from freeing up existing space within prisons would be "landing somewhere in the middle" of 200 and 900.

But Chairman of the Prison Officers' Association, Mark Fairhurst, said: "You can create as much additional space as you like, and build as many new prisons as you like, but where are the staff coming from to supervise people? Nobody wants to be a prison officer anymore."

Norris said the government had delivered more than 3,200 prison places in two years.

Investment on more prison spaces was announced in last year's spending review and the Â£110m is not new money, A Â£7bn capital investment plan to create 14,000 prison places by 2031.

News.title: Two-day sea search for missing teen on holiday is called off
News.content:
A major sea search for a missing 15-year-old boy has been called off after two days, the Coastguard has said.

At about 15:30 BST on Sunday, HM Coastguard received a report that three people were experiencing difficulty in the water at Marloes Sands beach, Pembrokeshire.

Two managed to get out of the water, but the teenage boy, who was visiting the area on holiday from Yorkshire, was unaccounted for. The search was suspended at 19:30 BST on Monday.

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency told the BBC that there were currently no plans to resume the search.

In a statement on social media, Angle Lifeboat RNLI said its crew "worked tirelessly" for 22 hours at sea in a major, multi-agency search for the missing swimmer.

On Sunday, Broad Haven and Dale coastguard rescue teams were in attendance, alongside RNLI lifeboats from Angle, Tenby and St Davids and a pilot boat.

A coastguard helicopter and a HM Coastguard fixed wing aircraft were sent, along with the Welsh Ambulance Service.

The search was suspended at about 03:30 BST on Monday and started again later that morning, before being called off in the evening.

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency said, despite an extensive search, "sadly, no sign of the missing person was found".

Angle Lifeboat RNLI added its crew had "shown immense dedication over the past two days".

It thanked the Milford Haven Coastguard for "their fantastic coordination and support" in what they said has been a "lengthy and tiring incident".

"Our thoughts are with the swimmer's family and friends at this difficult time," it added.

News.title: Noughties garage track named TikTok's UK song of the summer
News.content:
British singer Kyla's Do You Mind has been named as TikTok's song of the summer in the UK after the noughties garage track experienced a resurgence on the app.

The song gained popularity when it was first released in 2008, but it became known worldwide in 2016 when Canadian rapper Drake sampled it on his chart-topping single One Dance.

It has now found a new audience by trending on TikTok, generating more than 500 million views from about 650,000 videos posted in the UK over the summer, according to the platform.

Kyla, who created the song with her husband DJ Paleface, tells BBC Newsbeat it is "surreal" but "incredible" that Do You Mind is getting another moment nearly 20 years on.

News.title: Hundreds remember Heaton Park synagogue attack victims at memorial event
News.content:
The Chief Rabbi Ephraim Mirvis and Communities Secretary Angela Rayner were among about 800 people who attended a memorial event for the victims and survivors of last year's Heaton Park synagogue attack.

Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby were killed, and three others injured, as they tried to defend their place of worship from attacker Jihad al-Shamie on 2 October 2025.

Relatives of the bereaved and some of the survivors were among the speakers at Monday's service of remembrance at the synagogue in Manchester.

Prior to the event, Rabbi Daniel Walker said the Jewish community feels less safe now than it did immediately after the attack.

He said rising antisemitism, combined with a lack of action to "deal with core problems", had left many members of Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation â and British Jews more widely â feeling increasingly vulnerable.

Two seats remained empty for the service, bearing the names of Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby.

News.title: Flu vaccine rollout begins as NHS regroups from 'busiest summer'
News.content:
Last winter's flu season was unexpected, beginning more than a month earlier than usual, external with the Super-K strain.

Super flu is not a medical term, and it does not mean the virus has become harder to treat, just that people are yet to build up immunity against it.

Flu vaccines are updated annually to ensure they are a good match for the type of flu circulating. Influenza viruses constantly mutate and experts have to predict these changes ahead of time.

This year's vaccine has had a few tweaks, including one to better match subclade K.

It is not clear when flu will hit this year, and whether it will be a bad season. But experts often look to southern hemisphere countries, like Australia and New Zealand, to gain a better understanding of how the UK could be affected.

Their flu season peaks in July or August. Australia has had fewer cases than last year, external, but New Zealand has seen high numbers, external.

Dr Amanda Doyle from NHS England said it was best to be cautious.

"Last year's flu season came early and was made worse by a new variant, which had a major impact for patients and put enormous pressure on urgent and emergency care services across the country," she said.

"With the NHS experiencing its busiest summer on record, staff have started preparing for this winter earlier than ever â and with services already under significant pressure, it is vital that everyone offered the vaccine comes forward."

News.title: Boy, 16, appears in court charged with murder
News.content:
A teenage boy has appeared in court charged with the murder of a man in Dungannon, County Tyrone, and the attempted murder of two other people in the same incident.

The body of Sidi Djalo, who was 61, was found alongside his injured eight-year-old daughter at a house on Lisnahull Road on Saturday morning.

The man's 48-year-old wife sustained non-life threatening injuries during the attack.

The 16-year-old defendant, who cannot be named because of his age, was also charged with making threats to kill. He appeared in court in Omagh on Tuesday morning and was remanded in custody.

The teenager spoke only to confirm his name, date of birth and address.

BBC News NI understands the man who died was from Guinea-Bissau, but had lived in Northern Ireland for more than two decades.

During the hearing, defence solicitor Jarlath Faloon said there were "clear concerns" about the defendant's mental health.

Faloon said the defendant had been examined by a mental health nurse over the weekend but not at psychiatric level.

The judge made an order to conduct a mental health assessment of the defendant.

He is due to appear on 15 September at Dungannon Youth Court.

News.title: Swinney to cut number of mainland health boards from 11 to two
News.content:
The first minister said he had been "appalled" by the number of cases involving violence against women and girls over the summer months.

"This has been a long-running issue within Scottish society," he said.

"The government has taken many measures to tackle this, but I think events over the summer have said to me that I've got to exercise the strongest possible personal leadership as first minister to make sure that we tackle these issues."

He said violence against women and girls could not be tolerated "in any way, shape or form in our society" and added that "making sure that we change the behaviour of men and boys in our society will be central to that programme".

One of the government's proposals to tackle the cost of living issue was to introduce a price cap on some food and drink items in large supermarkets.

Twenty-three organisations have since written a joint letter to Swinney urging him to scrap the plan.

Signatories include groups representing retail, food and drink production, manufacturing and distribution businesses in Scotland.

In response, Swinney said: "Many members of the public are struggling with the price of their shopping and I want to try to do something practical to address that and that's about bringing forward a proposal for an affordable price cap on a limited number of items within our supermarkets.

"We've got to consult about this and make sure the legislation can have the effect that we want it to have and that's exactly what the government is going to do."

News.title: Man dies near Notting Hill Carnival after entering canal
News.content:
A man died near Notting Hill Carnival in London on Monday afternoon, the Metropolitan Police have confirmed.

Police officers had attempted to stop the man, believed to be in his 20s, as he approached the event. He fled on foot with officers in pursuit, and entered the water in the vicinity of Meanwhile Gardens a short time later, the force said.

Taken to hospital by ambulance the man was pronounced dead a short time later.

Cdr Claire Smart said: "This is a tragic incident and our thoughts are with the loved ones of the man who has lost his life."

The Met Police said officers had attempted to stop the man at about 15:19 BST near Harrow Road.

The man entered the water in the vicinity of Meanwhile Gardens, off Kensal Road.

Officers and members of the public went in after him and pulled him from the water, police said, and officers immediately started CPR.

Paramedics were called and continued treatment at the canal side before taking the man to a central London hospital. He was pronounced dead at 16:43.

The Met Police said on Monday night that urgent enquiries were ongoing to locate and inform his next of kin.

Smart, gold commander for the Notting Hill Festival, said: "Any death following contact with the police is passed to the Independent Office for Police Conduct so the circumstances can be fully investigated.

"I would encourage everyone to avoid speculation while this work takes place."

She added: "I acknowledge the efforts of the officers and members of the public who entered the canal to rescue this man. I know they will be devastated that his life couldn't ultimately be saved."

The Met Police said the two days of the festival had passed "largely without incident".

There were two assaults with knives - one stabbing and one slashing. Neither resulted in life-threatening injuries.

On Monday evening, police said there had been 315 arrests that day, bringing the total number of arrests to 560.
