"We found our best approach by almost bringing upgrades each race. One week it's mechanical, one week it's aero, and we are continuing like this. It's fitting with our capacity of production, with our wind tunnel capacity, and it's going well.

"Now, if McLaren want to do things differently, it's because they have good reasons to do it. The set-up of the teams is different; the configuration is different. But at the end of the day, over a season we are almost following each other in terms of development."

Sports.title: Mario Andretti and Jacky Ickx: A friendship that has endured for almost 60 years
Sports.content:
Mario Andretti and Jacky Ickx were remarkably versatile even by the standards of their generation, competing and succeeding across multiple disciplines. Having won some of the biggest prizes in motorsport between them, both can look back on their journeys with immense pride.

But competition was only one part of the story, and the relationship Andretti and Ickx built stands out from the rest in motor racing.

So, when the two joined Motorsport.com on a video call for a special double interview, it felt like two old friends had been reunited. The pair always got along well when they were team-mates at Ferrari in Formula 1 and the World SportsCar Championship. But it’s remarkable how, six decades after they first met at the Mexican Grand Prix in 1968, their admiration and affection for each other remain undimmed.

“You have to explain to me how you stay in such good condition, because you look good,” Ickx said of Andretti.

“I understand, yesterday you won [IndyCar’s Freedom 250] and you finished on the podium. You have many reasons to smile. We hope at Genesis to be like you.

“You are amazing, my dear Mario. It brings me some emotions to think that what we did more than almost 60 years ago - yes, almost 60 years ago.

“You are the most famous driver - the celebrated, the iconic Mario Andretti. I had the fortune to share with you, it was yesterday, I believe, 1972, in a Ferrari 312 PB. So thank you very much.”

Andretti, clearly touched by Ickx’s praise, simply replied: “No, thank you. You were the best.”

Endurance exploits ​brought them together

Jacky Ickx, Mario Andretti, Ferrari 312 PB Photo by: Rainer Schlegelmilch / Getty Images

When you see that kind of admiration from the pair, it’s easy to understand why they formed such a formidable pairing on track. It was in 1971 when they first shared a garage, teaming up at Ferrari for a double programme. Even as reliability held them back in F1, both scored a win each, with Andretti - who wasn’t even racing full-time - driving the 312B to victory on his debut outing for Enzo’s squad.

It was in sportscars, though, that their partnership really flourished. Their similar physical dimensions already made life easy for Ferrari’s designers, but it was ultimately mutual respect and understanding that turned them into such a formidable pair. Ickx, for instance, famously let Andretti qualify the car according to the American’s preference.

As a result, Ferrari dominated the 1972 season, with Andretti and Ickx winning four of the 11 races together, including Daytona, Sebring, Watkins Glen and Brands Hatch. Had Ferrari not skipped Le Mans after concluding its F1-derived engine wasn’t fit for a 24-hour contest (that year's Daytona race was reduced to six hours), the pair would most certainly have been among the victory contenders at the legendary La Sarthe.

Andretti admitted that sharing a car in endurance racing brought him and Ickx together, laying the foundation for a friendship that has lasted to this day.

“Long-distance racing taught me a lot,” he said. “You're sharing the moment with someone else to do the same thing.

“There's no bigger pleasure when you're in victory lane together with your partner. The ones that have accomplished the same thing for you - and with you.

“We all depend on each other to minimise the mistakes - and make no mistakes - to be able to bring it home.

“You're sharing your victory in a different way when you're driving in long-distance races. We're both in the same seat during the race at one time or another and we're both experiencing exactly the same thing. That's something that brings you together.

“Jacky, specifically, from the long-distance racing factor, I did most of my long-distance races with him. That's why I said he's my best buddy, my best team-mate.”

Still chasing the same goal

Jacky Ickx, Genesis Magma Racing Photo by: Genesis

Following his stint with Ferrari, Ickx went on to become one of the most successful names in sportscar racing history, winning Le Mans six times. He also triumphed in the Spa 24 Hours and Bathurst 1000 before turning his hand to rally raid and winning the Dakar Rally on his third attempt.

Andretti, likewise, accomplished almost everything he set out to achieve, winning marque races such as the Indy 500 and the Daytona 500 and claiming the championship in both Formula 1 and IndyCar.

Both may have long retired from active competition, but the passion for motorsport still burns brightly in their 80s. Andretti, besides being the patriarch of one of America’s biggest racing dynasties, works as a director for Cadillac’s new F1 team. Ickx, meanwhile, serves as a brand ambassador for Genesis Magma Racing, and recently sampled the GMR-001 at Paul Ricard.

Their lives may now be separated by geography - Andretti remains based in Pennsylvania while Ickx spends a significant amount of time in Africa - but the distance has done little to weaken their connection. If anything, they continue to follow each other’s careers and genuinely want to see the other succeed.

“I'll be watching with interest,” said Andretti. “I wish you guys all the very best. Whatever your endeavours are, maintain your objectives and always go for the sky.”

“I wish you to enjoy life in your projects,” Ickx adds. “We are in very good company. We are lucky to still be active, to be in good health.

“We are very lucky, Mario. I keep in mind these days the years we have shared together, where we have shared long-distance racing.

“Of course, I follow you in your championships, F1, IndyCar, NASCAR, Midget.”

Mario Andretti, Jacky Ickx, Ferrari 312 PB Photo by: David Phipps / Sutton Images via Getty Images

As the call drew to an end, both Andretti and Ickx bid each other goodbye. They could have spent the hour trading stories about their past glories, but instead, the conversation repeatedly returned to the time they had shared together on and off the track.

“You have been a real friend and such a talented driver,” concludes Ickx. “I was tempted to say I love you, but you're not supposed to say that.

“Mario, stay safe, please,” he adds. “Stay safe. And thank you very much for your friendship.”

Sports.title: The underlying upgrade that boosted McLaren's performance jump
Sports.content:
McLaren’s win in Zandvoort, their second in a row after Budapest, highlighted a key point: the updates introduced on either side of the summer break did more than restore the aerodynamic load the car had been missing. They also enabled the team to take a decisive step forward.

At the Barcelona Grand Prix, for instance, McLaren’s strengths had already begun to emerge, and the same was true at Spa, where the car appeared in its most convincing form. The faster and longer the corner, because absolute speed alone is not the sole factor, the more competitive the car becomes. The latest upgrades delivered the extra downforce required to turn the car into the benchmark through those sections.

The effectiveness of these developments surprised even McLaren, as the performance shown in the high‑speed sections exceeded internal expectations.

Yet another factor behind the Zandvoort victory went somewhat under the radar: the debut of the new front wheel rims, a detail that McLaren technical director of engineering Neil Houldey had already hinted at ahead of the weekend.

McLaren wheel cover comparison Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

“We introduced a small change to the rear section of the floor to generate a bit of extra load, along with some minor tweaks to the rear brake ducts. We also have new front wheel rims, which will help us build more temperature in the tyres. These updates are not significant in terms of lap time, but they do make us slightly more competitive”, Houldey said.

Why is this detail so interesting? After the race, team principal Andrea Stella noted that both Budapest and Zandvoort were high-downforce circuits that naturally suited the car's characteristics better than other tracks. However, looking back at Monaco, where the team hoped to fight at the front and repeat previous successes of last year, McLaren and struggled ended outside the podium positions.

The reason for those struggles went beyond cornering speeds and circuit characteristics. While Monte Carlo gives teams greater set-up freedom with fewer compromises, the car suffered from a lack of downforce and from difficulty generating temperature in the front tyres, which reduced overall grip. This limitation had already emerged earlier in the season, most notably in Australia and China, where the car experienced pronounced graining, while in Japan, where graining was not an issue and the new asphalt improved the overall grip, the MCL40 gained its first podium of the season.

One of the concerns heading into the Zandvoort weekend was the possibility of front‑axle graining, although it ultimately proved to be minimal for everyone. The real challenge was getting the tyres into the right temperature window, even over a single lap. That became clear in the final Q3 attempt on Saturday, when Lando Norris secured pole position, while other teams, struggled to bring the tyres up to temperature and needed an additional lap.

Aston Martin 2026 wheel comparison demonstrates a difference between the front and rear to manage temperatures Photo by: Gianluca D'Alessandro

This is where the topic connects with the updates introduced in the Netherlands. With wheel rim development open once again this season as part of the rule changes, teams have gained a powerful tool for managing tyre temperatures and operating pressures. The internal cavities of a custom rim design, that some teams call “pockets”, allow engineers to passively control air exchange and thermal transfer to the tyre.

At Zandvoort, McLaren focused specifically on this area to retain higher temperatures within the rim structure and, in turn, transfer that heat more effectively to the tyre. This is why only the front rim, manufactured by long‑standing partner Enkei, was updated, accompanied by a more closed wheel cover designed to limit the cooling effect of ambient airflow as it strikes the assembly and to reduce drag.

The rear rim remained unchanged because rear‑tyre degradation was already a key factor throughout the weekend, as seen during the sprint and the race. In that area of the car, the priority was to keep temperatures under control in the traction phases and the high‑speed sections rather than adding more heat. Strong gusts caused the cars to slide through the high‑speed corners, where additional downforce becomes critical, as well as through the key traction zones on the exit of the slower corners.

Sports.title: "How can you allow this?" – Wolff shares Lauda story behind Hamilton's iconic F1 pole
Sports.content:
When Toto Wolff held his annual media session with a select group of Dutch journalists at Zandvoort, one of the topics that came up was how a Formula 1 team can get the maximum out of a driver and, related to that, how much freedom a team principal should give a star driver.

The most recent example is Max Verstappen and the considerable freedom he is given at Red Bull, for instance with his own racing team and endurance adventures such as the Nürburgring 24 Hours.

As is well known, the Dutchman does that with a Mercedes-AMG GT3, although the question remains whether another F1 team – Mercedes, for example – would ever give a driver like Verstappen just as much freedom.

When Wolff is asked that question, he gives an almost philosophical answer, explaining that a team principal must always analyse the best approach to getting the maximum performance out of a particular driver – and must therefore try to understand his personality.

"I think every team is different, but I think what I am trying to do is to identify what it is that makes the driver fast within our structure," Wolff said.

"What kind of framework do we need to provide to extract the best performance of the driver, and part of that is obviously the well-being. And that is something that I am very keen on as well.

"I have never put drivers in a box and have never said this is how you need to be."

Max Verstappen, Mercedes-AMG GT3 Photo by: Miguel Reis / NurPhoto via Getty Images

"Toto, how on earth can you allow this?"

With Verstappen, that freedom involves competing in other racing series, but Wolff’s thoughts immediately go back to the most telling example from his own career as an F1 team boss: Hamilton’s passion for fashion, particularly in the build-up to the 2018 Singapore Grand Prix.

"I remember Lewis Hamilton with his fashion collection back in the day and there was this Singapore race. I remember it was 2018 or 2019, when he launched his Tommy Hilfiger collection," Wolff recounted.

"He had a fashion show in Shanghai where he FaceTimed us. He was grateful that Mercedes changed from Boss to Hilfiger to allow him to have his own collection. He showed everything and said, look at this, this is my catwalk, this is my collection. I can't believe it!"

The fashion show in Shanghai took place on 4 September, but Hamilton did not immediately head to Singapore afterwards. In between, he still had New York Fashion Week on his schedule to present his collection in the US.

"And then he flew from Shanghai to LA or New York, and did it there," Wolff recalls. "Niki Lauda said to me back in the day, I cannot comprehend why you allow this. We are racing in Singapore next weekend, so how is this even possible?"

The criticism intensified when Hamilton’s journey to Singapore was delayed and he was set to arrive late for the first engineering meeting.

Hamilton arrived late in Singapore after the fashion shows, but Wolff defended his driver against criticism Photo by: Glenn Dunbar / Motorsport Images

"Lewis said that he needed to do another stopover in London or so, I don’t even remember. He calls me on Wednesday and says that it will be touch and go, arriving on Thursday for the first engineering meeting.

"I replied, do me a favour, because I'm already getting lots of shit here for you doing a 360 around the world in funky clothes!

"But then he called me again and said, I'm late, the flight has been delayed. So Niki says to me, I really can't believe how you can allow that."

"Lewis, please don’t let me down this weekend"

What followed, however, was telling in two respects: firstly, in Wolff’s willingness to protect his drivers and give them freedom, and secondly, in how Hamilton then repaid that trust on track.

"When he arrived, I said, 'Lewis, do me a favour. I'll take it from you here, I'll take all the criticism from everyone, but just don't let me down this weekend.'

"Understood, he said, and this is when he had this unbelievable pole position. There was that sensational lap and then he won the race, disappearing in the distance.

Hamilton repaid Wolff’s trust in Singapore and went on to clinch his fifth world title just over a month later Photo by: Jerry Andre / Motorsport Images

"After the race he came back to me and said, that was a good deal, no?"

Wolff concludes with a laugh that from that moment on, even Lauda was fine with what Hamilton did away from the track, as long as it did not negatively affect his performance on it.

"Niki said to me afterwards, 'I'm never going to criticise it anymore, even if he flies to the moon before a race!'"

Hamilton took pole in Singapore by more than three tenths of a second over Verstappen and six tenths over title rival Sebastian Vettel. The Mercedes driver won Sunday’s race by almost nine seconds from Verstappen and would secure his fifth world title just over a month later in Mexico.

Sports.title: Haas completes latest TPC test as focus on 2027 F1 driver line-up decision grows
Sports.content:
Haas has completed its latest Testing of Previous Cars (TPC) run with Ryo Hirakawa, Leonardo Fornaroli and Rafael Camara in action, as focus on its 2027 Formula 1 driver line-up increases.

With the 2027 F1 silly season picking up speed since the end of the summer break, Haas is one of the few teams to officially decide its driver line-up for next season.

While Oliver Bearman looks assured of retaining his place at the team for 2027, attention has turned to Esteban Ocon’s position, with Haas making no secret of its intention to assess all of its options.

The American team has just completed a three-day TPC test at Portimao, where reserve driver Hirakawa was in action alongside 2025 Formula 2 champion and McLaren development driver Fornaroli and current F2 title contender and Ferrari junior Camara. Each driver completed laps in the VF-25 – Haas’ 2025 F1 car – at the Portuguese venue from 26-28 August.

It follows a similar TPC test Haas ran last month, when it gave an opportunity to Toyota-backed drivers Sho Tsuboi and Nirei Fukuzumi at Fuji.

While no further information has been revealed about the Portimao TPC test, it was made clear it was part of the wider plan by Haas to evaluate all interested drivers before making a final decision on its 2027 line-up.

Ayao Komatsu, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

“I think it's really good that other people are actually interested in us,” Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu said ahead of the Dutch GP last weekend.

“At the moment, we're not performing so well. We cannot challenge for points, but I think it's nice that other people can see the potential in us. Within the constraint how we're fighting and we're trying to improve the team. We just take it as a compliment that other drivers are interested.”

Komatsu has stressed his immediate focus is on the short term to maximise performance from both the car and its drivers in 2026, indicating Haas will take its time to decide its future driver pairing.

In Haas’ short history in F1, it has often been one of the last teams to announce its driver line-up for the following season – so a similar timeline isn’t unrealistic given the relatively stable driver line-ups elsewhere on the grid for 2027.

“We’re not in any rush,” Komatsu said at Zandvoort. “We’re focused on our two drivers, Ollie and Esteban, trying to get the best out of them. They’ve got the tough challenge, right? You know what they are capable of.

“Ollie has showed it repeatedly, Esteban, when he is happy with the car, you know what he can do. So we need to really just focus on providing them with the best possible car, best set-up adaptation, and get the best out of them. And then both of our drivers are fully focused. So at the moment, we’re focused on that.”

Sports.title: What Norris' contract extension means for McLaren and Piastri
Sports.content:
With what is undoubtedly coming with a salary befitting a world champion, Lando Norris has put pen to paper to a deal tying him to the Woking-based team until 2030, with options for multiple additional years after that, taking Norris into his 30s.

Imagining Norris wearing a different-coloured race suit has always felt like a mind-bending exercise. Now, the 26-year-old's bumper McLaren contract has definitively taken one of F1's leading stars out of the driver market for years to come, turning Norris into a bona fide franchise driver for the team.

Read Also: Formula 1 Norris extends McLaren deal until F1 2030

Norris started his McLaren career a decade ago, when he was picked up by Zak Brown and supported through the single-seater ranks with Carlin, replacing Stoffel Vandoorne as a grand prix driver in 2019 as part of a new wave of Britain-born talent including George Russell and Alex Albon.

Turning from a fast but raw and insecure talent into a championship-winning superstar, last season was undoubtedly Norris' coming-of-age year, overcoming driving style struggles, mechanical failures and a formidable team-mate in Oscar Piastri to take his first world championship.

That triumph seems to have changed something within Norris. From hoping he could one day achieve his dreams, he finally gained the confidence to know that he could. Seeing is believing.

"Lando is driving and operating at the level of a world champion," team boss Andrea Stella said after Norris' Zandvoort win. "What I like the most about his journey in Formula 1 is that he keeps improving. And I think especially after the start of the 2025 season, something clicked, which is not only a single click, but is a way of working with Lando and that we are adopting also on Oscar's side now in particular. And I think this approach has led Lando to continuous improvements."

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

Search for stability underpins quiet 2027 silly season

It's exactly the type of steady presence, then, that McLaren was keen to tie down for the foreseeable future, willing to fork out an undisclosed but no doubt significant chunk of cash to do so.

Aged 26, Norris is only just entering his prime, so securing its most successful driver since Lewis Hamilton provides McLaren with additional stability as it aims to overcome a slow-ish start to the 2026 season. Norris' brace of wins either side of the summer break are a sign the team is starting to get there.

One look at a particularly quiet transfer market further reinforces the idea that stability is a prized quality to have right now. Teams have been stretched to their limits with the complex 2026 power unit regulations, so they are keen to remove as many unknowns off the board elsewhere, as long as their drivers are performing.

When Max Verstappen, as ever the silly season's dominant domino, decided to stay put at Red Bull, the 2027 starting grid was inevitably going to look very similar to this year's. Alongside Verstappen's decade-long tenure at the Milton Keynes team, Charles Leclerc has also reinforced his commitment to Ferrari, and Mercedes will no doubt want to achieve the same longevity with its drivers, especially Kimi Antonelli.

Speaking to Motorsport.com, Ferrari team boss Fred Vasseur explained the value of Leclerc's long-term relationship with Maranello: "Having this kind of continuity is always positive. For me it's also much easier to work with drivers that I have known for ages. Sometimes you don't need to discuss [something] when you have known someone for 10, 15 or 20 years, when the first feeling is the good one, and you know what he's thinking."

It is clear that mutual trust and understanding also exists between Norris and McLaren, to the benefit of both parties.

Oscar Piastri, McLaren Photo by: Pauline Ballet / LAT Images via Getty Images

What about Piastri?

It will be intriguing to see how Piastri and his camp look at this high-profile deal for his team-mate. The Australian extended his deal to 2028 at the start of the 2025 championship, which looked like his to lose until a combination of a decline in performance, driver mistakes, team errors and bad luck saw him finish behind both Norris and Verstappen.

It was a huge blow to Piastri, and unease over team orders and the team's rules of engagement at points through the 2025 campaign, such as a controversial position swap at the Italian Grand Prix or contact between the two team-mates in Singapore and Austin, may well replay on his or his management's mind when digesting the implications of Norris' long-term big money deal. Those who believe McLaren is and always will be Norris' team certainly won't see his contract extension as anything other than a confirmation of that idea.

But right now, Piastri has more pressing concerns. Compared to his ironclad first half of the 2025 season, the 25-year-old has suffered an extended slump in performance with the 2026 generation of cars, seemingly going through similar driving style struggles that he faced last year on low-grip circuits like Austin and Mexico.

Team principal Stella said Piastri's issues are "purely technical" rather than anything mental, whether related to how 2025 finished or 2026 started, as he reaches a full calendar year without a grand prix win on Monday.

McLaren's solution isn't too dissimilar to how it fixed Norris last year, working with Piastri behind the scenes to make adaptations both from a car and driving style point of view. If it succeeds, it has its two aces back for what is shaping up to be a closely-fought second half of 2026, and a potential title challenge next year.

McLaren's end goal is still for both drivers to be fighting each other for wins and titles, which would involve Piastri following a similar trajectory towards a long-term contract extension. It is up to the Australian's camp to decide whether that's in his interest, or whether it might be time to explore new horizons. In any case, Piastri's current deal until the end of 2028 means time is on his side. The same can be said for McLaren.

In the meantime, McLaren has its reigning world champion tied up for the entirety of the current rules cycle. It's one less puzzle piece on the board as the Woking squad aims to retain and even reinforce its title-winning team.

Sports.title: Norris extends McLaren deal until F1 2030
Sports.content:
Lando Norris and McLaren have agreed to a long-term contract extension, keeping the world champion at the Formula 1 team until at least 2030.

On Saturday morning McLaren announced it had tied Norris to the team until 2030, with multi-year options to further extend the 26-year-old's stay. Norris personally announced the news to the Woking factory staff during the team's annual family and friends open day.

"McLaren is my home, and I’m very pleased to be signing a new contract to keep me with the team until at least 2030," Norris said. "When I started this journey nine years ago, I was clear about the goals I wanted to achieve: to get McLaren back to the front and to win championships.

"We’ve achieved that goal, but we want more, we want to keep on winning, and we know as a team that we’re capable of achieving it. I can’t wait to get back in the car in Monza and I’m very excited about what the future holds for us, both over the rest of this season, and in the coming years.”

Norris' previous deal ran until the end of 2027, effectively increasing the Briton's stay at Woking for at least four more years. Team-mate Oscar Piastri is still under contract until the end of 2028 after extending his deal at the start of last year.

Salaries are rarely revealed in F1, but it stands to reason Norris is in line for a bumper pay rise off the back of his world title and his all-round progress as a driver, which has carried through into a strong first half of 2026. Norris capitalised on McLaren's car upgrades to win the last two grands prix in Hungary and the Netherlands.

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Pauline Ballet - Formula 1

In addition to the new contract extension, Norris was also gifted with his championship-winning 2025 car, the MCL39.

Team principal Andrea Stella was "delighted" to continue working with Norris for the foreseeable future. "He is an exceptional driver, someone who combines outstanding natural speed with maturity, consistency and a strong commitment to McLaren, but above all, he is a special human being who is valued by everyone in the team," Stella said.

"Since joining McLaren as part of our junior programme, he has grown with us and played a central role in bringing the team back to the front of Formula 1. This extension gives us important continuity and reinforces our confidence in the direction we are taking together. With him and Oscar, we know we can count not only on one of the strongest partnerships but also on one of the most united and close-knit teams in Formula 1."

Norris started his McLaren journey as a junior driver in 2017, before being promoted to a race seat in 2019. He has since exclusively raced for the papaya squad and amassed 13 grand prix wins, 18 poles, and 48 podiums.

The team's CEO Zak Brown, who has played an integral role in bringing Norris through the ranks, said: “His journey with the team is a fantastic example of our commitment to identifying, developing and supporting world-class talent, and his achievements speak for themselves.

"Together with Andrea, Oscar and the wider team, Lando has helped drive McLaren into a new papaya era of success, helping us go from the back of the grid, to double consecutive constructors’ titles in 2024 and 2025 and our first drivers’ championship in 17 years.

"We are extremely excited about what lies ahead and remain fully focused on continuing to compete for wins and championships.”

Sports.title: Ukraine appeals to FIA Court of Appeal over lifting of Russia ban | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The Ukrainian Automobile Federation is reportedly appealing against the FIA’s decision to reverse its ban on Russians competing in motorsport and displaying their flag at its events.

The federation is bringing an appeal to the FIA Court of Appeal over the U-turn.

The FIA’s decision came into effect on August 3rd, though the governing body did not announce it for another 10 days. The federation formally objected to the decision three days later and subsequently requested the FIA’s ethics committee.

The governing body originally announced the ban, which also applies to Belarussia, in response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The war continues and the FIA’s announcement of its decision did not give any reasons for its change.

Until 2022, Russian racer Nikita Mazepin competed in Formula 1 and his father’s company sponsored Haas, which ran in Russian colours. F1 also held a race in Russia, at Sochi Autodrom, from 2014 to 2021. F1 cancelled its contract in response to the invasion and the FIA has not relaxed its ban on events taking place in Russia or Belarussia.

In 2023, FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem said he had opposed taking action against Russia over the war. The BBC reported Ben Sulayem proposed relaxing the ban on Russian participation in motorsport, and stated the FIA said its decision followed a similar announcement by the International Olympic Committee in July.

The Ukrainian Automobile Federation is challenging the FIA’s decision as it claims the Russian Automobile Federation is operating offices in parts of Ukraine which Russia has invaded, in Sevastopol, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia. The federation’s website prominently displays names of its members who have been killed in the war since it began.

Sports.title: Ferrari reveals 1996 Schumacher tribute livery for home race at Monza | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Ferrari will run a special livery for their home race at Monza commemorating Michael Schumacher’s 1996 Italian Grand Prix victory.

The team called the design “a special livery inspired by the Ferrari F310” which Schumacher drove during his first season with the team 30 years ago. He won three races for them, the Spanish, Belgian and Italian grands prix.

Ferrari described their livery for this weekend’s race as “predominantly red, with some white on the wings, together with black.”

“The wheels, from BBS as was the case back then, have a hint of gold, recalling the original colour of the magnesium rims used that season,” they added.

The design also incorporates Schumacher’s ‘MS’ logo and the seven-starred helmet design he wore later in his career. He arrived at Ferrari as a two-times world champion and won five titles with them in consecutive seasons from 2000 to 2004.

Ferrari drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc will also wear special overalls for this weekend’s race.

The team will arrange two demonstration runs during the event using an F2002 chassis which Schumacher raced in 2002. Four-times world champion and former Ferrari driver Sebastian Vettel will demonstrate the car before the grand prix on Sunday and Rubens Barrichello, Schumacher’s team mate from 2000 to 2005, will do the same on Saturday.

Sports.title: Argentina ready to host Formula 1 again, says president | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Argentina’s president Javier Milei says the country is ready to host the Formula 1 world championship again.

Milei made the claim while opening the FIA American Congress in Buenos Aires.

“The Automovil Club Argentino has made an enormous contribution to national motorsport, and Argentina is a country that loves cars,” said Milei. “The Argentine passion for racing is timeless.

“That is why I invite you to dream with me. Argentina has all the conditions necessary to once again welcome Formula One and the World Rally Championship onto its calendar.

“We have the tradition. We have the drivers. And now we are once again developing the institutional seriousness that these categories demand before choosing a country. We have absolutely everything.”

Franco Colapinto became Argentina’s first Formula 1 driver since 2001 when he joined the series two years ago. Alpine recently extended his contract to drive for them again next year.

Colapinto’s huge popularity in Argentina was demonstrated when he performed a demonstration run in Buenos Aires before hundreds of thousands of fans in April.

Last week the FIA condemned the abuse of its stewards after being inundated with complaints on social media from Colapinto’s supporters over two penalties he received in the previous round. The FIA did not mention Colapinto by name.

Argentina last hosted the world championship in 1998. F1 first visited the country in the fifties when Argentina’s Juan Manuel Fangio won his home grand prix four times on his way to claiming a then-record five world championship titles.

All 20 Argentinian grands prix took place at the Autodromo de Buenos Aires Oscar y Juan Galvez. A plan to redevelop the circuit and bring it up to F1 standards was proposed in 2017, but did not go ahead.

Sports.title: Social Media: “The car of my dreams” – Hamilton gets a Ferrari F40 | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton has a new addition to his road car collection: a Ferrari F40.

The seven-times world champion, who joined Ferrari last year, said the F40 is “the car of my dreams and has been for as long as I can remember.”

Ferrari began producing the F40 in 1987. It was the last road car created by the company under the guidance of its founder, Enzo Ferrari.

“As a kid I dreamt of having one,” said Hamilton, who was two years old when Ferrari first began producing the F40. “When I joined Ferrari last year I made sure to have one with me on my first day at Maranello. That’s how much it means to me.”

The car has a three-litre V8 twin-turbo engine producing around 351kW. Ferrari claims the car can hit a top speed of 324kph.

“These cars are works of art and incredibly rare,” Hamilton continued, “so when I found this one, covered in dust after being sat in a garage for over thirty years, I knew I had to bring her home. First to Maranello, where the master engineers and mechanics at the factory worked for weeks to bring her back to life.

“Massive thank you to everyone who had a hand in this project. This has truly been a dream come true. I can’t wait to share more with you all.”

Sports.title: Palou clinches fifth IndyCar championship title in seven years | IndyCar
Sports.content:
Alex Palou continued his domination of the IndyCar series by clinching his fifth title on Sunday.

The 29-year-old has won the championship in all bar two of the seven seasons he has contested it. He debuted in the series at Dale Coyne in 2020 before moving to Ganassi the following year. He has delivered the title for his current team every season except 2022, when Penske’s Will Power won the championship.

Palou claimed his latest title with one round remaining. He has claimed six victories so far this season – two fewer than last year. He took pole position for the series’ blue riband race, the Indianapolis 500, but was unable to repeat his 2025 victory.

His latest championship triumph came in unusual circumstances during the series’ double-header race weekend at the Milwaukee Mile oval. Saturday’s first race was halted due to rain, and not resumed until after the completion of Sunday’s second race.

Andretti’s Kyle Kirkwood was Palou’s closest threat heading into last weekend, but finished behind him in both races. Palou clinched the title with a 100-point lead over McLaren’s Christian Lundgaard by the end of the weekend.

McLaren’s Pato O’Ward took back-to-back victories, moving him into the thick of a close fight for the runner-up spot behind Palou. Lundgaard, Kirkwood and O’Ward are separated by just four points.

Palou will defend his latest championship title next year as the most senior driver in Ganassi’s line-up. His team mate, six-times champion Scott Dixon, who scored his last victory over a year ago at Mid-Ohio, will join O’Ward at McLaren.

Sports.title: Who Should Moses Itauma Fight Next?
Sports.content:
That simple post has generated plenty of interaction because everyone gets to play matchmaker. It keeps Itauma in the conversation while giving fans a voice in how Queensberry should handle his return.

Quick Knockouts Hid The Weaknesses

Whoever comes next must serve a purpose. Matching Itauma with another heavyweight who collapses under his opening attack would do nothing to correct what Hrgovic exposed.

Itauma’s string of early knockouts built excitement but denied him the live rounds needed to develop punch economy. He attacked Hrgovic as though every combination had to end the fight, throwing power shots at full speed instead of using a measured jab to score, control distance, and conserve energy.

Once his legs slowed, the defensive flaws became easier to see. Itauma’s upper body grew stationary near the ropes, leaving him available for Hrgovic’s straight right hands. When pressured, he looked for heavy hooks to escape rather than tying up, turning Hrgovic, or digging to the body to interrupt the attack.

Those are skills Itauma cannot develop by knocking out another overmatched opponent in two rounds.

Vianello And Ajagba Offer Useful Tests

Guido Vianello fits the requirement. The Italian has the size and durability to make Itauma work, but he would not bring the same threat level as the division’s leading contenders.

Efe Ajagba presents a harder version of that test. His length and right hand would punish careless attacks, forcing Itauma to use his jab and remain defensively responsible after throwing combinations.

Jerry Forrest represents the traditional gatekeeper route. He is experienced, awkward, and durable enough to extend younger heavyweights without bringing the explosive offense of the division’s biggest punchers. The purpose would be to get Itauma seven to ten useful rounds, not simply restore his knockout reel.

Parker And Bakole Bring Greater Danger

Martin Bakole, Joseph Parker, Bakhodir Jalolov, and Teremoana Teremoana would answer more serious questions, but each carries considerable risk immediately after the Hrgovic loss.

Jalolov’s southpaw power and amateur experience make him particularly hazardous. Parker has the patience and ring intelligence to allow Itauma to spend energy before increasing his own work.

Bakole brings pressure, leaning his entire frame on opponents and forcing them to fight in reverse. You either learn to breathe through infighting, or you drown. He would force a physical inside fight that Itauma has not shown he can control. Teremoana Teremoana brings pure physical dread. When you face a giant who punches with evil intent, you cannot afford wasted movement. Itauma would have to stay locked in every second, forcing mental endurance alongside physical stamina.

Frank Warren faces a difficult promotional decision. Soft opposition will draw criticism on major cards, but another stoppage defeat would badly damage Itauma’s value. The Hrgovic fight has also shown other heavyweights that Itauma can be worn down after his opening attack, making contenders more willing to face him.

Itauma does not need protection from every challenge. He needs an opponent who survives the early rounds and forces him to find another way to win. DAZN has given fans the matchmaking question, but the final selection will show how much Queensberry learned from the Hrgovic defeat.

Blowing out tomato cans inside three minutes might look pretty on social media, but it does zero real work for a 21-year-old who just learned that a championship fight starts when the initial barrage fails. You cannot build a championship engine by sparring heavy bags in actual fights.

The standard promotional playbook after a young prospect gets exposed in deep water is to slam the emergency brakes and retreat straight into safe territory.

Frank Warren and Queensberry have a valuable commodity in Itauma, and after seeing him leave the ring in exhaustion against Hrgovic, their natural instinct will be damage control. That means matching him with the exact same low-danger fodder that built his early record.

They will want him scoring fast, with highlight-reel knockouts on undercards, to restore fan excitement and protect their investment. The promotional machine will spin the Hrgovic defeat as a minor bump due to youth, claiming he just needs confidence builders.

The issue with that conservative approach is that it cures nothing. If they feed him three or four sacrificial lambs who fall down in round two, Itauma learns zero pacing discipline. He will not learn how to control his output, he will not learn how to rest while still winning minutes, and he will enter his next world class fight with the exact same twenty minute gas tank that failed him in London.

Queensberry will probably take the soft route to protect the asset, but doing so only delays the inevitable when he steps back up.

Sports.title: WBA President Leaves Jack Catterall Waiting for Teofimo Lopez
Sports.content:
Last month, Teofimo defeated Rolly by a 12-round majority decision on August 22, but Mendoza has not repeated that commitment or announced a negotiation period.

The silence is a bad sign. An X post from the WBA president is not an enforceable championship order. Mendoza can change his mind, while the WBA Championships Committee can approve an interim fight against a more profitable opponent.

Catterall has seen this before. He accepted step-aside money as the WBO mandatory to allow Jose Ramirez to face Josh Taylor for the undisputed light welterweight championship. Catterall waited until February 2022 for his opportunity, only to lose a highly controversial split decision to Taylor after dropping and outlanding him. His experience explains why Catterall has ruled out another deal.

“There’s not $1 that can persuade me to step aside to allow a unification bout to happen. I’m here to fight,” Catterall said before Romero faced Teofimo.

The WBA’s handling of Shakhram Giyasov gives him another reason to distrust promises. Rolly won the welterweight title in May 2025 with a victory over Ryan Garcia, but did not defend against Giyasov. The WBA formally ordered the mandatory last October, yet Romero kept the belt without fighting him.

Seven months later, Romero was elevated to “Super” champion, and Giyasov faced Catterall for the secondary title. Had Giyasov won, he likely would occupy the same position Catterall does now: holding another WBA belt without receiving the primary champion.

Lopez also has little financial incentive to cooperate voluntarily. Catterall is an awkward southpaw counterpuncher who can make an opponent look poor while offering less money in the United States than Ryan Garcia, Conor Benn, or Devin Haney. It is maximum tactical difficulty without a matching payday for Lopez.

That two-champion structure does not create urgency either. It allows the organization to sanction title fights involving both belt holders without immediately forcing them to meet.

Catterall needs Teofimo for the payday and the opportunities a victory would produce. Beating him would strengthen Catterall’s position for fights against the Garcia vs. Benn winner, WBO champion Haney, or IBF champion Liam Paro.

Until the WBA issues an order with deadlines and consequences, Catterall has only a secondary belt and Mendoza’s unenforceable promise.

Sports.title: Roberto Durán Outclasses Carlos Palomino at Madison Square Garden
Sports.content:
Palomino represented the right test. The former WBC welterweight champion had lost his title to Wilfred Benítez by split decision five months earlier and remained frustrated over not receiving a rematch. He believed Durán had looked soft in previous welterweight appearances, although the Panamanian arrived at the weigh-in looking sharp at 146 pounds. Palomino weighed 145.

Although the 7-5 favorite, Durán did not fight like a lightweight depending solely on aggression. He mixed pressure with feints, jabs, counters, and subtle changes of distance. His head and shoulders were rarely still, allowing him to slip punches without giving up his place inside the pocket.

That upper-body movement disrupted Palomino’s straight punches. Durán kept his head away from the center line, letting the jab pass before answering. At other times, he parried it with his rear hand or stepped inside with a right over the top. Palomino was accustomed to using the jab to set his rhythm, but Durán turned the punch into an opening for his own offense.

Speed soon became decisive. Palomino wanted to time Durán between combinations, yet his counters arrived too late. Durán could step in, finish his work, and change position before Palomino answered. He occasionally smiled, seemingly enjoying the freedom of competing without draining himself to 135 pounds.

Along the ropes, Durán’s work was just as measured. He did not waste energy throwing wide punches when Palomino covered up. He placed hooks into the ribs, brought short right uppercuts through the guard, and used his head and shoulders to keep Palomino from creating room.

Those clinches also answered questions about Durán’s ability to handle a natural welterweight. He did not try to overpower Palomino with muscular strength. Shoulder nudges, forearm leverage, and superior head position allowed him to turn his opponent or free one hand for short punches. His effectiveness there came from balance and technique, not size.

A right hand dropped Palomino early in the sixth round. Some accounts described the knockdown as the finish to a left-right combination, while others credited an overhand right to the chin. Palomino rose immediately and took referee Arthur Mercante’s mandatory eight-count. He survived despite cuts near his right eye and below his left ear.

The former champion produced his best work in the seventh, landing hooks at close range. Durán responded by sweeping the final three rounds. Freed from the severe lightweight cut, he maintained his pace and punch output through the tenth instead of slowing after building a large lead.

Palomino later said Durán’s hand and foot speed had surprised him. He also maintained that Durán thumbed him twice in the right eye during the inside exchanges, neither seen by Mercante.

Mercante and Harold Lederman each scored it 99-90, while Tony Castellano had it 99-91. The cards reflected Durán’s dominance. The contest was one-sided without becoming dull because he continued creating exchanges instead of protecting his advantage.

On HBO, promoter Don King placed the bout beneath Larry Holmes’ WBC heavyweight title defense against Mike Weaver. The card drew 14,136 spectators and a gate of $771,982, with many fans particularly interested in Durán against Palomino. After television networks and Madison Square Garden passed on Holmes-Weaver, King rented the building for $150,000. Durán and his manager reduced their original $250,000 guarantee to $100,000 against a later bill to help keep the promotion together.

Such a thorough victory established Durán as more than a dominant lightweight, carrying his reputation into a larger division. Palomino had been a world champion only months earlier and had never previously been handled in that fashion. Durán showed that his aggression worked because it was supported by defensive movement, timing, balance, and faster feet.

The performance also supplied an early version of the tactics Durán would use against Sugar Ray Leonard in Montreal the following year. Against both men, he slipped his way into punching range, interfered with their jabs, and used technical infighting to keep them from working comfortably. Palomino could not escape that attack. Leonard would later discover how difficult it was to impose his own rhythm once Durán dictated the terms.

Durán and Palomino embraced after the decision. Durán then appeared alone on the July 2, 1979, cover of Sports Illustrated, pictured in action against Palomino beneath the headline “Durán the Boxer.” Palomino retired shortly afterward, while Durán continued toward the defining welterweight victory of his career.

Sports.title: Andy Ruiz Jr. Races Toward Heavyweight Title Shot
Sports.content:
Under a three-fight agreement with Matchroom, Ruiz does not necessarily expect to complete the entire deal before challenging for a belt.

“It could take one fight. It could take two fights. I don’t know. God willing, just take this fight and then I’ll get to fight any of the champions,” Ruiz told Ariel Helwani.

Beating Knyba should not place Ruiz near the front of any championship line. Agit Kabayel stopped the 6’7” Polish heavyweight in three rounds, and Ruiz would merely be defeating someone who has already been exposed below the elite level.

Ruiz still has a reason to move quickly. Daniel Dubois and Filip Hrgovic represent the type of champions who would generate a major payday without presenting the commercial obstacles attached to the division’s biggest names. Neither man may hold his belt for long, leaving Ruiz with a limited period to turn his reputation into a lucrative championship opportunity.

A fight against Dubois or Hrgovic would also give Matchroom an immediate return on its investment. Ruiz can be sold as a former champion attempting one last run rather than spending several seasons rebuilding against modest opposition. His 2019 upset of Joshua remains valuable enough to market, even if his recent results do not warrant preferential treatment.

Winning a belt would serve another purpose. Ruiz has repeatedly expressed interest in a third fight with Joshua after splitting their first two meetings. Joshua has little competitive need to revisit a loss he decisively avenged, but Ruiz becoming champion would change the value of that matchup. A trilogy containing a heavyweight title would be easier to sell than one based almost entirely on memories of Madison Square Garden.

That possibility adds urgency to the Knyba fight. Ruiz does not simply need another win. He needs to look convincing enough for Matchroom to place him near Dubois, Hrgovic, or another champion before the available belts change hands.

The reunion with Manny Robles offers Ruiz a familiar selling point. Robles trained him for the first Joshua fight, when his compact combinations, quick hands, and ability to close distance produced the defining performance of his career. Six years later, a trainer cannot restore lost activity or guarantee that Ruiz still possesses the same physical tools.

Questions also remain about his durability. Chris Arreola dropped Ruiz hard in 2021, while Miller’s constant pressure forced him into a draining fight three years later. Ruiz broke his hand during that draw and eventually required surgery. Elite heavyweights will test that hand, force him to maintain a higher output, and find out how much punishment he can still absorb.

A traditional rebuilding process would consume much of Ruiz’s remaining career. Taking three or four fights to restore his ranking may require another year or longer. Yet the championship queue contains younger contenders who have remained active and beaten better opposition. Mandatory defenses and existing title obligations leave little justification for Ruiz jumping ahead of them.

That explains the hurry, but it does not make Knyba a title eliminator. Ruiz first needs to show that his hand is healthy, his conditioning holds up, and the return to Robles has produced more than another temporary burst of discipline. His name may shorten the climb, but defeating Knyba would not prove he belongs with the division’s best.

Sports.title: Abel Sanchez Says Hrgovic Needed Knockout Against Itauma
Sports.content:
“We weren’t going to win a decision. I don’t care how close the fight was; we were not going to win a decision because boxing has a tendency to do what’s best for boxing financially. I expected to be down. I expected not to win any rounds. I expected Filip to be the 9-to-1 or 8-to-1 underdog. I expected all that, but it was a 12-round fight, and we were going to capitalize on it being a 12-round fight,” Sanchez said to Fight Hub TV.

The crowd made Itauma’s advantage feel wider than it was. Every clean punch brought a loud reaction, while much of Hrgovic’s quieter work passed without the same recognition. Itauma deserved the rounds, but the applause created the impression that he was dominating a fighter who remained competitive and began coming on from the sixth.

Sanchez’s expectation of trailing on the scorecards shaped the tactics. Chasing rounds would have forced Hrgovic to trade combinations with the faster southpaw, giving Itauma the explosive exchanges he wanted. Sanchez instead repeatedly told Hrgovic to make Itauma initiate the action and spend energy closing the distance.

The difference in efficiency became decisive. Itauma threw fast four- and five-punch combinations, while Hrgovic answered with measured jabs and absorbed much of the incoming work on his gloves, arms and shoulders. Even when Itauma scored, he was paying a far greater physical price for each exchange.

A jab did not have to dominate every sequence. Its purpose was to interrupt Itauma’s approach, force another setup and prevent him from planting his feet comfortably. Every reset required the younger fighter to begin again.

That pattern also changed the use of space. Itauma controlled the center initially while Hrgovic willingly gave ground. Once Itauma’s output dropped, the older heavyweight began advancing more consistently. Areas that had provided Itauma room to attack and leave gradually became places where Hrgovic could hold him under pressure.

Abel compared the bout to taking Andy Ruiz Jr. to New Zealand for his 2016 fight with Joseph Parker. He told Ruiz they were already three points behind before boarding the plane. The trip reinforced why he could not depend on favorable scoring when his fighter was facing the home attraction.

The judges became irrelevant when Hrgovic stopped Itauma in the ninth round. Sanchez’s prediction that his fighter would trail was understandable because Itauma had legitimately won most of the earlier rounds. What the scorecards could not show was the changing direction of the fight. Hrgovic was allowing Itauma to spend himself while waiting for the portion only one of them had been prepared to handle.

Sports.title: Frank Sanchez Deserves His Shot at Filip Hrgovic
Sports.content:
Sanchez stepped aside with a guaranteed shot at the winner. Now Hrgovic wants unification fights against Agit Kabayel or Daniel Dubois, with another payment offered as the solution. Sky Sports confirmed Sanchez’s guarantee before the fight.

“Frank Sanchez will wait, get another step-aside, make money without fighting and everyone’s happy,” Hrgovic said after his victory, as quoted by The Ring.

Everyone being happy is Hrgovic’s interpretation. A payment compensates Sanchez for a delay. It does not give him the championship or the earning power that comes with winning it.

There is a competitive cost, too. Waiting without fighting offers no opportunity to sharpen distance judgment and counterpunch timing under pressure. Taking an interim bout carries its own risks: an injury or defeat can damage his claim. Neither option makes a postponement harmless.

His style also gives this defense sporting value. Against Efe Ajagba, Sanchez used movement and quick counters to frustrate a bigger puncher rather than trading on his opponent’s terms. PBC’s fight report documents that performance.

Applied against Hrgovic, that approach would test the champion’s ability to close distance, establish his jab and create exchanges. He cannot build a strategy around Sanchez exhausting himself the way Itauma did. A patient opponent willing to score and move presents a different task from surviving an early assault.

That does not make Sanchez tougher than Kabayel or Dubois. Limited commercial appeal is still a poor reason to dismiss him as an opponent.

The IBF has a role beyond approving whatever deal generates the largest purse. In 2023, it stripped Terence Crawford after his contractual rematch obligation to Errol Spence Jr. prevented a mandatory defense against Jaron Ennis. That was a rematch dispute, not a unification request, so it does not settle Hrgovic’s case. The decision nevertheless demonstrates that commercial plans need not override a challenger’s position. ESPN’s report explains the decision.

The appeal of another belt is understandable. Hrgovic wants to maximize his remaining years, but Sanchez’s career clock is running as well. Further delays leave him dependent on other fighters’ results, recovery periods and negotiations.

There is nothing wrong with voluntarily accepting an offer he considers worthwhile. The choice, however, should remain his. Insisting on the promised fight would not make him an obstruction to heavyweight unification.

Hrgovic deserves credit for beating Itauma. Sanchez deserves the opportunity that was agreed upon before the winner was known.

Sports.title: Oleksandr Usyk Targets Deontay Wilder for Late Career Victory Lap
Sports.content:
The historical attraction is easy to understand. Having beaten Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua twice each, Usyk can complete his collection of victories over the three heavyweight names that dominated discussion before his arrival in the division.

But the date belongs alongside the name. Defeating Wilder in 2027 would not carry the significance of beating him during his WBC championship reign. Completing that list gives promoters a neat career retrospective without necessarily adding much to Usyk’s strongest accomplishments.

Wilder brings recognition and a right hand that supplies the promotional clips. His defeats against Joseph Parker and Zhilei Zhang exposed the weakness in relying on one decisive punch. Parker denied him clean opportunities, while Zhang punished his hesitation.

Against Usyk, he would struggle to find room to set his feet and throw that right hand. The southpaw changes angles, draws reactions with feints and makes opponents adjust before they can punch. Wilder must process those changes before committing.

That is where his reduced output becomes especially costly. Waiting for a clear target allows Usyk to score and leave. Throwing without properly setting the attack risks missing, losing balance, and taking counters. Wilder needs to create openings with his jab and positioning rather than spend rounds hoping one arrives.

Age offers the strongest qualification to that prediction. Usyk would be 40 by the proposed March date. His movement depends on repeated small adjustments, and any decline in his legs might leave him within reach for longer.

Yet a slower Usyk would still require Wilder to recognize those opportunities and act immediately. Punching power cannot compensate for an opening noticed too late. The American’s chance depends as much on his willingness to throw as on the force behind the shot.

Taking the event to the United States offers a commercial explanation. Wilder supplies a familiar home fighter, while Usyk gets another opportunity to headline there. That familiarity may help attract attention, but converting it into ticket purchases requires convincing buyers that the contest remains competitive.

Lapin has discussed Zuffa as a potential partner, without confirming an agreement. Those talks do not establish who will finance the event, and an American venue does not rule out Saudi involvement. Boxing Insider

A broadcaster or promoter may pay for the names. Fans would still be buying the versions who enter the ring in 2027.

Sports.title: Moses Itauma Must Fire Ben Davison After Filip Hrgovic Disaster
Sports.content:
Davison failed his fighter in two critical areas.

First, the physical conditioning was inadequate for a twelve-round championship fight. You cannot put a twenty-one-year-old puncher in against a seasoned heavyweight without building an elite gas tank. Itauma trains inside a comfortable camp, but he clearly lacked the gritty cardiovascular foundation required for a war.

Second, the corner work was nonexistent when the crisis hit. When a young fighter starts burning energy throwing every shot with bad intentions, the coach must pull back the reins. Davison should have instructed Moses to establish the jab, circle the ring, and take full minutes off to recover his breath. Instead, Davison watched his fighter empty his arsenal into Hrgovic’s iron chin. There were no technical adjustments, no tactical wisdom, zero control over the pace.

Promoter Frank Warren knows how to rescue promising careers after devastating defeats. He rebuilt Daniel Dubois; he will do the same here. But the first move must be immediate and decisive.

Moses Itauma needs to cut ties with Ben Davison today. The ideal replacement is Abel Sanchez, the veteran coach who stood across the ring orchestrating Hrgovic’s victory. Sanchez knew Itauma would blow his engine. He told Hrgovic to stay calm, absorb the early barrage, take over the moment the youngster started gasping for air.

Sanchez would take Itauma up to Big Bear, strip away the hype, build an engine capable of throwing punches all night. Moses has unbelievable hand speed, exceptional natural gifts. What he lacks is an old school trainer who demands relentless discipline.

Someone has to take responsibility for the disaster against Hrgovic. Itauma paid the price with his unbeaten record inside the ring. Davison needs to pay the price with his job.

Ghana News.title: Africa’s colonial ecological debt could exceed hundreds of trillions of dollars – Report
Ghana News.content:
A groundbreaking analytical report titled “CO2lonialism-Ecocide-Reparations” has been unveiled at the University of Lagos, presenting a new and potentially monumental dimension to Africa’s reparations agenda.

The report argues that the long-lasting ecological harm caused by British colonial rule on its former African colonies constitutes a separate and vast category of damage, distinct from the humanitarian harm of the slave trade, with a valuation that could exceed hundreds of trillions of dollars.

The report’s lead author, Professor J. G. Nkem Onyekpe, PhD, Head of the Department of History and Strategic Studies at the University of Lagos, presented the findings to a distinguished audience of academics, legal experts, and public activists.

The core argument is that while direct historical harms are significant, the systematic and structural appropriation of resources, land, and energy under colonialism has created a devastating ecological debt that demands rigorous monetary valuation.

"The report documents that valuation exercises of comparable ambition and scale have already been attempted successfully," stated Prof. Onyekpe. He cited a peer-reviewed 2022 estimate that valued resources appropriated from the global South through unequal exchange at over $10 trillion per year in 2015 alone.

"If the same order of logic—that large-scale, structurally unequal appropriation of resources is capable of rigorous monetary valuation—were extended backward across the full duration of colonial rule and across the full set of affected African states, the resulting figure would run into the hundreds of trillions of dollars, and quite possibly beyond."

The report is set to be formally submitted to the African Union’s newly established sub-commissions—the Committee of Experts on Reparations (AUCER) and the Legal Reference Group on Reparations (AULER). These bodies, now operational under the AU’s Decade of Justice and Reparations (2026-2035), are tasked with developing a harmonized methodology for evaluating and advancing a common African position on reparations claims.

The implications of incorporating ecological destruction into the reparations framework are enormous, according to Nigerian public activists attending the launch.

They argue that if a rigorous, continent-wide valuation methodology is adopted, the $5 trillion figure publicly demanded by Senator Ned Nwoko will now become insufficient. Senator Nwoko had previously submitted a formal claim to the British government demanding at least $5 trillion in reparations from Britain’s colonial system and other colonial powers.

The legal and institutional environment for such claims has shifted markedly since 2021, creating a unique window for advancing an African-led claim. Key developments include the adoption of a working legal definition of ecocide by the Independent Expert Panel, followed by binding or soon-to-be-binding instruments at the Council of Europe (2025) and the European Union (2024), and a proposal before the International Criminal Court.

Most critically, the African Union’s own decision in July 2025 to establish an ad hoc committee to examine the classification of “massive destruction of environmental ecosystems” as a crime provides direct institutional support for the report’s premise.

The report also documents a directly on-point international legal precedent: the 1990s Certain Phosphate Lands in Nauru case before the International Court of Justice. In that case, a formerly colonised state successfully brought a claim against its former colonial administrator (Australia) specifically for environmental devastation caused by colonial-era phosphate mining.

This landmark ruling provides a template, however imperfect, for what an African claim of this kind might look like in practice.

“The Nauru case proves that such claims are not merely theoretical but are grounded in established international law,” remarked Dr. Karibi-Whyte, a Jurispudence and International law expert. “Africa is now building on that precedent to address a harm that is orders of magnitude larger.”

The launch comes at a pivotal moment for the reparations movement, with the African Union having declared 2025 as the Year of Reparations and formally established the AUCER and AULER mechanisms to guide the continent’s strategy.

This new report is expected to be a critical document for their work, framing environmental repair as an essential element of restorative justice for the continent.

Ghana News.title: Ibrahim Sulemana joins Sassuolo on loan from Atalanta
Ghana News.content:
Italian Serie A side Sassuolo have completed the signing of Ghanaian midfielder Ibrahim Sulemana on a season-long loan.

Sulemana joins the club from Atalanta, penning a deal that will keep him at Sassuolo until the end of the 2026/27 season.

Sassuolo also have the option to buy the defensive midfielder at the end of the season should they be convinced by his performances.

The move will see the Ghanaian play for his fifth club in the last five years, having enjoyed stints at Hellas Verona, Cagliari, Atalanta and Bologna.

Sulemana enjoyed the first half of last season at Bologna before moving to Cagliari for the second half of the 2025/26 campaign. He made 16 appearances, scoring one goal.

Sulemana will be hoping to get minutes at his new club and regain a recall to the Black Stars team after missing out on the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

Ghana News.title: Former UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer to stand down as MP to focus on world affairs
Ghana News.content:
Sir Keir Starmer has announced his departure from the House of Commons, stepping down as the Member of Parliament for Holborn and St Pancras just months after leaving Downing Street. The decision sets the stage for an imminent by-election in central London and marks the final chapter of a turbulent parliamentary career for the former Labour leader.

Shifting Focus to Global Horizons

Reflecting on his departure, Starmer told local media that he had decided over the summer to pivot toward global issues. He noted that the transition felt natural after serving as head of government.

"I think once you've been prime minister, it's important to answer the question: what are you going to do next? Having decided I'm going to concentrate on international affairs, I think it's right to step down," Starmer said.

He added that it had been a "huge honour and privilege to represent the best constituency in the country and to have taken over from Frank Dobson, who was such a great constituency MP and a member of the last Labour government."

Starmer outlined his future professional path, emphasising that his attention would turn outward.

"I will now focus on other things, and that will be international affairs including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world," Starmer stated.

Alongside global policy, he intends to maintain long-standing advocacy work.

"I will also continue, as I have done for a long time now with others, to work on combating violence against women and girls; that is an issue that matters to me hugely. It's work I started before I became an MP and it's work I'm keen to continue after I'm an MP. So international affairs on the one hand, and continuing my work on violence against women and girls on the other."

Local Legacy and Electoral Test

The resignation triggers a high-stakes electoral test for Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who assumed office over the summer after Starmer's exit. Holborn and St Pancras has long operated as a secure Labour stronghold, with Starmer capturing a substantial majority during the 2024 general election.

Starmer highlighted his domestic achievements within the district since entering parliament in 2015.

"I want to thank all of those I was privileged to work with in the constituency on issues that matter hugely: affordable housing, first-class education and the work we did on knife crime through the Camden youth support, which was really, really important," he said.

He also acknowledged the backing of grassroots members.

"They have been resolute in their support for me, firstly in becoming an MP and then becoming the leader of the Labour Party and then as prime minister."

Despite the historical safety of the seat, opposition parties are positioning themselves for an aggressive campaign. The Green Party has signalled interest, with leadership noting that Zack Polanski, a London Assembly member, is considering a bid.

"Zack has always made it clear he would like to be a London MP. London has been his home for over 20 years," a Green Party spokesperson said.

Other potential challengers include independent left-wing figure Andrew Feinstein, who mounted a prominent campaign against Starmer in the previous election cycle.

Political Fallout and Reactions

The announcement drew sharp rebukes from the Conservative opposition. Conservative Party chair Kevin Hollinrake criticised the sudden reversal from earlier commitments to remain a backbench MP.

"It is fitting that his final act as a member of parliament is yet another U-turn having pledged to stay on," Hollinrake said. He added that the contest would result in "a costly by-election for taxpayers at a time when Andy Burnham and John Healey are plotting tax rises on hard-working families across the country."

Conversely, loyalists defended Starmer's legacy of turning the party's electoral fortunes around following the 2019 defeat. Former housing secretary Steve Reed remarked that Starmer was leaving Parliament "with his head held high." Former business secretary Peter Kyle echoed those sentiments, noting, "From the pits of despair after the 2019 hammering to the euphoria of a landslide victory, he led with grit, driven by a love of country."

Concluding his formal statement, Starmer offered reassurance to his successor and the incumbent administration.

"Whoever is lucky enough to become the Labour candidate will have my full support and backing,g and I will continue to give my full support to the prime minister," he said.

As Westminster braces for a competitive by-election cycle, the unfolding political landscape reflects both the enduring strength of traditional party strongholds and the persistent volatility characterising contemporary British governance.

Ghana News.title: Built to Last, Left to Rot: Ghana’s maintenance crisis
Ghana News.content:
Ghana’s ambition to host major international football competitions is being weakened by the poor maintenance of football stadiums and sporting facilities across the country. Despite Ghana’s renowned football history and growing interest in the sport, the worsening condition of some playing fields continues to raise concerns about the country’s readiness to meet the standards needed for high-level competitions.

Football pitches are important to the development and promotion of the sport. However, several pitches across the country are poorly maintained, with uneven playing surfaces, inadequate drainage systems, neglected grass and damaged facilities. These circumstances can affect the quality of matches, increase the risk of injuries to players and make some venues unqualified for international competitions.

The problem is not limited to only the playing surfaces. Some stadiums and football facilities also encounter the same challenges, which include seating areas, changing rooms, floodlights, sanitation facilities and other essential infrastructure. International football competitions require venues to meet strict standards, and failure to maintain these facilities frequently decreases Ghana’s chances of being selected as a host.

Sports analysts and football supporters have always called for a change in the method of maintaining sporting facilities. They argue that maintenance should not only be done when Ghana is preparing to host a major tournament. Rather, stadiums and pitches must receive regular inspections, repairs and renovations throughout the year.

Poor maintenance also influences the development of young football talents. Local teams and aspiring footballers need quality pitches to train and compete. When suitable facilities are unavailable, young players may face challenges in developing their technical abilities and could be forced to play on unsafe or unfit surfaces.

Ghana has previously shown its ability to host major football events, showing that the country has the potential to attract international competitions. However, sustaining that reputation requires uninterrupted funding and proper maintenance of existing facilities rather than waiting for major tournaments before taking action.

The government, the Ghana Football Association, local authorities and private stakeholders therefore need to adopt a long-term maintenance strategy for football facilities. Such a strategy should include regular inspection of pitches, adequate funding, professional pitch maintenance and accountability for the use of resources allocated to sports infrastructure.

If Ghana can improve its maintenance culture, the country will not only increase its chances of hosting major international football competitions but also build better conditions for local clubs and young footballers.

Maintaining football facilities should therefore be considered as a long-term investment in Ghana’s sporting future rather than an expense that becomes necessary only when a major competition is approaching.

Ghana News.title: Number of debit cards issued by banks decreased by 11.8% to 5.7m in 2025
Ghana News.content:
Dr. Johnson Asiama

The number of debit cards issued by banks decreased by 11.8% to 5,709,937 in 2025 from 6,474,537 in 2024. According to the Bank of Ghana, the decline in the number of debit cards was mainly due to the destruction and withdrawal of expired cards.

In contrast, credit cards issued in 2025 increased by 4.8% to 71,629 from 68,380 in 2024.

This was due to the expansion of credit card services across the industry.

According to the 2025 Payment Systems Oversight Annual Report the total number of prepaid cards issued also declined by 31.8% to 403,582 from 591,502 over the same comparative period.

Meanwhile, the mobile money industry in Ghana recorded strong growth and resilience in 2025, as reflected in Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) and notable structural developments that shaped the industry.

The number of active mobile money customers recorded significant growth in 2025, rising by 13.6% to 26.7 million in 2025 from 23.5 million in 2024.

The Central Bank said the stronger growth underscored the resilience and continued expansion of Ghana’s mobile money ecosystem.

Ghana News.title: Total mobile money transaction values grew by 50.8% to GH¢4.54trn in 2025
Ghana News.content:
Total mobile money transaction values grew by 50.8% to GH¢4.54 trillion in 2025 from GH¢3.01 trillion over the review period, the Bank of Ghana has disclosed.

According to the 2025 Payment Systems Oversight Annual Report, the acceleration in transaction values underscored the increasing importance of e-money platforms in supporting economic transaction.

Following the significant agent network clean-up in 2024, the number of mobile money active agents dipped but rebounded in 2025.

According to the Bank of Ghana, active agents increased by 21.4% over the period to 491,057 in 2025 from 404,370 in 2024.

It said that the growth reflected a post-clean-up consolidation phase, characterised by improved agent legitimacy and activity rather than rapid network expansion.

However, mobile money transaction values in 2025 continued to be concentrated in a small number of high-value transaction types, with Agent-to-Agent (A2A) transactions remaining dominant and accounting for 41.0% of total transaction values compared with 37% in 2024.

“A2A transactions have continued to play a critical role in supporting liquidity redistribution and settlement within the mobile money agent network”, the report said.

It added that the third-party transfers recorded a marginal increase to 14.9% in 2025 from 14.4% in 2024, reflecting the growing use of fintech platforms for mediated merchant and commercial payment flows.

This shift points to continued integration of mobile money channels into business and institutional transactions.

In contrast, cash-based transactions made up a smaller share of total transaction values, with combined cash in and cash out activities accounting for 16.1% in 2025, compared with 20.1% in 2024. This reduction indicated a gradual transition from cash-intensive activity towards account-based and digital transaction flows.

Other transaction types, including wallet-to-bank, bank-to-wallet, person-to-person and business-to-business transactions, maintained relatively stable shares, collectively supporting both retail and merchant payment use cases.
