If the majority of his support was party-based, the MDR could potentially retain much of its political influence. If a significant portion was personally attached to Kogar, his departure could create a new political bloc.

If the 2025 victory was the product of several forces working together, then the outcome of the separation could depend on which of those relationships survive.

That uncertainty is precisely what makes the development important for Koung. Kogar is not an unknown political figure entering the electoral arena for the first time.

He has won four elections in Nimba, according to the political account surrounding his record, and has moved from the House of Representatives to the Senate. His political base is also described as extending across important parts of the county, including the Gbehlay-Geh and Buu-Yao areas, with maternal ties into the Mano belt.

Such a record does not guarantee future victories. But it does make the assumption that Kogar can simply be politically erased following an MDR expulsion difficult to sustain.

The danger for the Unity Party would be to confuse party membership with voter loyalty. A voter who supported Kogar in a senatorial election may not necessarily support him in a presidential election.

Similarly, a voter who supported Koung in 2023 may not automatically abandon the Unity Party because of a dispute between Koung and Kogar.

Liberian voters are not a single political constituency, and Nimba’s electoral history demonstrates that voters frequently make different calculations depending on the office being contested, the candidates involved and the alliances surrounding them.

Still, presidential elections are often decided by margins, and that is where Kogar’s political relevance could become significant. He does not have to take a majority of Nimba away from the Unity Party to affect the national equation.

If he were to move a meaningful portion of his supporters toward another political coalition, the effect could be enough to reduce the Unity Party’s margin in a county where the party might otherwise expect overwhelming support.

That is the political gamble.

In 2023, the Boakai-Koung ticket won 74.14% of Nimba’s runoff vote. If the Unity Party expects to reproduce that performance in 2029, it will have to contend with a political environment that may contain more competing centers of influence. The most important of those could be Kogar. There is also a generational dimension to the dispute.

For decades, PYJ represented the dominant political personality in Nimba. His death created space for other politicians to compete for influence. Koung is already one of the strongest beneficiaries of that transition, having moved from senator to vice president and becoming an important national figure.

Kogar’s rise represents another strand of the same transition. The two politicians are not politically identical, and their constituencies may overlap without being interchangeable.

If Kogar and Koung eventually reconcile, the episode could ultimately strengthen the governing coalition by bringing competing political interests back together.

If they remain divided, however, the dispute could evolve into a contest over who can mobilize the political constituency that once operated under the broader PYJ-MDR umbrella.

If Kogar aligns himself with an opposition presidential candidate in 2029, the calculation becomes even more serious for the Unity Party. And if he decides to become part of another presidential ticket—or pursues a presidential ambition himself—the potential for fragmentation could increase considerably.

But political analysis is not about predicting the future with certainty. It is about identifying the factors that could shape it.

Kogar’s political career has been shaped by battles over party structures, leadership and political loyalty, and his supporters now argue that he is once again being forced to fight for his political survival.

His critics, meanwhile, can point to Kruah’s explanation that Kogar was given due process and failed to appear for a scheduled hearing. Both narratives are likely to remain part of the political debate.

But the larger issue cannot be resolved by determining who won the argument inside the MDR meeting.

The real verdict will come from voters. If Kogar remains politically active, his next political move will provide an important indication of how much of his 2025 support was personal. If he can mobilize supporters outside the MDR structure, that would suggest that his political influence is broader than the party machinery.

If he struggles to reproduce that support, it would strengthen the argument that the MDR and the wider political coalition surrounding Koung were more important to his victory than his personal appeal.

For Koung and the Unity Party, therefore, the wisest response may not be to dismiss Kogar but to understand what his expulsion could mean.

Nimba politics has repeatedly punished those who assume that electoral loyalty is permanent. In 2017, PYJ demonstrated that his political influence could dramatically reshape a presidential contest.

In 2020, Koung won a competitive Senate election with 36.12% of the vote, demonstrating both his strength and the limits of political consolidation.

In 2023, the Boakai-Koung ticket transformed Nimba into one of its strongest political bases, winning 59.53% in the first round and 74.14% in the runoff. In 2025, Kogar demonstrated his own electoral strength by winning 52.08% and 62,136 votes in the senatorial by-election.

The numbers are different elections, under different circumstances, involving different candidates. They cannot simply be added together or treated as a direct projection of 2029.

Koung remains a formidable political figure in the county, but his political future will increasingly be judged against his ability to maintain the coalition that helped elevate him to the vice presidency.

Kogar, meanwhile, has been removed from the MDR, but he has not been removed from Nimba politics.

His 62,136 votes are not his permanent property. Neither are they irrelevant. Some belonged to the candidate, some may have belonged to the party, some may have been influenced by the broader political environment, and some may have reflected relationships built over years.

The challenge is determining how much of that coalition can travel with him. That is a question that cannot be answered by an MDR resolution.

It can only be answered through future political activity and, eventually, through votes. For now, the photograph of Kogar being removed from the MDR headquarters may be the most visible symbol of his political separation from the party.

But the more important picture may be the one voters will create in 2029.

World.title: Liberia: Fed, But Starving: Health Workers Say Misinformation, Fees and Aid Cuts are Causing a Dramatic Rise in Severely Malnourished Babies
World.content:
Summary:

21-year-old Lovetee did not know breast milk is all babies under six months can consume. She fed her four-month-old daughter, Princess, soft rice and well water, and the baby is now dangerously malnourished.

Health workers across the country say this is common. UNICEF found only about half of Liberian babies under six months are exclusively breastfed, and many caregivers wrongly believe infants need water or food to grow strong or stop crying.

The problem is getting worse. A 2025 study saw a nearly tripling in cases of acute malnutrition, alarming health officials. They say USAID cuts have left them without first-line tools to treat malnourished children, meaning more will die.

The introduction of fees for service at public facilities means many babies are born and die without ever being registered or getting any support.

By King Brown with New Narratives

BUCHANAN, Grand Bassa County— The sun is hot here in Big Joe Town, outside Grand Bassa’s capital city. Lovetee, 21, sits on a wooden chair watching her four-month-old daughter, Princess, lying weak on her lap, suffering from diarrhea. Princess’s ribs show through her skin, and her hair is thinning instead of growing.

Lovetee, a first-time mother, has not eaten properly in days and she says she barely sleeps because Princess cries until morning. She has been feeding Princess soft rice mixed with soup, plus water from the open community well, a practice she learned from her brother’s partner. Lovetee says no one ever told her a baby under six months cannot eat food or drink water. Mother and baby are paying for that lack of knowledge.

“When my baby crying, my breath can want cut off, because she can just be breathing fast, fast,” Lovetee says. “Her stomach just running. She weak, weak in her body. To even lift her, I have to balance her neck with my one hand and her waist with my other hand before she break.”

Experts say that knowledge gap, between what families believe and what a newborn’s body can process, sits at the center of a public health crisis playing out quietly in homes across Liberia. In 2020 – the most recent data – the Demographic and Health Survey found that 56 percent of young Liberians surveyed incorrectly believed babies needed water in their first six months, and 46 percent believed babies needed something beyond breast milk to grow strong. Only about half of Liberian babies under six months are exclusively breastfed.

A more recent survey is alarming public health experts. The 2025 Comprehensive Food Security and Nutrition Survey, not yet published online, found that 8.5 percent of children in Liberia, below the age of five years, suffer from acute malnutrition or wasting, a dramatic increase from the Demographic and Health Survey, which put the number at 3 percent.

Experts think the numbers are actually higher because they see women who have been told the dangers of giving infants food and water and do it anyway. Experts don’t trust that caregivers are telling survey takers the truth.

The problem is compounded by the introduction of fees and aid cuts. Lovetee wants to take Princess to the government hospital, but under the new policy, started in March, requiring all patients to pay for services at public health facilities that were previously free, she would need roughly L$500 upfront for a bed, plus money for medicine. Unemployed and single, she does not have the money.

Even if Lovetee got Princess to a health facility, nurses no longer have the “plumpy nut” nutrition boost and antibiotics that used to be provided with funding from USAID. All they can do is teach her to feed the baby breastmilk alone.

“If things are not handled within five to 10 years, it will lead to an outbreak [explosion of cases],” warns Samuel Moiwai, public health lecturer at Grand Bassa University.

A Body Not Yet Built for Food

According to the World Health Organization , for the first six months, an infant’s digestive system is built to process one thing: breast milk, since it supplies all the nutrients and fluids an infant needs. The only other thing they can take in is formula, but it must be prepared with sterilized bottles and clean water, often out of reach in rural areas.

But Debra Bah, a pediatric nurse in Buchanan, says she regularly sees babies under six months drinking plain water and eating softened family food, believing breast milk alone is not enough. It is a mistake, says Bah.

“When you give soft rice or water, the baby goes quiet for some time, so family believes the baby is satisfied, not knowing such silence can be very dangerous,” she says.

Solid food introduced too early can cause gas, diarrhea, a swollen abdomen, dehydration, respiratory infections and vomiting.

A father learns too late

Archiebald Moses, 33, says his partner grates and sun-dries eddoes bought at market, then cooks the powder as a daily meal for their five-month-old son, alongside breastfeeding. The baby is not doing well.

“I never heard from anybody before that giving young baby the food we are giving him is harming him,” Moses says. He says fathers should be included in nutrition education too.

Nurse Joyce Albert Mitchell looks for medication after screening an infant for signs of malnutrition. Photo By King Brown

Joyce Albert Mitchell has screened babies at Buchanan’s Well Baby Clinic for five years. About 50 infants pass through weekly, and staff logs one or two malnutrition cases almost daily. She says the real number is higher since many rural mothers never reach the clinic.

The number of women giving birth in health facilities has hit more than 80 percent – a record high. There they are educated about breastfeeding. But Joyce says that guidance is constantly undermined by relatives insisting babies need water and food.

“Giving water to a baby is very dangerous. The child’s immune system is very small and weak,” Joyce says. “If the mother forces water into the child’s stomach, the gut will get filled, and the child will be unable to suck the breast milk well; the water already filled the stomach, it can cause damage for the child.”

Eunice Feekpah Bundor, a community health services supervisor and clinic screener, says giving babies water and food early is common and getting worse. She says some mothers start giving water almost immediately after birth; by one, two or three months, caregivers add fufu, dumboy, rice and other foods.

“Yesterday I received a patient; you could see the spinal cord, the skin dry, the face looked almost like an oldman’s face,” Bundor says.

Nearby health worker Rebecca Karr recalls a three-month-old who died after weeks of eating rice and drinking well water that led to diarrhea and fever.

“By the time they brought the baby, she could not drink or breastfeed,” Karr says. “We tried, but we could not save her.”

The staff worry that numbers may be higher. The babies being born at home without ever having their births registered can die and no one ever knows they existed.

Malnutrition doesn’t only shrink bodies; it damages brain development, lowers IQ, and delays walking and learning, says Sundayway Vungee, Grand Bassa County’s Nutrition Supervisor and a ten-year veteran of the Liberia Government Referral Hospital’s maternity ward. She worries about the next generation of children.

“For Liberia to flourish, our young generation coming up, they have to be well-nourished. When they are well-nourished, they will be able to think well, go to school, and pick up well.”

Traditional misinformation persists

Oretha Tukpeh is a face of the problem. The 55-year-old grandmother of six says her own children were given water and family foods, country rice, plantain, eddoes, and creek water from a young age, and none died or needed hospital care.

“People can hear plenty funny things in the city,” she says, laughing. “But in the bush, you will not hear it, don’t give the baby this one, give the baby that one.”

Vungee says old habits are especially hard to change among teenage mothers as young as 12 who are too young to understand the gravity of raising a baby and are vulnerable to grandmother’s messages. (One in three Liberian girls is pregnant before 18, one of the highest rates in the world). Vungee says some discard the deep-yellow colostrum produced right after birth, believing it unclean, though it is dense with the antibodies newborns need most. Many lack support from the baby’s father, making breastfeeding harder.

Joanna Fahwor, who runs an organization supporting single mothers in Grand Bassa, says many mothers she works with were told by relatives that breast milk was “weak” and that water, rice, eddoes and oatmeal would make babies “strong.”

One case has stayed with her, a two-month-old girl who, within a week of starting solid food, developed severe diarrhea and skin sores, her weight dropping so fast her clothes hung off her. She says the baby later improved after clinic treatment.

The county runs nutrition programs at 18 health facilities and 25 mother-support groups around Buchanan. But programs have been crippled by aid cuts. The therapeutic food supplies known as “plumpy nut” and antibiotics supplied to treat severe malnutrition that used to be supplied by USAID have run out.

Joanna Fahwor, Executive Director of Single Mothers, a women based organization in Grand Bassa County. Photo By King Brown

“Most of the children are dying because of no product in the country,” she says.

Liberia is not alone in facing these challenges, but some countries have achieved far higher breastfeeding rates. UNICEF reported that up to 87 percent of Rwandan mothers exclusively breastfed in 2019, aided by national campaigns, evidence that public education and supportive policy can make a difference.

Back in Big Joe Town, Lovetee frets as she watches her daughter fade. The tragedy is that she along with thousands of other mothers, had the means to help her child thrive, for free, but for now, she lacks the knowledge.

This story is a collaboration with New Narratives . Funding was provided by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency. The donor had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: Liberia: Charlyne Brumskine Becomes First Liberian Woman Appointed to Prestigious Post on West African Regional Court
World.content:
Cllr. Charlyne Brumskine speaking at an AMUJAR event in May at the Ellen Johnson Sirleaf Presidential Center in Monrovia.

Summary

Charlyne Brumskine is one of five judges selected for the prestigious role serving on the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) Community Court of Justice, which hears cases against regional governments, from 2026 to 2030.

The lawyer, who brings more than 23 years of legal experience to the court, is the first Liberian woman to serve in that role.

Brumskine says she wants more West Africans to understand and have access to the Court, including through proceedings outside its headquarters in Abuja, Nigeria.

By Joyclyn Wea, gender correspondent with New Narratives

When Charlyne Brumskine learned she had been selected to the coveted post as a judge on the Ecowas Community Court of Justice, her thoughts turned to her late father.

Charles Walker Brumskine, the prominent lawyer and four-time presidential candidate who died in 2019, had hoped to serve as vice president of the Economic Community of West African States Commission himself, his daughter said.

“My father did not get it. You can imagine how proud I feel to have been able to achieve that,” Brumskine said.

Brumskine is one of five judges selected to serve on the regional court from 2026 to 2030, alongside judges from Nigeria, The Gambia, Togo and Benin. The Court’s bench rotates among Economic Community of West African States member states every four years.

Brumskine is not the first Liberian to serve on the Court. Liberian judges Micah Wilkins Wright and Yussif D. Kaba previously served on the bench. But she is the first Liberian woman.

“Is a privilege that I do not take lightly,” Brumskine said. “I am continuing the legacy of Liberian women who came before me, those who plaited the mat on which I sit. But I am also a forebearer of those who will come after me. I am simply keeping the seat warm for them and providing a blueprint of how Liberian women must represent our country with dignity, excellence, and purpose.”

Based in Abuja, Nigeria, the Community Court of Justice is the judicial arm of the Economic Community of West African States. It interprets regional laws and treaties, settles disputes involving member states and Economic Community of West African States institutions, and hears human rights cases.

Its human rights jurisdiction gives the Court particular importance to ordinary citizens. Individuals can bring qualifying human rights complaints directly before it without first exhausting all remedies in their national courts.

One recent example saw a group of survivors of the 1990 St. Peter’s Lutheran Church massacre, in which up to 600 people were killed by Armed Forces of Liberia soldiers, sue the Liberian government, accusing successive administrations of failing to investigate and prosecute those responsible. But in October 2024, the court threw out the case, ruling it lacked jurisdiction because the violations fell before the court’s human rights mandate existed.

Brumskine said about 90 percent of the Court’s cases concern human rights, covering issues ranging from human trafficking and unlawful detention to freedom of expression and due process.

Liberians have used the Court in other cases. Kabineh Ja’neh, the former Supreme Court associate justice, challenged his impeachment there in 2020. The Court ruled in his favor, finding the government had violated his right to a fair hearing and ordering the government to pay him compensation and restore certain rights. Liberia later sought a review, but the Court rejected the application and ordered compliance with its original judgment.

In another recent case, the Court in July 2025 dismissed an application involving Abrahim Sheriff, raised in Guinea but claimed to be of Liberian origin, who brought a case against Liberia and Guinea at the Court, alleging both governments unlawfully arrested and detained him on unfounded claims of armed insurrection and mercenary activity, subjecting him to torture and enforced disappearance and confiscating $180,000.

Those cases, Brumskine said, demonstrate the breadth of issues that can reach the regional bench. But she said she hopes that Liberians will not have to go there.

“I hope that our government, our judicial system, affords our citizens the opportunity to fundamental rights so that no one appears before me or before any of the justices from Liberia,” she said.

Despite several landmark human rights rulings, the Court faces mounting criticism over poor compliance by member states, with enforcement of its binding judgments remaining one of its toughest challenges since it began operations in 2001. That weakness was on display in the Lutheran Church massacre case, where the court’s narrow reading of its jurisdiction let the Liberian government avoid accountability.

The Court’s independence is also being tested by politically sensitive cases, including a suit by Ghana’s suspended and later dismissed Chief Justice, Gertrude Torkornoo, who is seeking $10 million in damages over her removal. Most recently, the court has been drawn into regional migration politics, hearing a case accusing Ghana of unlawfully detaining and deporting refugees transferred from the US under a secret deportation agreement — the first case filed under the 1979 ECOWAS Free Movement Protocol.

Brumskine comes to the Court with more than 23 years of legal experience. She has also been active in politics and was Alexander Cummings’ running mate in the 2023 presidential election.

During the Ellen Johnson Sirleaf administration, Brumskine worked with the Ministry of Justice on Liberia’s anti-human trafficking framework and with the Ministry of Commerce as Liberia negotiated accession to the World Trade Organization. During the George Weah administration, her law firm served as external counsel to the Central Bank of Liberia.

She is founder of CMB Law Group and has taught at the Louis Arthur Grimes School of Law and the Liberian School of Law. She is licensed to practice law in Liberia, New York and Washington, D.C., and has worked across private practice, public policy and international negotiations.

That background differs from Economic Community of West African States judges who often reach the regional bench after careers in national judiciaries. But previous service as a judge was not required. Candidates could qualify with at least 20 years of relevant professional experience as a judge, lawyer or legal academic.

The selection process was competitive.

The Liberian government submitted three nominees after being allocated a seat on the rotating bench. The three were interviewed in Sierra Leone in April by the ECOWAS Community Judicial Council, made up of chief justices from across the region. Jutonu Kollie, Ministry of Justice communications officer, did not respond to questions about the identities of the other two finalists by deadline.

Brumskine recalled sitting before nine regional chief justices who were sitting as the Economic Community of West African States Community Judicial Council, the body responsible for screening and recommending candidates for the court judgeship as part of her interview panel, wearing headphones as interpreters translated among English, French, and Portuguese speakers. The questions ranged from Economic Community of West African States treaties and human rights protocols to regional affairs and legal philosophy.

The Judicial Council ranked the three candidates and sent its recommendations to the Economic Community of West African States Council of Ministers before the Authority of Heads of State and Government gave final approval.

Former president Sirleaf, Charlyne Brumskine, along with other influential Liberian women, at a dollar campaign in April 2025 to raise funds to support Edith Gongloe Weh’s Senatorial race.

Brumskine said one of her priorities will be helping ordinary West Africans better understand a Court many do not know exists. She wants the Court to become more visible outside Abuja, including by holding activities and proceedings in member states.

“Let the Court come to Monrovia,” she said. “Let people come and see and hear and feel what the Community Court of Justice is. Let’s take it to Accra. Let’s take it to all the different countries in the region.”

She said she believes that access matters particularly for women and other citizens seeking remedies for human rights violations, including human trafficking, which has been growing in Liberia and where the government has done little to protect victims. She stressed that the court is for all West African citizens, not just the elite, to hold governments to account.

“A woman in Buchanan can take her case to the Economic Community of West African States Court of Justice if she meets certain criteria,” Brumskine said.

Her appointment means yet another Liberian woman has attained a prestigious post outside the country while women in the country continued to struggle for representation in leadership. Women hold just 10 of 103 seats in the Legislature. Brumskine said progress has been slow, but she sees her own responsibility as extending beyond occupying a regional seat.

Bowoulo Taylor Kelley, vice president of the Association of Female Lawyers of Liberia, said Brumskine’s appointment demonstrates what Liberian women can achieve when given the opportunity. “These barriers do not reflect a lack of talent,” Kelley said. “Rather, they reflect systems that must be deliberately opened and made fairer.”

At her Monrovia law firm, she said she is mentoring three young women lawyers to take on greater responsibilities eventually. “It’s my role to train. It’s my role to mentor so that when Charlyne Brumskine goes out, they are stepping up to take my place locally,” she said.

For Brumskine, however, the immediate task is the Court and the four years ahead.

“To be a judge, it is the pinnacle, it is the height, it’s the peak of our professional career,” she said. “And not just a judge in Liberia. To be a regional judge.”

Brumskine’s term begins in Mid-October 2026.

This story was produced in collaboration with New Narratives as part of the Investigating Liberia project. Funding was provided by a private donor and the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency. The donors had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: Liberia: Ambassador Witherspoon’s Barbados, Crozierville & Sankofa Story Features in New Book
World.content:
Academics associated with the University of the West Indies (UWI) at Cave Hill will release Tides of

Exchange: The West Indian/Caribbean Footprint in Africa in early November 2026. The book comprises 25 chapters by 25 authors, including Back to Barbados: Barbadian Diaspora in Liberia – Sankofa and the Quest for Ancestral Reconnection, by Liberia’s Ambassador Lorenzo Witherspoon.

It is edited by three distinguished Caribbean academics. Glenford Howe, a senior researcher and policy specialist at The UWI Global Campus, internationally recognized for his work in Caribbean development, higher education, and Africa/Caribbean cooperation; Tara Innis, a Caribbean historian and Deputy Dean (Planning) in the Faculty of Humanities and Education at the UWI Cave Hill Campus in Barbados; and Shelene Gomes, a sociocultural anthropologist at the UWI St Augustine Campus in Trinidad and an honorary research associate in the Department of Anthropology at the University of Cape Town.

The book will be published in November 2026 by Ian Randle Publishers, an independent publisher based in Kingston, Jamaica, that has published fine books about the Caribbean since 1991 and whose primary focus is English-language readers. See https://ianrandlepublishers.com/tide-of-exchange-the-indian-caribbean-footprint-in-africa/

The relationship between Africa and the Caribbean is a story of tides, displacement, return, solidarity, and cultural exchange. These regions, separated by the Atlantic Ocean yet linked by histories of slavery, colonialism, and liberation, have interacted consistently for centuries.

This book explores the West Indian/Caribbean footprint in Africa through historical, political, medical, legal, cultural, intellectual, and trade perspectives, among others, arguing that these exchanges are best understood as reciprocal tides. These ‘tides’ embody the diaspora’s complexities: a people both shaped by Africa and later returning to shape it.

One of the earliest visible organized Caribbean presences in Africa was the settlement of Jamaican Maroons in Sierra Leone in 1800. After resisting British authority in Jamaica, the Maroons were exiled first to Nova Scotia, but discontent and harsh conditions prompted their relocation to West Africa. In Sierra Leone, they became part of Freetown’s social fabric, joining formerly enslaved Africans from Britain and North America. The Maroons contributed military skills and cultural practices, reinforcing the city’s identity as a diasporic crossroads. This episode reflects an early and direct “return” of Caribbean people to African soil, centuries before Pan-African political movements formalized such connections.

During the 19th and early 20th centuries, West Indian seamen played an often-overlooked role in linking the Caribbean to African port cities. Working on merchant and imperial vessels, these sailors docked in Cape Town, Lagos, and other harbors along the continent’s eastern, southern, and southwestern seaboards. They carried not only labor but also culture: stories, music, and political ideas that contributed to the maritime subculture and cultural vibrancy of these port cities. In South Africa, Caribbean seamen mingled with African workers and sometimes became embedded in local communities. The mobility of these sailors underscores that the Caribbean footprint was not confined to military deployments or formal missions but also included grassroots networks of the working-class diaspora.

The Caribbean presence in Africa was also shaped by colonial service. From the late 19th century, West Indians served as clerks, teachers, nurses, medical officers, and administrators in British and French Africa. Their ambiguous role, as colonized subjects administering other colonized populations, speaks to the contradictions of empire. Simultaneously, the West India Regiment (WIR) fought in the East African campaign against German colonial forces. Their experiences reveal that Caribbean peoples were drawn into African theaters of conflict not as free agents but as conscripts and enforcers of empire, yet these encounters left enduring traces of connection.

One such person was George Stanfield Best, who, as a British subject, was conscripted into the British Army in 1914 when World War I broke out. After serving in the African Theatre, headquartered in North Africa, he emigrated to Liberia in 1926, where he met and married Lillian Porte, granddaughter of John Prince Porte, one of the 347 Barbadians who had emigrated there in 1865.

The 20th century brought more intentional and political engagement. Caribbean thinkers, activists, and legal scholars such as Marcus Garvey, George Padmore, Henry Sylvester Williams, Franz Fanon, C.L.R. James, and Claudia Jones played central roles in shaping Pan-African thought and in building organizational bridges between the Caribbean diaspora and African nationalists. Padmore’s collaboration with Kwame Nkrumah in Ghana and James’s mentorship of Kenyan and Nigerian students in London exemplify this intellectual exchange. Caribbean leaders also supported African struggles at the United Nations and within the Non-Aligned Movement. The post-independence period thus saw Caribbean states act as political allies in African liberation.

Caribbean professionals, particularly in medicine and public health, further strengthened these ties. Shared experiences in plantation medicine and tropical disease control left Caribbean doctors and nurses well equipped to assist newly independent African states facing similar health challenges. In recent decades, collaborations have emerged around HIV/AIDS prevention, non-communicable diseases, and community health systems, and the COVID-19 pandemic has underscored the relevance of South–South cooperation in global health.

The cultural tide is perhaps the most palpable. Jamaican Maroons’ Gumbe music, and subsequently reggae, calypso, and dancehall, became powerful symbols of resistance and identity across Africa, often serving as soundtracks for resistance, protest, and liberation struggles. At the same time, African spiritual practices, culinary traditions, and performance forms remained alive in the Caribbean, giving Caribbean visitors to Africa a sense of cultural familiarity. These exchanges have deepened in the 21st century through musical fusions, diasporic festivals (such as carnivals), and academic collaborations.

In 2024, the Sankofa Pilgrimage to Barbados brought four hundred Liberian descendants of Barbadians, along with many from across the Caribbean, for a weeklong homage with kith and kin.

The establishment of CARICOM’s diplomatic mission in Nairobi in 2019 marked a new phase in these exchanges. This initiative formalized the Caribbean presence on African soil and opened pathways for economic, educational, and cultural cooperation. At the same time, diasporic communities of West Indians and Caribbean people living in African cities, from Nairobi to Johannesburg, continue to embody the living currents of connection.

From Maroons in Sierra Leone to seamen in South African ports, and from soldiers in West and East Africa to Pan-African intellectuals in London and Accra, the West Indian and Caribbean footprint in Africa is broad and multifaceted. These stories illustrate not a single moment of “return,” but a series of tidal movements, ebb and flow, push and pull, across centuries. Conceptualizing these connections as tides of exchange highlights their dynamic, reciprocal character and underscores that the Caribbean is not only a child of Africa’s diaspora but also a complex contributor to Africa’s modern histories and futures.

Notably, three presidents of Liberia were of Barbadian ancestry, one of whom was born in Liberia.

Contributors to this volume include specialist historians, anthropologists, statesmen, development experts, and others, drawn from academies in the Caribbean, Europe, and North America, as well as from countries across the African continent, many of whom are in the diaspora, exemplifying the very essence of the reciprocal exchange this work aims to highlight.

When, at his daughter’s urging in 2013, Ambassador Lorenzo Witherspoon began building on the oral history of his family’s West Indian origins, it was a search for truth, and he did not imagine where it would take him. At the time, Loyce Witherspoon was pursuing an undergraduate degree in International Development & Political Science at McGill University in Montreal, Canada. On a bright spring day, she was invited by friends from the Caribbean to join them for a meeting of the university’s Caribbean Club.

After initially protesting that she was not from the Caribbean, she recalled secondhand accounts from her father about his maternal great-great-grandfather, John Prince Porte, who emigrated to Liberia from Barbados in 1865, and about his grandfather, George Stanfield Best, who had come in 1926 from Trinidad via the African Theatre in North Africa, where he had fought during World War I as a British subject. Succumbing to their constant coercion, she relented and attended the meeting. Upon returning to her apartment, she promptly called her dad, insisting, as her friends had, that he conduct thorough research into the Porte family’s ancestral origins in Barbados.

At the time, the family knew that their Porte patriarch’s ancestral origin was Barbados, as confirmed by the April 6, 1865, passenger manifest of the brig Cora and by his tombstone in the Christ Church cemetery on Porte Hill in Crozierville. What they did not know then was that George Stanfield Best, the husband of Porte’s granddaughter, Lillian, was also a Barbadian. His family had migrated to Trinidad in search of work during the sugar revolution in Trinidad and Tobago (T&T) in the late 18th century, distinct from the earlier 17th-century sugar revolution on islands like Barbados and Jamaica. Family records listed his Caribbean origin as T&T, not Barbados.

The only recorded and organized mass emigration of free people from Caribbean states to any part of Africa resulted from the 1862-1864 agitations on the island and from negotiations between President Daniel B. Warner of Liberia (led by then-Secretary of State Edward Wilmot Blyden) and Sir James Walker, Governor of Barbados. The talks followed the implementation of the British Slavery Abolition Act of 1834 and the expressed desire of African Barbadians to return to Africa.

On April 6, 1865, 346 African Barbadians departed Barbados for Liberia. This group produced three Liberian Presidents, several Secretaries of State, Supreme Court Justices, Diplomats, Judges, Academics, Educators, Clergy, and Businessmen.

In 2020, 157 years after their arrival, the story of the Porte family was self-published. Portes Find A New Home in Liberia – Story of the Post-Emancipation Emigration of the John Prince Porte Family from BARBADOS, West Indies, to Liberia, West Africa in 1865, & The Family’s Quest for Ancestral Citizenship marked the first published account by a descendant of one of the seventy-two families that emigrated to Liberia in 1865, describing their post-arrival life in their new home.

The Essay will discuss the 1865 post-emancipation emigration of 346 African Barbadians to Liberia. Building on the reflections of journalist Kenneth Y. Best in his biography, ALBERT PORTE, A Lifetime Trying to Save Liberia, it will delve into the published account by Ambassador Lorenzo Witherspoon and his daughter, Loyce B. Witherspoon, descendants of one of the Bajan families (Porte) that emigrated to Liberia. It will also provide the backstory and an account of the 2024 SANKOFA Pilgrimage to Barbados, the first-ever mass pilgrimage of Bajan-Liberian families, shepherded by this Porte family researcher and organized in conjunction with the Government of Barbados.

The history of the African diaspora is often framed by displacement and dispersal, yet it also encompasses powerful traditions of return, settlement, and belonging. Ambassador Witherspoon’s essay examines one of the most significant yet understudied examples of organized Black migration from the Caribbean to Africa: the 1865 emigration of 347 Barbadians to Liberia. Through the intertwined histories of his Porte family and the Crozierville community, it traces how migrants forged new lives on African soil while preserving cultural memories, social practices, and identities rooted in Barbados. Moving across generations, the piece combines family history, ancestral research, and personal reflection to illuminate enduring connections between Africa and its diasporas. It culminates in the contemporary Sankofa Pilgrimage to Barbados, revealing how descendants continue to negotiate questions of origin, belonging, citizenship, and heritage. In doing so, the chapter exemplifies the central concerns of this volume: recognizing Africa not merely as an imagined homeland but as a lived site of reintegration, community formation, and the ongoing reconstruction of diasporic identities.

The 2020 publication of Portes’s Find a New Home in Liberia prompted an ask from the Barbadian Prime Minister that could not be ignored or refused: “Bring my people home”! This was a call to Ambassador Witherspoon, following a quite eventful meeting in her Ilaro Court office in July 2021, to plan a sojourn for descendants of Barbadian ancestors.

Portes Find A New Home in Liberia, along with Back to Barbados: Barbadian Diaspora in Liberia – Sankofa and the Quest for Ancestral Reconnection, and Ambassador Witherspoon’s contribution to Tides of Exchange serve as inducements for fellow Barbadian-Liberians to document and publish the rich stories of their Barbadian ancestors’ lived experiences and contributions to the building of the Liberian nation-state.

The Sankofa Pilgrimage to Barbados, held May 6-13, 2024, brought together more than 400 Liberians of Bajan and Caribbean ancestry, including former Liberian President Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf, who served as a Special Eminent Guest, for an event the entire Caribbean had never before seen.

The itinerary for the 2024 Sankofa pilgrimage to Barbados demonstrated sponsor value through high-visibility events spanning heritage, scholarship, culture, business, and public commemoration:

Heritage and scholarship: Heritage Island Tour, Barbados National Archives Genealogy Marketplace, Barbados Museum & Historical Society film screenings, and a University of the West Indies colloquium.

Heritage Island Tour, Barbados National Archives Genealogy Marketplace, Barbados Museum & Historical Society film screenings, and a University of the West Indies colloquium. Commemoration and dialogue: Sankofa Commemorative Ceremony at Bay Street Esplanade (where Barbadians departed for Liberia) and a Fireside Discussion with President Sirleaf.

Sankofa Commemorative Ceremony at Bay Street Esplanade (where Barbadians departed for Liberia) and a Fireside Discussion with President Sirleaf. Culture and community: Business Roundtable, Prime Minister’s Reception, Barbados-Liberia Oistins by Night cultural event, and a commemorative service at James Street Methodist Church, where the Thanksgiving service was held before the 1865 departure for Liberia.

Together, these events delivered an immersive, professionally executed experience with strong reputational, cultural, and community impact, demonstrating Sankofa’s ability to convene leaders, families, institutions, and communities around a credible international heritage agenda.

Building on this momentum, the Africa Barbados Heritage Initiative (TABHI), a 501(c)(3) foundation founded by Ambassador Witherspoon and registered in Liberia and the United States, is planning Sankofa: The Return (to Barbados) for August 4-11, 2027, during the Season of Emancipation, with more than 500 participants expected. The sequel will broaden participation, deepen institutional partnerships, and position Barbados as the focal Caribbean point for diaspora heritage engagement.

Sankofa: The Return is a sponsor-ready heritage and diaspora engagement initiative that offers partners visibility, institutional alignment, community impact, and cultural diplomacy value through a globally resonant story of return, remembrance, and reconnection. Corporate and other sponsors are welcome to partner to bring the 2027 program to life.

The event offers sponsors a distinctive opportunity to support heritage, cultural diplomacy, and diaspora engagement through a high-profile program that links Barbados, Liberia, and the wider African diaspora. Its significance lies in being the only recorded organized mass emigration of free people from a Caribbean state to Africa.

Tides of Exchange: The West Indian/Caribbean Footprint in Africa will be available for purchase in November 2026.

World.title: Liberia: Baptist Prelate Reeves Tells Methodists At Opening Of Africa Bishops Conference
World.content:
Monrovia – The President of the Liberia Council of Churches (LCC), Rev. Dr. Samuel Baryogar Reeves, has called on Bishops of the Methodist faith, especially on the African continent to now begin to move aggressively in its growth, while at the same time contributing to nations’ development.

By Emmanuel Conway

Dr. Reeves, who is also the President of the Liberia Baptist and Theological Convention, stated that the African Church is standing in the middle of extraordinary growth; hence, amid the growing congregations, emerging young people and scholars and women in key leadership positions, the next move is to climb the ladder.

Bishop Reeves made these comments Monday, August 31, 2026 at the opening of the ongoing 2026 Africa College of Bishops hosted by the Liberia Episcopal Area of the United Methodist Church.

The meeting, which is expected to run up to September 4, being held under the theme: “Deepening Ecumenical Enlargement, Expanding Continental Influence and strengthening institutional sustainability” with text drawn from the Book of Isaiah 54:2 quote: “Enlarge the space of your tent.”

Time To Enlarge The vision.

The Baptist Prelate, who is also the Vice President of the Inter-Religious Council of Liberia (IRCL), reminded the gathering of Methodist Bishops, members of the Christian community and government officials that the church must move fast enlarge the vision, theological imagination, opportunities for emerging leaders and participation of women.

He also wants the church to make meaningful contributions to education, health, entrepreneurship, peacebuilding, governance, and human development.

“But we do not enlarge simply to become larger. We enlarge because the mission is larger than yesterday. We make room for people to encounter Christ. We make must room for young people to discover vocation. We must make room for girls who have been overlooked and for gifts that need to be included and we must make room for communities still waiting for Christ and for the Church to serve them,” the head of the churches in Liberia and the Baptist Church lectured.

The Church Must Engage

Bishop Reeves reminded the conference that vision alone isn’t the answer; it must move us into relationships, into partnerships, and into redemptive action.

Bishop Reeves is of the conviction that with vision and collaboration, much of the world’s problems would be solved adequately.

“Poverty does not ask which church you attend. Violence does not ask which theology you hold. Migration does not respect national borders. Climate vulnerability does not recognize denominational boundaries. Youth unemployment does not distinguish between churches. Human suffering does not wait for us to settle our differences. Therefore, the Church must collaborate. Collaborate at the scale of the challenge,” he challenged members of the Methodist faith and Christians across Africa and the world.

According to him, there must be conversations that lead to collaboration,

Collaboration that leads to coordination, coordination that leads to collective action and such collective action must give the Church credible influence.

“If a young person receives an education, our influence matters. If a family survives because the Church stood beside them, our influence matters. If a conflict ends because Christian leaders helped people find peace, our influence matters. If corruption is challenged because the Church found a prophetic voice, our influence matters. And if despair gives way to hope, a daring hope, our influence matters,” he furthered.

With young Africans already shaping the continent through technology, business, science, education, culture, politics, media, and civil society, he further challenged the Church to prepare them for those arenas.

“We must disciple young people for vocation as well as for worship. We must disciple young people for vocation as well as for worship. We must develop leaders who can think critically, govern competently, communicate intelligently, innovate responsibly, and remain rooted in Christ Jesus.”

“Women must have genuine opportunities to lead. Lay professionals must be partners in ministry and mission. Theological education must address the questions Africans are actually asking. We need people who can pray faithfully on Sunday and yet govern wisely on Monday.”

The Church Must Endure

This growth or larger tent, he stated, needs stronger stakes and greater reach that requires deeper roots, and greater influence that requires greater integrity.

He urged the Church to improve systems and strengthen institutions, financial transparency, accountability, governance, discipline, planning, responsible investment, entrepreneurship, endowment development, and strategic partnerships.

“The African Church needs a deeper culture of ownership. External partners can help, but internal capacity must grow. We need resources generated, managed, invested, and multiplied so that mission can continue through changing circumstances,” Bishop Reeves advised.

“Every bishop must eventually face one question: Who will be ready because you served? That is the question of legacy. Mentor your clergy. Empower women. Develop lay leaders. Strengthen theological institutions and prepare successors. A leader’s greatest contribution may be the leaders he or she develops after he or she is gone.” He among other things added.

Call For Steadfastness

Meanwhile, speaking earlier at a special Thanksgiving Service held at the First United Methodist Church on Sunday, August 31, 2026, Bishop L. Jonathan Holston of the Alabama West Florida Episcopal Area in the United States, called on worshippers to remain steadfast in faith and to root their lives in Christ’s teachings.

Bishop Holston asserted that the African church is no longer a mission outpost but “the epicenter of the worldwide church,” and as such, the continent stands in a season of preparation and transition.

He admonished believers, especially of the Methodist Church, to embrace three commitments: to love boldly, by widening the church’s welcome to a new generation without letting tribal divisions or regional politics narrow its reach; to serve joyfully, resisting fear and scarcity even amid economic uncertainty and global crises; and to lead courageously, strengthening spiritual foundations even as the church expands its influence.

At the same time, Bishop Samuel J. Quire Jr., Resident Bishop of the Liberia Episcopal Area and president of the West Africa College of Bishops, presided over and the conference.

He described Liberia as a mother figure in the history of African Methodism, telling the congregation that those who leave home always have reason to return and pay tribute. He also praised the Liberia Annual Conference’s resilience through past hardship.

Bishop Mande Muyombo, President of the Africa College of Bishops and Resident Bishop of the North Katanga Area, lauded Liberian United Methodists for their hospitality toward visiting delegations. He reaffirmed the church’s commitment to the Book of Discipline in guiding governance and marriage practices across Episcopal Areas, and urged members to remain united, faithful to Scripture, and devoted to the church’s mission despite ongoing challenges.

Clergyman Muyombo also announced that Bishop Ruben Saenz, president of the Council of Bishops, would arrive in Liberia on September 1, and invited the Liberia Episcopal Area to prepare a fitting welcome.

Also present were Conference Lay Leader Tolbert G. Nyenswah, Men’s President Samuel Swen Kun Jr., Women’s President Josephine Snorton, and delegations from the Youth and Young Adult Fellowship.

World.title: Kanchibiya council launches sports club registration exercise
World.content:
The Kanchibiya Town Council has launched an exercise which will see the registration of sports clubs in all sports disciplines across the district.

The local authority has since tasked sports coordinators to ensure that a minimum of two clubs are registered within their respective wards.

Speaking in a telephone interview today, Acting Kanchibiya Council Secretary Augustine Chanda said only registered clubs holding a valid Council Certificate of Registration will be permitted to participate in the community sports tournaments that would be organized by the local authority.

Chanda said only registered clubs will be eligible to contribute players for selection to district teams that will represent the province at national events.

He added that only registered clubs will receive support from the local authority in the form of sports materials and will be recognized by their respective Sports Federations and Associations at provincial and national levels.

Chanda disclosed that for a club to obtain a Certificate of Registration from the Local Authority, they are required to submit copies of their Club Constitution, Meeting Minutes, List of Members, and a TPIN certificate.

He said the registration fee for a club is K250 and shall be paid to the Department of Finance.

Meanwhile, Kanchibiya Town Council Community Development Officer Joseph Nkazi also stressed the importance of registration, urging clubs to complete the process to enable them to benefit from different incentives.

Nkazi said unregistered clubs risk missing out on significant opportunities including tournament participation, district team selection, sports materials support, and national federation recognition.

“We urge all sports clubs in the district to take advantage of this registration exercise. Registration opens doors to many opportunities that will benefit both the clubs and the players,” Nkazi said.

World.title: Power targets positive start  in Africa  ‎
World.content:
‎Power Dynamos coach Oswald Mutapa is seeking a positive start ahead of this weekend’s TotalEnergies CAF Champions League 2026/27 First Preliminary Round match against Al Merriekh SC of Sudan.

‎

‎The Zambian champions left for Rwanda on Tuesday, where the Sudanese giants are playing their home matches.

‎

‎Mutapa says the first leg is critical in setting the tone for the campaign.

‎

‎“This is an important assignment we are going into. From the first game you need to get a positive result and that makes you half way through to the next round,” Mutapa said before departure.

‎

‎“A positive result is important so that as we start the CAF Champions League campaign we will know where we are going. It is important that we start on a high and positive note,” he added.

‎

‎The coach urged his players to go to Rwanda with courage and intent.

‎

‎“We must go to Rwanda with courage, show intent from the word go so that even as we come to the return leg we would have done half of the job,” Mutapa said.

‎

‎The first leg is scheduled for September 4-6, with the return leg set for September 11-13.

‎

‎This is Power’s second consecutive appearance in the Champions League.

‎

‎The Second Preliminary Round will be played on October 16-18 and October 23-25, with the 16 winners advancing to the group stage at the end of November.

World.title: Zambians cautioned against looming El Nino
World.content:
The Restoration for Community Justice has urged Zambians to begin preparing now for a drier-than-normal 2026/27 rainy season, as scientists warn of a strengthening El Niño weather pattern expected to peak between October and December this year.

‎In a press release issued to the media today, Restoration for Community Justice Chief Executive Officer Mathews Mulenga says, according to reports, most of Southern Africa, Zambia included, is projected to receive below-normal rainfall between October 2026 and March 2027.

‎Mr Mulenga said this will be driven by the El Niño phenomenon in the tropical pacific.

‎Mr Mulenga said the country cannot afford to treat the warning casually, given that agriculture, energy and tourism, all climate-sensitive sectors, underpin the livelihoods of millions of Zambians.

‎”This is not a Kanchibiya problem or a Muchinga problem. This is a national emergency in the making and every Zambian, from the smallholder farmer in the village to the policymaker in Lusaka, has a role to play in preparing for it,” Mr Mulenga said.

‎He said over two million smallholder farmers nationwide are at risk and warned that this year’s record national maize harvest of five million metric tons should not create complacency, recalling that the drought of 2023/24 wiped out similar gains just as quickly as they were made.

‎Mr Mulenga has since called on farmers across the country to diversify into early-maturing and drought-tolerant crops and embrace alternative livelihoods such as beekeeping, fish farming, and small livestock rearing, which are less exposed to erratic rainfall.

‎He also urged the government to invest more in early warning systems and anticipatory action, further calling on farmers nationwide not to sell off their entire harvest but to retain some for reserves for the anticipated lean period.

‎And Kanchibiya District Co-operative Union Chairperson Robert Mushili said cooperatives across Zambia are willing to adopt early warning information but need it communicated in practical, timely terms.

‎”This message should reach every corner of Zambia, not just districts like ours. If farmers everywhere know in September what to expect, they can still make good decisions before it is too late,” Mr Mushili said.

World.title: Ndaitwah, Boko arrive for HH inauguration
World.content:
Namibian President Netumbo Ndaitwah has arrived at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport ahead of the inauguration of Zambia’s President-elect, Hakainde Hichilema.

The President was received at the Presidential Pavilion by senior government officials, members of the diplomatic corps and Namibian High Commission staff.

Namibia and Zambia share deep historical ties rooted in solidarity, liberation and mutual respect.

Zambia and Namibia enjoy strong bilateral relations anchored on trade, transport, energy, water and defense cooperation.

The Walvis Bay-Ndola-Lusaka Development Corridor remains a flagship project linking Zambia to Namibia’s Walvis Bay Port, providing Zambia with a direct and efficient route to international markets.

Both countries have continued to invest in upgrading road, rail and border infrastructure to facilitate trade.

In the energy sector, the two countries cooperate through the Zambezi Watercourse Commission and joint projects on hydropower and transmission.

Namibia also imports electricity from Zambia during periods of surplus, while Zambia benefits from Namibia’s port and logistics services.

The two nations also collaborate in agriculture, tourism, education and health and Hundreds of students from both countries study across each other’s institutions, and cross-border trade in livestock, maize and manufactured goods continues to grow.

Meanwhile, Botswana’s President Duma Boko touched down at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport ahead of the inauguration of Zambia’s President-elect, Hakainde Hichilema.

Botswana and Zambia have walked together for decades in pursuit of democracy, good governance and regional development

Zambia and Botswana share strong bilateral relations anchored on trade, energy, transport, tourism and water resource management.

The two countries cooperate closely through the Kazungula Bridge, which has become a key trade and transport link connecting Zambia, Botswana, Zimbabwe and South Africa.

The bridge has significantly reduced transit times and boosted cross-border trade under the SADC and AfCFTA frameworks.

Botswana and Zambia are collaborating on power transmission and renewable energy projects to address regional power deficits.

The two countries also share the Zambezi River basin and work together through SADC structures on sustainable water management.

World.title: Eswatini, Tanzania, Zimbabwe present at HH inauguration
World.content:
The Deputy Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Eswatini, Thulisile Dladla, the President of the United Republic of Tanzania and the President of the Republic of Zimbabwe have arrived in the country, ahead of the inauguration of Zambia’s President-elect Hakainde Hichilema.

All three leaders were received at the Kenneth Kaunda International Airport Presidential Pavilion by senior government officials, members of the diplomatic corps and envoys from their respective missions.

Eswatini and Zambia share a bond rooted in history, culture and the liberation struggle.

Zambia and Eswatini enjoy cordial relations anchored on trade, education, health and cultural exchange within SADC.

Both countries cooperate in agriculture, with exchange programmes in sugar, livestock and small-scale farming.

Eswatini has expertise in sugar production and agro-processing, while Zambia offers opportunities in maize, horticulture and agro-industrial development.

Zambia and Tanzania share one of the strongest partnerships in the region, dating back to the liberation struggle.

The Tanzania-Zambia Railway Authority, TAZARA, links Dar es Salaam Port to Zambia and facilitates trade in copper, fuel, maize and manufactured goods. Both countries are working to modernise TAZARA to boost efficiency.

Tanzania is a major gateway for Zambian imports and exports through Dar es Salaam Port, trade includes copper, cement and agricultural products from Zambia, and fuel, building materials and consumer goods from Tanzania.

Zambia and Zimbabwe share historical, cultural and economic ties which includes Victoria Falls and the Zambezi River are symbols of the shared heritage and tourism potential between the two nations.

Trade between Harare and Lusaka continues to grow, with Zimbabwe exporting manufactured goods, steel, agriculture products and energy equipment, while Zambia exports copper, maize, cement and electricity.

Both countries are key partners in the North-South Corridor, which links the region to ports in South Africa and Mozambique.

The two governments cooperate closely in energy through the Kariba Dam and the Zambezi River Authority, in agriculture, mining, and tourism.

Thousands of Zambians and Zimbabweans live and work across the border, strengthening family and business ties.

World.title: M’membe Warns Zambia’s UN Peacekeeping Role At Risk
World.content:
Zambia risks losing its international standing as a respected contributor to United Nations peacekeeping and military observer missions, Socialist Party president Dr Fred M’membe has warned. In a statement, M’membe cautioned of far-reaching consequences arising from what he described as state-sponsored military actions carried out during the August 13 general election period.

M’membe pointed specifically to the death of former Lunte member of parliament and ex-minister Mutotwe Kafwaya, who died during a military raid on a residential property in Kabulonga. He described the incident as the most tragic and damning of a series of events he said undermined the constitutional boundary between the Zambia Army and party politics, arguing that when the military behaves like a political militia, the fundamental trust between the state and its citizens fractures.

The Socialist Party leader was dismayed by what he called the extensive deployment of elite units of the country’s army to directly interfere with the electoral process in favour of ruling party candidates and intimidate citizens into silence. He said the harrowing events of the August 13 elections suggested a deeply disturbing shift, arguing that under the command of Lieutenant General Geoffrey Zyeele, elite army units did not act as neutral guardians of peace but instead appeared as active instruments of intimidation.

M’membe specifically named Lieutenant General Zyeele, Brigadier General Moses Shapwaya and Major Lyempe Kapumpa, stating that the uniform they wear does not grant immunity from accountability and warning that their conduct will cost the nation. He cited Article 2 of the Zambian Constitution, which grants every person, including citizens, residents and state entities, a fundamental right and solemn duty to defend the Constitution and resist any attempt to overthrow or illegally abrogate it.

He further argued that commandos entering civilian polling spaces, threatening electoral staff and interfering with opposition representatives at Mulungushi International Conference Centre represented an unacceptable overreach of state power. According to M’membe, a democracy cannot function when voters and election officials look at their own army not with a sense of security but with fear, a dynamic he said was on full display during the election period.

M’membe stated that the primary duty of the Zambia Army is to defend the Republic, protect its sovereign borders and uphold the Constitution of the Republic of Zambia as established, and that the army was trained to respect and uphold national and international law. He said that for decades Zambia had proudly stood as a beacon of peaceful transitions and democratic resilience in Africa, but that this reputation was severely compromised during the 2026 election cycle.

While government publicists have scrambled to frame the military deployments during the election as routine measures to maintain order, M’membe said the reality on the ground felt like a coordinated suppression of dissent. He argued that no institution should expect to be free from scrutiny of those who gave it their loyalty and support, and those who did not, a pointed reference to the army’s constitutional obligation to serve all citizens regardless of political affiliation.

The warning comes at a particularly sensitive moment, with President Hichilema being sworn in for a second term today even as questions over the conduct of security forces during the election period remain unresolved. Zambia has historically maintained a strong international reputation as a contributor to UN peacekeeping and observer missions across the continent, a status M’membe argues is now genuinely at stake if the concerns he has raised are not addressed.

Whether M’membe’s allegations translate into any formal inquiry, whether domestic or through international channels, remains to be seen. For now, his statement adds another layer of scrutiny to an election period that has already produced a treason case against the losing presidential candidate, dozens of parliamentary petitions, and mounting public debate over the boundary between military conduct and political interference in Zambia’s democracy.

Do you believe the allegations raised by Dr M’membe warrant a formal, independent investigation into military conduct during the election?

World.title: Analysis: What the flood of petitions really tells us about ECZ
World.content:
Political analyst Dr Lawrence Mwelwa has urged the ruling United Party for National Development to abandon its widespread election petitions, warning that challenging opposition wins after declaring the presidential poll free and fair smacks of selective justice. He made the remarks in an interview just as the country marks President Hichilema’s second-term inauguration, with the volume of contested results now spanning provinces well beyond the handful of cases that made early headlines. This situation has significant implications for governance and democracy in Zambia.

Mwelwa argued that if UPND has consistently maintained the presidential election was free, fair and credible, consistency demands the party also respect the verdict of the electorate in parliamentary, mayoral and council elections where it lost. He noted the closure of the Constitutional Court Registry during the presidential petition window, taken over by soldiers, denied the opposition a chance to test the presidential result in court, a decision he said continues to shape public perception of the process and can affect the political landscape in Zambia.

Citing the biblical story of Prophet Nathan and King David, Mwelwa said leadership is measured by fairness and restraint, particularly where a party already enjoys an overwhelming electoral mandate. He warned that justice should never appear selective, especially from a government with little to fear from a strong opposition, adding that a confident administration protects political plurality as an investment in Zambia’s democratic future rather than treating it as a concession. The integrity of Zambia’s political system relies on such principles.

The petitions Mwelwa is referring to extend well beyond the seven cases already before the Lusaka High Court. In Mwandi, UPND’s Sibeso Sefulo lost to independent candidate Iris Kaingu by fewer than 500 votes and has petitioned the result, alleging Kaingu’s agents engaged in vote-buying and interfered with the electoral process. Sefulo has also accused the Electoral Commission of Zambia of failing to properly supervise how results were counted and announced, and is seeking either a full re-run of the election or a recount.

In Ndola Central, former minister Frank Tayali lost by just 819 votes to Resolute Party’s Emmanuel Mulenga and has filed his own petition contesting the result. On the Copperbelt, UPND’s Joseph Kazhila has challenged the outcome in Chingola Central, alleging NRPUP supporters were seen handing out food and money to voters, with one incident reportedly sparking a physical altercation at a polling station. In Kabushi, UPND’s Emeldah Mpumpuni has gone further, alleging that agents for NRPUP’s Tillas Sichinga concealed cash inside pens to distribute to voters undetected.

Further petitions have been lodged in Mwense, Nchanga, Nkana, Kalabo South, Bangweulu, Siavonga and Zambezi Central, while even Lusaka Mayor Simon Mwewa’s own election is now being challenged. Taken together with the Kabuswe, Masebo and other cases already before the courts, the total number of parliamentary and local government petitions filed since polling day now runs into the dozens, a scale of litigation that legal observers say will keep Zambia’s High Court registries occupied for months.

It is worth pausing on what this volume actually signals. A handful of petitions after any election is normal; disputed margins happen everywhere. But when the ruling party itself, the very party that spent weeks insisting the presidential contest was free, fair and beyond reproach, turns around and files petitions against results it lost at parliamentary, mayoral and council level, a fair-minded observer has to ask what changed between the presidential count and everything below it. Either the same electoral machinery was competent everywhere and UPND’s petitions are opportunistic, or something in how ECZ ran this election left enough doubt that even the winning party does not fully trust its own declared outcomes down the ballot.

That question becomes sharper when set against what did not happen. No presidential petition was permitted to be filed and tested in court, in part because the Constitutional Court Registry was closed and taken over by soldiers during the very window the law sets aside for that challenge. If the process was as clean as officials maintain, there was no institutional reason to fear a court testing it. A commission confident in its own numbers does not need the petition window shut by force; it lets the numbers speak in front of a judge. The optics of that closure, whatever the stated justification, invite exactly the scrutiny ECZ has since tried to avoid.

Cases like Mandevu and the Lusaka mayoral contest deserve particular attention in this light. These are races where control of a capital city’s local administration, and by extension patronage, contracts and grassroots political machinery, is at stake in a way that a single rural parliamentary seat is not. If there is anywhere an “underhand method,” as some describe it, would be worth deploying to tilt a result, it is precisely in high-value urban contests like these rather than in far-flung constituencies with little national leverage. That is speculation, not proof, and it should be treated as such. But it is not an unreasonable question for citizens to ask when the party that won comfortably at the top of the ballot is simultaneously contesting results it lost near the bottom.

None of this proves fraud. Zambia’s courts, not newspaper columns, are the proper venue to establish whether any of these petitions have merit, and due process must be allowed to run its course for every single one, Kabuswe’s, Sefulo’s, Tayali’s, and the rest. But an election that produces this scale of litigation, this many allegations of vote-buying and procedural failure, and a shuttered court registry during the one window meant for testing the presidential result itself, cannot honestly be described as Zambia’s smoothest electoral outing. If anything, it may be the most contested since the return of multiparty democracy.

The opposition also has a responsibility in Mwelwa’s assessment. He said it must reject violence, intolerance and reckless language while remaining steadfast in defending democracy and holding government accountable within the law, a balance he argued neither side has fully managed since the election. But healing, he stressed, cannot be achieved through speeches alone, and requires dialogue between political leaders, civil society, the Church and other stakeholders in spaces where difficult issues can be discussed without fear.

Should a party that declares an election free and fair be bound to accept every result on that ballot, even the ones it loses, and should ECZ be compelled to explain why the presidential result alone was shielded from the same courtroom scrutiny it now allows everywhere else?

This is an analysis piece. Views expressed are the author’s own.
