World.title: A NY hospital tried to close its birthing center. This city united to fight back
World.content:
A NY hospital tried to close its birthing center. This city united to fight back

toggle caption Katherine Bruno/Upper Hudson Planned Parenthood

TROY, N.Y. — Like many residents of this aging industrial city on the Hudson River, Starletta Washington was stunned when she heard Troy's last remaining hospital planned to close its birthing center.

"It was devastating," said Washington, who heads the local YWCA. Washington was born at the hospital and had her children there. She couldn't believe families would now have to get to a hospital half an hour away or face the prospect of an emergency delivery.

"Nobody else was going to be born in the city of Troy unless they were born on a city bus, in the back of a cab, or, disgustingly, on the side of the street?" Washington said. "Blew my mind."

Sponsor Message

For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

Troy wasn't the first community to face this prospect. Since 2010, hospitals have closed hundreds of maternity units as cities and towns shrink and hospitals consolidate into larger systems.

Troy found a more hopeful ending.

toggle caption Hannah Norman/KFF Health News

Elected officials from both major parties joined patient advocates, mothers, midwives, doulas and community leaders like Washington to challenge Trinity Health, the large Catholic health system that owns Troy's hospital and birthing center. The campaign even united Planned Parenthood and the Catholic diocese.

"Whether you were Republican or Democrat, or if you didn't vote, it literally brought everyone together," said Carmella Mantello, the city's Republican mayor. "Everyone just said, 'We can't let this happen.'"

Throughout the country, healthcare remains a flash point as politicians square off ahead of November's elections. But in many places, Americans are also quietly finding common ground.

In this small city, citizens were brought together by frustration over large, corporate health systems that can seem to put profits over patients. And they resolved to work together to keep critical medical services in their community.

A community institution

Babies have been delivered at Samaritan Hospital on a hill above Troy since this city's once bustling factories produced most of America's shirt collars a century ago.

More recently, Samaritan's Burdett Birth Center had become a model for patient-focused care. Midwives and doulas work alongside OB-GYNs and support mothers who want to avoid a delivery by cesarean section unless necessary.

Patient safety advocates have pushed for years to reduce surgical deliveries, which can lead to complications. At Burdett, only about a quarter of newborns are delivered by C-section, compared with about a third statewide, according to 2025 hospital data. Burdett also had fewer preterm births and fewer babies with low birth weights.

Sponsor Message

"I wouldn't go anywhere else," said Lidia Zambrano-Madera, who gave birth to both her children at Burdett with the help of a midwife.

For Zambrano-Madera, who recently opened a children's play center in Troy, Burdett offered another advantage: It was just five minutes from home.

toggle caption Jayana Espinoza

But three years ago, Trinity Health, a multibillion-dollar Michigan-based hospital system, said the birth center was losing money and would close.

Families from Troy and surrounding Rensselaer County would have to deliver at another Trinity hospital in Albany, up to a half-hour's drive away. The hospitals are branded under St. Peter's Health Partners in the Albany region.

"We've been frantic about trying not to cut the care at the bedside," said Steven Hanks, a physician who oversees Trinity hospitals in New York and New England. "But, you know, you get to a point where you can only consolidate so much. You can only spread people so thin, and then you have to start taking harder looks at your actual services."

Corporate backlash

Trinity's plans — news of which broke in a local newspaper — came without warning, surprising the obstetrical staff and community leaders. They set off a firestorm.

Within days, midwives, mothers, community leaders and politicians held a rally at the YWCA in downtown Troy. Others would follow. Volunteers led by doulas and midwives made T-shirts and handed out pink "Save Burdett" signs at the local farmers market.

Activists were outraged that the hospital hadn't adequately assessed the impact of the closure, particularly on low-income families. They conducted a community survey that found 1 in 4 Troy residents didn't have access to a car and would have trouble getting to Albany.

The campaign drew on deep connections that many residents had to Burdett. "They realized what a gem Burdett is, and what a great community service they provide," said Jessica Hayek, a doula and birth educator who helped lead the campaign.

Sponsor Message

Hayek and others also tapped into deep-seated frustration with Trinity, a healthcare behemoth that operates 91 hospitals and last year recorded more than $25 billion in revenue and a healthy operating margin that topped 5%.

"Trinity Health is in the Midwest, and they are not in the community," Hayek said. "So when you're looking at just the numbers from an office in the Midwest somewhere, they're not looking at the benefit that this place has on the community."

toggle caption Hannah Norman/KFF Health News

Hayek describes herself as a liberal Democrat. But Trinity's focus on its bottom line also irked many Republicans, including Mantello, who was the City Council president at the time.

"The whole hospital scene has changed," Mantello said. "It was very personable. You had nurses and doctors who were able to give more care and spend more time with patients." Now, by contrast, many hospitals have what she described as a "more corporate type of atmosphere."

Even the Catholic bishop decried the planned closure of the birthing center as out of step with the values of his faith and the hospital system's.

"Nothing is more central to the Catholic healthcare mission than supporting life and all those who bring it into the world," Bishop Edward Scharfenberger said after Trinity announced the closure plan. Scharfenberger has since retired.

A bipartisan solution

Despite the backlash, Trinity Health executives for months insisted they had no choice. The system even sued the state to push through the closure.

toggle caption Katherine Bruno/Upper Hudson Planned Parenthood

Ultimately, though, powerful state officials, including New York Attorney General Letitia James, a Democrat, joined the fight to save the birthing center, launching an investigation into the proposed closure and hosting a daylong hearing in Troy.

State Assemblyman John T. McDonald III, a Democrat who represents Troy, worked with Republican elected officials, including the county executive and the state senator representing Troy, to secure $5 million in state funding to help keep Burdett open.

Sponsor Message

"You had a Democrat and a bunch of Republicans all working together on the same issue," McDonald said, "because, at the end of the day, our job is to listen to what the public has to say."

Nearly a year after announcing the closure, Trinity reversed itself and said Burdett would remain open.

Lois Uttley, a New York City-based researcher and activist who has worked with communities facing hospital consolidation, said Troy's success reflects a growing bipartisan suspicion of big corporate healthcare organizations.

"The executives of these health systems will tell the community that joining a big health system will be good, that the quality of care will improve, that efficiencies will mean they can keep the costs low," Uttley said. "But what I have seen over the last 30 years of work is that those promises often are broken."

As hospitals close or downsize, she said, communities are catching on. "They're becoming more skeptical."

There's another, more hopeful lesson in Troy's success, said McDonald, the state assemblyman.

"If we take down our swords," he said, "and put out our arms, maybe we can get something done."



KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

World.title: Judge to decide if Tyler Robinson will go to trial in Charlie Kirk murder case
World.content:
Judge to decide if Tyler Robinson will go to trial in Charlie Kirk murder case

toggle caption Rick Egan/Pool/Getty Images

A Utah judge is slated to hear arguments Tuesday to decide whether there is probable cause to justify a murder trial for Tyler Robinson, who is accused of killing conservative activist Charlie Kirk last fall.

The hearing comes after months of legal wrangling, in a case where prosecutors are seeking the death penalty for Robinson, 23.

District Judge Tony Graf Jr. is scheduled to begin hearing oral arguments at 10 a.m. local time in the courthouse in Provo, Utah. The proceeding is due to be livestreamed by Salt Lake City TV channel KUTV , despite objections from Robinson's lawyers, who say such coverage jeopardizes his right to a fair trial.

Kirk was killed nearly one year ago

Kirk was fatally shot on Sept. 10, 2025, at a rally held at Utah Valley University. The 31-year-old was in Orem, Utah, to kick off his American Comeback Tour. Some 3,000 people were on hand, and were listening to Kirk speak when he was shot, police said.

Sponsor Message

Authorities said video footage showed Robinson, who then lived in Washington County, Utah, arriving and moving around on the campus, as member station KUER reported. They also say he mentioned needing to retrieve his rifle in messages with his then-roommate, with whom Robinson had a romantic relationship.

On the morning after the killing, investigators found a Mauser .30-06 caliber bolt-action rifle that they believe to be the murder weapon.

Prosecutors say Robinson has confessed to killing Kirk, citing a note he left for his roommate and other interactions. Robinson was arrested after a relative turned him in to police, saying the young man "had confessed or implied that he was the shooter," as NPR reported.

Prosecutors are likely to seek the death penalty

Robinson faces one charge of aggravated murder and six other serious counts, including tampering with a witness. Ahead of Tuesday's hearing, the defendant had not yet entered a plea. His attorneys also were urging the judge not to allow video recordings and broadcast of the proceeding, saying it could prevent the pool of potential jurors from being impartial.

Aggravating circumstances will likely play a key role in the case, as they could be used to justify imposing the death penalty for Robinson if he is found guilty. Prosecutors say there is evidence to support a victim targeting enhancement in the case, saying Robinson's alleged motive was political, as KUER reports. They cite evidence such as bullet casings bearing anti-fascist messages, such as "Hey Facist! CATCH!" [sic].

Sponsor Message

The possibility that the shooter endangered thousands of people at the rally is also an important distinction under Utah law. Police say the sniper's bullet that killed Kirk was fired from a rooftop some 150 yards away from the spot on a campus courtyard where Kirk was killed, as NPR has reported. Defense attorneys contend that because only a single bullet was fired — and struck its target — the crowd was not at risk.

Last month, hundreds of people who attended the rally in Utah where Kirk was killed filed requests for victim benefits from the state, seeking mental health and trauma support.

World.title: Lost island in northern B.C. lake — that appeared then disappeared — located, B.C. Hydro says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A newly formed island in B.C.'s largest lake has been located.

B.C. Hydro said Monday that the forested land mass, bigger than a Canadian football field, landed ashore after drifting some 30 kilometres northwest of its last known location in the middle of Williston Reservoir.

The island's curious appearance, and seemingly sudden disappearance in the massive man-made lake in northern B.C., has captured international attention and intrigue since boaters first made the discovery in August.

B.C. Hydro spokesperson Bob Gammer said satellite imagery dated Aug. 15 shows the island resting in the north entrance of the Ospika Arm, where the Ospika River flows into the reservoir.

He said the island appears to be intact, and that it has moved even further away from the W.A.C. Bennett Dam connected to the reservoir.

"For it to disappear and now to reappear, that just creates a lot of excitement," Gammer said.

"It's great to know that we found it and it's not causing any trouble right now and hopefully that's the way it stays."

Satellite data provided by B.C. Hydro shows the location and size of a newly formed island found in the Williston Lake reservoir in northern B.C., about 130 kilometres northwest of the W.A.C. Bennett Dam. (Submitted by B.C. Hydro)

The island's origin still hasn't been confirmed though B.C. Hydro believes record high water levels likely caused it to break off somewhere along the reservoir's sprawling shoreline.

Gammer said strong winds would have moved it through the open waters over the last month.

"It's certainly not current. The water does very slowly move to the east to the [dam]," Gammer said. "The wind is really what's going to drive things."

WATCH | A floating island in northern B.C.'s Williston Reservoir: Island in Canada mysteriously appears, then vanishes | Duration 1:48

The Williston reservoir was created in 1968 and is the seventh-largest in the world.

John Clague, an earth sciences professor at Simon Fraser University, said decades of erosion have left the banks of the reservoir vulnerable to landslides.

He said the reservoir is "notorious" for having strong winds that can create waves and currents that undermine shallow rooted trees along the shoreline.

B.C. Hydro estimates the island to be around 70 metres wide and 140 metres long, or about 9,800 square metres in area.

"This has to be a world's record in terms of size for floating wood mats with trees that were quite healthy and growing nicely and now are part of an island," said Clague.

B.C. Hydro will want to get a better understanding of where it came from and how it formed, Clague said.

"There should be a big scar along the shoreline."

The W.A.C. Bennett Dam on the Williston Lake reservoir, near Hudson’s Hope. (B.C. Hydro)

Clague said he's surprised how far the island has travelled, and B.C. Hydro will want to investigate to understand where it came from and how it formed.

That's quite a distance for it to travel and not essentially fall apart," he said. "It's a big piece of real estate, but it's thin. It's not like an iceberg that extends further beneath the water in an ocean."

The island's whereabouts have been a curiosity for residents in northern B.C. as well as interested observers from around the world.

Video of the island bobbing in the middle of the reservoir first went viral in local Facebook groups in early August.

After a decade spent running fishing charters on Williston Lake, Marianne Anderson said she has never seen anything like it.

She said a local fishing guide showed her the video of what looked like a giant carpet of trees, bobbing in the middle of the lake.

The next time fishing guides were in the area, the island was gone.

"It looked unreal," she said.

LISTEN | An island mysteriously appeared — then disappeared — in northern B.C.: Radio West 3:57 A floating island in northern B.C.'s Williston Reservoir Northern B.C. residents and B.C. Hydro speak about a massive floating island of trees on on Williston Lake, north of Prince George.

Finlay Farquhar, a radio engineering assistant based in the United Kingdom, said he was able to track the island's new location using open-source satellite websites after reading about it on social media.

He also found it nestled on the shoreline in the Ospika Arm.

"Quite curious, and it was really quite surprising that there'd been a floating island," Farquhar said. "I was quite surprised by how far it moved."

Satellite data provided by B.C. Hydro shows the location and size of a floating island found in the Williston Lake reservoir in northern B.C., about 100 kilometres west of the W.A.C. Bennett Dam. (B.C. Hydro)

Gammer said B.C. Hydro was able to locate the island after independently confirming new reports of its location.

Gammer said it's possible the island might move again if strong winds break it free from shore.

"It's nothing that's going to require us to take some serious action," he said.

"We will monitor this just to see what happens, whether it breaks apart and if we then have a debris field instead of one big chunk, that may cause us to take some other action."

He said the island is unstable and boaters should be cautious.

"Go ahead, boat up to it, get near it, take your own pictures, get your drone out, whatever you'd like to do to image it," he said. "But we really warn people about trying to climb on it, as tempting as it may be."

Subscribe to CBC's Fort St. John Weekly for a roundup of the best news and stories from B.C.'s Peace and Northern Rockies.

World.title: Used bookstores navigate 'suspicious' bulk orders amid AI book-shredding fears
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Used booksellers in Canada are navigating how to handle mysterious bulk orders, as suspicions grow that companies are buying up their old books so they can be scanned for AI training — and then trashed.

Their concern stems from a U.S. copyright lawsuit brought against AI giant Anthropic, which revealed the company was spending millions on physical books, chopping off the spines to quickly scan the pages to train its large language model Claude, and discarding the remains.

A 404 Media investigation revealed two weeks ago that large orders of books are also going to an Amazon facility in Las Vegas to undergo "destructive scanning" for LLM training, offering further evidence that the practice may be widespread. Similar concerns are being raised by bookstore owners in Australia and elsewhere.

Physical books, particularly those published before OpenAI launched ChatGPT in 2022, are in demand for AI companies. That's partly because some experts say the language models degrade when repeatedly trained on their own output, so they need to be fed with content that is guaranteed to be free of AI-generated text.

Some AI companies have also encountered legal issues using copyrighted digital content.

'There's something not right here'

Peter Sellers, proprietor at Sellers & Newel bookstore in Toronto, says bulk book requests in the past have come from designers staging homes or film sets, and typically are accompanied by colour and size requirements.

But around June, he started getting "very suspicious" calls for bulk orders for seemingly random lists of books, he told CBC News in an interview.

"It's kind of tempting, because I can unload a lot of stuff that may otherwise be unsaleable," he said. "And then you start thinking about it — no, no no, there's something not right here."

WATCH | More about Anthropic's destructive scanning: The facts about AI companies destroying books | Duration 2:40 Anthropic bought millions of physical books to train its AI chatbot Claude. Here are the facts about the books that were ‘destructively scanned.’

On June 10, he received a message on LinkedIn from someone claiming to represent data engineering company Innodata, saying they were "currently looking to purchase large volumes of secondhand books" and "exploring potential sourcing partners."

Sellers said he ignored the request and thought little of the message until he later read an article about AI book scanning. Suddenly, he said, all those "odd" requests seemed to make a lot more sense.

"My whole staff is now attuned to this," he said.

"If somebody wants stuff in bulk, the answer's no — unless you're a designer that we know or someone we've dealt with, or you've got some kind of legitimate credentials and you want these books for a legitimate reason," he said.

Innodata, based in Ridgefield, N.J., offers "data and domain expertise" for AI projects, according to its website, which says it works with "seven of the world’s largest tech companies." Innodata recently posted a senior book buyer job on LinkedIn.

CBC News has requested comment from Innodata but has not heard back.

B.C. company named as suspected supplier

Other booksellers told CBC News they have received similar requests in recent months, often for obscure educational books that sat unsold for years. Some say it's hard to turn down those requests, especially in an industry that's not exactly booming.

The names of the companies making these requests seem to change quickly, sellers say, and none of the buyers have publicly admitted to supplying AI companies.

Zoom Books, a company based in Pitt Meadows, B.C., that says it resells and recycles secondhand books, has been frequently mentioned in online bookseller forums and on Reddit for making large numbers of perplexing bulk orders.

Booksellers in Spain , Germany , Australia , New Zealand and elsewhere have raised suspicions that Zoom's orders are intended to be resold for AI scanning, though none have shown proof that this is the case.

WATCH | Authors and creators on AI: AI-written books divide publishing world | Duration 2:13 Generative AI is making its way into publishing, leaving authors and creators with differing views on the technology. The CBC's Ben Dornan reports. Correction: A previous version of this story said that MacIntyre Purcell Publishing used AI to generate and scramble words in some puzzles in a puzzle book. MacIntyre Purcell Publishing says they do not publish AI-generated material and the information was provided to Nimbus in error.

Patrick Hempelmann, the owner of a BMV Books in Toronto, told CBC News that Zoom started buying hundreds of books from him about six months ago.

The orders were primarily for specialized technical books with small print runs, typically selling for between $5 and $30, he said. Some were old medical texts or graduate student-level math and physics books that had sat on shelves for a decade.

"We couldn't really figure out what their motivation was or what their specialty was, because they were kind of buying things all over the place. There seemed to be no real rhyme or reason," he said.

Hempelmann said Zoom Books made the purchases online through AbeBooks, a third-party seller, and BMV fulfilled the orders.

The orders were shipped to Wood Dale, Ill., care of PrepFort, a third-party logistics and fulfilment centre that works with major companies including Amazon, Walmart and Shopify.

Hempelmann says he was unaware of the AI book scanning controversy until CBC News contacted him, but after reading about it, he says it's "just sad."

BMV Books owner Patrick Hempelmann says he was 'sad' to learn about destructive book scanning. (Submitted by Patrick Hempelmann)

"I mean, we are booksellers. Books shouldn't be destroyed," he said.

Another Canadian bookseller who did not want to be quoted in this article told CBC News they received similar orders from Zoom Books several weeks ago.

Until mid-March, Zoom Books' chief growth officer, Reed Pannell, was a business development director at U.K.-based World of Books , according to his LinkedIn account. Court documents reported on by The Washington Post named World of Books one of the companies that Anthropic purchased from for its secretive destructive scanning project.

In an email to CBC News, Pannell said that Zoom does not sell to Anthropic, but he did not directly confirm that the company hasn't dealt with any other AI companies or shipped books to companies that may have scanned and destroyed them.

Pannell would not disclose Zoom's customers, citing confidentiality.

He said Zoom collects and processes more than three million books each month and that its mission is to keep books in circulation.

"We acquire secondhand books and resell them intact. We do not digitize books," Pannell said. "Our priority is always reuse, and when a book can no longer be rehomed, it is responsibly recycled."

PrepFort co-founder Sufyaan Kalota said in an email to CBC News that the company "cannot share any details regarding our customer agreements due to our confidentiality commitments."

Buyers may be 'cat's paw': store owner

Chris Brayshaw, owner of Pulpfiction Books in Vancouver, says he saw a two-week "sales bump" several weeks ago where he was making about a dozen sales a day of primarily non-fiction books that he considered "dated" and had been sitting for years.

The books were purchased at prices between $10 and $80 US each and shipped to various locations across North America and Europe, he told CBC News.

Brayshaw would not provide the names of the buyers, but says he suspects they were "limited liability companies created specifically for this purpose, maybe as kind of a cat's paw to disguise the ultimate source of where the items were going."

Pulpfiction Books owner Chris Brayshaw, pictured in 2023, says he was getting unusual bulk orders for a two-week period this summer. (Baneet Braich/CBC)

He says he has refused sales of valuable books in the past when the purchasers had destructive or esthetic reasons for buying.

Although Brayshaw has strong negative feelings about AI, the books purchased by the mysterious bulk buyers were ones he was generally "delighted" to finally move.

"I don't think it was a great loss to civilization," he said.

World.title: To shelve or not to shelve: How the American alcohol response varies widely by province
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As the trade dispute with the U.S. drags on after a deal recently fell through, the availability of American alcohol in Canada remains largely unchanged.

While it's sometimes reported there's a ban on American alcohol in the country, the reality is more complicated.

"Embargo doesn't fit. It's not a tariff, it's not a blockade and it's not a boycott," said Robert Huish, a Dalhousie University professor in Halifax who studies sanctions, tariffs and economic weapons.

"It's almost like a flex move, really, where the provinces are able to say, 'Hey, look, we're making this choice for the short term,' and there seems to be a lot of public support for that choice there," said Huish.

The reality is that the availability of American alcohol varies widely across the country — from full availability in Alberta to unavailable at the LCBO, Ontario's Crown-run liquor retailer, which happens to be one of the largest purchasers of alcohol in the world.

Many other provinces, including Nova Scotia, happen to be somewhere in the middle.

"That choice to not shelve product, that's been a very powerful symbolic message, right to the Trump White House," Huish said. "He's reacted to it personally."

What follows is a province-by-province look at the availability of American alcohol across Canada.

British Columbia

While American alcohol has remained off the shelves at the Crown-run B.C. Liquor stores since early last year, warehoused American product can still be purchased by private liquor stores, restaurants, bars and pubs from the province's Liquor Distribution Branch.

Alberta

Alberta, which has a private liquor retailing system, has a public liquor importer, Alberta Gaming, Liquor & Cannabis (AGLC). In March 2025, the importer announced it would no longer accept American alcohol imports, though retailers were permitted to sell existing inventory.

In June 2025, Alberta lifted the import ban.

Saskatchewan

Saskatchewan uses a model similar to Alberta's. The Crown-run Saskatchewan Liquor and Gaming Authority acts as the main distributor, while retail stores are privately owned.

In March 2025, Saskatchewan Liquor announced it would stop purchasing U.S. alcohol, but resumed imports three months later.

Late last month, Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe announced a 50 per cent retaliatory levy on American alcohol products.

Manitoba

Manitoba's Crown liquor retailer, Manitoba Liquor Mart, removed American alcohol from store shelves in March 2025, while the Crown-run distributor halted imports at the same time.

In December, warehoused American alcohol went back on the shelves.

After the breakdown of the U.S. trade deal and resulting imposition of tariffs on Canadian goods, Manitoba Liquor pulled the remaining U.S. alcohol off the shelves late last month.

Ontario

Ontario has maintained the strictest boycott of American alcohol of any province.

After removing American alcohol from LCBO shelves and halting U.S. imports in March 2025, the province has refused to sell off any of its roughly $80 million in warehoused stock, unlike most other jurisdictions.

The province has also resisted calls to sell the product for charity.

Most provinces that have resumed selling American alcohol have made charitable donations from the sales.

Quebec

Quebec has maintained the second-strictest boycott, stopping imports of American alcohol and pulling stock from the SAQ in March 2025.

However, in February, the province resumed selling roughly $9 million worth of American product that was at risk of perishi ng, such as ready-to-drink beverages and sake.

New Brunswick

New Brunswick's Crown-run alcohol retailer and distributor, ANBL, stopped purchasing American alcohol in February 2025 and pulled existing stock from shelves a month later.

In May 2025, ANBL resumed selling American alcohol to select buyers, such as private agency stores. By January 2026, American alcohol had returned to all ANBL retail channels.

Nova Scotia

Nova Scotia's Crown-run alcohol retailer and distributor, NSLC, stopped buying American alcohol in January 2025 and pulled it from the shelves in March 2025. In December, it resumed selling the warehoused product.

Prince Edward Island

P.E.I.'s Crown-run alcohol retailer and distributor, the P.E.I. Liquor Control Commission, stopped buying American alcohol in March 2025 and pulled it from the shelves that same month. In December, it once again began selling its warehoused stock.

Newfoundland and Labrador

The Crown-run Newfoundland and Labrador Liquor Corporation removed American alcohol from its shelves early last year and has not ordered additional inventory since the trade dispute began.

In December, sales of the existing American stock resumed.

Yukon

The Yukon Liquor Corporation stopped placing orders for U.S.-made alcohol products in March 2025. While existing stock is not available in the six corporate stores, private licensees can sell from their existing inventory and the corporation's warehoused stock.

Northwest Territories

The Northwest Territories Liquor and Cannabis Commission stopped buying American alcohol in March 2025. Existing stock was never removed from the shelves and continues to be sold through regular retail and wholesale channels. As of the middle of last month, the commission said there was less than $5,000 worth of U.S. alcohol on the shelves.

Nunavut

The Nunavut Liquor and Cannabis Commission stopped purchasing American alcohol in March 2025 and pulled it from the shelves at the same time, but resumed some sales in July 2025.

"American alcohol products are held in NULC inventory, but are not currently being sold in NULC stores," a spokesperson wrote to CBC News.

Even with American alcohol available for sale in many parts of the country, interest remains tepid as Canadians seek out local alternatives, said Huish.

"That's something that is sort of growing out of the disdain for this consistent belligerent behaviour from the U.S.," he said.

MORE TOP STORIES

World.title: Élections Québec to mail voter information in French only for 1st time in a provincial election
World.content:

For the first time in a general election, Élections Québec will send voters information documents in French only in order to comply with changes to Quebec's language laws, the agency said in a news release on Tuesday.

Although the documents typically mailed by Élections Québec ahead of voting day will be in French only, it will contain a QR code leading to the agency's English website for voters wishing to access the information in the language.

Élections Québec sa ys only Indigenous voters and persons declared eligible to receive instruction in English can contact the agency and request to receive their documents and other services in English.

Legislation to protect French and make it the sole language of communication for public institutions became law in 2022.

Élections Québec says voters should receive their provincial election guide and notice of entry — documents detailing where and how to vote — no later than the week of Sept. 1 4.

Reminder cards will be mailed out for the week of Sept. 28.

The election is set for Oct. 5.

World.title: Schools in Edmonton and across Canada cancel international field trips
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Zoe Cogger says two trips to the United States were going to be the highlight of her senior year in high school.

The 16-year-old was set to go with fellow Edmonton students to the National High School Dance Festival in Pittsburgh and to Spokane, Wash., for the annual Bloomsday Run.

But the trips are no more.

Edmonton Public Schools has cancelled all international excursions for the school year, including to Thailand, France, the United Kingdom, Costa Rica and Portugal.

"I was pretty sad when I found out," Cogger said.

Cogger is among thousands of students across Canada whose school trip plans have been cancelled or tweaked for this school year for various reasons, including global conflicts and uncertainty.

'Further unpredictability and risk'

Supt. Ron Thompson with the Edmonton public board said in a letter to parents in June that a recent field trip had students come face to face with civil unrest. The board didn't specify what country the students were in.

"Couple this with reported global fuel shortages, recently reported public health concerns and ongoing military conflict, which introduces further unpredictability and risk to international travel," Thompson said.

He added that he doesn't take the cancellations lightly and that the board would reassess its decision before the 2027-28 school year.

The Vancouver School Board and the Calgary Catholic School District both said they're approving field trips on a case-by-case basis.

"We are operating within an evolving global context and are carefully considering a range of factors in our review processes," the Vancouver board said in an email.

Last year, the public Calgary Board of Education cancelled all international trips while it reviewed policies on how trips are planned and students prepare for the rigours of international travel. It said recently that trips have resumed for this year.

In Winnipeg, the Louis Riel School Board has cancelled trips to the United States since last October, after Ottawa posted a travel advisory warning Canadians that the U.S. government is no longer accepting gender markers.

The Winnipeg School Division said it's allowing school trips — but not to the United States.

"Travel to other international destinations may still be considered if it supports student learning or business operations," spokesperson Jillian Recksiedler said in an email.

'Complex times'

Public boards in Toronto and Saskatoon say none of their trips have been cancelled.

Some experts say school trip changes are understandable.

"We live in really complex times and international trips are a complex thing to pull off," said Maren Aukerman, an education professor at the University of Calgary.

"The other side is it is a real loss. There's lots of research that compares virtual field trips with real field trips and, not surprisingly, you cannot replace being in a different place, exploring a different culture."

Aukerman said some schools are choosing instead to plan trips within Canada.

Trade war, citizenship concerns

Wayne Smith, a hospitality and tourism professor at Toronto Metropolitan University, said the cost of living has made it more difficult for parents to sign up their children for trips.

Planning trips has also become complicated, he said. With Canada's population growth, teachers are seeing students with more diverse citizenship statuses.

"I know in Toronto, for example, the amount of paperwork [teachers] have to file to do a class trip is pretty phenomenal," he said.

"It's just got really complicated over the last few years, and especially since the vast majority of the trips are south of the border."

Aukerman said that the trade war has complicated travel to the United States.

Edmonton high school student Nyla Ahmadzai said she isn't going on any international school trips this year. But she spent all last year helping friends raise money for their planned excursions.

"They did bottle drives, sold chocolates, candies, even posting on social media, asking family members for donations and stuff," she said. "I had a friend clean cars.

"Now it's taken away from them, and it's really, really frustrating."

Cogger said she had hoped Edmonton Public Schools would consider trips on a case-by-case basis instead of cancelling them altogether.

"It's better to find a way to make it work because these experiences are a high school experience."

But there's an upside.

Cogger said her school is planning a run in Jasper National Park instead of the one in Washington, and she's not upset.

"I'm glad that they were able to find a replacement."

World.title: 2 tankers carrying Saudi oil hit in Strait of Hormuz as war shows no signs of stopping
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Two supertankers carrying Saudi oil were struck by unknown projectiles within ‌minutes of each other while transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz late on Monday, according to shipping intelligence and tracking firms Marisks and Kpler.

"The near-simultaneous incidents represent a further escalation in the threat environment ​within the Omani corridor," Marisks said.

The tankers each ​loaded two million barrels of Saudi crude at the Juaymah terminal last week, Kpler data showed.

Oil prices gained on Tuesday after ‌U.S. President Donald Trump threatened further strikes against Iran, following the first exchanges of fire since late July.

In the latest attacks on shipping, the Saudi Arabian-flagged very large crude carrier Sidr was struck by unknown projectiles about 31 kilometres northeast of Khasab, Oman, at around 3:52 p.m. ET, Marisks said.

Minutes later, the Liberian-flagged VLCC ⁠Senegal Prosperity was reportedly struck by three unknown projectiles approximately some 31 kilometres east ⁠of Khasab, Marisks said. All crew aboard were reported safe, it added.

The United ⁠Kingdom ⁠Maritime Trade Operations agency ​reported three projectiles striking a tanker in the same location as it sailed out of ​the Strait of Hormuz, ⁠in what appeared to be the same incident.

WATCH | A look at sea mines: Can Iran really launch sea mines from rockets? | About That | Duration 2:56 U.S. Central Command says it carried out fresh strikes on Iran, claiming it was retaliation for Iran preparing to launch sea mines from rockets into the Strait of Hormuz. Andrew Chang digs deeper into what may be Iran's novel ability to deploy underwater mines with missiles. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, CAT-UXO, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

Bahri, operator of Sidr, and Sinokor, operator of Senegal Prosperity, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Earlier on Tuesday, Iranian media reported that a Saudi oil tanker was stopped while transiting through the southern corridor ⁠of the Strait of ‌Hormuz.

Energy exports curbed

Iranian and U.S. blockades ⁠of the Strait ⁠of Hormuz have sharply curbed energy exports ‌from the Gulf as both sides tried to assert their authority over the waterway.

Efforts by mediators including Qatar and Oman to broker a deal to reopen the strait, which carried about a fifth of ⁠global oil supplies before the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran more than six months ago, have so far proven inconclusive.

Iran said on Tuesday it would reciprocate if the U.S. honoured its commitments under a June interim deal on halting their conflict, but tensions remained high after Trump threatened Tehran with further strikes.

Children swim as ships are seen anchored in the Strait of Hormuz on Aug. 10, off the coast of Bandar Abbas, Iran. (Ali Saeedi/Getty Images)

The six-month-old conflict had shifted into an economic standoff before a U.S. attack on Iran's Larak Island on Sunday, which Iran responded to by launching missiles overnight at two U.S. air bases ​in Jordan.

"We're going to hit them hard … There will be a response," a Fox News ​reporter quoted Trump as telling the channel on Monday, although the president separately told reporters that the renewed strikes did not signal a return to full-scale war.

A senior Iranian source told Reuters the exchanges of fire were a "limited and contained confrontation" but said Tehran would deliver a ​harsh response if attacked again.

While neither side appears to want a return to all-out war, their pledges to respond to further ⁠attacks highlight how quickly a conflict which has ⁠increasingly been fought through sanctions, blockades and economic pressure could spill back into military action.

'Run and run'

Tehran has repeatedly said it will allow free navigation through the strait only if Washington implements the terms of the deal that was signed by both sides in June but quickly unravelled.

The agreement declared an end to fighting but deferred many of the most difficult issues and paved the way for a broader 60-day negotiation period — which passed without further agreement.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian attends the Shanghai Co-operation Organisation summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on Monday. (Vyacheslav Prokofyev/AFP/Getty Images)

But the heightened tensions this week have renewed fears of oil supply disruptions from the world's key crude-producing region.

"The tit-for-tat missile exchanges between the U.S. and Iran bring validation to those who believe that even if not a 'forever war,' this conflict will run and run," said PVM analyst John Evans.

Thousands ⁠have been killed in the conflict, mainly in Iran and Lebanon, since it began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28. Washington has increasingly relied ⁠on economic pressure to try to force Tehran to stop blockading the strait and end the war.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has warned that countries doing business with ⁠Iran could ⁠face U.S. sanctions and said secondary sanctions are likely to be ​unveiled weekly in the effort to pressure Iran, with an initial focus on banks.

LISTEN | The state of the U.S.-Iran war: Front Burner 27:28 Is Iran becoming a 'forever war'?

Iran's central bank governor, Abdolnaser Hemmati, said on Tuesday that Tehran had sufficient foreign currency reserves.

The central ​bank was ready to inject up to $2 ⁠billion US into the foreign exchange market to calm recent volatility, Hemmati was quoted as saying by the semi-official Tasnim news agency.

"I am telling the president of the United States: Iran has [foreign] currency and it has enough," he said.

His comments appeared partly aimed at reassuring markets after Iranian officials pointed to growing difficulties for Iran's economy.

World.title: 'It is Lake Ontario and it won’t change,' business owners in Niagara region respond to Trump renaming lake
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Now that Google Maps has changed the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America for users based in the U.S., the owners of one Niagara Falls restaurant decided to take a similar approach to their menu.

The move comes after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to change the name of the lake, amid escalating tensions and a brewing trade war.

“If you can rename whatever you want for your country, well then, we can do the same thing over here,” said Richard Carpenter, co-owner of Carson’s Pizzeria.

What was once their Buffalo chicken sandwich is now listed as their "Ontario wing sauce chicken sandwich."

“Also, the same thing with the Chicago Deep Dish, he named it the Thorold-style Deep Dish Pizza,” said co-owner Jonathon Olszewsky.

The pizzeria's Facebook post, announcing their “little name change,” has gathered concurring reactions from Canadians across the country, though Carpenter said the menu change is temporary and more “humour-based.”

Carson's Pizzeria is just one business in the region using small gestures like this to respond to the name change.

Katherine McMichael, owner of the shop Lady Lou Collective in Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont., said “it is Lake Ontario and it won’t change.”

“It’s quite silly that somebody thinks they can change the name of the lake, especially when it was made way beyond any of us were ever here,” McMichael told CBC Niagara.

McMichael owns and curates Canadian-made art work and gift items for her store Lady Lou Collective.

She keeps a sign in her shop's door thanking her customers for supporting Canadian businesses and Canadian-made goods.

A sticker thanking customers for purchasing Canadian goods at Lady Lou Collective, a gift shop in Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont. (Diona Macalinga/CBC)

She said while the impact of the Canada-U.S. trade war on her own business pales in comparison to those in many other industries, particularly the automotive sector, she's still affected, as she no longer ships orders to the U.S.

“It’s sad that we can’t do that anymore,” said McMichael, fearing that her American customers would get hit with duties. “I used to say that we’re two countries that support each other … We’re all just trying to make ends meet.”

Across the street, Shauna Dickson, owner of mom-and-pop shop Irish Design said she often uses Lake Ontario as a landmark to help customers and businesses overseas find her boutique.

Dickson, who was born and raised in Niagara-on-the-Lake, said the move to change the name of Lake Ontario “felt really close to home.”

Over the years, she said she felt a shift in her interactions with customers visiting from across the border, she told CBC News. But, despite the growing tensions between the two countries she wants to make sure her American customers still feel welcome in her store.

“We had a lot of customers come in and apologize when the conversation gets brought up about where they’re from,” Dickson said.

“It feels like we’re trying to comfort people a lot to make sure they know they're welcome here,” Dickson added. “We’re not blanketing you with one bully.”

World.content:
Article content

I have so many people in my life who express what a good listener I am and what a great time or conversation we have together. These comments leave me feeling confused. World.title: Vote to move Uribe’s massacre probe to Congress triggers infighting among Colombia’s left
World.content:
Internal fractures within Colombia’s leftist opposition burst into the open following a vote by five representatives of the Historic Pact (PH) party to transfer a criminal investigation against former President Alvaro Uribe to Congress’ Accusations Commission.

The controversy erupted after the five PH members of the committee backed a motion of Uribe’s Democratic Center (CD) party to assert legislative jurisdiction over long-standing criminal cases against Uribe, including investigations into the massacres of El Aro (1997) and La Granja (1996), and the 1998 assassination of human rights defender Jesus Maria Valle.

PH members

David Alejandro Toro

María del Mar Pizarro

Heráclito Landínez

Jorge Bastidas

Gabriel Becerra

As the former governor of Antioquia, Uribe would have been in on the massacres carried out by the Bloque Metro and AUC paramilitary groups, according to the Prosecutor General’s Office, which refused to turn over the investigations.

The commission claimed jurisdiction over the Uribe file because the paramilitaries didn’t demobilize until after 2002, when he became president.

Critics of the decision, including the prosecution and PH Senate chief Ivan Cepeda, argued that Uribe’s alleged involvement in the crimes happened years before he was granted presidential immunity.

Cepeda spent much of his career fighting Uribe in court over his alleged ties to the AUC.

Because of the committee vote, the Constitutional Court will have to rule on who gets to investigate Uribe’s alleged crimes against humanity, which could delay the investigation.

Journalists who reported on the PH support for the fabricated conflict suggested that this may be part of a political deal between congressmen political deal between Uribistas and Petristas, supporters of former President Gustavo Petro.

Becerra, who is close to Cepeda, said in a statement that there “existed nor will there exist any political deal that would compromise justice, truth or the rights of victims.

According to the house representative, the PH lawmakers “initially considered it reasonable and legally appropriate to clarify the jurisdiction of the authority responsible for conducting the investigation,” but changed their mind in response to the controversy and calls for their resignation.

Lawyer Miguel Angel del Rio, the victims representative in the Uribe case, told Tercer Canal that “the ethic committee of the Historic Pact should investigate these five congressman,” adding that “what we have here is solidarity with impunity and this cannot be allowed.”

The Historic Pact became Colombia’s largest political party after congressional elections in March, but has seen an increase in internal tensions after Cepeda’s failure to win the presidential election in June.

World.title: Finance minister presents Colombia’s $203B budget proposal
World.content:
Colombia’s Finance Minister Miguel Gomez presented a budget proposal of COP634.9 trillion ($203 billion) for the coming year, a 14% increase compared to last year.

Much of the increase is due to the government’s debt obligations, which went up 55% to 155.4 trillion ($49.8 billion), almost a quarter of the entire budget.

At a presentation, Gomez told press that an earthquake that left tens of thousands homeless in western Colombia earlier this month also forced the administration of Abelardo de la Espriella to increase spending.

In a video, the finance minister also said that the government “has taken deci

The budget bill, a revision of the one that was presented by the former government of former President Gustavo Petro, will have to be approved by Congress before October 20 or be issued as a decree.

The government will also present a Finance Bill, which determines how the government plans to pay for its spending, before December.

World.title: Colombia claims killing eight suspected EMBF guerrillas
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella said Thursday that Colombia’s armed forces killed eight guerrillas of FARC dissident group EMBF in a joint operation.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella said that the military offensive targeted “camps used by structures of the Jorge Suarez Briceño Block,” a unit of the EMBF, in a rural part of El Retorno in the Guaviare province.

In a precision airstrike followed by an operation carried out by our commandos, the preliminary tally shows that 8 terrorists have been killed so far, 11 rifles and 5 machine guns have been seized, along with a large amount of logistical supplies. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that “Colombia must know we are going on the offensive” against organized crime and illegal armed groups that are all deemed “narco-terrorist” organizations by the government.

“Major ringleaders and their criminal organizations will find no hiding place or sanctuary anywhere in the country,” the president added.

De la Espriella took office earlier this month, vowing to end peace negotiations with illegal armed groups and go on a military offensive with the help of the US military instead.

One of the groups that was negotiating peace with the administration of former President Gustavo Petro was the EMBF, led by former FARC commander “Calarca.”

The group, together with FARC dissident group EMC, controls large swathe of territory in southern Colombia and along the border with Venezuela.

World.title: De la Espriella calls for “iron fist” against crime in Colombia
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the security forces to impose the law “like a giant with an iron fist, the iron fist of the State.”

During a meeting with commanders of the security forces, De la Espriella stressed that security “is the cornerstone of our government and the most forceful government policy.”

The president urged the security forces to confront crime with an iron fist and stressed that “our soldiers and police officers have the full and unconditional support of this government. Never again will they be mistreated or forced to bow down to crime.”

Here we must act like a giant with an iron fist—the iron fist of the state. And that ability to convey a sense of unity is what has a psychological impact on crime and sends a clear message to citizens: we are here to protect you, to look out for you, but also to enforce the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella called to erase the distinction between organized crime and illegal armed groups, and “treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups,” claiming they are interconnected.

We have to stop treating these criminals differently. We must treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups, because the criminal pyramid we have in Colombia—whose base is drug trafficking, followed by illegal mining, extortion, and smuggling—is all perfectly interconnected. The foundation of all crime and the primary source of all forms of violence is drug trafficking. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“When it comes to fighting crime, there are no differences—neither in the state’s actions nor in its response and certainly not in the categorization” that allowed peace talks with groups like the FARC and ELN, according to the president.

“That is over in this administration. They are all terrorists, and we are going to treat them as such, no matter what happens,” said De la Espriella.

World.title: De la Espriella claims 123,700 barrels stolen monthly from Colombia’s state oil company
World.content:
Oil thieves from north Colombia would be stealing at least 123,700 barrel of gasoline, diesel and naphtha, a month, claimed President Abelardo de la Espriella.

According to De la Espriella, the theft of the refined oil products that wee imported or produced by state-owned oil company Ecopetrol “is utterly alarming, and demands an immediate and forceful response from the State.”

Every month, approximately 123,700 barrels of refined products—gasoline, diesel, and naphtha—imported or produced by Ecopetrol would be stolen. This would occur solely on a 14-inch pipeline that connects Pozos Colorados, in Santa Marta, to the interior of the country, and the losses are concentrated mainly in Cesar and Magdalena. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“We would be talking about more than 1.5 million barrels a year, with losses exceeding $500,000 million for Ecopetrol and, therefore, for the nation,” the president said in a post on social media platform X.

De la Espriella added that “these fuels are used as raw materials in the illicit processing of cocaine” by illegal armed groups that operate in the country’s periphery.

If we confirm that a large portion of this fuel is being used to power cocaine production facilities, then we are not only dealing with a massive theft from Ecopetrol: we are dealing with a criminal network that may be linking the theft of hydrocarbons to drug trafficking and the financing of armed terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president ordered a “joint operation” of the military, police, prosecution and administrative authorities “to comprehensively combat this criminal economy” led by Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora.

“I want results and periodic report on progress,” said De la Espriella.

Organized crime and illegal armed groups have been involved in fuel theft for decades.
