How Live Dealer Casino Games Actually Work at Olimp

1st Tuesday, September 2026 - 00:17 UTC Full article

Live dealer tables get sold as a compromise. That framing is wrong. A well-run live studio is closer to a real casino floor than any random number generator ever gets, and the stream, the shuffle, and the payout math all run on separate, auditable systems. Understanding how those pieces fit together changes how you play, not just what you believe about fairness. This guide breaks down the mechanics, not the marketing copy.

The Technology Behind Every Live Table

Cameras, dealers, and card-recognition software form the backbone of every live table, whether it's blackjack, baccarat, or roulette. Multiple angles feed a control room where operators watch for stream drops or dealer errors in real time. Optical character recognition reads card values and chip placements faster than a human could confirm them, which is what lets the game move at a pace close to a physical table rather than lagging behind it. None of this is visible to the player, but it's why results register within a second or two of the dealer's action.

Licensing sits underneath all of it. A live studio partnership only means something if the studio itself is independently audited, and the operator has to be transparent about who supplies the feed. On olimpbet, the live casino section groups tables by studio and game type rather than burying the provider name, which is a small detail but a telling one. Knowing which studio runs a table tells you more about its rules and betting limits than the game's title ever will.

Latency is the practical issue nobody warns you about. A stream running on a weak connection doesn't just look worse, it can desync the countdown timer from what you're actually seeing, and that's how players misjudge a betting window and lose a hand to a technicality rather than the cards. Standard live tables buffer a couple of seconds by design, precisely to absorb small network hiccups without cutting into decision time. A stable connection matters more here than on any slot, because slots don't punish a half-second lag the way a live baccarat clock does.

Table Variety and Format Differences

Table variety at Olimp spans the usual roulette and blackjack formats along with game-show style products that blend a live host with a digital wheel or multiplier board. These hybrid formats run on the same streaming infrastructure but layer in randomized number generation for bonus rounds, so the dealer segment is genuinely live while the multiplier reveal is computer-generated and independently tested. That distinction matters when comparing volatility between a straightforward blackjack shoe and a wheel-based show with uneven, occasionally large payout swings.

- Live blackjack: fixed betting spots, dealer-controlled pace, side bets vary by table provider.

- Live roulette: European single-zero wheels dominate, though some tables still run American double-zero.

- Baccarat: fastest average round time of the core table games, often under a minute per hand.

- Game-show formats: live hosting plus RNG-driven bonus segments, with payout tiers engineered for occasional large hits rather than steady small returns.

- Speed variants: reduced decision windows, aimed at players who want volume over deliberation.

Betting limits differ by table, and that's worth checking before you sit down rather than after. Entry-level blackjack tables commonly accept small minimum bets to keep the format accessible, while VIP or high-limit rooms raise both floor and ceiling considerably, sometimes with a separate dealer rotation entirely. Roulette sits in the middle, with limits that scale by bet type since a straight-up number wager carries different risk than an even-money spread. Checking the limit table before joining avoids realizing your usual stake doesn't fit the room.

Shuffling, Dealing, and the Round Sequence

Shuffling and dealing follow procedures stricter than they look on camera. Multi-deck shoes get replaced on a schedule, and automatic shufflers remove the manual reshuffle that used to be a weak point for tampering accusations. Baccarat and blackjack studios post their deck count and penetration rules, so a player who wants to track shoe composition can actually do so, unlike a fully automated RNG shuffle where the internal state stays hidden. That transparency is part of why regulated live studios operate under the same scrutiny as physical casino floors.

Here's a rough sequence of what happens between placing a bet and seeing the result post to your balance:

- You select a seat and confirm your stake within the betting window, typically ten to twenty seconds depending on the table.

- The dealer executes the round on camera while the control system logs card or wheel data in parallel.

- Recognition software cross-checks the visual feed against the logged data to confirm the outcome.

- Payouts calculate automatically and post to your account balance, usually within a few seconds of the round closing.

- History updates on your account, letting you review past rounds, a step most players skip but shouldn't.

Why Your Connection Quality Matters

Connection quality on your end still matters more than most players assume. A dropped frame during a critical reveal can feel like the game glitched against you, when really it's a buffering issue that resolved a second later with the correct result already logged server-side. Mobile data connections are more prone to this than fixed broadband, so if you're playing high-limit baccarat, a stable line is worth prioritizing over convenience.

Session length on live tables tends to run longer than slots because the pace is dealer-controlled rather than self-paced. That changes bankroll math. A player used to spinning through a slot's volatility in a few minutes needs to budget differently for a baccarat shoe that might run twenty or thirty hands before it resets. Olimp's table listings show average round duration alongside the minimum stake, worth reading before committing a session bankroll rather than discovering the pace mismatch mid-shoe.

Putting the Mechanics to Practical Use

None of this replaces basic bankroll discipline, but knowing the mechanics behind the stream removes a lot of the guesswork that makes live tables feel opaque to newer players. The camera work, the licensing behind each studio, and the way limits scale by table type are all checkable before you place a single bet.

Spend five minutes reading a table's rules panel before joining, and most of the surprises that trip up first-time live players simply stop happening. Understanding the sequence from bet placement to payout, and knowing why your own connection matters as much as the studio's setup, turns live dealer play from a leap of faith into a game with visible, checkable moving parts.

World.title: Sticky Wilds and Stacking Multipliers: mechanics in Wild West Gold
World.content:
Sticky Wilds and Stacking Multipliers: mechanics in Wild West Gold

1st Tuesday, September 2026 - 00:09 UTC Full article

You trigger the bonus round with three scattered symbols, the reels lock into free spin mode, and on the very second spin a wild lands dead center on an active payline. It doesn't disappear after that spin. It just sits there, glowing faintly, waiting for the next wild to land beside it. That single mechanic, a wild that refuses to leave, is the reason this particular slot keeps coming up in conversations about high-volatility free spins bonuses that actually pay when they hit.

Most free spins features reset every symbol between spins, which keeps volatility somewhat contained. This one doesn't. Once a wild appears during the bonus round, it becomes sticky and stays fixed on the reel for the remainder of the feature, and every sticky wild carries its own multiplier of 2x, 3x, or 5x, assigned at random the moment it lands. Three or four of these accumulating across a five-reel grid changes the math of every subsequent spin, since you're no longer hoping for one lucky wild, you're building a growing wall of them.

How the Multiplier Stacking Actually Works

Here's where a lot of players misread the mechanic: when two sticky wilds land on the same winning line, their multipliers add together rather than multiply. A 3x wild sitting next to a 5x wild produces an 8x boost on that line, not 15x. It sounds like a smaller number, and mathematically it is, but the tradeoff is that additive stacking makes big multipliers achievable more often across a full bonus round rather than reserving them for one rare combination. Anyone who tries wild west gold for the first time tends to assume multiplicative stacking because that's the more common convention in slot design, so it's worth checking the paytable before assuming your math is right mid-session.

Developed by Pragmatic Play, the game runs on a 4x5 layout with 40 fixed paylines, a structure that gives sticky wilds more lines to intersect with as the feature progresses. Landing three scatters starts the bonus with 8 free spins, and additional scatters landing during the feature, anywhere from two up to five of them, extend the round by 4 to 20 more spins. That extension window matters more than it looks on paper: extra spins mean extra chances for wilds to land and stay, and since existing sticky wilds carry over, a bonus round that stretches to 15 or 20 spins can end up with a reel that's nearly saturated with multipliers by the final few turns.

Why the Payout Ceiling Sits Where It Does

The certified return to player on this configuration is 96.51%, though Pragmatic Play does license alternate versions at 95.56% and 94.53% depending on how individual operators configure the game, so it's reasonable to check which version a given casino is running before assuming the headline figure applies. Volatility is rated high, and the spread between base game and bonus round outcomes shows exactly why. A regular base spin caps out at 6,750x the stake, which is already a substantial ceiling for a single spin, but the free spins feature raises that limit to 10,000x when sticky wilds combine efficiently across the grid.

That gap between 6,750x and 10,000x isn't decorative. It reflects how much of this game's total volatility budget is loaded into the bonus feature rather than spread evenly across every spin. Slots with flatter volatility curves tend to pay similar maximum multipliers whether or not you've triggered a bonus, but this one concentrates its upside almost entirely into the free spins mechanic, which is part of why triggering the scatters feels disproportionately significant compared to slots where the base game can occasionally produce comparable results on its own.

- Base game maximum win: capped at 6,750x the stake, achievable without triggering any bonus feature

- Free spins maximum win: up to 10,000x the stake, dependent on how many sticky wilds accumulate and stack

- Bonus trigger: 3 scatters award 8 free spins; 2 to 5 scatters landing during the feature add 4 to 20 more spins

- Wild multiplier range: each sticky wild is randomly assigned 2x, 3x, or 5x, stacking additively with others on the same line

Reading the Feature Like Someone Who's Tracked It

Players who follow this slot across multiple sessions tend to describe the free spins round in two distinct phases. Early spins are about scatter luck and getting extensions, since a round that only runs the base 8 spins rarely has time for enough wilds to stack into anything dramatic. Later spins, especially once a round has been extended past 12 or 15 turns, shift toward multiplier accumulation, where the question isn't whether a wild lands but where it lands relative to the wilds already sitting on the grid. Wild West Gold rewards that second phase disproportionately, which is part of why extensions carry more practical weight here than in slots where every spin behaves identically.

None of this changes the fact that the 10,000x ceiling remains a rare outcome rather than a routine one, and high volatility means long stretches without a bonus trigger are part of the design rather than a malfunction. What the additive stacking and sticky wild mechanics do is make the feature's variance legible: you can watch the multipliers building spin by spin and get a real sense of where a round is heading, rather than waiting on a single opaque payout at the end. That transparency, more than the headline multiplier, is what keeps the format worth returning to.

World.title: Brazil: Flávio Bolsonaro promises 500,000 prison places inspired by the Salvadoran model
World.content:
Brazil: Flávio Bolsonaro promises 500,000 prison places inspired by the Salvadoran model

31st Monday, August 2026 - 22:13 UTC Full article

“There are few prisoners in Brazil, there should be more; there are not more only because the legislation is weak,” the senator said after the meeting

Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the Liberal Party's presidential candidate and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's main rival in October's elections, met on Sunday in São Paulo with El Salvador's justice and public security minister, Gustavo Villatoro, and announced he will incorporate into his programme measures inspired by President Nayib Bukele's security policy.

The plan envisages creating 500,000 prison places over four years and building five federal maximum-security prisons in a complex the candidate has named “Treva”. It also provides for a Ministry of Public Security separate from the Justice Ministry, with transfers of resources and intelligence to states and municipalities, and the classification of the Primeiro Comando da Capital and Comando Vermelho as narcoterrorist organisations. Washington added both to its list of terrorist groups in May.

“There are few prisoners in Brazil, there should be more; there are not more only because the legislation is weak,” the senator said after the meeting, proposing minimum sentences of eight years for mobile phone thieves. Brazil had 964,074 people deprived of liberty at the end of 2025, according to the National Secretariat for Penal Policies, 6% more than the previous year and the third-largest figure in the world in absolute terms, after the United States and China. Among the inmates is his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, serving a sentence for attempting a coup.

The meeting lasted around an hour at a hotel in the city. According to the candidate, he told Villatoro that many in Brazil consider it impossible to eliminate criminal factions, and the minister replied that it is not, because they did it in El Salvador. Parts of the conversation were recorded and will be used in the senator's television campaign advertising.

“In El Salvador they managed to implement one of the greatest and most effective recoveries of sovereignty and to return public security to the Salvadoran people,” Bolsonaro said. International human rights organisations have documented arbitrary detentions, torture and deaths in custody under the state of exception in force in that country since 2022. The Salvadoran government rejects those accusations and attributes the fall in homicides to its strategy. The candidate did not address the matter at the press conference.

The two countries differ considerably in scale. El Salvador has around six million inhabitants and an area smaller than the state of São Paulo; Brazil has more than 215 million.

Public security tops Brazilian voters' concerns: 35% place it as their first or second worry, ahead of healthcare and corruption. Other candidates, including Renan Santos and Romeu Zema, have also signalled an intention to adopt measures inspired by the Salvadoran model. Senator Sérgio Moro, a candidate for governor of Paraná for the same party, attended the meeting.

World.title: ‘Throttle Therapy’ in Mexico: Sometimes, it’s not about the miles
World.content:
I know it’s been a minute since I’ve written a “Throttle Therapy” column, but there’s a pretty good reason for that: It’s hot. I mean, like really, properly hot.

And while I love riding on our motorcycle, Dora, I have absolutely no desire to spend several hours sitting on top of a hot engine while wearing boots and a helmet, with the sun doing its best to turn me into a roast dinner.

So, for the past few months, Dora has been sitting there.

She hasn’t complained. She hasn’t guilt-tripped Omar and me. She hasn’t even looked particularly disappointed that the long rides that used to be such a big part of our life in Mexico have disappeared from the calendar.

She’s just been waiting.

And I’ve been making excuses.

Some of them are legitimate, like the brutal heat. But I’ve also realized I had quietly fallen into the habit of thinking that if we couldn’t go for a proper ride, there wasn’t much point in going at all.

A few hours? Not really worth getting the gear on. A couple of hours? We wouldn’t get anywhere. Just a quick ride? Well, we might as well wait until the weather cools down.

And so, we waited.

I’ve missed it, though. I’ve missed those rides where we leave home without much of a plan and somehow end up six hours later in a place neither of us intended to visit.

Confusing therapy with mileage

The rides where we stop for coffee, then tacos, then happen on something interesting down a road we’ve never taken before. The ones where we pull over simply because the view is too good to keep moving.

Somewhere along the way, I think I started confusing the therapy with the mileage. If we couldn’t give Dora a full day, it somehow didn’t count. Then, recently, I realized that was a bit ridiculous.

I needed a ride.

Not an epic adventure or a new destination. Not a six-hour exploration of roads neither of us had ever traveled. I just needed to get on the bloody motorcycle.

So yesterday, Omar and I took Dora out for a short ride along one of our favorite stretches of Highway 200 between Mismaloya and Boca de Tomatlán.

If you’ve never ridden that road, it’s one of those places that makes you understand why people fall in love with this part of Mexico. And yes, I know that sounds like the beginning of a tourism , but I’m afraid it’s true.

Bougainvillea spills over walls. Palm trees pop up between buildings. There are little tiendas, concrete houses painted in colors that somehow seem brighter in the Mexican sunshine, battered signs and the occasional roadside shrine decorated with flowers.

There’s activity everywhere: A man sitting in the shade, someone washing something outside their house, kids running around, dogs that seem to believe they own whichever patch of road they happen to be standing on.

And then, as if by some glorious magic, the jungle opens up and there it is: the Pacific. Blue all the way to the horizon, crashing against the rocks below.

A quick stop along the Pacific

I’ve ridden that road countless times, and it still gets me.

We rode for a while, then pulled Dora over and walked down to the beach. There was music coming from somewhere. Families were sitting under umbrellas. Young couples were running in and out of the water. Boats bobbed offshore. And, because this is Mexico, there was a man selling shrimp on a stick.

Obviously, we bought some. I’m not sure whether food tastes better when it’s slathered in salt and hot sauce, and you’re eating it on a Mexican beach, but I’m willing to conduct further research.

We sat there for a while, talked a little, watched the water and did absolutely nothing.

And it was exactly what I needed.

The whole thing probably took less than two hours. A few months ago, I might have looked at that and thought it didn’t really count. We hadn’t gone far enough. We hadn’t discovered somewhere new. We hadn’t found some tiny mountain village neither of us had heard of. We hadn’t clocked enough miles to justify getting Dora out of the garage.

But sitting there with grilled shrimp and lime, my feet in the sand and the Pacific in front of me, I realized I’d been looking at it all wrong.

It was never really about the distance. It was about getting out of my own head.

That’s what riding has always done for me.

When you’re on a motorcycle, there isn’t much room for thinking about the emails you haven’t answered, the article you need to finish, the laundry sitting in the basket, or whatever else has been rattling around in your head.

Living outside the waiting room

You have to pay attention.

To the road. The traffic. The bend ahead. The truck coming the other way. The smell of the trees. The heat. The sudden glimpse of the ocean.

And for a while, that’s all there is.

I think we spend far too much time waiting for the right conditions to do things. We’ll go when work settles down. When the weather is better. When we have a whole weekend. When we have enough time to do it properly.

I’m starting to wonder how much of life gets missed while we’re waiting for “properly.”

That little ride reminded me that sometimes two hours can be enough. You don’t always need to go somewhere. Sometimes you just need to go.

And maybe that’s what I’ve missed most about Dora.

Not the long rides themselves, although I certainly miss those. It’s the way a motorcycle can make an ordinary day feel like you’ve gone somewhere. You can leave home with no particular plan, follow Highway 200 for a while, stop on a beach, eat shrimp from a stick and sit looking at the Pacific. Then you get back on, and you go back home.

Nothing monumental happened. And somehow, everything feels a little better.

That’s one of the things I love about living in Mexico. It isn’t always the big, postcard moments. It’s the fact that they can turn up in the middle of an otherwise completely ordinary day.

I know we’ll get back to the long rides, and we already have plans for Dora when the weather finally decides to stop trying to melt us. There are roads we haven’t traveled, places we still want to see and, knowing us, probably a few wrong turns waiting to happen.

But I’m not going to wait for the perfect day or the perfect amount of time anymore.

Because it turns out “Throttle Therapy” doesn’t require a full tank, six hours and a destination.

Sometimes it just requires getting on the bike. And sometimes, if you’re extra lucky, it even comes with a side of shrimp.

Charlotte Smith is a writer and journalist based in Mexico. Her work focuses on travel, politics, and community. You can follow along with her travel stories at www.salsaandserendipity.com.

World.title: Fierce storm downs trees and damages shopping malls in Guadalajara, with more rain on the way
World.content:
The intense storm that struck the Guadalajara Metropolitan Area (ZMG) Sunday afternoon left behind downed trees, pooled water on roadways and damaged shopping centers in both Guadalajara and Zapopan.

In Zapopan, Civil Protection and Fire Department authorities reported that at least 13 trees had fallen, mostly in the city center. One went down on Patria Avenue, near the urban forest of Los Colomos, blocking traffic.

In Guadalajara, initial reports counted another seven fallen trees. The affected areas include Pablo Neruda and Circuito Madrigal intersections; Terranova and Buenos Aires; Manuel Diéguez and José María Vigil; and Patria and Alberta.

Authorities worked to remove branches and trunks, clear streets and reduce risks for pedestrians and motorists.

The storm also caused damage to shopping centers.

Andares, a shopping mall in the high-end residential area of Puerta de Hierro, Zapopan, reported that water leaked through the roof of a department store, damaging merchandise.

Meanwhile, gusts of wind caused glass panels to detach and fall from the roof in Midtown, a shopping mall located along López Mateos Avenue in Guadalajara. Debris fell onto the food court, where diners and visitors were taking shelter from the storm. However, no injuries were reported as a result of the incident.

In addition to fallen trees and damage to shopping centers, Sunday’s storm reportedly caused power outages in several neighborhoods in the ZMG, where power didn’t return until Monday morning.

More rain was expected today across the city, with the National Water Commission (Conagua) anticipating an 80% chance of rain in Guadalajara and 40% in Zapopan.

Despite the severe storms that have occurred this year in Jalisco, rainfall has not generated a significant recovery in the level of Lake Chapala, the main source of water supply for the ZMG. Data from Conagua revealed that the lake’s water capacity currently stands at 69% — up 6% compared to the beginning of June.

Josué Sánchez Tapetillo, a specialist in water resource management, told the local newspaper El Informador that the lake has recovered approximately 46 centimeters during the current rainy season. He noted that although the recovery rate has been slow compared to previous years, there is no cause for alarm as the rainy season is not over yet.

With reports from Telediario and El Informador

World.title: In Coatepec, INAH discovers ceremonial plaza and stele with never-before-seen features
World.content:
A civic-ceremonial plaza and a monolithic stele featuring atypical characteristics for the region were discovered in the area of Coatepec, Veracruz, in a find that could provide new clues about the societies that lived there prior to the Conquest.

Both the structure and the sculpture, which are reminiscent of those from nearby Maya settlements, were found in a good state of preservation.

The National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) said in a statement that the find offers the opportunity to explore a unique regional expression that has been little studied and that is challenging to connect definitively with the established traditions of the Gulf Coast.

In an interview with newspaper La Jornada, INAH archaeologists Lino Espinoza García and Alberto Vázquez Domínguez said that the settlement dates back some 1,500 years before the Christian era, coinciding with the beginning of the Campo Viejo settlement.

According to the archaeologists, “from that time onwards, there was a continuous population [inhabiting the area] until the colonial era,” which began in the early 1500’s.

The findings on the platform and the stela, however, could date back to the Protoclassic period, ranging from 200 B.C. to 200 A.D.

A discovery with features never seen before

The discovery occurred on a private residential property as part of an archaeological salvage operation led by INAH archaeologists in the San Lucas subdivision, near the Campo Viejo archaeological zone.

The findings consist of a platform — 30 meters long by 12 meters wide — built with white slabs and blocks of dressed limestone, with a texture similar to plaster, which would have been selected or worked to create a specific visual finish.

The ornamentation features square-like figures and circular stones on two of its sides, attributes that are not typical of the region and had not been previously recorded there.

The monolithic sculpture measures 1.88 meters high, 1.47 meters wide at its widest point and 0.68 meters wide at its narrowest. With a thickness that ranges from 22 to 25 centimeters, it features engravings alluding to a symbolic event in which two elite figures, seated and wearing elaborate attire, receive a fluid from a divine entity holding a vessel on a higher plane.

Lino noted that “the entire stele, made of andesite stone, references themes of fertility and cultivation of the land.”

Field excavations conclude this month, and specialists will proceed with laboratory analyses, which will extend until early 2027.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Mexican-built particle detector slated to help global scientists illuminate the birth of the universe
World.content:
A Mexican physicist was recently chosen to lead the development of a particle detector for one of the world’s largest scientific projects: an underground atom smasher in Europe that is helping scientists understand the universe shortly after the Big Bang.

The proposed detector would be built in Mexico and installed at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN), home of the Large Hadron Collider beneath a portion of the French-Swiss border.

The Mexican-built device, called the Muon Identifier Detector (MID), is planned for ALICE 3, a future version of one of the collider’s four main experiments.

If built and approved, it would give Mexican institutions responsibility for a central subsystem of ALICE 3.

The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is a particle accelerator and collider covering a circular circuit of 27 kilometers, or 17 miles, near Geneva, Switzerland. It speeds beams of protons or electrically charged atomic nuclei to within a whisker of the speed of light — about 1.08 billion km/h, or 671 million mph — before steering them into head-on collisions.

Collisions involving heavy atomic nuclei can briefly create matter thought to resemble conditions in the universe’s earliest moments.

The Mexican project is still not guaranteed to reach CERN.

While the MID is included in the reference design for ALICE 3, the Mexican team must obtain funding, finish the design and construction work and clear technical reviews before it can be installed. Operations are targeted for 2036.

The Mexican project is headed by Antonio Ortiz Velásquez, a senior researcher at the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) whose appointment was approved by the ALICE Collaboration Board, UNAM said Aug. 13.

UNAM said Ortiz, a physicist at UNAM’s Institute of Nuclear Sciences, is the first Mexican scientist chosen to direct development of a strategic ALICE 3 subsystem.

Mexico has already worked with ALICE for years, helping build and operate earlier detector equipment and analyze collision data, but the new project goes even further.

The Mexican-built device would track muons, small particles that can pass through much of the detector after a collision. Their paths can help researchers study a fleeting, superheated state of matter that scientists believe filled the universe immediately after the Big Bang.

“We are recreating tiny droplets from the early universe and studying them through the traces they leave in particle detectors,” Ortiz said.

The team hopes to begin construction in Mexico in 2028. It includes researchers from UNAM, the Center for Research and Advanced Studies, the Benemérita Universidad Autónoma de Puebla, the Autonomous University of Sinaloa and the National Technological Institute of Mexico, along with partners in the United States, Hungary, the Czech Republic and Pakistan.

With reports from La Jornada, MxPA and Space Daily

World.title: 11 injured in car bomb attack on Zacatecas police station
World.content:
Eleven people, including a policewoman, were injured Sunday night when a car bomb exploded outside a municipal police station in Ojocaliente, a town in the state of Zacatecas.

Zacatecas Attorney General Cristian Camacho said Monday that authorities were investigating whether the attack was linked to the capture on Saturday of an 18-year-old man who is allegedly a sicario (hitman) for the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG). The federal Security Cabinet is collaborating with Zacatecas authorities on the investigation. No arrests had been reported as of early Monday afternoon.

Rodrigo Reyes, general secretary of the Zacatecas government, reported on Monday that 10 civilians and a female police officer were injured in the explosion on Sunday, which occurred as Ojocaliente residents were taking part in festivities honoring the town’s patron saint. The official said that 10 of the victims were in stable condition while one was in a “delicate” state but “out of danger.”

Reyes said that explosives were placed in a car that was reported as stolen in the state of Jalisco. They detonated at approximately 8 p.m. Sunday.

In addition to injuring 11 people, the explosion damaged 30 properties, including homes, and 13 vehicles, including police cars, according to Reyes.

The attack was the third carried out with explosives in Zacatecas in four days. Three police officers and one civilian were injured in the two other attacks, which were perpetrated on Thursday and Saturday of last week.

Ojocaliente Mayor Juan Manuel Zambrano canceled classes on Monday — the first day of the 2026-27 school year — in light of Sunday’s attack, while municipal government offices were closed to the public.

Reyes said that security in Ojocaliente had been beefed up, with army troops and members of the National Guard deploying to the municipality.

The federal Security Cabinet said on social media on Monday that authorities from all three levels of government were “reinforcing the security operation in the area to protect the population.”

A revenge attack by the CJNG?

The car bomb explosion on Sunday night came a day after an 18-year-old man was arrested on Saturday near the border between Zacatecas and the state of Aguascalientes.

In an interview with Radio Fórmula on Monday, Camacho said that “we’re not ruling out that yesterday’s attack was a reaction to that result.”

The attorney general said that the suspect had admitted to being a sicario for the CJNG. He also said that “everything suggests” that the attack in Ojocaliente on Sunday was carried out by that criminal group.

The CJNG is based in Jalisco but operates in virtually all of Mexico’s states. The cartel’s leader is now said to be Juan Carlos Valencia González, stepson of CJNG founder and former leader Nemesio Rubén “El Mencho” Oseguera Cervantes, who was fatally wounded in a military operation in Jalisco in February.

Zacatecas is known for violence, but homicides have declined by more than 50% this year

On Aug. 11, the federal government reported that there were 51 homicides in Zacatecas in the first seven months of 2026, a reduction of 53.2% compared to the same period of last year. The annual reduction in murders in Zacatecas was the fourth largest among Mexico’s 32 federal entities.

Earlier this decade, Zacatecas was one of Mexico’s most violent states, but it recorded the eighth-lowest homicide count among Mexico’s 32 federal entities between January and July.

There are, however, signs that the security situation is deteriorating in the state, whose location between the Pacific coast port of Manzanillo, Colima, and Mexico’s northeast border with Texas makes it a trafficking route for fentanyl and other drugs.

On a single day last month, the bodies of ten murdered men were found across three municipalities in Zacatecas. Five of the bodies were found hanging from a bridge in Pánuco, a municipality just north of Zacatecas city. Among the 10 victims were a former mayor of Sombrerete, Zacatecas; an official with the Fresnillo municipal government; and an ex-councilor in the municipality of Canatlán, Durango.

With reports from El Universal, Julio Astillero, Radio Fórmula, AFP, El Economista and El Financiero

World.title: Is it parmesan-style or Parmesano? Mexico-US trade talks hit snag over cheese names
World.content:
Mexico-U.S. trade talks have hit a snag over cheese, with the sticking point going back to the trade agreement Mexico signed with the European Union (EU) in May.

The Mexico-EU accord grants special protections to hundreds of European products whose names are linked to specific regions, including Parmigiano Reggiano, Feta and Manchego cheese. It also provides the EU with legal recourse against violations.

U.S. officials say the protections could restrict future sales by U.S. producers to Mexico under names like parmesan and feta, forcing them to use descriptions with labels such as “imitation” or “style.”

The U.S. government’s stance is that these names are generic, while the EU insists they ought to be reserved for products produced in the region for which they are named.

“What Mexico did was completely wrong,” said Jaime Castañeda, executive vice president of the U.S. Dairy Export Council. “The Mexican government must guarantee that both the United States and Mexican manufacturers of common cheese brands can continue operating in the market.”

While U.S. negotiators are pressuring Mexico to amend its deal with the EU (it has yet to be approved by the Senate), the European Commission insists it is not possible to modify the terms of the agreement.

Mexico — among the world’s top consumers of cheese — imports approximately US $1 billion worth of cheese annually from the U.S, while total EU dairy exports to Mexico amount to only US $200 million.

The Washington, D.C.-based International Dairy Foods Association (IDFA) is on record describing the U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade deal (USMCA) as dairy’s most important trade agreement.

The IDFA says the U.S. dairy industry, which supports more than 3 million jobs and contributes US $779 billion to the U.S. economy, depends on access to global markets to sustain growth and create new opportunities for farmers and processors.

U.S. negotiators are using the USMCA as leverage in hopes of forcing Mexico to accede to their demands, but critics say that in addition to the conflict with the EU accord, lower-quality U.S. cheeses are undercutting local production.

With reports from Reuters, CEO, The Independent and Fox 10 Phoenix

World.title: Nuevo León invests in 3 new bridges to boost trade via Laredo
World.content:
Nuevo León Governor Samuel García confirmed on Friday plans for potentially three new bridges connecting his northern state to Texas, aiming to speed up trade and facilitate cross-border commuting.

Following a working visit to the southern United States, García announced the construction of two new bridges at the Colombia-Laredo Port of Entry and reiterated plans to expand state Highway 1 North, connecting the Salinas Victoria industrial zone with the border municipalities of Anáhuac and Nuevo Laredo.

With a US $200 million binational investment of equal parts from Mexico and the U.S., the aim is to construct two new international bridges at the Colombia-Laredo crossing to expand its operational capacity and facilitate trade. Construction is expected to commence in May 2027 and be completed in 2028.

“I confirm the hypothesis we envisioned five years ago: the Texas-Nuevo León Golden Triangle is the most prosperous region in the world,” García said during a ceremony. “For Nuevo León, it’s crucial to have the infrastructure ready to be part of this triangle and be connected with Dallas, Houston, Brownsville, Corpus Christi, Austin, San Antonio and Laredo,” García stressed.

García said that the ongoing modernization of the Colombia-Laredo trade port has already doubled the number of cargo lanes from 7 to 14, helping to raise crossings from between 80 and 800 to 8,000 per day, a figure that he expects to increase to 15,000 by 2030.

In addition, a new viaduct will provide direct connectivity between Salinas Victoria and Laredo, Texas (via Anáhuac), running parallel to Highway 1 North as part of a larger project with the Texas-based startup Green Corridors.

The project, requiring $17 billion in investment, is being developed as a public-private partnership with the Nuevo León government providing the right-of-way. However, it is not expected to reach completion until 2031.

During the event, García also announced the development of a tax-free industrial park in the municipality of Anáhuac, as part of the federal government’s overarching Plan Mexico economic strategy. The state aims to attract investment in manufacturing, assembly and logistics by offering federal, state and municipal tax incentives, including exemptions on income tax (ISR), payroll tax and property tax.

“We are creating a tax haven,” García said.

If all four infrastructure projects move forward as planned, the Colombia-Laredo area will end up with a total of four crossings: the current bridge, the two new bridges to be built next year and the Green Corridors viaduct linking northern Nuevo León and Tamaulipas with Laredo.

With reports from Reporte Indigo, Rio South Texas, Mexico Industry and El Universal

World.title: MND Local: The massive ongoing investment in Los Cabos
World.content:
When foreign direct tourism investment numbers were announced for the first quarter of 2026, Baja California Sur (BCS) led all states, accounting for US $191.5 million, or 31% of the US $617.2 million invested in Mexico during that timeframe. That BCS received the most investment was not a surprise. If anything, the only surprise was that it did not receive a greater share of the total.

In 2024 and 2025, for example, BCS received upwards of US $1 billion dollars in foreign direct tourism investment during each year (US $1.039 billion and US $1.292 billion, respectively) — the most in Mexico — representing 36.2% and 40.6% of the national total. Of the US $2.5 billion-plus invested in BCS since 2024, an estimated 90% is centered on projects in Los Cabos; the municipality that, not coincidentally, accounts for 83% of tourism in the state.

This raises two very interesting questions: Where is all this money coming from? And what is it being used to build?

Why is Los Cabos receiving so much investment, and from whom?

A third interesting question is how long BCS (and, by extension, Los Cabos) has dominated foreign direct tourism investment in Mexico. However, finding an answer is difficult, as annual figures for this category before 2024 aren’t easily accessible. But based on the quarterly announcements that have been reported in recent years, it seems that BCS has been leading the way in tourism investment since at least 2022, when it received 36.3% of invested monies during the fourth quarter of that year; a trend also noted in the second and fourth quarters of 2023, when the state garnered 47.3% and 38.1% of the national quarterly totals.

As for where the money is coming from, the answer is overwhelmingly from U.S. sources. In 2025, for instance, nearly 85% of investments originated in the U.S., with Canada and Spain each contributing a little over 5%. No other country’s investment accounted for more than 2.1%.

What’s being built? Primarily luxury hotels and resorts — the Four Seasons Resort and Residences and Park Hyatt Los Cabos have both opened in Cabo del Sol since 2024, and Amanvari recently opened at Costa Palmas on the East Cape — although master-planned communities, vacation rentals, and marinas and beach clubs have also attracted significant capital.

The projects currently in the pipeline

As of the first quarter of 2026, Mexico’s Secretaría de Turismo (Sectur) noted 13 active tourism projects in BCS worth US $3.893 billion. Amanvari, the Aman brand resort at Costa Palmas on the East Cape of Los Cabos, recently opened on Aug. 1, with 18 casitas each fetching more than US $3,000 per night. So one project is complete. Of the dozen remaining, four relate to new hotels scheduled to open in Los Cabos between 2027 and 2029: the Conrad Los Cabos, SIRO Palmilla, Delano East Cape and Raffles Estera East Cape Resort & Residences.

The Conrad Los Cabos, a Hilton property with 111 guest rooms, 21 suites, 43 residences and access to a new Ernie Els-designed golf course, is slated to open in 2027 at Oleada, an 860-acre development on the Pacific Coast north of Cabo San Lucas. The SIRO Palmilla, a wellness-oriented hospitality brand from Kerzner International, is also expected to open its doors in 2027, with 120 rooms and 14 luxury villas.

Luxury brands Delano and Raffles, meanwhile, have both announced East Cape resorts to open by 2029. However, neither has broken ground as yet, nor have their exact locations been divulged. The only thing that is known is that Delano is planning for 117 guest rooms and 60 branded residences; Raffles for 80 guest rooms, 46 residences and seven drinking and dining options.

Home Depot invests 690 million pesos in Los Cabos

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Home Depot México (@thehomedepotmx)

Most, but not all, foreign investment in Baja California Sur is tourism-related. In 2025, for instance, a total of US $1.587 billion was invested in the state, 81% of which was earmarked for tourism projects.

One example of a non-tourism-related project is the new Home Depot, which opened on Aug. 20 in San José del Cabo. The store, which is located by the Fonatur roundabout, represents an investment of 690 million pesos (about US $41 million) by Home Depot Mexico, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Home Depot, Inc., the home improvement chain headquartered in Atlanta, Georgia.

It’s the second Home Depot store to open in Los Cabos: the other is near Cabo Bello in La Ruta Escénica in the corridor which connects cape cities Cabo San Lucas and San José del Cabo. The state’s third Home Depot, of the 144 now open in Mexico, is in the capital city of La Paz.

The recently opened San José del Cabo location supports 95 new jobs for residents, plus an inventory of 50,000 products now available to local consumers.

Chris Sands is a writer and editor for Mexico News Daily, and the former Cabo San Lucas local expert for the USA Today travel website 10 Best and writer of Fodor’s Los Cabos travel guidebook. He has also contributed to numerous other websites and publications, including The San Diego Union-Tribune, Marriott Bonvoy Traveler, Forbes Travel Guide, Porthole Cruise and Travel, and Cabo Living.

São Paulo Oktoberfest 2026: Three Weekends in Ibirapuera

From September 18 to October 4, São Paulo Oktoberfest sets up in Ibirapuera Park for three weekends of Bavarian-style celebration: long tables, brass-band and folk programming, German-style beers from Brazilian craft breweries, and plates of sausages, pretzels and pork knuckle.

The event runs Fridays from 5 p.m. to 11 p.m. and Saturdays and Sundays from 2 p.m. to 11 p.m., with tickets via the festival’s official site.

Why Brazil Does Oktoberfest So Well

Southern Brazil holds one of the largest German diasporas in the world, and Oktoberfest culture runs deep — Blumenau’s edition is second only to Munich’s in size, and São Paulo’s version brings that tradition to the country’s biggest city.

For expats from Germany, Austria or Switzerland, the São Paulo edition is the closest thing to a Wiesn weekend in the southern hemisphere’s spring.

Practical Tips for Expats

Ibirapuera is reached via metro (AACD-Servidor or Brigadeiro stations, then a short ride) or rideshare; festival weekends fill the park’s surroundings, so allow extra time.

Go early on Saturdays for families’ atmosphere; Friday evenings skew after-work. September evenings in São Paulo can be cool — bring a light jacket.

Make a Weekend of It

Pair the festival with MASP’s new ‘Histórias latino-americanas’ exhibition or a Bienal do Livro visit — both run through the same period.

ArtRio 2026: The Fair at a Glance

From September 16 to 20, ArtRio gathers Brazil’s leading galleries and a new generation of emerging projects in Rio de Janeiro, sustaining the fair’s role as the country’s most important marketplace and meeting point for contemporary art outside São Paulo.

The fair’s programming typically extends beyond the stands into talks, guided visits and special projects that connect the market to the city’s museums and institutions.

Rio’s Biggest Culture Month

ArtRio caps an exceptional September for Rio: the fair opens the same week Rock in Rio closes its seven-day run at the Cidade do Rock, and the city’s museums align new shows with the influx of visitors.

For the art world, the SP-Arte (August) to ArtRio (September) sequence defines the Brazilian market’s second semester.

What Expats and First-Time Visitors Should Know

ArtRio is open to the general public, not just collectors — it is the easiest way to survey dozens of Brazilian galleries in a single visit.

Prices range from accessible editions by emerging artists to blue-chip works; gallery staff are used to international visitors and first-time buyers.

Pairing ArtRio With the City

Combine the fair with Rio’s museum circuit — the Museu de Arte do Rio (MAR) and the Paço Imperial, currently hosting the Instituto Moreira Salles’ Luiz Braga retrospective, are natural companions.

MASP’s Landmark Show: What ‘Histórias Latino-Americanas’ Is

Opening September 4, the collective exhibition spreads across five floors of MASP’s Lina Bo Bardi building, articulating baroque and contemporary works from Mexico to Argentina’s far south.

Organized in five thematic nuclei, the show investigates how the idea of Latin America was constructed, represented and disputed — from colonial imagery and the visual language of the baroque to indigenous and Afro-diasporic community traditions and utopian counter-narratives to authoritarianism.

A Year of Latin American Stories at MASP

The exhibition crowns MASP’s 2026 season, which dedicated the entire year to Latin American histories with solo shows by Peru’s Sandra Gamarra Heshiki, Mexico’s Damián Ortega and Colombia’s Carolina Caycedo.

The curatorial program deliberately sidelines European artists in favor of Latin American, Black Atlantic and indigenous production, accompanied by research seminars and publications.

Why Expats Should Put It on the List

For foreigners living in Brazil, the exhibition doubles as a crash course in the region’s visual history — including the country they now call home — in one of the southern hemisphere’s most important museums.

MASP offers materials in English, and the iconic free-span gallery on Avenida Paulista is itself a landmark of Brazilian modernist architecture.

Visitor Tips

Opening weeks will be busy; weekday mornings and MASP’s Tuesday free-admission windows (check current rules) are the strategic slots.

The museum sits on the metro’s Trianon-Masp station (Line 2), easy to combine with the Paulista avenue cultural corridor.

Bienal do Livro São Paulo 2026: What to Expect

The 28th Bienal Internacional do Livro de São Paulo turns the Anhembi District into Latin America’s biggest literary marketplace for ten days: hundreds of publishers’ stands, author encounters, debates, signings and children’s programming.

The fair goes well beyond bookshelves — expect panel discussions with major Brazilian and international authors, manga and comics zones, and gastronomy areas that keep visitors on site all day.

Why Expats Should Go

The Bienal is one of the best places in Brazil to browse Portuguese-language literature with English-friendly programming mixed in — international publishers and bilingual editions have a growing presence.

It is also a window into Brazil’s reading culture: few events show the country’s literary scene — from cordel poetry to graphic novels — in one place.

Planning Your Visit

Weekday mornings are the calmest; weekend afternoons get packed, especially when big-name authors hold signings — check the signing schedule and arrive early for queues.

The free shuttle from Portuguesa-Tietê (metro lines 1 and 3) is the easiest route; parking at Anhembi is limited on peak days.

Beyond the Fair

Pair a Bienal day with the surrounding Santana and Barra Funda neighborhoods, or time your visit for the evening debates that run until closing.

World.title: Argentina’s Navone Hands Djokovic His Earliest Grand Slam Exit in 20 Years
World.content:
Novak Djokovic’s bid for a record 25th Grand Slam title ended almost as soon as it began Sunday night, with Argentina’s Mariano Navone pulling off the biggest win of his career in the first round of the US Open. Navone, ranked No. 49 in the world, defeated the fourth-seeded Djokovic 7-6(5), 5-7, 4-6, 6-2, 6-1 in a four-hour, 36-minute battle inside Arthur Ashe Stadium.

The result was historic. Djokovic had never lost in the first round in 20 appearances at the US Open, and he had not been beaten in the opening round of any Grand Slam tournament since the 2006 Australian Open.For much of the night, it appeared the 39-year-old Serbian might escape.

Navone won a tight opening set in a tiebreak before Djokovic fought back to take the next two. Djokovic then broke serve early in the fourth set to take a 2-1 lead and appeared to be moving toward the second round. Instead, the match changed dramatically.

Djokovic had been struggling physically throughout the night and his condition worsened as the match stretched past three hours. He vomited during the match and later said he was dealing with cramping as well as pain in his back and shoulder. Navone immediately broke back in the fourth set and began taking control. The 25-year-old Argentine won five of the next six games to force a deciding set, while Djokovic’s movement and energy continued to fade.

The fifth set quickly became one-sided. Navone broke Djokovic repeatedly and closed out the biggest upset of the opening day with a 6-1 final set.Djokovic finished with 70 unforced errors and converted only four of his 12 break-point opportunities. Navone converted six of 17. Afterward, Djokovic acknowledged that the physical problems were not limited to Sunday night. He said he has been dealing with vomiting and other issues during matches throughout the year and that his body eventually begins to break down.

“I’m trying, man. I’m trying,” Djokovic said when asked whether the problem could be fixed.The defeat continued a troubling North American hard-court stretch for Djokovic. He also lost his opening match at the Cincinnati Open earlier in August, falling to another Argentine, Thiago Agustin Tirante.

New York appeared to offer Djokovic a chance to reset. He entered as the No. 4 seed and was chasing the one major milestone still hanging over his career: a 25th Grand Slam singles championship. Instead, his tournament lasted one match. Djokovic remains tied with Margaret Court at 24 major singles titles and will now have to wait until at least the 2027 Australian Open for another opportunity to reach 25. For Navone, the night represented the opposite end of the tennis spectrum.

The Argentine arrived in New York better known for his results on clay than hard courts. He entered the match with one ATP Tour title and only two previous US Open victories. Facing one of the most successful players in tennis history under the lights at Arthur Ashe Stadium, he refused to go away even after Djokovic took control in the middle of the match.

“It is a dream come true,” Navone said after the victory. Navone now moves into the second round, where he will face the winner of the match between three-time Grand Slam champion Stan Wawrinka and Matteo Berrettini. Djokovic, meanwhile, leaves New York after the earliest Grand Slam exit of his career in two decades and with renewed questions about whether his body can continue to withstand the demands of five-set tennis.

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Police Department has indicated that it is aware of the sale of drugs in San Ignacio and Santa Elena that has triggered violent crimes in the community.

ASP Stacy Smith, Police Staff Officer says that the department is aware of the issues occurring in this area.

“The Department has always been cognizant of the issues that are attendant when it comes to the sale of drugs and that is why, as minuscule as it may seem to some, that when persons are arrested for drug trafficking that matter is made public and I make it my business to have those persons who are alleged to be engaged in such activities be known to the public because as stated we know that it is the sale of drugs that fuels these rivalries. Not only does it cause the loss of life of persons in terms of the violence, but the degradation of the family structure, the fact that persons in the neighborhood are not at peace when their properties are being hunted for persons who want to have a quick fix,” Smith explained.

In addition, Smith said that the Belize Police Department remains available to provide the statistics to see what occurred over the past few years, which has resulted in a transition from marijuana being one of the mainstream drugs to cocaine and crack being used.

“And in terms of the operational efforts in Western Belize, they are afoot and we are adjusting. We are cognizant that this most recent incident pertains to someone of interest and we are tailoring our operational efforts in that regard,” Smith added.

World.title: A new school year, A new transition: Supporting Autistic children back in class
World.content:
A new school year, A new transition: Supporting Autistic children back in class

By Zoila Palma: As children across Belize return to classrooms for the 2026–2027 school year, the transition back to school can bring a mix of excitement and uncertainty for autistic children and young people.

After weeks of summer freedom, returning to structured routines, new expectations, different surroundings or unfamiliar teachers can feel overwhelming.

For some students, however, the return to a predictable school routine may actually provide a welcome sense of stability.

Parents and caregivers can help make the transition smoother by gradually re-establishing familiar routines before and during the first weeks of school, Autism unlimited says.

Returning to regular wake-up and mealtimes, discussing what the school day will look like and explaining changes in advance can provide reassurance.

Visiting the school, meeting teachers or support staff, practicing the journey to school, or using photographs and videos of classrooms and other spaces can also help reduce anxiety by making the environment more familiar.

Practical support is equally important. Sensory tools such as ear defenders, fidgets and other familiar items can help students regulate during the school day, while comfortable clothing can make mornings easier for children who are sensitive to certain textures.

Some children may also benefit from a small comfort kit, visual cards to request a break or simple phrases such as “I need a break” or “Can you help me?”

Schools and families can work together to consider individual adjustments, including quieter arrival routines, predictable breaks or, where appropriate, a phased return to school.

The first weeks can be tiring as autistic students adjust to increased sensory input, social expectations and classroom demands.

Allowing time to decompress after school and keeping evenings and weekends relatively calm can support their wellbeing.

The goal is not simply for autistic children to cope with the transition, but to feel safe, understood, supported and ready to thrive in the new school year.

World.title: Santander explains canal system as Belize River fish kill questions continue
World.content:
Santander explains canal system as Belize River fish kill questions continue

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Santander Farms says its factory effluent is handled through a closed loop canal system that leads to a single monitored discharge point on the Belize River.

The company opened its operation to 7 News following the mass fish kill along the river earlier this month, which has turned attention toward agricultural activity in the watershed.

Chief Operating Officer Juan Cruz explained that the farm sits on flat land with separate main, secondary and third party canals.

“We have a closed grid canal that manages the factory effluents,” Cruz told 7 News, adding that the factory only runs during the dry season when sugarcane is harvested. Effluent from that process is irrigated onto surrounding crops, returning nutrients taken during harvesting.

Cruz said all canals were designed using RTK technology with zero slope and lead to one effluent point, a requirement under the company’s Environmental Compliance Plan.

On the canal itself, which drew controversy when opened around eleven years ago, Cruz said the company holds a permit and requires Department of Environment clearance to enter and clean it.

World.title: Tents? No Way!
World.content:
The tent at Middle Quarters Primary and Infant School in St Elizabeth where some classes were held

MIDDLE QUARTERS, St Elizabeth — Describing tents as heat traps, Middle Quarters Primary and Infant School Principal Pauvine Watson-Barrett is insisting that all of her 252 students must be housed in ventilated classrooms when the new academic year opens next Monday.

“The tent cannot be used; it is extremely hot. We tried to use the tent last academic year. We had grade one initially in the tent and after the [Primary Exit Profile] exam we had grade six going to the tent and giving grade one a feel of a classroom space,” she told the Jamaica Observer on Monday.

“However, due to the heat the children were not able to use the tent for the entire day. They had to be out of it by midday. Right now it is hotter than what we were experiencing last academic year, so I don’t see where I can use that tent to host the classroom,” she added.

Last week, the Caribbean Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology and The University of the West Indies Climate Studies Group Mona advised governments, businesses, farmers and households across the region to step up preparations for potentially severe climate extremes as El Niño conditions are and set to intensify the hot and dry conditions already affecting parts of the Caribbean.

Both entities warned that the region should remain particularly vigilant as August to October marks the peak of the Caribbean’s heat season.

This year’s El Niño is on track to be the strongest on record, threatening to unleash extreme weather across the globe and make 2027 the hottest recorded year by far.

Under such severe heat, tents would not be suitable to serve as classrooms for children.

On Monday, when asked how all her students would be accommodated, Principal Watson-Barrett said the National Education Trust (NET) had promised to deploy temporary wooden classrooms, but up to Monday afternoon there was no structure or even foundation to give assurance of the buildings.

“I am yet to see them. Between the Ministry of Education, NET, and the contractor, they promised that we would be getting two buildings each holding two classrooms, so that would be a total of four classrooms. Up to this morning (Monday) there was no updated information. The contractor said he is waiting on NET to give approval for the building of the [wooden] classrooms,” Watson-Barrett told the Observer.

She said the school is exploring two options to accommodate students if the temporary buildings are not erected in time.

“We will have to look at rotation and/or merging of classrooms into one room. For instance, last academic year I had a classroom with two grade two classes and they were placed in one room and then the teachers team-teach,” she said.

“Because of the heat, also, I am not considering a shift system. Imagine coming to school at 12 o’clock to start classes in this heat on a shift system,” added Watson-Barrett.

She said the school is expected to have seven accessible classrooms based on ongoing construction work.

“Currently, we have one block that is 85 per cent complete. That block can host two classrooms. The other two blocks that are available are currently being worked on and we are hopeful that by this Friday those two blocks will be completely cleaned and ready for the opening of school, September 7,” she said.

A deteriorating building had to be demolished last week at the school.

“That would leave me wanting five more classrooms to accommodate the other students, because as of last week I lost a building that had four classrooms, the guidance counselling room and the library on it,” said Watson-Barrett.

She said Middle Quarters Primary and Infant will be receiving students from the now shuttered Giddy Hall Primary School, three-and-a-half kilometres away.

“Even without the inclusion of the Giddy Hall Primary children I would be short of classrooms. I have 170 students expected to attend school in the primary department with an additional 29 from Giddy Hall Primary School, seeing that the school was consolidated and we are the receiving school,” she said while pointing out that five academic and two auxiliary staff were moved to her school from Giddy Hall.

“The ministry has made the decision to close down smaller schools based on the enrolment there… For the infant department we are expecting to have about 52 students,” she added.

When asked about the availability of potable water, Watson-Barrett said the school has been getting reliable water supply from the National Water Commission.

“Currently, I am seeing where improvement has been made on the water system; it is still being worked on, but whenever it is locked off we purchase water,” she said.

“During Hurricane Melissa [last October] the drums were blown off the building. However, we have a large metal tank that we store water in. Those drums that were blown down are yet to be replaced,” she added.

World.title: Tough guardrails
World.content:
Casino Gaming Commission (CGC) Chief Executive Officer Cleveland Allen (second left) gestures while speaking at this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange. Flanking him are CGC executives (from left) Caleigh Reid, legal officer; Damion McKenzie, senior director, investigations and enforcement; and Shainee Myles, director of human resource. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

WITH Jamaica’s first licensed casino operator set to commence operations by March next year, once all outstanding conditions are met, the Casino Gaming Commission (CGC) is assuring that stringent guardrails are in place to keep criminal elements out, with operators required to verify players, monitor suspicious transactions, and protect vulnerable gamblers.

Speaking during this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange, both CGC Chief Executive Officer Cleveland Allen and Senior Director of Enforcement and Investigation Damion McKenzie outlined a multi-layered system of checks that will follow casino operations from the moment a player registers to the regulator’s ongoing monitoring of the business.

The safeguards include know-your-customer (KYC) checks, scrutiny of suspicious transactions and sources of wealth, anti-money laundering controls, surveillance systems, responsible-gaming interventions, and direct regulatory access to the casino’s operations.

The officials were speaking as Adamas Grand Casino Limited, Jamaica’s first licensed casino operator, moves towards opening at Princess Grand Jamaica Resort in Green Island, Hanover. The CGC granted the operator its licence on July 29, but the licence is conditional and does not yet authorise the casino to begin operations.

CGC Legal Officer Caleigh Reid said the operator must first satisfy all remaining requirements, with March 31, 2027 set as the deadline to commence operations.

“They have a specific time frame in which to open. There are certain deliverables that they have to satisfy us with, certain things that they have to provide us with before they get the go-ahead. Right now they have the licence, but they are not authorised to begin operations until all of those other deliverables are satisfied, which is all outlined in their conditions of licence,” she said.

The safeguards are intended to address several risks associated with casino gaming, particularly money laundering, organised crime, problem gambling, and the potential exploitation of vulnerable players.

At the heart of the CGC’s financial crime controls will be requirements for casinos to know who their customers are and to scrutinise the money moving through their operations.

According to McKenzie, the regulator will not simply assess an operator’s anti-money laundering system once and walk away.

“A part of our legislation requires us to do ongoing monitoring as it relates to money laundering and proceeds from illicit means. We will continue to monitor, but the training that we provided to our officers… allow them to understand the different typologies that are related to money laundering in the gaming sector, to understand the myriad things that happen that can be classified as money laundering,” McKenzie said.

The commission will also examine whether an operator has properly carried out those checks and whether the financial profile of a player makes sense.

“Our audit plan also allows us to go in and check on persons who have signed up, if you did the proper KYC and anti-money laundering check against this person: What does this person do? How did they come about the cash? The source of wealth? So all those checks continue throughout the lifecycle of the licence,” McKenzie added.

Furthermore, Allen noted that the commission is designated as the competent authority for casino gaming under the Proceeds of Crime Act, with responsibility for anti-money laundering, counter-financing of terrorism and counter-proliferation financing compliance in the casino sector.

He explained that casino gaming in Jamaica is restricted to approved Integrated Resort Developments, meaning a casino cannot operate as a stand-alone gambling establishment.

Therefore, this creates a two-stage screening process.

“At the first stage of the development of it, the Government wants to be satisfied that the operators, the financiers, their funding is from good sources, they have good standing in other jurisdictions, not just for the development but for the operations of the casino… and when you come to stage two, when you come to us, we then conduct our own due diligence, specifically in respect to the conduct and operations of a casino,” Allen said.

He also noted operators will be required to maintain surveillance systems capable of supporting regulatory monitoring, as well as provide space for commission officers at the premises.

“In Las Vegas, on any one casino property, there are about 5,000 cameras. These cameras can zoom in and read the serial number on a note at a table four miles down the road. We have similar surveillance and monitoring requirements for the casino. More than that, the operator is required to have facilities on its premises for the commission and our officers to be able to have access to and at any time go on site and monitor,” Allen said.

The CGC’s guardrails are not limited to criminal activity. Allen explained that the regulator’s responsible-gaming framework is designed to identify people who may be developing harmful gambling habits and provide avenues for intervention.

That framework includes staff training, player information, behaviour monitoring, exclusion and self-exclusion mechanisms, as well as controls on advertising. The commission has worked with the Responsible Gaming Council of Ontario and signed an MOU with RISE Life Management, which has experience in counselling and self-exclusion relating to gambling.

“The mechanism behind responsible gaming is that the staff will be trained to spot persons who have a problem, persons who sit all day and gamble. There’s some form of intervention from the staff to allow some kind of cooling-out period for this individual. Also, because Jamaica will be a cashless system, they’ll also be able to track the pattern of a player to see his betting patterns and some form of intervention can be implemented because of that pattern of constant gambling, constant topping up, constant chasing, constant losses,” he added.

Allen also assured that responsible-gaming controls will extend to how casinos advertise and promote their services.

He said s should not target children or young people and should not rely on influential figures who children might look up to.

He also noted that the CGC intends to leverage existing responsible-gambling programmes, including initiatives involving schools, while keeping casino-related promotion within the resort environment.

World.title: 60 years of Tastee: A celebration of food, music and Jamaican legacy
World.content:
Patrons enjoy the free concert hosted by Tastee Jamaica as part of their 60th anniversary celebrations.(Photo: Karl Mclarty)

FOR 60 years, Tastee Jamaica has commanded the support of Jamaicans, becoming as synonymous with the island as the patty itself. But the company’s legacy stretches far beyond food. Having established itself as a key contributor to the discovery of some of Jamaica’s most talented entertainers, Tastee has firmly cemented its place in the hearts of Jamaicans globally. On Friday night, the company showed its appreciation to its local fanbase, treating scores of Jamaicans to a free concert of the highest entertainment quality.

With Emancipation Park transformed into a sprawling celebration of music and memories, the event was far more than an anniversary concert. Hosted by veteran broadcaster Jennifer “Jenny Jenny” Small, it was as much a celebration of Jamaican music as it was a birthday party for the company. Agent Sasco, Tarrus Riley, King Yellowman, Nadine Sutherland and a host of others created an atmosphere that reflected both legacy and loyalty.

For some of the night’s performers, however, appearing on the Tastee stage carried even greater significance, having gained their break in the industry decades ago through the talent search spearheaded by the company.

“We a eat patty over 60 years. Big up Tastee. Tastee is the one that make people know me international,” said King Yellowman as he paused his set to remind the audience of his third-place finish in the inaugural Tastee Talent Contest in 1979.

Giving a commanding performance, Yellowman treated the crowd to a short yet energetic set, which included songs such as I’m Getting Married in the Morning and Zungguzungguguzungguzeng.

Also turning in a vibrant performance was the 1979 competition winner, Nadine Sutherland. She performed hits such as Action, Starvation — which she released a year after her win — and Babyface. In what she described as a full-circle moment, Sutherland recalled how Tastee changed her life when she was just 11 years old.

“I’m still in disbelief that it’s been 46 years since the 11-year-old me was brave enough to get on that stage. I was known as ‘the little girl from Above Rocks’ who was brimming with confidence. I had to draw back for that little girl tonight and just soak it all in. I’m grateful that I’m still here, and I still love this,” she said.

Tastee’s own story began in 1966 when Vincent and Valerie Chang opened the company’s first operation at Union Square in downtown Kingston. As demand grew, the business expanded, eventually establishing its headquarters in Cross Roads and developing a footprint across the island. Somewhere along that journey, Tastee’s relationship with Jamaica began extending beyond what it served across the counter.

Over its decades-long run, the Tastee Talent Contest — later known as the Tastee Talent Trail — became an important proving ground for emerging Jamaican performers, including Beenie Man, Papa San, Cobra, Mr Vegas, T.O.K., Glacia Robinson, Brian and Tony Gold, and several others.

It was therefore little surprise that the company received an abundance of praise from the night’s performers.

That spirit of giving was not confined to Tastee’s entertainment history. After the company awarded 13 students $60,000 each towards tuition through its back-to-school initiative, Agent Sasco extended the gesture from the stage, committing to cover the tuition of another high-school student.

Sasco’s giveback didn’t stop there, as he treated patrons to a delightful set, which included spirited performances of crowd favourites such as Winning Right Now, Hand To Mouth, Hand Inna Di Air, Idiot Thing Dat, Banks of the Hope, and others.

Alaine also turned in a quality set, performing songs such as Dreaming, Rise In Love, Bye Bye and Ordinary Love.

Abijah, Carey Sayles, Tony Rebel, Sista Pat, Tarrus Riley, Richie Stephens and saxophonist Dean Fraser were among the evening’s other performers, rounding out a musical package that traversed generations and genres.

Speaking with the Jamaica Observer following the concert, patrons sought to explain Tastee’s longevity. Noting that not many companies would think to give back to their supporters in such a tangible way, concertgoers said Tastee’s knack for recognising the support of its consumers has helped establish its 60-year legacy.

“Tastee is not just about the patties. They’ve always been about giving back in some way, shape or form. If it weren’t for Tastee, Jamaica and the world would not have discovered talent such as Beenie Man, Yellowman, Nadine Sutherland, and so many others,” said Suzette Morgan.

“Their dedication to the Jamaican people has always been evident and it was proven again tonight when they hosted this free concert. The fact that we didn’t have to pay anything didn’t take away from the quality of the show. We got solid performances while we nibbled away on patties. It was a perfect way to celebrate their anniversary.”

Marcia Stewart agreed.

“Tastee is big in Jamaica because it’s big on supporting Jamaicans. We love our patty and the company has proven over the years that they value the support of their consumers. Hosting a free concert showed exactly how much they appreciate Jamaicans, and I hope they last another 60 years,” she said.

Friday night proved that while patties built the Tastee name, the company’s legacy has also been shaped by the love of the Jamaican people.

For decades, Tastee fed Jamaicans more than simply food. Through its talent competition, it also helped feed an entertainment industry that would eventually send some of the artistes it discovered onto stages around the world.

Behind the songs, the memories and generations of performers sharing one stage was the story of a Jamaican institution that has managed to remain part of the country’s everyday rhythm for six decades.

At 60, that relationship remains as much a part of Tastee’s legacy as the patties themselves.

World.title: Jamaica secures Tottori training base
World.content:
(From left, front) Tottori Athletics Association President Shinichi Hamasaki, Jamaica Athletics Administrative Association President Garth Gayle and Tottori Prefecture Governor Shinji Hirai; (back) Local Government Minister Desmond McKenzie, Sports Minister Olivia Grange and Japan’s Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Jamaica Kohei Maruyama during yesterday’s ceremonial signing of a partnership agreement between Jamaica and Tottori Prefecture in Kingston.Garfield Robinson

JAMAICA’S preparations for the 2027 World Athletics Championships received a boost yesterday with the signing of a 2027 World Athletics Championships Training Camp Agreement between Jamaica and Tottori Prefecture in Japan.

The agreement represents the latest chapter in a sporting partnership that began in 2007 following the World Athletics Championships in Osaka and has since developed into a nearly two-decade relationship built around athletics, cultural exchange and friendship.

Garth Gayle, president of the Jamaica Athletics Administrative Association (JAAA), was pleased with the agreement, which he believes sets the tone for a successful campaign at the championships.

“We want to ensure the best facilities and all that is needed for a successful campaign in Beijing 2027,” Gayle said.

Gayle says the Japanese will provide additional technical support, while the camp will also allow Jamaica to stage trial meets for its athletes. He said the trial meets proved pivotal for Oblique Seville, who went on to strike gold at the 2025 World Athletics Championships in Tokyo.

“The camp also allows the athletes to acclimatise as there is not much difference between Japan and China, so this is a good opportunity for coaches, managers and athletes to get ready for a successful championship,” Gayle said.

Sports Minister Olivia Grange described the renewed agreement as an important step in strengthening Jamaica’s sporting diplomacy and international partnerships.
