“Today’s signing represents another decisive step in strengthening Jamaica’s sporting diplomacy, international partnerships and preparations for continued success globally,” Grange said.

She said the relationship with Tottori had evolved beyond simply providing Jamaican athletes with a venue to train, becoming a lasting friendship between Jamaica and Japan.

“What began in 2007, in the wake of the World Athletics Championships in Osaka, has evolved into more than a training arrangement. It has become a lasting friendship between Jamaica and Tottori,” Grange said.

The partnership has already produced tangible benefits for Jamaica’s athletes, particularly through the 2025 training camp ahead of the World Championships in Tokyo.

Grange says Team Jamaica was provided with world-class facilities and comprehensive support services, allowing athletes and staff to concentrate fully on competition preparation.

She also highlighted the contribution of hundreds of volunteers, interpreters, medical personnel, officials, sponsors and community members who helped make the Jamaican delegation feel at home during its stay.

Grange also pointed to exchanges between Jamaican athletes and Japanese communities, including a visit by Assinie Wilson, Kelly-Ann Beckford and teammates to students at Hakuto Special Needs School. That interaction subsequently inspired the Buddy Art Project, through which artwork created by students with disabilities was incorporated into flags displayed to welcome the Jamaican delegation.

Other exchanges included Jamaican athletes interacting with kindergarten children in Sendai, where they played games and received handmade medals.

“These moments remind us that this relationship extends far beyond training and competition; it is a bond of friendship, community, and shared humanity,” Grange said.

The sporting ties between the two countries have also been strengthened through the Japan Exchange and Teaching Programme, which saw Jamaican Olympian Christine Day appointed Jamaica’s first sports exchange advisor.

Day is based in Tottori, where she shares her sprinting knowledge and mentors athletes, providing another avenue for the development of athletics and cultural links between Jamaica and Japan.

Tottori Governor Shinji Hirai and Chairman Shinichi Hamazaki attended the signing and greeted guests in Jamaican dialect with “What a gwaan” before reverting to Japanese, with their remarks translated by an interpreter.

Minister of Local Government and Community Development Desmond McKenzie was also on hand for the signing and highlighted the broader relationship between Jamaica and Japan, including the friendship and cooperation between Tottori Prefecture and Westmoreland.

McKenzie says Jamaica and Japan are celebrating 62 years of bilateral relations, with cooperation extending beyond sport into community development, emergency communications and economic revitalisation.

He also highlighted the impact of Japan’s Grant Assistance for Grassroots Human Projects programme on micro and small businesses and municipal corporations, while noting the Social Development Commission’s continued collaboration with Japan on community initiatives, including sport.

World.title: MESSI’S IMPACT
World.content:
Argentina Captain Lionel Messi poses with the FIFA World Cup Trophy after Argentina won the 2022 World Cup final football match against France at Lusail Stadium in Lusail, Qatar, on Sunday, December 18, 2022. (Photo: AFP)

FOLLOWING Lionel Messi’s decision to retire from international football, Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts believes the Argentine legend has made a significant impact on Jamaican football through his exploits on the international stage.

Messi made the announcement in a statement on social media on Monday, bringing an end to his 21-year stint with the national team.

“This is one that hurts me a lot. I love, I loved, and I will always love being part of the national team. I gave everything I had, and I don’t have anything more to give,” he said.

“I leave with peace and pride, knowing that together with my teammates we gave you moments we once dreamed of. It was crazy to experience all of this with you. I love you! Thank you God for making me Argentine.”

The 39-year-old cemented his legacy in 2022 after guiding Argentina to the FIFA World Cup, ending a 36-year drought. He almost made it two World Cup title lifts in a row in this summer’s World Cup in the USA, Mexico and Canada but went down 1-0 to Spain in the final.

Eight-time Ballon d’Or winner Messi leaves as the country’s all-time leading goal scorer and most capped player with 125 goals in 207 appearances. He also led Argentina to the 2021 and 2024 Copa America titles and the gold medal at the 2008 Olympics in Beijing.

Ricketts says Messi’s contribution on football, particularly in Jamaica, cannot be ignored.

“Messi in contemporary football would be arguably the most talked about player and probably the most highly rated player right now. He would have impacted the lives of so many young boys and girls,” Ricketts told the Jamaica Observer. “If you walk around any township, you will always see somebody, some youngster wearing a shirt marked Messi and that just goes to show what sport generally, and what football in particular, can do to the psyche of a nation.”

“Every good thing must come to an end and it has been an era for Messi and even his impact on the just-concluded World Cup speaks volumes for his footballing skills and of course the impact that he would have made in global football. Truly, Messi has impacted not just Jamaica but the world.”

One of Messi’s milestone international games came against the Reggae Boyz, when he made his 100th appearance for Argentina in a 1-0 win at the 2015 Copa America in Chile.

Former national midfielder Jobi McAnuff played the full 90 minutes and swapped shirts with Messi at full time, which he says is one of the greatest moments of his career.

McAnuff, though, says he developed an even greater respect for the Argentine maestro after his kind gesture towards the entire Jamaican team following the game.

“There was a queue of Jamaican players, staff, everything, waiting for him outside the changing room,” he said. “He just took his time, signed every autograph, shaking hands, pictures, like [he was] class. He did not have to do that. They’re the little things for me that just set him apart for me, yes he’s a great footballer, but we come back to people as people and just respect that you can show to people.”

The Reggae Boyz would face off with Messi again seven years later in an international friendly in New Jersey, just months before lifting his first-ever World Cup title. Messi came off the bench and scored twice to lead Argentina to a 3-0 win.

“Everybody wanted to get to the touching distance of Messi — not even so much to touch him, but to get close to him — and a number of our players tried to embrace him, tried to take pictures with him. Our coaching staff really wanted to be identified with arguably one of the best footballers of all time,” Ricketts recalled.

“I don’t know if it’s fair to say we have lost an icon but he has now gone into retirement, but the name Messi will probably live forever in the minds of those who have an interest in the sport of football.”

Many players over the years have been dubbed the “next Messi”, including former Reggae Boy Chevone Marsh, who earned the nickname during his days at Cavalier FC and Calabar High.

Ricketts says the chances of the world producing another Messi are slim but hasn’t ruled it out, especially with the possibility that talent could come from Jamaica.

“What has happened in recent times is that coaching education now has improved leaps and bounds, not just locally, but throughout the Caribbean, throughout Concacaf and throughout the world,” he said.

“We would have established probably the best coaching education programme, so it’s not far-fetched. It’s not impossible but certainly, based on the newness of our coaching skills and our coaching workshops, it’s not far-fetched. It’s certainly not impossible.”

World.title: Fashion Radar: House of Clay
World.content:
​An intimate behind-the-scenes moment dressing the bride on her wedding day in an off-white stretch-satin slip gown. (Photo courtesy of House of Clay)

Tuesday Style Fashion (TSF) spotlights Keisha Allen, creative director of luxury for bridal fashion brand House of Clay.

TSF: Please share your House of Clay story — how you started, and the reason behind the name.

House of Clay: My journey to House of Clay officially began when I studied garment production and fashion design for two years at Garmex HEART Academy between 2005 and 2007. Following my training, my first job was at a prominent bridal boutique here in Jamaica. That experience proved to be pivotal. I fell in love with the transformational power of a wedding gown — that exact moment when a woman saw herself in the right dress and her entire demeanour changed. I could physically see her confidence bloom and watch her realise just how beautiful she was. I knew then that I wanted to dedicate my life to creating that feeling for women of all shapes and sizes.

Working directly with gowns from international designers and doing minor alterations also exposed me to global standards. I had already resolved in my heart before that any brand I built would be of such high quality that it could stand beside any international designer brand and not feel out of place. Seeing those gowns up close simply confirmed that this was standard work I could definitely do and surpass.

The reason behind the name ties back to my faith. I remember reading a story in Jeremiah 18 about a potter working at his wheel, taking a vessel of clay that didn’t turn out as he wanted, squashing it, and starting over to reshape it. I thought about the significance of how a potter takes a lump of clay — which, to most people, and as we say in Jamaica, is really just “dirt” — and turns it into something meaningful. Clay seems insignificant to the untrained eye, yet in the hands of a skilled artisan, it becomes a masterpiece. That mirrors my process with textiles. Taking a flat, two-dimensional piece of fabric and sculpting it to perfectly contour or fit a three-dimensional woman’s body is an art form.

Initially, the brand was simply supposed to just be called Clay. However, when we went to register the business in 2011, we were told we couldn’t register the single word “Clay” on its own because it’s a common substance, so we had to add something to it and registered as “Clay Fashioned.” But that felt a bit too on-the-nose so I could not settle with it. Having always been a fan of global couture houses, I realised that many of them use “House of” before their brand name — like House of Chanel. I knew this was the kind of house and legacy I was building, so we decided on House of Clay in 2015. While our inner garment labels simply read “Clay,” the company name reflects our commitment to couture, uncompromising quality, and the legacy we are building in how we make women feel… like “The Most Beautiful Woman in the Room”.

TSF:When did you thread that first needle and know this was your destiny?

House of Clay: I don’t think I knew it was my destiny the exact moment I threaded my first needle. As a child, I was always making clothes for my dolls. My father was very perceptive and good at recognising those subtle traits and creative gifts, so he bought me my first sewing kit when I was about nine years old. Even then, I wasn’t dreaming of fashion yet — I actually wanted to be a paediatrician!

It wasn’t until high school, around third form, that I realised I had a bit of a love-hate relationship with the sciences. I started evaluating what I genuinely loved doing and what I was naturally good at. I loved working with my hands, creating, and engaging in meticulous tasks like hand-sewing and embroidery — even the most tedious parts. That was when the thought clearly hit me: I want to be a fashion designer. From that moment on, I set my mind to pursuing it.

I grew up with a very meticulous mother, so a detailed and deliberate approach to my work came naturally. Because of that, I was never drawn to “fast” fashion or quick, ready-to-wear pieces you could whip up in a few hours. In my early days, of course, I made those kinds of garments because I had to master every aspect of garment construction. But I found that I was always most at peace, happy, and in my element when doing intricate, labour-intensive work — like hand-beading an entire gown over several days. Where others might feel anxious or restless during such tedious processes, I enter a state of complete calm and focus. Looking back, I realise that inclination is rare; even among talented creators, not everyone gravitates toward the technical, painstaking side of couture. That affinity was the quiet signal that this was where I belonged.

TSF:Why wedding dresses?

House of Clay: There are two primary reasons why I chose bridal wear. First, from a purely technical standpoint, bridal is the pinnacle of couture. Virtually every major couture runway show concludes with a showstopping bridal gown because it represents the highest, most complex form of garment construction — and naturally, that level of craftsmanship is where I gravitated.

Second, and most importantly, a wedding dress is arguably the most significant garment a woman will ever wear in her lifetime. From my earliest days working with brides, I fell in love with being part of that sacred moment. It is a true privilege to create something that doesn’t just fit a woman, but honours her and helps her feel breathtakingly beautiful and confident on one of the most important days of her life.

TSF: Take us back to the completion of that first gown.

House of Clay: When that very first bride trusts you with her wedding gown, the feeling is almost overwhelming. It comes with an incredible sense of reverence, paired with a genuine fear of messing up — because you know this is not just an ordinary dress; it is monumentally important to her. Looking back, I felt the fear and did it anyway, pouring absolutely everything I had into it. As a naturally creative person, the design aspect is often the easy part. Designing simply takes deep compassion — listening intently to what the bride desires, understanding her fears, and being mindful of her insecurities. Once you have that connection, and hopefully taste, creativity naturally flows to create a beautiful design. What truly makes it a masterpiece — what sets the process apart, is the technical execution — the desire and discipline to operate at the absolute highest standard.

After weeks upon weeks of meticulous, painstaking labour, stepping back to look at that finished gown on the hanger and thinking, “Wow, I made that,” was incredible. But the most significant moment — the moment that still defines my work to this day — is when she puts it on. Seeing her posture shift, her expression change, and watching that same transformational confidence and joy wash over her is my ultimate reward. Experiencing that same feeling that first made me fall in love with bridal wear as a young consultant confirmed everything for me.

TSF: Who in the field of wedding gowns do you most admire and why?

House of Clay: When I was first starting out, the designer I admired most was Vera Wang. Back then, her name was completely synonymous with luxury bridal, but what fascinated me was that she wasn’t creating typical, traditional wedding dresses. She essentially turned the bridal industry on its head.

She stepped into the space without trying to conform to it, which I thought was brilliant, brave, and deeply admirable. Her approach proved that there are always brides who want to wear something that authentically represents who they are, rather than simply following traditional expectations. That willingness to innovate and stay true to a distinct artistic vision is something I have always respected.

The Core Ethos of House of Clay



At the heart of House of Clay are three fundamental brand pillars that define every single gown we create:

Transformation: We believe that every woman’s body is inherently beautiful, regardless of shape or size. Our philosophy is that a woman should never have to force herself to fit into a gown; rather, the gown must be engineered to honour and fit her unique structure and architecture. It is about accentuating who she is so she feels completely radiant and confident.

Craftsmanship: This is at the very soul of what we do — from technical pattern drafting to intricate hand-finishing. In today’s fashion climate, true pattern drafting has become somewhat of a lost art, with many relying on shortcuts like “freehand cutting”. We hold fast to the mastery of pattern drafting because it unlocks endless structural possibilities and ensures precision fit right from the initial foundation. Coupled with traditional couture finishing techniques and meticulous attention to internal details (down to the millimeter on every seam allowance), our garments are built to world-class standards.

Made in Jamaica: We take immense pride in our roots. Jamaica is world-renowned for its global impact in music and athletics — we have given the world reggae and the fastest athletes alive. We believe Jamaican fashion deserves that exact same global stage. Growing up, there was often a stigma attached to local dressmaking, where “Made in Jamaica” was associated with ill-fitting, homemade, or poor-quality garments. House of Clay is actively dismantling that narrative. Everything we produce is designed and crafted in-house right here in Jamaica, serving as a standard for couture, luxury, and excellence.

Photos: Terry-Ann Miller | Merrick Cousley Photography | Courtesy of Keisha Allen

World.title: Sheree Martin named first female CEO of NCBJ, effective Sept 1
World.content:
Sheree Martin appointed CEO of National Commercial Bank Jamaica

KINGSTON, Jamaica — After months of acting in the post, Sheree Martin has been appointed chief executive officer by the Board of National Commercial Bank Jamaica Limited (NCBJ), effective September 1, 2026.

She will be the first woman to hold the post.

Martin served as interim CEO since January 19, 2026, leading the bank’s strategic and operational priorities with a focus on efficiency, governance and the customer experience.

In a statement, the bank said her appointment provides continuity as it continues to work on the same priorities.

Group Chief Executive Officer of NCB Financial Group Limited and Chairman of NCBJ Robert Almeida said Martin’s leadership during the interim period reinforced the board’s confidence in her ability to lead the bank.

“Sheree brings deep institutional knowledge, a strong understanding of our customers and a clear appreciation of how the different parts of the Bank must work together to deliver,” Almeida said.

“She combines strategic judgement with practical, hands-on leadership and a strong focus on execution. These qualities will serve NCBJ well as it builds on the progress already underway.”

Martin said she was honoured by the appointment and energised by the opportunities ahead.

“NCBJ has an extraordinary legacy, talented people and a vital role in the lives of our customers and in Jamaica’s development,” she said. “I look forward to working with our board and teams to build on that foundation – accelerating our progress, strengthening the customer experience and bringing the full capabilities of the bank together more effectively.”

She added, “Our priorities are clear: empower our people within the right culture, improve the way we deliver and earn our customers’ confidence through the quality and consistency of the service, financial solutions and platforms they experience every day.”

Martin brings more than 20 years of executive leadership experience across the financial services and energy sectors. Before assuming the role of interim CEO at NCB, she had leadership responsibility for several functions including retail banking, operations, credit underwriting, marketing and enterprise information management.

World.title: Former gang member found guilty of murdering Tupac Shakur
World.content:
Rapper Tupac Shakur attends a voter registration event in South Central Los Angeles, August15, 1996. (AP Photo/Frank Wiese, File)

LAS VEGAS, United States (AFP) — Duane Davis, a former Los Angeles gang member, was found guilty on Monday by a Las Vegas court of the 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur.

Thirty years after the rap legend’s death at a Las Vegas casino, the jury found Davis, 63, guilty of murder after just a few hours of deliberation.

World.title: What Iceland’s snub means for the EU’s place in the world
World.content:
“At a time when the international security environment has become far more uncertain than it was a decade ago, many expected support for reopening accession negotiations to grow,” said Nicola Procaccini, co-chair of the right-wing European Conservatives and Reformists group in the European Parliament. “The fact that the Icelandic people nevertheless chose not to take even that first step should give Brussels pause.”

Reykjavik’s narrow rejection of restarting EU accession talks in a referendum on Saturday is hardly a death blow to the 450 million-strong bloc. With fewer than 400,000 people and a smaller GDP than Estonia, Iceland was never the prize that would make or break Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s European project.

But the result is still an uncomfortable reality check for a Brussels establishment that has spent the past four years betting that a hazardous world would make the EU more attractive — and had taken Iceland’s renewed interest as a flattering signal of its own relevance.

“A nation weighed what membership would add to what it already has,” center-right Finnish MEP Mika Aaltola said, “and answered: not enough.”

Vote of (no) confidence

Enlargement is about more than adding countries to the EU. It is also a branding exercise: a way for Brussels to show that its model of democracy, prosperity and predictability remains attractive in a world of hard power politics.

Every country that knocks on the EU’s door gives the bloc a chance to present itself as a desirable club, in contrast to Trump’s claims that the continent is “decaying.” Iceland was unusually useful in that regard: a wealthy democracy that paused its membership bid in 2015, but was coming back and asking to be let in.

World.title: Ed Miliband to attend EU foreign ministers meeting in Ireland
World.content:
“Working closely with our European neighbours will make Britain a wealthier, safer country- that is why I am putting the European relationship at the heart of my agenda as Foreign Secretary,” Miliband said ahead of the meeting, which will take place in Wicklow in Ireland.

The foreign secretary is set to hold a series of bilateral meetings, including with his EU counterpart Kaja Kallas and German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul.

He is also due to meet his Irish counterpart Helen McEntree, Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand and Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha — the latter two also attending the meeting as guests.

Ahead of the meeting the Foreign Office said the discussions would focus on deepening U.K. cooperation with European and international partners, as well as supporting Ukraine.

He is expected to announce new British funding to support reconstruction in the invasion-hit country, as well as measures to allow British companies to participate in rebuilding efforts there.

Ministers will also discuss wider challenges facing the continent such as climate pressures — following the hottest summer on record in the U.K.

The so-called “Gymnich” meeting is meant to be a more informal setting than most EU summits so leaders can speak candidly without officials.

The format is named after the German castle Schloss Gymnich which hosted the first such meeting in 1974.

World.title: Team up with EU on energy to combat China, Andy Burnham told
World.content:
These moves would help support investment in the North Sea, address price instability and protect companies on both sides of the channel from incoming carbon border taxes.

But it also suggests going further — with a view to establishing regional independence on green energy.

Competing with China

The authors argue that the U.K. rejoining the North Sea Energy Cooperation Group (NSEC) as a full member would make it easier to coordinate energy investments like carbon capture storage, energy interconnectors and offshore wind farms — crucial to the green transition.

Since Brexit, the U.K. has only been a partial member of the deliberative body via a memorandum of understanding, but full membership would make “technocratic planning challenges around grid build-out” a lot easier to navigate, the authors say.

The report also argues for another extension of the grace period on electric vehicle battery rules of origin, which has been plaguing car manufacturers on both sides of the channel since Britains’s exit.

It also warns that in the long term, battery production and the rest of the EV supply chain need to be moved as far as possible to Europe from China.

World.title: France, Germany back call for faster, more efficient EU decisions in foreign and security policy
World.content:
Germany, in particular, has led calls to move from unanimity voting on CFSP to so-called qualified majority voting (QMV), but France, among other states, has traditionally opposed such a change. The letter opens the door to greater use of QMV without explicitly endorsing any wholesale change in voting methods.

"We continue to strive for consensus wherever possible," reads the letter signed by the foreign ministers of Austria, Sweden, Denmark, Finland, Belgium, the Netherlands, Romania and Spain in addition to France and Germany. " But we must also ensure that this culture of consensus fosters common action rather than preventing it — otherwise we will have legitimacy but no strength."

The steps outlined in the letter are:

Emphasizing the principle of "sincere cooperation" between EU states — meaning that countries must honor commitments they have made to one another, even if they are not strictly legally binding. Using "constructive abstentions" rather than outright vetoes, "so as not to prevent the Union from acting." Banning linkage of "unrelated matters" to an issue being debated — or cracking down on the practice of holding collective decisions hostage by threatening a veto unless the others agree to a separate national demand. Encouraging the EU's chief diplomat, currently Kaja Kallas, to explore treaty-based options to improve decision-making. The treaty-based option most commonly invoked is the so-called Passerelle clause, which allows the EU to change decision-making rules without changing any treaties — for example, to allow QMV voting on specific foreign and security policy matters. Emphasizing the need to spell out the reasons why a country invokes its veto rights for "vital and stated reasons of national policy," namely when a decision is taken by qualified majority.

The letter is due to be discussed this week as foreign ministers gather in Wicklow, Ireland for informal talks in the Gymnich format.

Those talks will also explore options for reforming the European External Action Service, the EU diplomatic branch headed by High Representative Kallas.

According to a Franco-German letter seen by POLITICO, options for reforming the EEAS include making Kallas an executive vice president of the European Commission with "de facto" oversight of external-facing policy units as regards trade, development aid and defense; and embedding much of the EEAS's staff inside the Commission in a new department for external relations.

Staff focused on security and defense policy would remain in the EEAS, and the ratio of one-third of EEAS staff being seconded diplomats from EU states would be maintained in this new unit.

The discussion paper also emphasizes the role of EU states in shaping foreign policy, envisaging a formal role for the High Representative to report to EU leaders on foreign policy matters and receive instructions directly from them during European Council gatherings.

World.title: EU chief diplomat taps ex-political, military leaders for defense group
World.content:
Kaja Kallas announced a high-level group made of former political and military leaders who will reflect on how the bloc can defend itself amid a changing U.S. presence. | Ezra Acayan/AFP via Getty Images

The taskforce will focus on European defense as the bloc faces growing pressure to take more responsibility for its own security.

Kaja Kallas, the EU's chief diplomat, announced Tuesday a high-level group made of former political and military leaders who will reflect on how the bloc can defend itself amid a changing U.S. presence.

The new body, which will be launched next week, will include prominent figures from the European Union as well as the United Kingdom and Ukraine, she announced at the start of an informal defense ministers' meeting in Ireland.

"Of course NATO remains the cornerstone of our European security. At the same time, the United States is also calling on European allies to assume greater responsibility for our own defense," said Kallas, who coordinates foreign and security policy on behalf of the EU's 27 member countries.

"Why have these political and military leaders? They can also say things that we, as institutions, cannot," she added. A spokesperson for Kallas did not specify who will join the group.

The former Estonian prime minister added that the aim of the group was not to work on replicating U.S. defense capabilities but to focus on defending European territory by using "unique strengths" while also using the "extensive operational experience of Ukraine" to "challenge conventional thinking."

World.title: Keir Starmer will force by-election after quitting as member of parliament
World.content:
Starmer, who has represented Holborn and St Pancras since 2015, added: “I will also continue, as I have done for a long time now with others, work on combating violence against women and girls; that is an issue that matters to me hugely. It’s work I started before I became an MP and it’s work I’m keen to continue after I’m an MP.”

His resignation will trigger a by-election — a big electoral test for Andy Burnham, his successor in Downing Street.

He follows other former prime ministers, including David Cameron and Tony Blair, in leaving the Commons soon after or immediately following their departure from No. 10 Downing Street.

The ex-PM held the Holborn and St Pancras seat in 2024 with an 11,572 majority, but faced a strong challenge from a left-wing independent and the Greens.

Zack Polanski’s left-wing environmentalists are likely to form the biggest challenge to Labour in the normally safe London seat.

A Green Party spokesperson suggested Polanski could contest the seat himself.

“Zack has always made it clear he would like to be a London MP. London has been his home for over 20 years,” they said.

Burnham paid tribute to Starmer in a House of Commons statement Tuesday, telling MPs he gave the U.K. “a lifetime of public service.”

World.title: EU’s Kallas says Hormuz diplomacy has produced ‘no results’
World.content:
European Commission High Representative and Vice President Kaja Kallas arrives at Druids Glen during an informal meeting of EU defence ministers at Wicklow, south of Dublin on September 1, 2026. | Paul Faith/AFP via Getty Images

Her comments come after U.S. forces struck Iranian positions near Larak Island on Sunday.

EU top diplomat Kaja Kallas said Tuesday that diplomatic efforts to defuse the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz had produced “no results at the moment.”

Speaking to reporters in Wicklow, Ireland, ahead of an informal meeting of EU defense ministers, Kallas said that “the freedom of navigation needs to be respected,” insisting ships should not be charged to use previously open routes.

“For us it is important that there are no tolls, no fees, for these routes that have been open before,” she added. Ministers will also discuss protecting critical undersea infrastructure.

World.title: Le Pen sparks backlash with hijab ban proposal
World.content:
The proposal is dominating the French political news cycle after a lawmaker from Le Pen’s National Rally said Sunday that wearing the hijab in public would become a fineable offense if she took office. Le Pen is currently polling with a double-digit lead ahead of the first round of the spring 2027 French presidential election.

Left-wing political leaders and civil liberties advocates in France lambasted Le Pen’s proposal as Islamophobic and discriminatory. The hijab is a headscarf worn by some Muslim women.

Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leading leftist candidate for next year’s presidential election, according to the most recent polling, accused Le Pen of wanting to set up an “Iranian-style clothing police” in a post on X. SOS Racisme, a French anti-racism watchdog, said Le Pen was looking to “chase Muslim women out of public areas.”

Center-right candidate Edouard Philippe said the state should focus on combatting “Islamism and extremists, not French Muslims,” and conservative candidate Bruno Retailleau argued it would be a poor use of police resources.

Debate about the hijab, which is worn by 26 percent of French Muslim women aged 18 to 49 according to a 2023 report from the French national statistics agency, regularly comes up in France.

It is one of the few European countries to have entirely outlawed wearing full-face veils in public and was the only country to ban its own athletes from wearing the hijab during the 2024 Olympics in Paris. Religious head coverings, including hijabs and kippas, have been banned in schools since 2004.

World.title: EU’s green fashion rules face test as global emissions rise 6.3%
World.content:
The global apparel and fashion industry is moving in the wrong direction on climate emissions, with greenhouse gas emissions rising 6.3% in 2024 compared to the previous year, despite a growing number of companies investing in renewable energy, cleaner materials and coal phase-outs, according to the Apparel Impact Institute’s latest assessment.

 

The increase in emissions was driven largely by higher fibre consumption, particularly polyester, putting the European Union's fashion industry further away from its goal of cutting emissions 45% by 2030 from 2019 levels.

Since roughly 80% to 90% of the EU's fashion footprint lies outside of Europe, according to the European Environment Agency, the EU’s sustainability laws are specifically designed to penalise "outsourced" pollution through a few key mechanisms.

Nonetheless, end-of-life products remain in the EU, with roughly 12.6 million tonnes of textile waste generated in the EU per year.

According to the World Integrated Trade Solution, China is the top textile exporter to the EU, with over €26.5 billion in apparel and accounting for roughly one-third of all textile and clothing products sold in Europe. Bangladesh ranks second, followed by Turkey, India, Pakistan, Vietnam and Morocco.

For the EU, which is tightening rules around fashion to make the industry more circular, new data from the Apparel Impact Institute suggests that clothing production will keep rising even if the bloc's laws succeed in cutting emissions.

"Decarbonising apparel requires action on both sides of the equation: reducing the carbon intensity of material production and manufacturing, while also addressing the growth in material volumes that can outpace those gains," reads the report.

In a bid to end the growth in textile waste, Brussels has introduced a package of measures aimed at changing how clothes are designed, sold and eventually discarded. The EU has also moved to make fashion companies financially responsible for the waste they generate.

But the apparel industry's rising emissions suggest that waste policy alone will not solve the climate problem. The industry's biggest source of emissions is linked to the processing of materials.

Polluting non-EU factories

According to the Apparel Impact Institute's report, textile processing accounts for about 51% of apparel emissions, followed by raw-material production at 26%.

That puts the spotlight on the factories producing fabrics and fibres, many of which are outside the EU.

The bloc can regulate what is sold on its single market, but most of the emissions associated with European consumers' clothes occur in global supply chains, resulting in a clash between EU industrial and climate policy.

With this backdrop, European policymakers are under pressure to decarbonise supply chains while simultaneously responding to concerns from industry about regulation, costs and competitiveness.

The same tension arises from the industry's perspective, according to the report. Manufacturers frequently lack the financing to invest in energy efficiency and renewable power, while clean electricity and alternatives to coal can remain unavailable or too expensive in key production countries. In many cases, sustainable materials can also cost more than conventional alternatives.

The report argues that brands need to share the financial and operational burden with suppliers through longer-term purchasing commitments, project financing and closer partnerships.

It also calls for climate targets to be converted into actual factory-level investment, particularly in energy- and heat-intensive textile processing.

"This includes improving access to appropriate finance, sharing project costs and risks, providing stable and longer-term purchasing commitments and aligning commercial relationships with decarbonisation objectives,” reads the report.

More sustainable fashion

Swedish major international fashion retailer H&M reduced the number of supplier factories using on-site coal boilers from 118 in 2022 to just 10 by the end of 2025, the report reveals.

Industrial electrification is also emerging as an alternative. Heat pumps are being deployed for processes such as laundry, dyeing and drying, while Lenzing, a company that produces wood-based cellulosic fibers, and power generation company VERBUND have commissioned a 14 MW power-to-heat facility in Austria that uses renewable electricity to provide industrial heat.

However, under business-as-usual assumptions, apparel emissions could reach 1.277 gigatonnes in 2030, compared with the 489 million tonnes the sector would need to reach to remain on a 1.5°C-compatible trajectory under the UN Paris Agreement.

Even if factories become more efficient and switch to cleaner energy, the report warns, it will not be enough if the industry keeps producing more carbon-intensive materials like fiber.

World.title: GPHG 2026: Our favourite luxury timepieces vying for top watch industry awards
World.content:
The watch world and its legion of followers found out on Tuesday which 84 timepieces are in the running for the 2026 Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève, the industry's top honour.

 

Spread across 14 categories, each of the shortlisted timepieces are truly remarkable. The nominees a Moscow workshop taking on the Swiss giants, a wearable solar system, and a 10-kilo clock that winds your watch while you sleep.

Each of the contenders will compete for one of the 19 prizes celebrating contemporary watchmaking creativity, including the prestigious 'Aiguille d'Or' Grand Prix.

The winners will be revealed at a glittering award ceremony in Geneva on Saturday 7 November and you can watch the event live on Euronews Culture. But, before then, here's a look at some of the pieces that have captured our hearts and minds.

Konstantin Chaykin — ThinKing Mystery

Category: Mechanical Exception

Take two credit cards and stack them: 1.65 mm. That's the thickness of this mechanical marvel, which happens to be wearing a mysterious little smile.

Maybe because while the big Swiss houses were busy fighting over the world's-thinnest record, an independent watchmaker landed a serious blow from his workshop in Moscow. The ThinKing Mystery is billed as the thinnest series-produced mechanical watch in the world.

Konstantin Chaykin's ThinKing Mystery Credit: GPHG©

Let’s unravel the mystery: there is no watch inside the case. The case is the watch. It doubles as the movement's mainplate. Two transparent sapphire discs display the time, and you never see what's turning them. 12 pieces. €426,000.

Christiaan van der Klaauw — CVDK Grand Planetarium Eccentric Silicium

Category: Mechanical Exception

A walk under a starry sky will never feel quite the same once you're wearing this. The eight planets of the solar system, hand-painted, light up on your wrist — each one exactly where it sits in the real sky.

Christiaan Van Der Klaauw's Grand Planetarium Eccentric Silicium Credit: GPHG©

The dial is made of iridescent oxidised silicon. The planets orbit across it in real time and at their true speed. Mercury laps the dial in three months. None of us will live to watch Neptune complete its orbit, which takes 165 years. The Dutch house already won the Calendar and Astronomy category in 2021. 6 pieces. €157,000.

Ulysse Nardin X Urwerk — UR-FREAK

Category: Complication

When two of the most explosive names in independent watchmaking finally get together, you end up with a watch that has neither hands nor a crown.

When two become one: Ulysee Nardin and Urwerk's UR Freak Credit: GPHG©

The Freak collection, launched in 2001 and already crowned in the Iconic category in 2023, tore up the rulebook: the entire movement rotates on itself and doubles as the hand.

Urwerk brings its house speciality, the satellite hours: cubes mounted on rotating arms, with the active figure travelling along the minute scale. The movement pivots every three hours around a silicon balance wheel. Two radical grammars in a single watch. It's quite something to say the least. 100 pieces. €115,000.

L.Leroy — Vox Temporis

Category: Artistic Crafts

Napoleon, Marie-Antoinette and Proust all read the time on a watch from L.Leroy, pioneer of French haute horlogerie.

This one you don't only look at. You listen to it. A single hand stays fixed while the dial turns beneath it to show the hour. The minutes are chimed: a minute repeater sounds them out loud. Hence the name, "the voice of time".

L. Leroy's Vox Temporis Credit: GPHG©

Hidden beneath the case, a flying tourbillon improves accuracy. Above it, the rotating dial carries a flinqué soleil decoration finished with translucent dark blue varnish, under a hand-engraved hand. We've been touched. €341,000.

Louis Vuitton × De Bethune — LVDB-03 Sympathique Louis Varius

Category: Mechanical Clock

One GPHG category isn't reserved for wristwatches. It's well worth mentioning one of the competitors.

Imagine if your phone charger turned into a mechanical work of art. You get home, unclip the bracelet, drop your watch into its cradle. Overnight, the clock winds it and resets it to the right time. No electronics involved.

A mechanical masterpiece: Louis Vuitton x De Bethune's LVDB-03 Sympahtique Credit: GPHG©

The mechanical wonder stands about 30 centimetres tall and weighs 10 kilos. On a titanium base inlaid with meteorite, three rose gold rings turn slowly around the structure. They're hand-engraved after drawings by Belgian illustrator François Schuiten: a steam train on a viaduct, hot-air balloons over the African savannah, sherpas on a mountain face, all drifting past.

Behind the project: an alliance between French luxury giant Louis Vuitton, whose watchmaking arm sits just outside Geneva, and De Bethune, one of the most prestigious houses on the horological planet and already an 'Aiguille d'Or' winner. 2 pieces. €4,717,000, clock and watch together.

Grand Seiko — Spring Drive U.F.A. Ushio 300 Diver

Category: Sports

Twenty seconds. Whether you’re working, running or diving, that's all this watch is allowed to gain or lose. Not per day, not per month. Per year.

The big blue: Grand Seiko's Spring Drive U.F.A Ushio 300 Diver Credit: GPHG©

Grand Seiko presents its first diver's watch fitted with a U.F.A. movement, which the Japanese brand describes as the most accurate mainspring-powered movement ever made. The recipe: a quartz oscillator aged for three months to stabilise its precision.

Ushio means "tide" in Japanese — a nod to the waters surrounding the archipelago of the Land of the Rising Sun. The house was already a GPHG winner in 2021. €10,000.

IWC Schaffhausen — Big Pilot's Watch Perpetual Calendar Ceralume®

Category: Sports

This one leads two lives. By day, a white pilot's watch. By night, a glowing blue object. IWC blended ceramic powder with Super-LumiNova pigments to make the case itself. The result: the whole watch glows for more than 24 hours — the hands, the case, the dial, the strap.

Illuminating by day and night: IWC Schaffhausen Big Pilot's Watch Perpetual Calendar Ceralume Credit: GPHG

Inside sits IWC’s well-known perpetual calendar, a legendary complication which knows the length of every month and every leap year, with no correction needed until 2100. The calendar shows the date, the day of the week, the month and the moon phases across four subdials. The movement offers a seven-day power reserve and can be admired through the sapphire crystal caseback. 250 pieces. €69,000.

SpaceOne × Baltic — Seconde Majeure

Category: Challenge

Is creative watchmaking reserved for six- and seven-figure pieces? The Challenge category, which honors more affordable models, says no.

Two Parisian brands sign the Seconde Majeure, built around a jumping hour module developed by Théo Auffret, a rising star of independent haute horlogerie. It works through three visible components: beneath the minute disc sits the Central Command Mobile, which makes a full rotation every 60 minutes. At the end of that rotation it engages the Hours Star, which is linked to the hours disc. Finally, the Jumper Spring makes the hour jump, once every 60 minutes.

Rising to the challenge: Space One x Baltic's Seconde Majeure Credit: Vincent Lions/GPHG

The kind of beauty that usually costs 10 to 50 times more. €3,200.

The independents are on a roll

The 26th awards ceremony will take place on Saturday 7 November 2026 in Geneva. Every shortlisted timepiece is in the running for the coveted 'Aiguille d'Or' Grand Prix, awarded each year since 2001 to the most striking piece of the year.

Each autumn, the timepieces nominated by the Academy – and subsequently the winners – travel around the world as part of a series of exhibitions offering an unrivalled overview of contemporary watchmaking’s creativity.

The GPHG has set out to open the competition to a wider range of houses, from a wider range of countries, with a growing contingent of independents.

Several legendary names, on the other hand, aren't competing at all. While Rolex has never participated, many of the missing brands are past winners: Patek Philippe, Cartier, Vacheron Constantin, F.P. Journe, Richard Mille, A. Lange & Söhne, Greubel Forsey, and Breguet, last year's 'Aiguille d’Or'.

The Olympics of watchmaking are going ahead without several of their record-holding stars. Which leaves the door wide open for the ones they did not see coming.

World.title: Shein and Temu items could face €20 levy in France’s crackdown on ultra-fast fashion
World.content:
France is cracking down on ultra-fast fashion with a new fee that eventually reach almost €20 per garment.

 

The levy, which comes into force on 1 September, targets major e-commerce platforms including Shein.

It follows legislation passed by the French parliament in June to regulate companies known for selling large volumes of lower quality clothing at rock-bottom prices.

It is part of a push to rein in Asian e-commerce giants including Shein, Temu and AliExpress, which have exploded in popularity in France in recent years.

"The harmful effects of ultra-fast fashion on our environment and our economy are well known and documented," said Mathieu Lefevre, the minister for ecological transition on Friday (28 August) as details of the measure were published.

How will France's ultra-fast fashion levy be determined?

Under the legislation, ultra-fast fashion will be determined according to two criteria: the volume of clothing placed on the market and the cost of repairing garments relative to their purchase price.

The per-item fee will vary on a set scale according to how each product scores on both these standards.

In 2026, companies will pay fines such as a 50-cent levy on underwear falling into the ultra-fast fashion category, rising to €2 for T-shirts, €9 for jeans and €12 for a jacket.

The levy could reach up to €19.50 per item by 2030, though the cap remains at 50 per cent of the product's pre-tax price.

A tool to collect data independently, rather than relying solely on companies' own declarations, is under development, Lefevre's office said.

Shein – which on Monday was valued at $26.3 billion (€22.7b) in its long-awaited Hong Kong initial public offering – declined to comment when contacted by news agency AFP.

Temu and AliExpress did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Will European retailers will be exempt from the levy?

The measure has faced criticism over which retailers it will affect.

In July, Lefevre's office said the levy would not apply to retailers such as H&M or Zara, prompting some to say that the measure appeared to spare European and French companies.

French officials have made repeated statements that they view Shein, Temu and AliExpress as driving the surge in ultra-fast fashion.

The European Commission had also raised questions over whether the legislation complied with EU law, but Lefevre's office said those concerns had been "dispelled" and the measure was not expected to be blocked.

China meanwhile warned in July of potential retaliation over the French law, slamming the regulation as "discriminatory" and in violation of trade principles.

Imports of small parcels from China into the EU have already fallen by around 30 to 40 per cent since a separate €3 EU levy on such shipments came into force on 1 July, according to the French government.

World.title: Thailand confirms it will cut visa-free stays to 30 days for EU travellers
World.content:
European Union passport holders will see visa-free stays in Thailand slashed from the middle of September.

 

The Southeast Asian nation has announced that it’s halving the length of trips without visas for tourists from more than 60 countries and territories to 30 days.

The move was floated back in May, but it has now been confirmed that it will come into force on 15 September.

Euronews Travel previously reported that the decision was apparently down to a string of high-profile crimes involving foreign nationals.

Local reports show a number of recent arrests of foreigners who’ve been accused of everything from drug offences and sex trafficking to operating businesses including hotels and schools without proper permits.

Nevertheless, tourism is vital to Thailand’s economy, accounting for more than 10% of its GDP, and it remains one of the most visited countries on the continent.

Currently, visitors from more than 90 countries, including those in the 29-nation Schengen Area, are able to visit Thailand for up to 60 days without a visa.

In a fortnight, though, more than 60 of those countries – including the EU nations – will see that duration cut to 30 days.

The Thai foreign ministry's consular affairs has yet to announce a decision on the status of travellers from around 20 more countries.

Visitors from Peru, Brazil and South Korea will, unusually, see their visas extended and, from the middle of the month, be granted 90-day visa-free stays, up from 60 previously.

It’s not all bad news for European tourists, though.

As Euronews Travel previously reported, visitors on visa-free stays will be able to extend their stays on one occasion, at the discretion of an immigration officer.

There’s also the option to get a Destination Thailand Visa (DTV), which permits stays of up to 180 days per entry, and that can be extended by an additional 180 days.

There is a slight catch, however: applicants must show evidence that they have at least 500,000 baht – or €13,000 – in a bank account, as well as proof of employment outside of Thailand for remote workers.

Thailand has attracted nearly 21 million foreign visitors since the beginning of 2026, although that’s down 3% on the same period last year, and continues a trend for visitor numbers not yet returning to pre-pandemic levels.

World.title: EU to gather ‘brightest minds’ to boost defence as Russia threat grows
World.content:
The European Union is setting up a new high-level group of political and military leaders from member countries, the UK and Ukraine to work out how to boost Europe's defence capabilities as threats from Russia escalate.

 

Kaja Kallas, the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, announced the initiative at an informal meeting of defence ministers in Ireland on Tuesday, saying it would help design a new approach to European defence.

"The aim is to have some of the brightest minds on security and defence come together and really provide out-of-the-box solutions on how we can be faster in fulfilling these gaps and how we can be more effective, especially now that the security situation in Europe is so much more real," Kallas told reporters at the press conference.

The announcement comes as Europe faces unprecedented security challenges, with the US administration reducing its military presence on the continent and Russia's escalation in Ukraine fuelling growing anxiety about spillover into EU territory.

"Europe is investing more in defence than ever, but spending alone is not automatically a guarantee of success. We have not been fast enough to cover the gaps in Europe's conventional power within NATO that we have identified," Kallas said.

She stressed that NATO remains the cornerstone of European security, and that the exercise forms part of a broader effort by Europe to take greater responsibility for its own defence by strategically deciding which capabilities to invest in.

Drawing on Ukraine's frontline experience and battlefield innovation is seen as particularly relevant to this effort. The new group will produce a report with concrete recommendations for Europe's defence.

The initiative will be formally launched at a conference organised by the European External Action Service (EEAS), titled "European Defence: Moving Further, Faster," on 7 September, when the names of participants and further details will be announced.

"The idea is to give ideas to member states but also EU institutions of what we should do better and faster — to really have tangible results so that we cover the capability gaps we have identified, considering the geopolitical situation," Kallas said.

World.title: ESA's BepiColombo mission nears major turning point on Mercury approach
World.content:
Eight years after it left Earth, BepiColombo is now tantalisingly close to entering orbit around Mercury, a hot and dense ball of metals and silicates with its own magnetic field, considered one of the most difficult planets to observe because the gravitational pull and wild radiation from the Sun are so intense.

 

"Mercury is a challenging destination. It's very difficult to reach, it's very difficult to operate there," said Santa Martinez, ESA mission manager.

"The main two aspects are really the extreme temperatures that go from -180 to 450°C, and also the solar radiation, which can be up to ten times what we have on Earth."

Spaceflight engineers at ESA's ESOC control centre in Darmstadt, Germany say they are ready and prepared for all kinds of incidents and accidents on 3 September, when the spacecraft splits apart and instruments that have been shielded inside are suddenly exposed to an ultra-harsh environment.

Likening the whole spaceflight experience to "operating with a very hot pizza oven running right on your back," ESA Flight Director Ignacio Tanco told Euronews, comparing it to "working on a knife edge".

His biggest concern is the solar panels, which are finely tilted. Move them a fraction of a degree too far away from the Sun and you risk losing power, or wind them a tiny bit too much towards our star and they risk getting roasted beyond repair.

"There's a lot of stuff that is going to be new on Thursday that the teams must prepare for," he said, comparing the moment to launching an entirely new spacecraft, one that happens to already be orbiting a different planet, with an 11-minute radio delay each way.

FILE - The BepiColombo Mercury arrival phase mission control team in the main control room at the European Space Operations Centre (ESOC). European Space Agency (ESA)

What happens next

BepiColombo is Europe's first mission to Mercury, and it is a complex one.

On Thursday, 3 September, at 2:00 pm CEST the spacecraft will be divided in two. Two probes joined together will set off for the science mission, while the large Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) that has brought them on a circuitous eight-year journey to this point drifts off in the other direction.

The MTM mothership is then in the hands of fate, as it has no attitude control and is no longer needed.

"It's a fully passive module, so you cannot control it, you cannot manoeuvre it," explains ESA's Flight Dynamics Manager Frank Budnik.

Without any way to steer, it will begin to tumble, and its trajectory will carry it past Mercury rather than into orbit. It would spend the rest of its days in interplanetary space.

Meanwhile, for the two probes, it is time to wake up and get to work.

Literally stacked on top of each other on the MTM, they are ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), which will study the planet's surface and interior up close, and the Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio), built by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), which will focus on the space environment around it.

Martinez was candid about the risks in the seconds, minutes, hours and days after separation this week.

"We know that it's likely that not everything is going to go according to the nominal plan," she said. "But we are ready, we are flexible, and we need to be prepared for the unexpected."

Flying to Mercury is a lot more challenging than flying to Mars. A spacecraft falling towards the Sun does not slow down; it speeds up, pulled by solar gravity.

To be captured into orbit, BepiColombo must match Mercury's own velocity almost exactly, a far more energy-demanding transfer than reaching even the distant, larger planets.

That is why the mission has spent eight years and nine planetary flybys of Earth, Venus and Mercury itself quietly bleeding off speed with an ion engine, rather than taking a more direct route, and it is why the next few months will see some high-stress moments for the mission team.

BepiColombo arrival at Mercury timeline CREDIT ESA ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS ATG Europe

For the two probes, Thursday's separation from the MTM is only the first step of a long arrival sequence.

For the following weeks, the two science orbiters MPO and Mio will remain locked together as a single composite spacecraft, flying free of the propulsion module for the first time, with instruments and cameras previously blocked by the MTM finally getting a clear view of space.

The next major milestone comes in late November and into early December, when mission controllers fire a critical sequence of chemical thruster burns to lower the spacecraft's orbit and bring it into Mercury's grip.

Once captured in orbit, MPO and Mio will separate from each other, becoming two fully independent, fully operational spacecraft in their own distinct orbits around the planet, and their own distinct teams on Earth, too.

Engineers will spend the following months commissioning systems and fine-tuning both orbits, a process that runs into March 2027.

Only once that is complete does the mission's dedicated science phase begin, in April 2027.

Mercury's unsolved mysteries

Mercury is an absolute headache to study via telescope from Earth because of the burning presence of the Sun in the background. So, as BepiColombo Project Scientist Geraint Jones told Euronews, "to study the planet in any detail, we have to go there with a spacecraft."

There is a lot we do not know about this fiery-hot planet. Chief among the open questions is Mercury's density: the planet is unusually heavy for its size, likely because of an oversized iron core which makes up 60% of its volume, but scientists do not yet know why.

Studying that will give us data to explain how the core generates Mercury's magnetic field. Of our solar system's rocky planets, only Mercury and Earth have a magnetic field, while Venus and Mars have none.

Other curious aspects of Mercury include the fact that the planet is literally shrinking as the inner core cools, and it rotates on its axis so slowly that a day lasts longer than a year.

One full day and night on Mercury corresponds to 176 Earth days, while a circuit around the Sun takes 88 Earth days.

For Jones personally, one of the most intriguing features of the planet is the surface features called 'hollows,' first spotted by NASA's MESSENGER mission to Mercury.

These hollows are places where the ground appears to be eaten away as volatile materials evaporate in the extreme heat. There is also strong evidence of water ice in some of the permanently shadowed craters at Mercury's poles, and scientists are keen to know exactly how much there is and why.

Mercury has no atmosphere, but there is outgassing from the planet that Jones is keen to study.

"Both spacecraft will be 'tasting' the gases that are surrounding Mercury, being able to tell us what gases are there, whether certain areas of the surface are giving off material and seeing how that changes over time as well," he explains.

Studying this barren and baking world goes beyond Mercury itself. Understanding how a rocky planet forms and survives so close to its star helps scientists understand the origins of Earth and of many of the odd and unusual exoplanets found in recent decades orbiting other stars in our galaxy.

As ever with this mission, getting answers requires patience.

The mission's full science campaign will not begin until April 2027, once both orbiters reach their final orbits. For now, all eyes are on 3 September, when a single separation turns eight years of winding around the inner solar system into a final descent into Mercury's gravitational grasp.

World.title: Iran says it will return to June ceasefire deal if US does the same
World.content:
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tuesday his country is ready to return to the ceasefire deal reached with the US in June if Washington does the same, in conciliatory remarks following the first exchange of fire between the two countries in a month.

 

Speaking at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Kyrgyzstan, Pezeshkian said that “if the US returns to its commitments in the memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately reciprocate,” Iranian state media reported.

The June framework deal called for an immediate ceasefire and started a 60-day period for talks aimed at reaching a wider peace deal.

Tehran agreed to clear the Strait of Hormuz of mines and allow ships to pass during the period, and Washington agreed to end its naval blockade, lift sanctions, issue waivers for Iranian oil exports and begin work on a reconstruction package for Iran, among other things.

The agreement quickly fell apart, and while there has been a lull in fighting, the two sides exchanged fire over the weekend.

While Pezeshkian has long favoured a negotiated end to the war, Iran’s most powerful force remains the elite paramilitary IRGC, which is pressing for greater concessions from the US, including Iranian control over Hormuz and financial compensation for the war. Those conditions would likely be unacceptable to Washington.

On Monday, Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi also said the US must honour its commitments and the framework deal.

"Then we can get out of this situation," Araghchi told Iran's state-run television on the sidelines of the summit in Bishkek.

Araghchi is in Kyrgyzstan as part of the Iranian delegation led by Pezeshkian.

Pezeshkian also said in another part of his speech at the summit that Tehran is not seeking war, and claimed the Islamic Republic has an impressive record of fulfilling its international commitments and treaties.

Pezeshkian's remarks come as the exchange of fire between Iran and the United States has once again escalated since the early hours of Monday, when the US targeted two Iranian launchers on Larak Island.

Hours after the US attack on the island near Hormuz, the Iranian president stated that Iran does not seek war but will "never sit quietly" in the face of any aggression and will "deliver a firm response to the aggressors".

World.title: UK records hottest summer on record, Met Office says
World.content:
The UK recorded its hottest summer on record in 2026, the country's national weather service announced on Tuesday, marking its second record-breaking summer in a row.

 

"An average mean temperature of 16.5°C puts this summer as provisionally the warmest on record, as well as the warmest season for the UK in a series which goes back to 1884," the Met Office said.

That beats the previous record of 16.1°C , set in 2025, and put the year comfortably above the next three hottest summers - 2018, 2006, and 2003 - which all saw an average mean temperature of 15.7°C over the season.

England, Wales, and Northern Ireland also recorded their warmest summers on record, while Scotland reported its joint-sixth warmest summer. England also saw its warmest June on record as well as its driest July, recording just 6.5mm of rainfall for the month.

The UK, like much of Europe, has experienced a series of scorching heatwaves and drought conditions over the last few months, with temperatures peaking at 38.1°C in London's Kew Gardens on 13 August.

“These records are now breaking with increasing frequency, reflecting the influence of human-induced climate change on the temperatures we’re experiencing in the UK," Dr Amy Doherty, who leads the Met Office's National Climate Information Centre, said.

“Particularly notable is how much we’ve exceeded the previous summer mean temperature record, set just last year," Doherty added.

According to a study carried out by Met Office scientists, the record-breaking season was made roughly 130 times more likely due to "human-induced climate change."

"In a climate unaffected by human emissions of greenhouse gases, a summer like this would be exceptionally unlikely, i.e. 1 in over 1,000 years," Dr Mark McCarthy, the head of climate attribution at the Met Office, said. "In our current climate, which is changing because of the effect of burning of fossil fuels, we should now expect this to be roughly a 1 in 9 year event".

Sweltering conditions across Europe have wreaked havoc on the continent this summer, putting increasing strain on emergency services and helping fuel a series of devastating wildfires.

World.title: What the SDF’s dissolution means for Syria’s Kurds and neighbouring Turkey
World.content:
Nearly a week after the Syrian Democratic Forces agreed to dissolve, the consequences are beginning to take shape for Syria's Kurds and neighbouring Turkey. As the former US-backed force is absorbed into the Syrian state, questions remain over what the country's Kurds have secured in return – from language and political rights to protections for women – and what the end of more than a decade of Kurdish-led autonomy means for Turkey's own conflict with Kurdish militants.

Advertising

SDF leader Mazloum Abdi announced the force's dissolution last Tuesday, saying its fighters would be integrated into the Syrian army.

At its height, the predominantly Kurdish force numbered around 100,000 fighters and controlled nearly a fifth of Syrian territory in the northeast, including major oil fields and fertile land. Under SDF rule, Kurds gained cultural and political rights denied to them under previous governments in Damascus.

“It means the end of Kurdish autonomy. After more than one decade of freedom, now they are under the control of Damascus,” said Syria expert Fabrice Balanche of Lyon University, who frequently visited the region.

Kurdish rights

“There are no guarantees for the Kurdish language because it's just a presidential decree: ‘let the Kurds use their language and teach Kurdish in schools,’ but there is nothing in the constitution,” Balanche said.

The decree, issued by President Ahmed al-Sharaa in January, recognised Kurdish as a national language and allowed it to be taught in schools in areas with significant Kurdish populations.

It also restored citizenship to Kurds who had been left stateless under measures stemming from a controversial 1962 census and made Nowruz, the Kurdish New Year festival, an official national holiday.

The Education Ministry followed up on 27 August with rules providing for three Kurdish-language classes a week in public and private schools in areas with significant Kurdish populations, with marks counting towards pupils' final grades.

‘Words and promises not enough’ as Syria’s Kurds face uncertain future

Abdi was also appointed as an adviser to al-Sharaa on Friday, days after announcing the SDF's dissolution. It remains unclear whether the role will be more than ceremonial.

But questions remain over what the end of the Kurdish-led administration will mean for women. The SDF and affiliated institutions used a system in which governing bodies were jointly headed by a man and a woman.

“During these 10 years of autonomy, men and women were equal,” Balanche said. “In the region’s administration. It was always a co-presidency. In Raqqah, for example, the mayor was Leyla Mustafa, a woman, and the co-president was a man. Now that is no longer the case.”

Balanche also said the change could threaten restrictions on polygamy introduced under the Kurdish-led administration. Another unresolved question is what will happen to female SDF fighters as the force is absorbed into Syria's armed forces, which currently have no female troops.

Shifting alliances

For years, the SDF was Washington's main partner on the ground in Syria in the fight against the Islamic State group. But its position weakened as the United States built closer relations with Syria's new rulers.

A Syrian government offensive in January seized large areas held by the SDF and pushed the Kurdish-led force back into negotiations over integration with Damascus.

Washington, meanwhile, has increasingly embraced al-Sharaa's government, dismantling broad sanctions against Syria in 2025 and last week removing the country from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.

Turkey has emerged as one of al-Sharaa's main foreign allies and has long pressed for the SDF to disarm and integrate into the Syrian state.

Ankara considers the SDF a terrorist organisation linked to the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), which launched an insurgency against the Turkish state in 1984. The SDF has rejected Turkey's claim that it is an extension of the PKK.

A year after Assad's fall, Syrian hopes for transitional justice are fading

The United States and European Union designate the PKK as a terrorist organisation, but not the SDF.

Turkey has carried out several cross-border military operations against the SDF in northern Syria since 2016 and still has thousands of troops stationed in the country. Ankara says those forces will remain until the security threats it faces have been eliminated.

The SDF's dissolution therefore achieves a longstanding Turkish objective in Syria. Turkey's ruling AK Party welcomed the move last week as an important step towards strengthening Syria's unity.

“Stability in Syria means Turkey perhaps being able to divert some of the resources it's been spending on counterterrorism into other areas of its defense that are absolutely necessary at a time like this, a time of regional turmoil,” said Turkey expert Asli Aydintasbas of the Washington-based Brookings Institution.

Turkey's Kurdish conflict

The SDF's dissolution could also remove an obstacle to the fragile peace process between Ankara and the PKK.

The process is intended to end the PKK's decades-long armed campaign against the Turkish state through the group's disarmament and dissolution.

Jailed PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan called on the group to disarm and disband in February 2025, and the PKK announced three months later that it would do so. A group of militants symbolically burned their weapons at a ceremony in northern Iraq in July 2025.

Turkey's parliament passed a law in August establishing a legal framework for the PKK's disbandment. Kurdish politicians have said broader democratic and legal reforms will also be needed for lasting peace.

Macron to become first Western European leader to visit post-Assad Syria

For Ankara, however, the process does not stop at Turkey's borders. It has repeatedly insisted that the SDF must also dissolve, because it regards the Syrian force as part of the same militant movement as the PKK.

The SDF has disputed that characterisation, with Abdi saying in 2025 that the PKK's decision to disarm did not apply to his forces in Syria.

The dismantling of groups Ankara regards as PKK affiliates across the region is essential to the process, said Middle East expert Serhan Afacan of Istanbul's Marmara University.

“The PKK should not exist anywhere in the region. This is what Ankara has been saying for more than a year,” Afacan said.

“If there is going to be any kind of peace process or reconciliation, the PKK is not supposed to exist anywhere in this region, in Turkey, in Iran, in Iraq, Syria.”
