World.title: 'Uncharted territory': Physicists find hints of mysterious dark matter
World.content:
Dark matter, an elusive substance that permeates the universe, has flummoxed scientists for decades.

But a single flash of energy spotted by the world's most sensitive detector of its kind is the "most compelling hint reported to date", according to an international team of physicists.

The team made the discovery, which is yet to be confirmed, using the LUX-ZEPLIN detector in the US.

They presented their findings today at the 2026 TeV Particle Astrophysics conference in Japan, and in a paper which is yet to be peer reviewed on the preprint server arXiv.

Theresa Fruth, one of the Australian physicists on the team, said the result was "very exciting".

"This event just won't go away even after many, many checks," Dr Fruth, from the University of Sydney, said.

" It's also kind of scary to think, 'Oh, this could be it'. "

But, she said, more detections were needed to confirm the result.

Nicole Bell, a theoretical physicist at the University of Melbourne who was not involved in the research, said it was an "interesting observation" but it was "very early days".

"If it's really dark matter, we'll see more events soon, and that would be a huge breakthrough," Professor Bell said.

What is dark matter?

Scientists estimate that 85 per cent of the observable universe is dark matter.

They know it exists by watching the way galaxies move, but no-one has observed it directly.

"I don't know what dark matter is. No-one knows what dark matter is," Dr Fruth said.

"What we do know is that there must be a lot more matter out there in the universe than what we know about."

Theresa Fruth is one of two Australian scientists working on the LUX-ZEPLIN experiment. (Supplied: University of Sydney)

One leading theory suggests dark matter might be slow-moving particles, bigger than the components of atoms, called weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs).

What did the team find?

Built in an old gold mine almost 1.5 kilometres underground, LUX-ZEPLIN is the most sensitive of the recent generation of dark matter detectors.

It uses a huge vat of super-cooled liquid xenon and 494 light sensors to try to detect tiny collisions between WIMPS and normal particles.

The deep location and metal shielding of the LUX-ZEPLIN detector protects the detector from background noise. (Supplied: Matthew Kapust/Sanford Underground Research Laboratory)

Until now, the LUX-ZEPLIN detector had not detected anything that looked like dark matter.

It is not alone, no other detectors have provided concrete evidence for dark matter, and most have found nothing at all.

Only one, the DAMA/LIBRA experiment in Italy, has found an annual signal which they attribute to dark matter, but no other detector has been able to confirm the results after years of attempts.

Professor Bell said the signal detected by LUX-ZEPLIN was "very different", but perhaps easier to explain as dark matter.

The single event, which was detected on June 16, 2023, was part of a 220 day run of the detector.

Jaden Newstead, a physicist at the University of Melbourne who also was not involved in the research, said physicists would need to rework some of their theories about dark matter if the result was confirmed.

"It's not how we would expect dark matter to have appeared," Dr Newstead said.

"This was a special analysis that was looking at higher energies."

Originally, many detectors searching for WIMPs looked at a much lower energy band, as that is what was predicted by theoretical physics.

This detection had an energy range of 270 keV, meaning the WIMP was even more massive than the researchers assumed.

LUX-ZEPLIN's central detector is filled with liquid xenon. (Supplied: Matthew Kapust/Sanford Underground Research Facility)

The team looked for "background" interference that might have caused the result, such as neutrons and neutrinos, but found "none could be identified as a likely explanation".

The team reached what is known as 2.6 sigma, a 0.5 per cent chance that the event could be explained by known backgrounds.

This is still below a 5 sigma threshold needed to confirm a discovery.

Dr Fruth said it was still possible that some "ultra-rare" background could have caused the detection.

"This is uncharted territory," she said.

When will we know if we've seen dark matter?

The LUX-ZEPLIN experiment will continue to collect data until at least 2028.

The team will use this data to either build their confidence in the finding or break it down.

Even if it does not pan out, Dr Fruth said the result would still be interesting.

"It's certainly something new and exciting to investigate further."

Similar dark matter detectors, like the XENON project in Italy and the PandaX project in China, could help check their results.

Dr Fruth said checking in with other scientists was one of the reasons they have released the data now instead of waiting for it to be published in a peer-reviewed paper.

Dr Newstead said it would likely take months for other experiments to check their data and confirm or refute whether the dark matter detection was real.

"It's an exciting hint," Dr Newstead said.

"Whenever the experimentalists are confused about something, it's always exciting for theorists."

World.title: Israeli strikes kill four in Gaza as military says it arrests Hamas militant
World.content:
At least three Palestinians have been killed by gunfire and airstrikes in Gaza City during an Israeli-backed raid, according to Gaza officials.

An Israeli special force had tried to carry out an operation in Gaza City before being detected by Hamas and launched heavy airstrikes to cover their withdrawal, director of the Hamas-run Gaza government media office, Ismail Al-Thawabta said.

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said a senior Hamas militant had been arrested with an Israeli security official saying the man was the head of Hamas' internal security service.

Some Israeli media reports said the raid may have been carried out by members of an Israeli-backed militia that operates from Israeli-controlled areas inside Gaza.

Witnesses said Israeli warplanes fired at least 12 missiles near the Katiba area in the west of Gaza City, an area crowded with displaced families.

Palestinians gather at the site of Israeli strikes and gunfire in Gaza City. (Reuters: Ebrahim Hajjaj)

At least three people — two children and a woman — were killed and several others wounded in the bombardment, medics said.

Two vehicles were hit and reduced to twisted wreckage. Another child was killed in Israeli fire in central Gaza, medics said.

In a statement on Tuesday, local time, the Israeli military said it struck several targets in the Gaza Strip in order to remove threats to Israeli security forces.

Mr Katz did not provide details about the arrest operation or identify the Hamas militant.

"This is our policy: we do not wait for threats, but rather pursue Hamas terrorists, thwart them, and destroy their terror infrastructure," he said, speaking from the Netiv HaAsara community near the northern Gaza border.

In a separate incident, medics said a girl was killed and two other people were wounded when Israeli forces operating east of Deir Al-Balah in central Gaza opened fire on the area.

Ceasefire has not stopped strikes

A US-backed ceasefire that took effect in October 2025 halted the large-scale fighting that had devastated the enclave, but it has not ended Israeli strikes.

The military says such operations are intended to prevent attacks by Hamas and other Palestinian militant groups.

Hamas accuses Israel of repeatedly violating the ceasefire and undermining efforts to advance a broader plan by US President Donald Trump to end the war.

The plan includes further Israeli troop withdrawals from Gaza and the disarmament of Hamas.

More than 1,300 Palestinians have been killed ‌in Gaza ⁠since the ceasefire came into force last October, according to Gaza health officials.

The Israeli military says four Israeli soldiers have been killed in militant attacks during the same period.

Reuters

World.title: Former British PM Keir Starmer to leave politics
World.content:
Former British prime minister Sir Keir Starmer has announced he will resign as an MP and trigger a by-election in his North London electorate.

His decision, initially announced to a local paper in his constituency, comes just over a month after he was replaced by Andy Burnham as Labour leader and prime minister.

Sir Keir led Labour to an election landslide just two years prior, in July 2024, but was unable to translate that victory into enduring popularity.

The embattled leader experienced some of the worst approval ratings of any British prime minister, leading to internal pressure for him to resign.

Sir Keir announced his resignation from the top job in June and was replaced by Mr Burnham, the former mayor of Greater Manchester, the next month after a leadership contest.

In a statement initially given to the Camden New Journal, which covers his Holborn and St Pancras constituency in North London, and later published on his X, Sir Keir said he wanted to "pass the baton to a successor".

"I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world," he said.

"I will also continue, as I have done for a long time now with others, work on combating violence against women and girls; that is an issue that matters to me hugely."

Sir Keir became an MP in 2015 after a legal career in which he served as the UK's Director of Public Prosecutions and the head of the Crown Prosecution Service.

He took over the Labour leadership in the aftermath of a disastrous election defeat under Jeremy Corbyn in 2019, turning the party's fortunes around through the Covid-19 pandemic by steering it back towards the political centre.

As opposition leader, he prosecuted Labour's case against Conservative prime ministers Boris Johnson, Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak.

Sir Keir's announcement came as his successor, Andy Burnham, prepared to address the Commons for the first time as PM. (Reuters: Kin Cheung/Pool)

The former two leaders resigned under pressure while Mr Sunak conceded the 2024 election after a poor performance by the Conservative party.

But Sir Keir's leadership in government was tested on multiple fronts, including sustained voter frustration at the UK's cost of living, the decision to appoint Peter Mandelson as UK Ambassador in Washington despite his alleged links to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and controversial changes to the UK's welfare system.

His tenure was also marked by a continuation of British support for Ukraine, the renationalisation of the UK's railways, and an attempted arson attack on his private residence in North London.

Sir Keir's announcement on Tuesday, local time, came on the same day Mr Burnham was due to make his first statement to the UK's House of Commons as prime minister.

ABC/wires

World.title: Ben Stokes joins Adelaide Strikers for BBL summer
World.content:
Former England cricket captain Ben Stokes will take part in the upcoming Big Bash League season after signing with the Adelaide Strikers, the team has confirmed.

The all-rounder's move had been tipped earlier in the week, but has now been locked in by the Strikers, who said they were looking forward to capitalising on Stokes's "world-class talent" and ability to put in "match-winning performances with both bat and ball".

Stokes retired from international cricket in June, a decision that caused shock waves when it was revealed during a Test match.

His arrival in Adelaide will follow a previous BBL stint, at the Melbourne Renegades in 2015.

"Ben is one of the greatest all-rounders the game has seen, a proven match-winner and a competitor who thrives under pressure," Adelaide head coach Tim Paine said in a statement released by the Strikers.

"We're thrilled to have a player of his ability join our squad."

In the same statement, Stokes said the opportunity to join the Strikers was one he "couldn't pass up".

"Adelaide Oval is an incredible place to play cricket, the Big Bash is a fantastic competition and the Strikers have an exciting group," he said.

"I can't wait to get started, create some special memories with the group and give Strikers fans plenty to cheer about."

Stokes — who made his Test debut in Adelaide in 2013 — will be available for the full BBL summer, the Strikers said.

The hard-hitting, fast-bowling all-rounder captained the England side that was widely expected to challenge Australia for the Ashes in the 2025/26 summer, but was defeated 4-1.

His decision to quit international cricket was revealed shortly before the tea break on day four of the third Test between England and New Zealand at Trent Bridge.

During the series, Stokes made front-page news after being dropped by England for the second Test amid an investigation following a night out with a teammate after the first Test at Lord's.

The 35-year-old is widely recognised as one of the most impactful and talismanic cricketers of the current era, and scored more than 11,000 international runs across T20, ODI and Test formats.

His match-winning performances have included a whirlwind 135 not out against Australia at Headingley in 2019, which steered England to an astonishing one-wicket triumph, and a rearguard 84 not out against New Zealand in the World Cup final the same summer.

His innings of 155 against Australia in a losing cause at Lord's in 2023 occurred in the match made notorious by the controversial run-out of wicketkeeper Jonny Bairstow.

World.title: Partner of missing Australian in Nepal says waiting for news has been 'hell'
World.content:
A week after the catastrophic Nepal-Tibet flood, 23-year-old Sarada Viswanathan is refusing to give up on her partner Rishab Iyer, also 23, who is still missing.

"It's been genuinely just hell for us," she told 7.30.

Mr Iyer was travelling with his parents and brother in Nepal on a Hindu Indian pilgrimage.

They too have not been heard from since last Wednesday.

The Iyer family — son Rudhra, father Sreedharan, mother Lakshmi and son Rishab — was on a pilgrimage tour in Nepal. (Supplied)

"It's been really difficult just not having any answers and not knowing where they are, how they're doing, whether they need help, whether they're drinking water, whether they're eating. Are they injured?" she said.

" It's just 24/7, we're just thinking about them, thinking about ways that we can bring them home. What can we do for them? How can we help them? "

Ms Viswanathan has set up a DIY search operation at her family home in north-west Sydney, scanning location tracking websites, clinging to any detail that might pinpoint the Australians.

Sarada Viswanathan and her friends search online for any signs of the Iyer family. (ABC News: Jerry Rickard)

"We all have them on Find My iPhone and Life360," she explained.

"The last location I have of Rishab is outside that hotel. The last location we have of his brother is slightly up onto the highway."

The Iyers were staying at the Royal Himalaya Hotel & Lodge, close to the river that flooded.

Rishab Iyer and Sarada Viswanathan have been friends since childhood. (Supplied)

"We're just hoping that they managed to climb somewhere and they managed to escape and that they just are in a remote region that's blocked off and they're not able to get in contact with anyone," Ms Viswanathan said.

Other relatives of the Iyer family are already on the ground in Nepal and have been feeding back any scintilla of information to Ms Viswanathan.

But the disaster zone has been difficult to access on foot, and Ms Viswanathan has set up a petition to push the Australian government to send defence force personnel to help with the search and rescue.

Mud covers properties in Trishuli, Nepal, after last week's flash flood. (Reuters: Navesh Chitrakar)

Australia has committed $8 million towards sending aid supplies and has dispatched a crisis response team of 18 people, including consular staff and the AFP.

Ms Viswanathan believes the government should assist with on-the-ground patrols, helicopter searches and thermal drones.

A sniffer dog is used to search for survivors following the floods in Trishuli, Nepal. (Reuters: Navesh Chitrakar)

"You never stop at anything to get your family back when they're missing. We appreciate all of the money and all the humanitarian aid that has been given. We're just hoping that we can get actual people there," she said.

Nepal has already knocked back offers of rescue assistance from foreign governments.

"The Australian government continues to offer search and rescue assistance to the Nepali authorities, but that offer hasn't been taken up," a spokesperson for the Department of Foreign Affairs told 7.30 in a statement.

"We are working with telecommunications companies to support Nepali search, rescue and recovery efforts, and assist us in ascertaining the location of those Australians who remain unaccounted for."

Missing Sydney man due to become an intern doctor

Ms Viswanathan and Mr Iyer have been friends since childhood and both became medical students in Sydney.

Mr Iyer was due to start a new job next year as an intern doctor at Gosford Hospital.

"My search will never end," Ms Viswanathan said.

" I will keep looking for him until anything is confirmed. I will never give up on him, and I know none of us will ever give up on them. "

Mr Iyer and his brother, Rudhra, 20, were keen cricketers and played for West Pennant Hills.

Rishab Iyer and his brother Rudhra were both studying medicine. (Supplied)

Their mother Lakshmi and father Sreedharan ran a childcare business and were well-loved in Sydney's Indian community.

John Kurian, 23, has been friends with Rishab since high school.

"We played cricket together since 2018 and we've lost four grand finals together," he told 7.30.

"So we've always joked around saying that we need to win another premiership. He has tried every season that he can. He's always our best player. He leads from the front verbally and with his bat and the ball."

Mr Kurian has joined Ms Visawanathan in her cause.

Rishab Iyer and John Kurian grew up together and played for their local cricket club. (Supplied)

"I'm here because he's my brother. Rishab and Rudhra are my brothers, and Sreedharan and Lakshmi are also my mum and dad," he said.

"They are out there somewhere right now. Maybe they can't be reached … because they are stuck or the communication towers are knocked down. The least we can do is try and get more people out there to help."

Son flies to India to search for missing parents

Umesh and Krishna Sharma were part of the same pilgrimage group as the Iyers and are also missing. (Supplied)

The Iyer family was staying at the same hotel as another missing Sydney family, the Sharmas, who were all on the same pilgrimage tour.

The two families were close.

Chitrak Sharma, 23, was in Sydney when he heard about the disaster in Nepal.

His mother Krishna and father Umesh are still missing.

"They're true Australians who lived by generosity, inclusivity, and just giving back to the community," Mr Sharma told 7.30.

"The first thing I did was I tried calling. Of course, [I got] nothing.

Chitrak Sharma, pictured left, with his mother Krishna, father Umesh, and brother Chaitanya. (Supplied: Chitrak Sharma)

"I tried calling someone else that I know was with them. No contact was able to be made. Still, I didn't take it too seriously because I mean, just what are the odds?"

Mr Sharma decided to fly to India and is now south of Delhi, where he is deciding whether to continue to Nepal.

"What made me take a flight here? It had been four days and no concrete news, and I figured I may have to head to Nepal very soon for any reason," he said.

"So that's why I'm basically on stand-by mode here in India with the rest of my extended family."

Mr Sharma remained hopeful but said he was prepared for the worst.

"I've thought about it, and just for assumption's sake I have brought some DNA samples with me. I brought hair in case, but I don't want to think too much about that right now," he said.

"My hope is that we find them safe and sound."

Families of the missing face racist comments

Amid their desperation, some of those related to the missing said they had seen racist comments on social media that denied their Australian identity.

Missing Australians A Queensland mother and a Sydney father are among dozens of Australians missing in Nepal following last week's deadly flooding.

"It's been quite disheartening to see a lot of racial comments towards the families that have gone, about 'they're not Australians'," Mr Kurian told 7.30.

"Rishab and Rudthra are as Australian as they come. They've grown up here their whole life, their education, their work, their sport, their academia, everything is here.

"So for anyone that's been saying those things, they need to really have a deep look and reconsider what they're saying."

Mr Sharma said he had also seen racist comments and wished they would stop.

World.title: Family of Perth man missing in Nepal hoping for 'miracle'
World.content:
The family of a Perth man missing in Nepal say they are hoping for a "miracle" that he will be found alive and well.

Luke Costanzo, 30, was visiting Mount Kailash on a pilgrimage trek with the non-profit, spiritual Isha Foundation.

So far, more than 1,000 people have died, and about 4,400 people remain unaccounted for after the area was hit by a landslide and flash flooding.

Nepali survivors return to unrecognisable villages The ABC sees firsthand the devastation and rescue operation underway in the worst-hit areas of Nepal.

Mr Costanzo's family released a statement on Tuesday announcing that he was one of the Australians still missing.

"It is with heavy hearts that we share our dear son and brother, Luke Costanzo, is one of the Australians still unaccounted for in Nepal following the flooding disaster last week," they said.

"Luke is an extremely strong, compassionate, disciplined and spiritual person.

"Once he makes a decision, he commits to it fully, and he was so excited to be visiting Mount Kailash on a pilgrimage trek."

The family said they last heard from Mr Costanzo from the Gyirong port border crossing, when his group was making its way back to Kathmandu on the final day of their journey.

Queensland mum, Sydney dad among Australians missing in Nepal A Queensland mother and a Sydney father are among dozens of Australians missing in Nepal following last week's deadly flooding.

"This is an unimaginably difficult situation for us, and we request the media please respect our privacy during this time," the family said.

"We truly appreciate all the love and support from friends and family that we've received and ask everyone to keep Luke, and all those affected, in your thoughts and prayers.

"We can do nothing but continue hoping for a miracle that Luke, and the others who remain missing, are found alive and well.

"For those wishing to help in some way — and are in the position to do so — we suggest donating to aid the wonderful people on the ground who continue with rescue efforts."

World.title: Missing Australian found in Tibet was not in flood zone, China says
World.content:
One of 43 missing Australians has been found alive six days after catastrophic floods hit the Nepal-China border.

In a statement, the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said it was unable to provide details about the person due to privacy obligations.

The Australian was in Tibet, China.

"It's hard to imagine the sense of relief their loved ones must be feeling after what will have been an incredibly harrowing few days," Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong said in a statement on Tuesday.

But China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs has told the ABC the Australian citizen was not in the disaster zone.

"This Australian citizen was not in the epicentre of the disaster and has already been in contact with the Australian Embassy in China," the foreign ministry said.

"The Chinese side is currently making every effort to search for and rescue missing persons, both Chinese and foreign."

More than 4,400 people remain missing in the affected area.

The rescue effort comes after the "golden window" of the first 72 hours for finding a survivor, which experts say offers the best chances of survival without access to clean water.

Cara Severino, who was found alive in Nepal on the weekend. (Supplied)

The Australian has spoken with their family and is receiving support from consular officers.

Another Australian, Cara Severino, was safely located on the weekend, bringing the number of Australians missing following the flash floods down to 42.

Despite the welcome news, the Foreign Affairs Minister warned that the government "must remain realistic about the days ahead".

Rescue teams are battling mud, rock and debris in many hard-to-reach areas. (Reuters: Stringer)

"As each day passes, our grave concerns for those still unaccounted-for inevitably grow," she said.

Nepalese and Indian Army rescue personnel search through damaged buildings. (AFP: Prakash Mathema)

Yesterday, the Australian government announced it would increase its humanitarian assistance for Nepal to $8 million.

Assistant Foreign Minister Matt Thistlewaite said this funding would mostly go towards the supply of hygiene kits.

"There's a desperate need for these kits for people in the region and also solar lights," he said.

"Obviously all of the power and telecommunications infrastructure has been wiped out.

"So those kits are being put together; they'll be transported by the Australian Defence Force over the coming days."

World.title: Authorities investigate reports former ADF soldier killed in Ukraine
World.content:
Australian officials are investigating reports a former ADF soldier has been killed while fighting in Ukraine.

The soldier, known by the nickname "Mozzie the Aussie", had been serving as a volunteer and combat medic in the Ukrainian International Legion's Med Team Alpha.

The ABC has been asked not to report his full name out of privacy concerns for his family, but has confirmed the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is making inquiries with authorities in Ukraine.

His death has not been confirmed by any Australian or Ukrainian officials, but veteran and Shadow Minister for Defence Personnel, Phil Thompson, paid tribute to the former Australian soldier on social media.

In a statement, Mr Thompson remembered his friend as someone "who earned the respect of all who served alongside him".

"He was the kind of bloke who never hesitated to put others before himself. He was a good man, a great soldier, and someone his mates could always rely on when it mattered most," he said.

"Through his courage, skill and selfless commitment to others, Mozzie saved countless lives on the battlefield.

"My thoughts are with Mozzie's family, friends, and brothers in the battalion in both Australia and Ukraine as they mourn this terrible loss."

Former soldier went to Ukraine to help

Mr Thompson said "Mozzie" served in the Australian Army and was a member of the Townsville-based 1st Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment.

He completed deployments to Papua New Guinea before travelling to fight in Ukraine.

In a video posted online by Med Team Alpha, a masked soldier identifying himself as "Mozzie from Australia" explained why he wanted to fight in Ukraine.

Oscar Jenkins gives first interview since conviction Oscar Jenkins has given his first interview since he was sentenced to 13 years' imprisonment by Russian authorities.

"I have a military background in Australia so a lot of the skills that I had wouldn't transfer over to other jobs," he said.

"So I thought Ukraine would be the perfect opportunity to help out the country as a whole and use my skills to a good use."

The Ukrainian Armed Forces has been contacted for comment.

According to Ukraine's Military Ombudsman, "around 16,000 foreign volunteers from at least 72 countries" are serving alongside Ukrainian forces.

In June, former ADF soldier Samuel Pedrazzini was killed while fighting on the front lines in Donetsk, in eastern Ukraine.

Melbourne man Oscar Jenkins, who was captured by Russian forces while serving in Ukraine's army in 2024, recently gave his first interview since being convicted in what the Australian government has slammed as a "sham trial".

Australian authorities say they have asked Ukraine to prioritise Jenkins in any future prisoner swap with Russia.

World.title: The greatest scientific mystery of our time may have just flashed in a gold mine
World.content:
NationalScience The greatest scientific mystery of our time may have just flashed in a gold mine Angus Dalton September 2, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Examine, a free newsletter covering science, is sent every Tuesday. You’re reading an excerpt – sign up to get the whole newsletter in your inbox. Sometimes it feels as if all the fundamental questions about existence have been solved. Then you remember dark matter. This unknowable substance constitutes as much as 85 per cent of all mass in the universe, and yet we cannot see or directly measure it, and we don’t know what it’s made of. Scientists believe dark matter underpins the structure of the universe. KIPAC/SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory But the structure of spiralling galaxies, the make-up of the cosmos, and indeed our very existence only make sense if the universe is woven with an undiscovered, invisible essence, holding it all together like a secret skeleton.



Needless to say, dark matter is the greatest scientific mystery of our time. That’s why physicists are intensely excited about a tiny spark of light detected in a pool of liquid xenon in the depths of an abandoned goldmine. The data is limited and fresh, and scientists are duly cautious. But there is a possibility this newly reported signal could be the first-ever detection of dark matter. How do we know dark matter exists? Fritz Zwicky was an unconventional and at times unpopular scientist who once said of his more orthodox colleagues: “Astronomers are spherical bastards. No matter how you look at them, they are just bastards.”



The Swiss stargazer was investigating the Coma galaxy cluster in 1933 when he realised the galaxies were rocketing around each other at 2000 kilometres per second – so fast they should have violently flung away from each other. The structure and speed of galaxies don’t make sense unless they contain far more mass and gravity than they appear to. AP He calculated the galaxies, to summon enough gravity to stay together, must have 400 times more mass than they appeared to have. What was providing this invisible gravitational glue? He proposed the existence of dark matter. Zwicky’s theory was treated as zany. Then American astronomer Vera Rubin spied another anomaly in the 1970s. Stars on the outer edge of a galaxy should orbit much slower than those at the centre. But Rubin discovered the outer stars of a galaxy travelled just as fast as those closer to the centre.



The visible matter in the galaxies didn’t have enough gravity to hold on to these distant, fast-spinning stars. Something else was holding on to them. Rubin concluded: “What you see in a spiral galaxy is not what you get”, and that dark matter must be real. Now astronomers can see how light is warped in space by gravity emanating from dense, invisible regions of suspected dark matter. The image below shows galactic gas highlighted in pink, while the blue areas show regions of intense gravity scientists believe can only be explained by dark matter. The Bullet Cluster, a pair of galaxy clusters that collided. Normal matter is shown in pink, suspected dark matter in the cluster shown in blue. This observation has provided one of the clearest direct examples of dark matter. NASA But that’s a shadow of a shadow. In the race to truly detect dark matter, instead of looking up through telescopes, we’re burrowing deep into the Earth.



The deep detector

Dark matter doesn’t emit or reflect light, and it barely interacts with normal matter. We also don’t know what it’s made of. So how do we find it? Dr Theresa Fruth, a dark matter hunter from the University of Sydney, helped design and construct one of the best dark matter detectors on Earth, called the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment. About 250 scientists and engineers are participating in the project. Dr Theresa Fruth, from the University of Sydney, preparing to descend to the LZ detector in South Dakota. Theresa Fruth “It’s basically a big bucket of liquid xenon,” Fruth says. “Xenon is a trace element in the air around us, and it’s a noble gas. But if you cool it down enough, about minus 100 degrees, it’s a really dense liquid.”



Any skerrick of radiation might mimic dark matter and must be banished. “Xenon is good because you don’t have any long-lived radioactivity naturally in the xenon. It decays away and you can have this very clean, very quiet liquid.” The LZ detector was moved 1.5 kilometres underground into a gold mine to shield it from cosmic rays. Matthew Kapust/Sanford Underground Research Facility Researchers assess LZ’s central detector while it is wrapped in foil. Matthew Kapust/Sanford Underground Research Laboratory Looking up into the LZ outer detector, used to veto radioactivity that can mimic a dark matter signal. Matthew Kapust/Sanford Underground Research Laboratory



The ultrapure liquid xenon is contained in two tanks of medical-grade titanium and teflon, in turn encased by more than 250,000 litres of water for extra shielding. The entire thing is entombed in an abandoned goldmine in South Dakota, 1.5 kilometres underground, to protect the detector from cosmic radiation lashing Earth from space. In theory, if a skerrick of dark matter hits this pool of xenon – one of the stillest, quietest, most stable places on Earth – at the right angle, it would spark a tiny flash of light. On Wednesday, at midnight, scientists reported a flash. Finding WIMPs



The LZ experiment is designed to detect weakly interacting massive particles, or WIMPs, one of the leading theories for what dark matter could be made of. WIMPs are thought to be heavy, slow-moving subatomic particles between 10 and 1000 times heavier than a proton. Scientists think they might be constantly passing through Earth like ghosts. When a WIMP collides with a xenon atom, the xenon atom emits a flash of light and electrons. Greg Stewart, SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory If one of these WIMPS struck the nucleus of a xenon atom in the LZ detector, theoretically, this would unleash a tiny flash of light. Five hundred photomultiplier tubes in the tank set-up are tuned to pick up any flashes.



Scientists pore over the resulting data to see whether flashes might be explained by stray radiation given off by the material of the detector itself, or some other rogue background ray. Now they have reported a flash that, as yet, cannot be explained by a background signal: a possible hint of dark matter. “We don’t really know what to do with that, because we’re so used to not seeing anything,” Fruth says. “We usually make these jokes about how we’re not seeing anything better than anyone else. “The moment you see something and you don’t quite know yet what it is, it’s very exciting, but also a little bit scary.” Aussie detector in the hunt



The finding is below “5-sigma” significance, which in physics lingo is the level of statistical confidence needed to report an actual discovery. The LZ flash sits at 2.6 sigma, which means there’s a 0.5 per cent chance the flash could be due to a known background signal rather than a WIMP. The dark matter lab under construction a kilometre underground at the Stawell Gold Mine in 2021. Joe Armao The scientists are releasing their data so that other dark matter hunters can analyse and try to explain it, so we’ll know more about this detection in coming months. Meanwhile, the LZ detector team is waiting patiently for another event, which could help refine that sigma number. Should further data push the statistical firepower higher, we could be at the start of a historic moment in science.

World.title: Australia’s ‘shameful’ cocaine habit prompts $600m Pacific package
World.content:
PoliticsFederalDrugs Australia’s ‘shameful’ cocaine habit prompts $600m Pacific package Matthew Knott September 1, 2026 — 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Koror City, Palau: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will pledge $600 million for a new Pacific-wide initiative to combat the surge of illicit drug smuggling in the region, especially cocaine bound for Australia. The major funding commitment came as Albanese pushed back against China’s Pacific envoy for threatening retaliation and lodging complaints over Taiwan’s presence at the Pacific Islands Forum in Palau, declaring it was up to Pacific nations to determine their own affairs. US Coast Guard members board a self-propelled semi-submersible in international waters in 2019. US Coast Guard/AP Tensions between Taiwan and China escalated as officials traded barbs, with Taiwan accusing Beijing of bullying smaller nations and China accusing the self-governing territory of humiliating itself. As they struggle to cope with a dramatic rise in transnational crime fuelling the illegal drug trade, Pacific leaders are preparing to endorse a new regional initiative known as Waqa Moana to beef up maritime patrols and intelligence sharing.



The $600 million package Albanese will announce on Wednesday would fund enhanced aerial surveillance to help track suspected drug vessels and provide extra support to police in Fiji, among the nations hardest hit by the rise in drug smuggling. The Waqa Moana initiative – named after a large, sturdy canoe – would include greater co-ordination of existing resources to combat transnational crime, including the 23 Guardian-class patrol boats Australia has given to Pacific countries. Federal police would also increase their co-operation with South and Central American countries to target the drug trade at its source. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was welcomed at Palau Airport on Monday night. AAPIMAGE “The Pacific is our home and our family. That’s why it’s in Australia’s interests to work with our Pacific partners to combat organised crime,” Albanese said.



“For the good of every country in the region, including our own – we need to work together to stamp out the illicit drug trade.” Related Article Analysis

Pacific diplomacy Narco-subs and ballistic missiles: PM’s Pacific trip a swirl of geopolitical turmoil Pacific leaders are expected to officially endorse the initiative at the end of the week. Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett declared in May that “it is our nation’s shame that Australians consume too many illicit drugs and pay high prices for them”. At the same time, Barrett revealed that 17 tonnes of illicit drugs, mostly cocaine, had been seized by authorities in the Pacific since January, up from less than five tonnes in all of 2025.



Barrett warned that “greedy and ruthless narco-gangs are trying to make more money by identifying new ways to traffic illicit drugs”, including by sending semi-submersible vehicles (widely known as narco-submarines) to cross the Pacific. “The magnitude and endless maritime trafficking of illicit drugs to, and through the Pacific, has become a serious national security threat for the Pacific and Australia,” she said. A multinational police investigation implicating 11 Fijian police officers in collusion with drug traffickers was also handed over to prosecutors in May. A month later, Fijian police confirmed that 76 parcels that washed up in the country had been found to contain cocaine. Pacific Minister Pat Conroy said: “Drug trafficking is having a devastating impact on Pacific communities.



“This initiative responds to the calls of regional leaders to do more, and to step up regional coordination to address this scourge.” Related Article Pacific diplomacy ‘The Pacific determines what happens’: Albanese pushes back against China over Taiwan warning Speaking after the forum’s opening ceremony, China’s special envoy for the Pacific Qian Bo said he had “serious concerns” about the level of access being granted to Taiwan, a self-governing island that China claims as an integral part of its territory. “We have made our position very clear to the government of Palau and the secretariat,” he told reporters. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun doubled down on Tuesday, telling reporters in Beijing that Taiwan “has no standing whatsoever” to participate in PIF activities.



“By sending ‘Taiwan independence’ separatists like [Taiwan Foreign Minister] Lin Chia-lung around to scheme for attention and clout, the Taiwan authorities will only end up bringing humiliation upon themselves,” Guo said. He also rejected New Zealand Foreign Minister Winston Peters’ claim that the non-attendance of several leaders was “highly suspicious”, insisting it was “completely groundless” to blame China for the no-shows. Lin urged Pacific leaders to hold firm against Beijing’s demands as he accused Qian of practicing an aggressive form of “wolf warrior diplomacy”. “We should not be making concessions just because of China’s bullying,” he said. He told reporters Taiwan had been a PIF development partner since 1993, and he had “every confidence” it would participate in next year’s conference in New Zealand. Blocking Taiwan from participating would “violate the spirit of the Pacific way”, he said.



China, the United States and other countries serve as official dialogue partners of the PIF, while Taiwan attends as a development partner. Palau is one of a handful of remaining countries in the world that still recognise Taiwan, rather than Beijing, as the legitimate government of China. China’s special envoy for the Pacific Qian Bo made it clear how unhappy Beijing was that Taiwan was invited to the forum. AAPIMAGE Saying he believed China had the support of most Pacific nations over the issue, Qian said that “there will always be consequences” when China is unhappy about a decision. Asked about Qian’s comments on Tuesday, Albanese told reporters: “The Pacific Islands Forum determines what happens here, not any other country.”



Albanese, who has previously holidayed in Palau, rejected the Chinese tourism ministry’s warnings of robberies, describing the Micronesian nation as a “paradise”. Asked about China’s warning of consequences, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said: “I think the Pacific should be able to determine its own relationships.” Opposition foreign affairs spokesman Ted O’Brien called Beijing’s behaviour “intimidating” and called for Albanese to be more outspoken about China’s attempted coercion. “The prime minister’s continued reluctance to confront increasingly concerning behaviour by Beijing risks projecting weakness and undermining Australia’s national interests,” he said. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Dean Cox won’t rule out suspended five returning to the Swans this season
World.content:
In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: Swans coach Dean Cox didn’t rule out Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, James Jordon or Riley Bice from returning to the club this season.

Carlton’s Ben Ainsworth has been working on his mindset this season with Richmond premiership great Alex Rance.

Max Holmes is firming to return for the Cats’ knockout final against Carlton. Sydney coach Dean Cox has not ruled out the five suspended players making a return to the club before the end of the season. As the second-placed Swans prepare to embark on a finals campaign with massively reduced external expectations on them after the five – Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice – were banned for breaching the club’s behavioural standards, Cox revealed there is uncertainty about how long they’ll be absent from the club. Dean Cox and his Swans will begin their finals campaign on Saturday. Getty Images “I think things are changing by the hour and the day,” Cox said on AFL 360 ahead of Saturday’s qualifying final against the Brisbane Lions at the SCG.



“[With] people upstairs [at the club], and I’m privy to some of those conversations [and the focus] has been about how we best manage our football team at the minute and make sure that we can focus as heavily as we possibly can on this weekend’s game, whilst also supporting those players whilst they aren’t at the club. Related Article AFL 2026 Legal moves for five Swans players as fresh hotel details emerge “There’s no timeframe on when they will return. We’ll keep talking about it each day, and assess the situation from there.” The five players have begun appointing different lawyers to represent them as police investigate the allegation of sexual assault at the Pullman East Melbourne that was made last month. The five have denied any criminal wrongdoing, according to a source with knowledge of the matter. There are at least three separate counsels for the five players, whose interviews with Victoria Police loom after the alleged assault at the hotel where the Swans were staying for their round 23 clash with Essendon.



The players’ legal moves come as further details emerge about the early morning events at the hotel and how one of the women came to be in the foyer with Swans staff including Cox. No Swans officials are accused of inappropriate behaviour. Cox confirmed he was maintaining contact with the players. View post on X “One thing I’ll always do is support my players – I’m staying in dialogue with those five players whilst they’re away from the football club. “I speak about their welfare, how they’re going, if we can support [them] in any way.



“We need to understand that that’s one thing I’ll always do. “I haven’t spoken to them at all about the police investigation, and also I think we need to understand that there’s still an investigation in process. “We need to get all the facts on that before we make any assumptions. “It’s purely about support, and I’ll continue to do that.” Separate to the police investigation, the players received club-imposed bans for the rest of the season for drinking, staying out late and inviting women back to the team hotel.



When the Pullman Hotel incident became public last month, Swans chairman Andrew Pridham conceded that the sanctions imposed by Sydney could “torpedo” their premiership hopes. “They shouldn’t have been in that situation of being out that late, and the only way we can deal with it is to put our foot down incredibly hard, which we’ve done,” Pridham said at the time. Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich and chairman Andrew Pridham fronting the media in Sydney. George Chan “I think a very important point to make is that we, as a football club, that is our business, and to effectively torpedo our season by making a decision such as this just tells you how seriously we are taking it.” Cox said he hadn’t spoken to Pridham about those comments.



“Certainly in my conversations with Andrew there has been not one suggestion that he’s lost any belief in this playing group, and what it can still do,” he said. “I think through this his support and guidance, not only for me but for all players and all staff and the entire club, has been the highest level. And it has been like that for decades. “I really admire the way he has led through this situation, taking ownership, set the standards, and supported all the people around him.”

- Scott Spits A Tigers great is helping this former Sun spark a Blues revival for the ages Hannah Kennelly



Carlton forward Ben Ainsworth concedes the Blues’ miraculous resurgence is ripped from the pages of a Ted Lasso script. “It’s pretty crazy to be in this position,” he said ahead of his team’s elimination final against Geelong on Friday. Ben Ainsworth is relishing being part of Carlton’s revival in 2026. Justin McManus “Obviously, playing in our first elimination final off the back of the wildcard final, and where we were at 1-8 [win-loss record] at the start of the year, to be here now is pretty incredible.” The Blues’ remarkable uprising continued last weekend with a thrilling win over Melbourne in a high-pressure wildcard final. Ainsworth was a key part of the victory, booting three goals in front of 91,733 fans at the MCG.



He said new coach Josh Fraser had instilled “a great sense of belief” in the group since he took over from Michael Voss mid-season. Ben Ainsworth played one of the most important games of his career. AFL Photos “A lot of the pillars at the start of the year were laid in terms of the foundation of how we want to play and things like that,” he said. “But it’s probably the small acts that we’re celebrating internally that probably doesn’t get blown up in lights externally, and I think everyone’s valuing that, and that’s incentivising our fans as well, which is good.” After nine seasons and 158 games for Gold Coast, the dynamic forward was traded to Carlton at the end of 2025, reuniting with his former Victorian Country teammates from underage football Harry McKay and Jacob Weitering.



View post on X Ainsworth revealed he’d been doing “a lot of work” on his mindset this season with Richmond premiership great Alex Rance. After announcing his shock retirement in 2019, Rance departed Richmond to focus on his family and faith – as a devout Jehovah’s Witness. Rance has since worked with Gold Coast as a leadership consultant and mental-performance coach. “He’s [Rance] obviously still up on the Gold Coast, but he’s a fantastic person to have in my corner ... pretty much just to filter out all the stuff throughout the week and over the game, and then reset for the coming week,” Ainsworth said.



Related Article AFL 2026 How the Blues are harnessing the energy of their boisterous fans to ‘break’ rivals Even since his move to Carlton, Ainsworth still catches up with Rance each Monday, describing the former Tiger as “a great support network”. “[We] filter out everything, whether it was good or bad, just be refreshed for the coming week. And then also focusing on my strengths; just bringing them to the forefront of mind before the game on the weekend,” he explained. When asked what the quirkiest piece of advice he’d received from Rance, Ainsworth grinned. “Oh no, not a lot, but I can tell you at the Gold Coast days, he was just a ball of energy,” he laughed. “Like he’d roll into the room, just bloody dancing or whatever, singing. He’s a great man.”



Despite the growing fanfare around the Blues finals performance, Ainsworth agreed there was a sense of calm among the playing group. “People are going to come for us when the bad times arise, and, obviously, they’re going to celebrate with us in the good times. But no matter what, we’re going to have each other there,” he said.

- Hannah Kennelly Finals return for Geelong star looking ‘positive’ AAP Geelong star Max Holmes is firming to return for an elimination final bout with Carlton, with Cats coach Chris Scott admitting the midfielder looked good enough to play last week.



Holmes hasn’t played since fracturing an ankle and needing syndesmosis surgery in round 19. But the 24-year-old has completed full training over the past week and is looking increasingly likely to face the red-hot Blues. Holmes ran freely during the brief time when media were allowed to watch training on Tuesday. “He [also] trained last Thursday, and he looked pretty good to my eye,” Scott said of Holmes. “If you put it in the really old-school, back when I started playing, he might have played last week because you watched him run around Thursday and go, ‘OK, well he can do it’.



Max Holmes was helped from the ground by trainers during the Cats’ clash with the Saints in July. AFL Photos “I just think we’ve shifted a little bit philosophically from those days. “It’s getting to the point where he just keeps doing what has been asked of him.” Missing out on a double chance, Geelong don’t have the luxury of giving Holmes another week off to be certain he is right to play. Holmes would give the Cats’ midfield a giant boost coming up against an in-form Blues set-up featuring the likes of young gun Jagga Smith, Sam Walsh and Patrick Cripps.



“I’m thinking hard without having come to a conclusion yet,” Scott said of the Holmes decision. “But that’ll obviously be a team decision as well, led in large part by Max.” If Holmes plays, the Cats will virtually be at full-strength after Scott declared small forward Oliver Wiltshire right to return from a foot injury. Geelong still had the pre-finals bye and avoided the historic wildcard round, which 10th-placed Carlton were forced into and beat Melbourne last Saturday night.



“I’d prefer to finish top four, win the first week, miss a bit of footy ... but this is this is a close second,” Scott said. “Carlton is so hot right now, they finished 10th, and that’s less an indication of their season. “More that half the competition, on their day, have a really good chance of beating anyone.” The Blues will enter Friday night’s match at the MCG having won 11 of their last 14 matches since Josh Fraser took over as coach. Carlton also have the recent edge over the Cats, winning four of their past five battles, including a thriller in round 12.

World.title: Drawn to a close
World.content:
Now the dust has settled, it’s time for C8-ers to venerate the realness of Granny’s page neighbour Cathy Wilcox. This salutation comes from Joy Cooksey of Harrington: “A real cartoonist’s picture paints the thousand words no artificial artist will ever achieve, just as a copyist’s attempt doesn’t create an original. AI can never replace Wilcox because it lacks a real heart and soul.”

Unsurprisingly, Jim Dewar of Davistown took the poetic route.

A word from an old wooden-spoonist:

Cheerio to our favourite cartoonist.

Let’s hope a wee break,

Is all that she’ll take,

Then return to the letters page soonest.

Lyn Langtry of East Ryde is another to witness the chrysalis of the Brothers Gibb (C8): “Picture the scene in the mid-sixties. A group of schoolgirls spending a day at the Royal Easter Show. In a building little more than a shed, some bands were entertaining the crowd. One was the Bee Gees. My diary just records the name but no commentary.”

Now, a hard-hitting question from Marjie Williamson of Blaxland: “On a foil sheet of 10 tablets, I always start at the top-right-hand tablet. Do left-handed people start at the top-left? Or the bottom-left?” Powerful.

Ron Besdansky of Northbridge has more on licensing law loopholes (C8): “In the ’70s, I went to folk music concerts at a pub in the city. At 11pm, they started selling food so they could continue serving alcohol, so I used to pay one dollar to get what I called the ‘statutory sausage roll’. No relation to the democracy sausage.”

World.title: ‘Legend’ former ADF combat medic killed while volunteering in Ukraine
World.content:
WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war ‘Legend’ former ADF combat medic killed while volunteering in Ukraine David Crowe September 1, 2026 — 8:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A former Australian Defence Force soldier hailed as a legendary combat medic has been killed in Ukraine while under fire from Russian forces, drawing praise for his “selfless” commitment to others. The soldier, known by his call sign “Mozzie” in Ukraine where he was fighting as a volunteer, was killed in action last Wednesday, according to his former Australian Army colleague, federal Liberal MP Phillip Thompson. Thompson said Mozzie served with the Townsville-based 1st Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, and was deployed to Butterworth in Malaysia and Papua New Guinea. The news of “Mozzie’s” death drew emotional reactions from supporters of the volunteer soldiers who have fought for Ukraine. Instagram “He was a valued member of the battalion’s heavy weapons platoon, affectionately known as the ‘Fatboys’, and earned the respect of all who served alongside him,” he said in a statement.



“After leaving the Australian Army, Mozzie travelled to Ukraine where he saw significant combat and later joined Med Team Alpha, serving as a combat medic and support specialist with the 1st Foreign Legion Squadron. “Through his courage, skill and selfless commitment to others, Mozzie saved countless lives on the battlefield. He was the kind of bloke who never hesitated to put others before himself. Loading “He was a good man, a great soldier, and someone his mates could always rely on when it mattered most.” The news drew emotional reactions from supporters of the volunteer soldiers who have fought for Ukraine, including the Protect a Volunteer (PAV) group.



“Mozzie was a legend,” one group member posted on social media site Reddit. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war Government has abandoned Oscar Jenkins in Russian prison: Australian interviewer “The stories about him are crazy but true. He once transfused his own blood, several times over several days, to stabilise a guy and make him able to get evacuated. “Another time he [exfiltrated] himself due to injury then went BACK and saved Fifty. “I never actually met him myself. I only met his teammates because Mozzie was always out in the field. But he holds the all-time record for people contacting PAV just to say good things about him.”



The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has not made any public comment on his death. Mozzie’s full name was not released due to a request from his family for privacy. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war ‘Your typical Aussie cricket boy’: Why Oscar Jenkins went to fight in Ukraine Another former Australian Army soldier, Samuel Pedrazzini, died in June in the Donetsk region of Ukraine. Pedrazzini, 26, had trained Ukrainian soldiers in the United Kingdom, as part of a longstanding NATO project, before resigning from the ADF and travelling to Ukraine to volunteer as a soldier last year. A funeral service for Pedrazzini was held in the western Ukrainian town of Chukalivka, near Ivano-Frankivsk, early in July.



His commander, whose call sign is Alex, praised the Australian for his military skill, according to a report in The New Voice of Ukraine. “Sam was an excellent machine gunner, a great marksman and a skilled medic. He was a person who could do absolutely everything,” Alex said. Loading “Prior to enlisting, he volunteered at stabilisation points to save wounded soldiers. Samuel deeply loved Ukraine and wanted to stay here. “At some point, he realised that he wanted to fight for Ukraine, defend its freedom and independence, and become a part of this society.”



The news follows the emergence of a video interview with another Australian volunteer fighter, Oscar Jenkins, who was captured by Russian forces in December 2024 and is now in prison. Jenkins was sentenced by a Russian court to 13 years in a penal colony, in a decision that Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described as an outrage. In the interview, Jenkins told Australian interviewer Mark Lowe, a teacher and amateur journalist based in Vladivostok, that he had offered to fight for Russia but had been turned down. World.title: Powerhouse big spending is at the expense of so much else
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

What people don’t see behind the eye-watering Powerhouse figures, tossed around like confetti, is the opportunity cost of missed chances (“Powerhouse joins our troubled history of building public institutions”, September 1). It’s amazing that the government can rustle up, at the drop of a hat, $70 million to spend on rugs, studio apartments, videos and other frivolities. Swept under a rug (not one of their $4000 ones) is the fact that many other worthy causes are being neglected. Take the Australian Print Museum at Penrith (recently reopened by the Hon Bob Carr) – a marvellous “working museum” that showcases the story of Australia’s print heritage. All the presses are kept running by an army of volunteers with not a penny from government. For 25 years we’ve been praised by thousands of visitors who are horrified when we explain that governments of both persuasions have ignored us. Their excuse being “we haven’t got the money”. Now, thanks to the Herald exposing what is a scandal of monumental proportions, we’ll approach the treasurer, safe in the knowledge the NSW government has bags of money. We should at least thank the Powerhouse management for alerting the rest of us to the fact that the state government is loaded with hollow logs just waiting to be prised open. James Cryer, Castlecrag A final polish for the Powerhouse ahead of opening. Steven Siewert Apparently Powerhouse Parramatta is spending $70 million on opening exhibitions (“Pressure builds on Powerhouse board”, September 1) and yet there exists a 147-year-old collection of objects across applied arts, design, fashion, craft and other areas that we rarely get an opportunity to view. One of the points of these new building projects was surely to allow more access to the collection for the public, students and academics. These collections are part of our heritage but are not even mentioned in this suite of lavish new exhibitions. Surely some of the $70 million could have been spent on supporting the Australian Design Centre in Sydney, which was unceremoniously defunded after supporting designers, makers and craftspeople for more than 50 years on a very small budget. Dr Ruth McDermott, Randwick Hypocrisy on display Pauline Hanson is absolutely entitled to protection from threats of violence, and those threats should be condemned without qualification (“Hanson security boosted amid war of words with PM”, September 1). But her hypocrisy is breathtaking. After 30 years of a political career built around division, exclusion and fear of the “other”, Hanson now accuses Anthony Albanese of inciting violence because he describes One Nation as divisive. This from a politician who has long portrayed herself as a fearless champion of free speech, prepared to say the provocative things others supposedly will not. Apparently, free speech becomes dangerous when it is used to criticise Pauline Hanson. Barnaby Joyce’s defence only adds to the absurdity. Albanese did not call One Nation “evil”. He criticised its policies and argued that it divides Australians. That is political debate, not incitement. And it just happens to be true. Threats against politicians are unacceptable, whoever the target, but Hanson’s increasingly familiar pose as the victim whenever she is challenged is becoming a little tiresome. Free speech works both ways. What’s that old saying about people in glass houses?

Denise McHugh, Tamworth I do not wish to make light of threats against politicians, but it strains credulity for Pauline Hanson to portray Albanese’s observation that she is dangerous as inciting violence. Nor should we forget that Hanson has form in exploiting threats for political sensationalism. Who could forget her extraordinary 1997 video declaration: “Fellow Australians, if you are seeing me now, it means I have been murdered”, that was deliberately broadcast when she was very much alive. Salvatore Sorbello, Campsie Talk about the pot calling the kettle black. Hanson, as usual, has a very selective memory and needs to be reminded of some of the outrageous statements, all more likely to incite violence than anything the PM has said. Her complaint is clearly just another wild thought bubble intended to gain attention. The media needs to stop giving her free publicity by quoting every ridiculous thing she says. Ian Ferrier, Long Jetty



Photo: Matt Golding Time for patients Mukul Desai’s own experience is the exception that proves the point, not a rebuttal to it (Letters, August 30). A five-minute consult after a 30-to-40-minute wait doesn’t mean his care needs were simple, it may mean anything beyond the acute complaint went unaddressed. Preventative care, medication reviews and early mental health signals rarely announce themselves; they surface only when a GP has time to ask. The data Dr Elly Goodsall cites bears this out: female GPs report substantially more psychological, women’s health and multi-condition presentations, and spend three extra minutes per patient accordingly (“I’m just one more female GP quitting”, August 29). A funding model that pays per visit rather than per minute doesn’t reward thoroughness, it punishes it. Mr Desai’s quick appointments aren’t evidence the system works; they may be evidence of exactly what’s being lost. Dr Zinnia Lo, Castle Cove Beat the cheat The NSW government is to be applauded for its changes to HSC assessment to try and combat students cheating using AI (“‘It tests you far more’: New HSC home rules combat AI”, September 1). For quite some time, schools have had the flexibility on how they administer assessment tasks, and even before AI there were problems with home assessment tasks. I’m sure I disappointed quite a few parents with the marks I’d given them for trying to pass off their own work for their children. Anyone who has been teaching a while picks up very quickly whether a submitted work is that of the student. AI is capable of writing in a person’s style, provided it has samples to work with. This makes it virtually impossible for a teacher to detect unless they are using sophisticated software, as some universities do. One thing for sure is that there will always be students who will cheat, with a few getting away with it, so the challenge remains for the government and teachers to try and keep one step ahead. This will be no mean feat as technology continues to evolve. Peter Miniutti, Ashbury Construction constructiveness If Premier Chris Minns is serious about addressing the crisis in housing supply then he needs to do much more than wring his hands in the hope of an industry white knight galloping into view with saddlebags full of restorative cash. The prospect of construction group Bathla’s collapse and the effect its financial woes are already having on its suppliers and subcontractors require decisive and immediate action (“Builder collapse risks sector-wide contagion,” September 1). It would be enough to send the housing sector reaching for its collective smelling salts, but why doesn’t the Minns government stump up what’s needed to keep the Bathla construction group afloat and take equity or perhaps even a controlling stake in the company for its trouble? Given the scale of Bathla’s woes, such a move might not only placate the industry and the legions of buyers dependent on the company’s viability, but also send a signal to the state’s construction sector that it is a partner in the struggling construction boom but not its controller. Bradley Wynne, Croydon



Unforced error The 2022 decision to grant the Aboriginal land claim over Naremburn’s Talus Street Reserve and the subsequent demand for the Northern Suburbs Tennis Association to vacate with under seven weeks’ notice is a profound miscarriage of community stewardship (“Tennis players face eviction”, August 31). For 45 years, more than $10 million in investment by the local community volunteer tennis organisation, including a recent $500,000 upgrade, has made this arguably Australia’s most well-used community tennis centre. The state minister overrode standard land-claim usage protections by exploiting a 1992 clerical oversight where a minister did not sign off on a management agreement with a private operator (a common system in tennis court facility administration). Despite early promises to engage, the Metropolitan Local Aboriginal Land Council has refused dialogue, issuing an aggressive, abrupt eviction notice instead. This is scarce public recreation land. It is also the birthplace of the Humpty Dumpty Foundation, a charity formed by the centre’s players that has raised more than $100 million for critical children’s hospital equipment. Evicting a thriving community and philanthropic hub on an administrative technicality, seemingly to bank green space for future development, defies justification. Our community assets deserve better from state leadership. Rick Anderson, Frenchs Forest The eviction notice requires current operators to vacate the site by the end of September. Sitthixay Ditthavong Cost of climate crisis The housing crisis in my part of the world has been significantly worsened by the effects of climate change, particularly in the aftermath of the disastrous 2022 floods. There are still flood-damaged, unlivable homes scattered through Lismore and surrounding townships. As reported in the Herald, in 2025 alone declared catastrophes damaged 145,392 homes nationwide – almost as many as the 172,657 new homes completed that year, according to the Insurance Council of Australia in its annual Insurance Catastrophe Resilience Report (“‘The homes we build twice’: Repair bill for climate disasters climbing faster than inflation”, September 1). No wonder the supply of new houses nationwide isn’t increasing fast enough. That huge impact on housing supply has absolutely nothing to do with immigration levels but, of course, those banging the anti-immigration drum, like Pauline Hanson and her followers, dismiss climate change as a hoax because acknowledging the real-world effects of climate change, already being experienced, would weaken their anti-immigration arguments and wouldn’t please her mining billionaire sponsors. Lynne Wallis, Wollongbar



Snow and steady Because so many weather phenomena are immediately attributed to climate change these days, I decided to analyse 75 years of Snowy Hydro’s data on snow depths at Spencer Creek (“Spring set to sizzle after warm winter”, September 1). Yes, there is a slow, long-term decrease in average snow depths and length of snow season, which may be attributable to climate change, among other factors. But what is certain is that snow depths vary widely from year to year – which may relate to the El Nino/La Nina cycles. My conclusion is that it’s just as likely that there will be bumper snow years in the decades to come, just as 2025 was, and Ms Rennie will be digging out her front door once again, and I will be digging out my car. And to put it in perspective, poor as the snow has been, 2026 is better to date than 1973 was and only marginally worse than in 1954 – both way before global emissions were anything like today. Peter Thornton, Killara I operate a lawnmowing business and always enjoy a break in the winter months. If the weather warms up permanently it might become a solid slog for 12 months a year. Michael Deeth, Como West A new threat Purely for research purposes, a one-line AI search, available to any child, negated Labor’s age verification legislation. Courts are recognising the negative addictive effects of social media on children, but the risks that AI pose will be far greater. It’s easy to imagine that you’re having a conversation with a real and helpful person, who vulnerable children could easily adopt as a cyber friend, leading them down endless labyrinthine pathways to who knows where. If social media is addictive, AI will be heroin (“How Australia’s social media ban loomed over Meta’s $24b settlement”, September). William S. Lloyd, Denistone Inspirational Tony “Stand up and fight until you hear the bell” may well have been the motto of the late former Australian boxing champion Tony Mundine (“Vale Tony Mundine, a champion fighter and a great Australian”, August 31). While the damage caused by boxing is now well known, we can still recognise how in another age it was one of the few paths out of poverty for some. In hindsight, we can see that this never should have had to be an option. However, we can still applaud the discipline and resolution shown by Mundine, for whom boxing bettered his own life, that of his family and of those boxers whom he later trained. As someone who shunned smoking, drinking, gambling and drugs, his philosophy of life and his achievements, if not his preferred sport, have been inspirational. Paul Casey, Callala Bay

World.title: The ‘lush oasis’ being built next to Sydney’s busiest motorway
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life The ‘lush oasis’ being built next to Sydney’s busiest motorway Cindy Yin September 1, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After spending years as a construction site for one of Sydney’s biggest transport projects, 2.5 hectares on the edge of Warringah Freeway will be transformed into parkland – but residents will have to wait at least another two years before they can access the space. The NSW government has unveiled draft designs for Cammeray Parklands on the lower north shore, with plans to build a synthetic-turf sporting area and courts suitable for basketball or pickleball, as well as open lawns, gardens, shared paths and an outdoor fitness station. An artist’s impression of the new Cammeray Parklands. NSW Government An artist’s impression of the new Cammeray Parklands. NSW Government Roads Minister Jenny Aitchison said the parkland would be a “lush oasis” next to one of Australia’s busiest roads, the Warringah Freeway, and open at the same time as the $7.6 billion Western Harbour Tunnel project.



But North Sydney Council’s independent mayor Zoe Baker said the two road projects had created “scarring” impacts on residents and motorists who have endured years-long disruptions. Once construction finishes in late 2028, the three-lane tunnels in the 6.5-kilometre Western Harbour Tunnel motorway will link the Warringah Freeway on the north shore to the WestConnex toll road at Rozelle in the south, providing motorists an alternative to the Harbour Bridge and Harbour Tunnel in the CBD. Aitchison said the new parkland would act as a “connecting piece of landscape” linking existing green space, Cammeray golf course and the nearby Anzac Park. An aerial view of the current Western Harbour Tunnel construction site near the Warringah Freeway. NSW Government The 2.5 hectares of open space will have open lawns, gardens, shared paths, a multi-use half court for pickleball and basketball, a synthetic-turf sports area and an outdoor fitness station. NSW Government



“What this is designed to do is to really give back to the community a green space where they can enjoy their time,” she said. The government was “getting on with delivering the Western Harbour Tunnel but we are also making sure the communities hosting this major construction work see a lasting benefit”, Aitchison added. Related Article Roads ‘Every millimetre counts’: Inside the beast tunnelling under Sydney Harbour Baker welcomed the plans and said every bit of green space that facilitated passive and active recreation was “vital” in North Sydney, but stressed the new parkland did not represent a real increase in open space because it was previously green space and a golf course before it became a construction site. “Overall it’s a net loss but it is better than what we were fearing,” she said. “The Warringah Freeway upgrade meant the loss of 3000 mature trees … When those trees went, there was a loss of biodiversity, and there was a very emotional – rightly so – response from our community. I hope this project will be part of the repair.”



The government is replanting 6000 trees to offset the 3000 lost to road upgrades but workers have discovered there is not enough room to plant them, due to a shortage of land. The Cammeray Parklands are also right next to the golf course that the Minister for Lands Steve Kamper signalled his intent, in March, to hand to Golf NSW, sparking backlash from the council who wanted the land to remain in the club’s hands. Western Harbour Tunnel project operations director Tariq Macan-Markar said Cammeray Park would have a similar feel to a park above the Rozelle Interchange.
