World.title: Messages of hate strike wrong note at Sydney Marathon
World.content:
NationalNSWAntisemitism Opinion Messages of hate strike wrong note at Sydney Marathon Orly Lavee Doctor September 1, 2026 — 7:30pm

September 1, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I was one of 40,000 people who ran the Sydney Marathon on Sunday. For one morning, a city of more than 5 million people becomes unusually intimate. Nobody cares what you earn, where you were born, which god you believe in or which language your grandmother spoke. It is communal joy in its purest form. Competitors in the 2026 Sydney Marathon. George Chan So perhaps that is why what happened next felt so discordant. Among all of that, I saw accusatory messages of hate directed against Israelis. I cannot know precisely who every person holding those signs intended to address. But in the current social climate, it was difficult not to understand them as being directed at Israelis participating in the Marathon, or at people perceived to be affiliated with Israel.



And for Jewish runners, particularly at a time when the distinction between criticism of Israel and hostility towards Jews is considered by many in the Jewish community as opaque, it was difficult simply to run past that language as though it existed in a vacuum. Related Article Sydney Marathon Sydney Marathon results 2026: Gobena and Jepchirchir crowned champions as thousands participate in Sydney Marathon What struck me most was not simply the politics of the signs. It was their spirit. It was inserted into an event whose entire character was the opposite of conflict: tens of thousands of ordinary people running the same course, drinking from the same cups, being cheered by the same strangers. It was immediately dispiriting not because politics should be confined to parliament, or because protest should always be polite. Some of the most important protest movements in history have been disruptive and uncomfortable. But protest is supposed to communicate something. At its best, it persuades, illuminates, demands, challenges or mobilises. It identifies an injustice and asks other people to see it. These signs seemed to ask nothing. Does telling a stranger they are hated move anyone closer to a solution?



Does importing the language of collective guilt into a community sporting event create empathy for Palestinians – or does it simply create another person who feels frightened, humiliated or despised? Political movements can become so enclosed within their own language and moral certainty that they stop noticing how they sound to everyone outside them. Slogans become articles of faith. The same ideas circulate among people who already agree with one another until expression itself becomes confused with achievement. Related Article Analysis

Antisemitism royal commission Liberals wanted to extend the royal commission. But Jewish groups did not join the call If they were protesting against the Israeli runners – most of whom would be ex-service people given Israel’s policy of conscription – who were raising money for Shalva, a disability NGO that serves Jewish, Muslim, Christian and Druze Israelis, then it highlights the futility in protest that no longer seems interested in persuasion or nuance. If the person passing you is not someone whose mind you hope to change, and not someone with power to implement the change you seek, then what precisely is the purpose of confronting them? Perhaps the answer is simply to make them feel unwelcome. If so, we should call that what it is.



It has been widely explored that criticism of the Israeli government and the Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) is not inherently antisemitic but neither is there an impermeable wall separating anti-Zionism from antisemitism. There are circumstances in which the distance between them becomes for some of us very small indeed. Perhaps the most useful test is a simple one: would we apply the same principle to anybody else? Is this a world in which ordinary people may be publicly confronted with the actions of governments, leaders or countries with which they are associated? Russians for Putin. Iranians for the Islamic Republic. Americans for American wars. Chinese Australians for Beijing. Palestinians for Hamas. Israelis for Netanyahu. Australia works, imperfectly but remarkably, because people can arrive carrying different histories, religions, languages, loyalties and inherited griefs and nevertheless meet one another in a public space without demanding that every person answer for everything done by someone who shares their ethnicity, nationality or faith. That social contract is fragile. None of this diminishes the suffering of Palestinians. None of it makes criticism of Israel antisemitic. Those are lazy binaries, and this subject deserves better than lazy binaries.



In our determination to make every public space another battlefield, I wonder whether we understand what we are giving up. Orly Lavee is a doctor who lives in Sydney. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: The greatest scientific mystery of our time may have just flashed in a gold mine
World.content:
NationalScience The greatest scientific mystery of our time may have just flashed in a gold mine Angus Dalton September 2, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Examine, a free newsletter covering science, is sent every Tuesday. You’re reading an excerpt – sign up to get the whole newsletter in your inbox. Sometimes it feels as if all the fundamental questions about existence have been solved. Then you remember dark matter. This unknowable substance constitutes as much as 85 per cent of all mass in the universe, and yet we cannot see or directly measure it, and we don’t know what it’s made of. Scientists believe dark matter underpins the structure of the universe. KIPAC/SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory But the structure of spiralling galaxies, the make-up of the cosmos, and indeed our very existence only make sense if the universe is woven with an undiscovered, invisible essence, holding it all together like a secret skeleton.



Needless to say, dark matter is the greatest scientific mystery of our time. That’s why physicists are intensely excited about a tiny spark of light detected in a pool of liquid xenon in the depths of an abandoned goldmine. The data is limited and fresh, and scientists are duly cautious. But there is a possibility this newly reported signal could be the first-ever detection of dark matter. How do we know dark matter exists? Fritz Zwicky was an unconventional and at times unpopular scientist who once said of his more orthodox colleagues: “Astronomers are spherical bastards. No matter how you look at them, they are just bastards.”



The Swiss stargazer was investigating the Coma galaxy cluster in 1933 when he realised the galaxies were rocketing around each other at 2000 kilometres per second – so fast they should have violently flung away from each other. The structure and speed of galaxies don’t make sense unless they contain far more mass and gravity than they appear to. AP He calculated the galaxies, to summon enough gravity to stay together, must have 400 times more mass than they appeared to have. What was providing this invisible gravitational glue? He proposed the existence of dark matter. Zwicky’s theory was treated as zany. Then American astronomer Vera Rubin spied another anomaly in the 1970s. Stars on the outer edge of a galaxy should orbit much slower than those at the centre. But Rubin discovered the outer stars of a galaxy travelled just as fast as those closer to the centre.



The visible matter in the galaxies didn’t have enough gravity to hold on to these distant, fast-spinning stars. Something else was holding on to them. Rubin concluded: “What you see in a spiral galaxy is not what you get”, and that dark matter must be real. Now astronomers can see how light is warped in space by gravity emanating from dense, invisible regions of suspected dark matter. The image below shows galactic gas highlighted in pink, while the blue areas show regions of intense gravity scientists believe can only be explained by dark matter. The Bullet Cluster, a pair of galaxy clusters that collided. Normal matter is shown in pink, suspected dark matter in the cluster shown in blue. This observation has provided one of the clearest direct examples of dark matter. NASA But that’s a shadow of a shadow. In the race to truly detect dark matter, instead of looking up through telescopes, we’re burrowing deep into the Earth.



The deep detector

Dark matter doesn’t emit or reflect light, and it barely interacts with normal matter. We also don’t know what it’s made of. So how do we find it? Dr Theresa Fruth, a dark matter hunter from the University of Sydney, helped design and construct one of the best dark matter detectors on Earth, called the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment. About 250 scientists and engineers are participating in the project. Dr Theresa Fruth, from the University of Sydney, preparing to descend to the LZ detector in South Dakota. Theresa Fruth “It’s basically a big bucket of liquid xenon,” Fruth says. “Xenon is a trace element in the air around us, and it’s a noble gas. But if you cool it down enough, about minus 100 degrees, it’s a really dense liquid.”



Any skerrick of radiation might mimic dark matter and must be banished. “Xenon is good because you don’t have any long-lived radioactivity naturally in the xenon. It decays away and you can have this very clean, very quiet liquid.” The LZ detector was moved 1.5 kilometres underground into a gold mine to shield it from cosmic rays. Matthew Kapust/Sanford Underground Research Facility Researchers assess LZ’s central detector while it is wrapped in foil. Matthew Kapust/Sanford Underground Research Laboratory Looking up into the LZ outer detector, used to veto radioactivity that can mimic a dark matter signal. Matthew Kapust/Sanford Underground Research Laboratory



The ultrapure liquid xenon is contained in two tanks of medical-grade titanium and teflon, in turn encased by more than 250,000 litres of water for extra shielding. The entire thing is entombed in an abandoned goldmine in South Dakota, 1.5 kilometres underground, to protect the detector from cosmic radiation lashing Earth from space. In theory, if a skerrick of dark matter hits this pool of xenon – one of the stillest, quietest, most stable places on Earth – at the right angle, it would spark a tiny flash of light. On Wednesday, at midnight, scientists reported a flash. Finding WIMPs



The LZ experiment is designed to detect weakly interacting massive particles, or WIMPs, one of the leading theories for what dark matter could be made of. WIMPs are thought to be heavy, slow-moving subatomic particles between 10 and 1000 times heavier than a proton. Scientists think they might be constantly passing through Earth like ghosts. When a WIMP collides with a xenon atom, the xenon atom emits a flash of light and electrons. Greg Stewart, SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory If one of these WIMPS struck the nucleus of a xenon atom in the LZ detector, theoretically, this would unleash a tiny flash of light. Five hundred photomultiplier tubes in the tank set-up are tuned to pick up any flashes.



Scientists pore over the resulting data to see whether flashes might be explained by stray radiation given off by the material of the detector itself, or some other rogue background ray. Now they have reported a flash that, as yet, cannot be explained by a background signal: a possible hint of dark matter. “We don’t really know what to do with that, because we’re so used to not seeing anything,” Fruth says. “We usually make these jokes about how we’re not seeing anything better than anyone else. “The moment you see something and you don’t quite know yet what it is, it’s very exciting, but also a little bit scary.” Aussie detector in the hunt



The finding is below “5-sigma” significance, which in physics lingo is the level of statistical confidence needed to report an actual discovery. The LZ flash sits at 2.6 sigma, which means there’s a 0.5 per cent chance the flash could be due to a known background signal rather than a WIMP. The dark matter lab under construction a kilometre underground at the Stawell Gold Mine in 2021. Joe Armao The scientists are releasing their data so that other dark matter hunters can analyse and try to explain it, so we’ll know more about this detection in coming months. Meanwhile, the LZ detector team is waiting patiently for another event, which could help refine that sigma number. Should further data push the statistical firepower higher, we could be at the start of a historic moment in science.

World.title: Australia’s ‘shameful’ cocaine habit prompts $600m Pacific package
World.content:
PoliticsFederalDrugs Australia’s ‘shameful’ cocaine habit prompts $600m Pacific package Matthew Knott September 1, 2026 — 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Koror City, Palau: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will pledge $600 million for a new Pacific-wide initiative to combat the surge of illicit drug smuggling in the region, especially cocaine bound for Australia. The major funding commitment came as Albanese pushed back against China’s Pacific envoy for threatening retaliation and lodging complaints over Taiwan’s presence at the Pacific Islands Forum in Palau, declaring it was up to Pacific nations to determine their own affairs. US Coast Guard members board a self-propelled semi-submersible in international waters in 2019. US Coast Guard/AP Tensions between Taiwan and China escalated as officials traded barbs, with Taiwan accusing Beijing of bullying smaller nations and China accusing the self-governing territory of humiliating itself. As they struggle to cope with a dramatic rise in transnational crime fuelling the illegal drug trade, Pacific leaders are preparing to endorse a new regional initiative known as Waqa Moana to beef up maritime patrols and intelligence sharing.



The $600 million package Albanese will announce on Wednesday would fund enhanced aerial surveillance to help track suspected drug vessels and provide extra support to police in Fiji, among the nations hardest hit by the rise in drug smuggling. The Waqa Moana initiative – named after a large, sturdy canoe – would include greater co-ordination of existing resources to combat transnational crime, including the 23 Guardian-class patrol boats Australia has given to Pacific countries. Federal police would also increase their co-operation with South and Central American countries to target the drug trade at its source. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was welcomed at Palau Airport on Monday night. AAPIMAGE “The Pacific is our home and our family. That’s why it’s in Australia’s interests to work with our Pacific partners to combat organised crime,” Albanese said.



“For the good of every country in the region, including our own – we need to work together to stamp out the illicit drug trade.” Related Article Analysis

Pacific diplomacy Narco-subs and ballistic missiles: PM’s Pacific trip a swirl of geopolitical turmoil Pacific leaders are expected to officially endorse the initiative at the end of the week. Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett declared in May that “it is our nation’s shame that Australians consume too many illicit drugs and pay high prices for them”. At the same time, Barrett revealed that 17 tonnes of illicit drugs, mostly cocaine, had been seized by authorities in the Pacific since January, up from less than five tonnes in all of 2025.



Barrett warned that “greedy and ruthless narco-gangs are trying to make more money by identifying new ways to traffic illicit drugs”, including by sending semi-submersible vehicles (widely known as narco-submarines) to cross the Pacific. “The magnitude and endless maritime trafficking of illicit drugs to, and through the Pacific, has become a serious national security threat for the Pacific and Australia,” she said. A multinational police investigation implicating 11 Fijian police officers in collusion with drug traffickers was also handed over to prosecutors in May. A month later, Fijian police confirmed that 76 parcels that washed up in the country had been found to contain cocaine. Pacific Minister Pat Conroy said: “Drug trafficking is having a devastating impact on Pacific communities.



“This initiative responds to the calls of regional leaders to do more, and to step up regional coordination to address this scourge.” Related Article Pacific diplomacy ‘The Pacific determines what happens’: Albanese pushes back against China over Taiwan warning Speaking after the forum’s opening ceremony, China’s special envoy for the Pacific Qian Bo said he had “serious concerns” about the level of access being granted to Taiwan, a self-governing island that China claims as an integral part of its territory. “We have made our position very clear to the government of Palau and the secretariat,” he told reporters. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun doubled down on Tuesday, telling reporters in Beijing that Taiwan “has no standing whatsoever” to participate in PIF activities.



“By sending ‘Taiwan independence’ separatists like [Taiwan Foreign Minister] Lin Chia-lung around to scheme for attention and clout, the Taiwan authorities will only end up bringing humiliation upon themselves,” Guo said. He also rejected New Zealand Foreign Minister Winston Peters’ claim that the non-attendance of several leaders was “highly suspicious”, insisting it was “completely groundless” to blame China for the no-shows. Lin urged Pacific leaders to hold firm against Beijing’s demands as he accused Qian of practicing an aggressive form of “wolf warrior diplomacy”. “We should not be making concessions just because of China’s bullying,” he said. He told reporters Taiwan had been a PIF development partner since 1993, and he had “every confidence” it would participate in next year’s conference in New Zealand. Blocking Taiwan from participating would “violate the spirit of the Pacific way”, he said.



China, the United States and other countries serve as official dialogue partners of the PIF, while Taiwan attends as a development partner. Palau is one of a handful of remaining countries in the world that still recognise Taiwan, rather than Beijing, as the legitimate government of China. China’s special envoy for the Pacific Qian Bo made it clear how unhappy Beijing was that Taiwan was invited to the forum. AAPIMAGE Saying he believed China had the support of most Pacific nations over the issue, Qian said that “there will always be consequences” when China is unhappy about a decision. Asked about Qian’s comments on Tuesday, Albanese told reporters: “The Pacific Islands Forum determines what happens here, not any other country.”



Albanese, who has previously holidayed in Palau, rejected the Chinese tourism ministry’s warnings of robberies, describing the Micronesian nation as a “paradise”. Asked about China’s warning of consequences, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said: “I think the Pacific should be able to determine its own relationships.” Opposition foreign affairs spokesman Ted O’Brien called Beijing’s behaviour “intimidating” and called for Albanese to be more outspoken about China’s attempted coercion. “The prime minister’s continued reluctance to confront increasingly concerning behaviour by Beijing risks projecting weakness and undermining Australia’s national interests,” he said. World.title: Dean Cox won’t rule out suspended five returning to the Swans this season
World.content:
In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: Swans coach Dean Cox didn’t rule out Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, James Jordon or Riley Bice from returning to the club this season.

Carlton’s Ben Ainsworth has been working on his mindset this season with Richmond premiership great Alex Rance.

Max Holmes is firming to return for the Cats’ knockout final against Carlton. Sydney coach Dean Cox has not ruled out the five suspended players making a return to the club before the end of the season. As the second-placed Swans prepare to embark on a finals campaign with massively reduced external expectations on them after the five – Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice – were banned for breaching the club’s behavioural standards, Cox revealed there is uncertainty about how long they’ll be absent from the club. Dean Cox and his Swans will begin their finals campaign on Saturday. Getty Images “I think things are changing by the hour and the day,” Cox said on AFL 360 ahead of Saturday’s qualifying final against the Brisbane Lions at the SCG.



“[With] people upstairs [at the club], and I’m privy to some of those conversations [and the focus] has been about how we best manage our football team at the minute and make sure that we can focus as heavily as we possibly can on this weekend’s game, whilst also supporting those players whilst they aren’t at the club. Related Article AFL 2026 Legal moves for five Swans players as fresh hotel details emerge “There’s no timeframe on when they will return. We’ll keep talking about it each day, and assess the situation from there.” The five players have begun appointing different lawyers to represent them as police investigate the allegation of sexual assault at the Pullman East Melbourne that was made last month. The five have denied any criminal wrongdoing, according to a source with knowledge of the matter. There are at least three separate counsels for the five players, whose interviews with Victoria Police loom after the alleged assault at the hotel where the Swans were staying for their round 23 clash with Essendon.



The players’ legal moves come as further details emerge about the early morning events at the hotel and how one of the women came to be in the foyer with Swans staff including Cox. No Swans officials are accused of inappropriate behaviour. Cox confirmed he was maintaining contact with the players. View post on X “One thing I’ll always do is support my players – I’m staying in dialogue with those five players whilst they’re away from the football club. “I speak about their welfare, how they’re going, if we can support [them] in any way.



“We need to understand that that’s one thing I’ll always do. “I haven’t spoken to them at all about the police investigation, and also I think we need to understand that there’s still an investigation in process. “We need to get all the facts on that before we make any assumptions. “It’s purely about support, and I’ll continue to do that.” Separate to the police investigation, the players received club-imposed bans for the rest of the season for drinking, staying out late and inviting women back to the team hotel.



When the Pullman Hotel incident became public last month, Swans chairman Andrew Pridham conceded that the sanctions imposed by Sydney could “torpedo” their premiership hopes. “They shouldn’t have been in that situation of being out that late, and the only way we can deal with it is to put our foot down incredibly hard, which we’ve done,” Pridham said at the time. Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich and chairman Andrew Pridham fronting the media in Sydney. George Chan “I think a very important point to make is that we, as a football club, that is our business, and to effectively torpedo our season by making a decision such as this just tells you how seriously we are taking it.” Cox said he hadn’t spoken to Pridham about those comments.



“Certainly in my conversations with Andrew there has been not one suggestion that he’s lost any belief in this playing group, and what it can still do,” he said. “I think through this his support and guidance, not only for me but for all players and all staff and the entire club, has been the highest level. And it has been like that for decades. “I really admire the way he has led through this situation, taking ownership, set the standards, and supported all the people around him.”

- Scott Spits A Tigers great is helping this former Sun spark a Blues revival for the ages Hannah Kennelly



Carlton forward Ben Ainsworth concedes the Blues’ miraculous resurgence is ripped from the pages of a Ted Lasso script. “It’s pretty crazy to be in this position,” he said ahead of his team’s elimination final against Geelong on Friday. Ben Ainsworth is relishing being part of Carlton’s revival in 2026. Justin McManus “Obviously, playing in our first elimination final off the back of the wildcard final, and where we were at 1-8 [win-loss record] at the start of the year, to be here now is pretty incredible.” The Blues’ remarkable uprising continued last weekend with a thrilling win over Melbourne in a high-pressure wildcard final. Ainsworth was a key part of the victory, booting three goals in front of 91,733 fans at the MCG.



He said new coach Josh Fraser had instilled “a great sense of belief” in the group since he took over from Michael Voss mid-season. Ben Ainsworth played one of the most important games of his career. AFL Photos “A lot of the pillars at the start of the year were laid in terms of the foundation of how we want to play and things like that,” he said. “But it’s probably the small acts that we’re celebrating internally that probably doesn’t get blown up in lights externally, and I think everyone’s valuing that, and that’s incentivising our fans as well, which is good.” After nine seasons and 158 games for Gold Coast, the dynamic forward was traded to Carlton at the end of 2025, reuniting with his former Victorian Country teammates from underage football Harry McKay and Jacob Weitering.



View post on X Ainsworth revealed he’d been doing “a lot of work” on his mindset this season with Richmond premiership great Alex Rance. After announcing his shock retirement in 2019, Rance departed Richmond to focus on his family and faith – as a devout Jehovah’s Witness. Rance has since worked with Gold Coast as a leadership consultant and mental-performance coach. “He’s [Rance] obviously still up on the Gold Coast, but he’s a fantastic person to have in my corner ... pretty much just to filter out all the stuff throughout the week and over the game, and then reset for the coming week,” Ainsworth said.



Related Article AFL 2026 How the Blues are harnessing the energy of their boisterous fans to ‘break’ rivals Even since his move to Carlton, Ainsworth still catches up with Rance each Monday, describing the former Tiger as “a great support network”. “[We] filter out everything, whether it was good or bad, just be refreshed for the coming week. And then also focusing on my strengths; just bringing them to the forefront of mind before the game on the weekend,” he explained. When asked what the quirkiest piece of advice he’d received from Rance, Ainsworth grinned. “Oh no, not a lot, but I can tell you at the Gold Coast days, he was just a ball of energy,” he laughed. “Like he’d roll into the room, just bloody dancing or whatever, singing. He’s a great man.”



Despite the growing fanfare around the Blues finals performance, Ainsworth agreed there was a sense of calm among the playing group. “People are going to come for us when the bad times arise, and, obviously, they’re going to celebrate with us in the good times. But no matter what, we’re going to have each other there,” he said.

- Hannah Kennelly Finals return for Geelong star looking ‘positive’ AAP Geelong star Max Holmes is firming to return for an elimination final bout with Carlton, with Cats coach Chris Scott admitting the midfielder looked good enough to play last week.



Holmes hasn’t played since fracturing an ankle and needing syndesmosis surgery in round 19. But the 24-year-old has completed full training over the past week and is looking increasingly likely to face the red-hot Blues. Holmes ran freely during the brief time when media were allowed to watch training on Tuesday. “He [also] trained last Thursday, and he looked pretty good to my eye,” Scott said of Holmes. “If you put it in the really old-school, back when I started playing, he might have played last week because you watched him run around Thursday and go, ‘OK, well he can do it’.



Max Holmes was helped from the ground by trainers during the Cats’ clash with the Saints in July. AFL Photos “I just think we’ve shifted a little bit philosophically from those days. “It’s getting to the point where he just keeps doing what has been asked of him.” Missing out on a double chance, Geelong don’t have the luxury of giving Holmes another week off to be certain he is right to play. Holmes would give the Cats’ midfield a giant boost coming up against an in-form Blues set-up featuring the likes of young gun Jagga Smith, Sam Walsh and Patrick Cripps.



“I’m thinking hard without having come to a conclusion yet,” Scott said of the Holmes decision. “But that’ll obviously be a team decision as well, led in large part by Max.” If Holmes plays, the Cats will virtually be at full-strength after Scott declared small forward Oliver Wiltshire right to return from a foot injury. Geelong still had the pre-finals bye and avoided the historic wildcard round, which 10th-placed Carlton were forced into and beat Melbourne last Saturday night.



“I’d prefer to finish top four, win the first week, miss a bit of footy ... but this is this is a close second,” Scott said. “Carlton is so hot right now, they finished 10th, and that’s less an indication of their season. “More that half the competition, on their day, have a really good chance of beating anyone.” The Blues will enter Friday night’s match at the MCG having won 11 of their last 14 matches since Josh Fraser took over as coach. Carlton also have the recent edge over the Cats, winning four of their past five battles, including a thriller in round 12.

World.title: Drawn to a close
World.content:
Now the dust has settled, it’s time for C8-ers to venerate the realness of Granny’s page neighbour Cathy Wilcox. This salutation comes from Joy Cooksey of Harrington: “A real cartoonist’s picture paints the thousand words no artificial artist will ever achieve, just as a copyist’s attempt doesn’t create an original. AI can never replace Wilcox because it lacks a real heart and soul.”

Unsurprisingly, Jim Dewar of Davistown took the poetic route.

A word from an old wooden-spoonist:

Cheerio to our favourite cartoonist.

Let’s hope a wee break,

Is all that she’ll take,

Then return to the letters page soonest.

Lyn Langtry of East Ryde is another to witness the chrysalis of the Brothers Gibb (C8): “Picture the scene in the mid-sixties. A group of schoolgirls spending a day at the Royal Easter Show. In a building little more than a shed, some bands were entertaining the crowd. One was the Bee Gees. My diary just records the name but no commentary.”

Now, a hard-hitting question from Marjie Williamson of Blaxland: “On a foil sheet of 10 tablets, I always start at the top-right-hand tablet. Do left-handed people start at the top-left? Or the bottom-left?” Powerful.

Ron Besdansky of Northbridge has more on licensing law loopholes (C8): “In the ’70s, I went to folk music concerts at a pub in the city. At 11pm, they started selling food so they could continue serving alcohol, so I used to pay one dollar to get what I called the ‘statutory sausage roll’. No relation to the democracy sausage.”

World.title: ‘Legend’ former ADF combat medic killed while volunteering in Ukraine
World.content:
WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war ‘Legend’ former ADF combat medic killed while volunteering in Ukraine David Crowe September 1, 2026 — 8:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A former Australian Defence Force soldier hailed as a legendary combat medic has been killed in Ukraine while under fire from Russian forces, drawing praise for his “selfless” commitment to others. The soldier, known by his call sign “Mozzie” in Ukraine where he was fighting as a volunteer, was killed in action last Wednesday, according to his former Australian Army colleague, federal Liberal MP Phillip Thompson. Thompson said Mozzie served with the Townsville-based 1st Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, and was deployed to Butterworth in Malaysia and Papua New Guinea. The news of “Mozzie’s” death drew emotional reactions from supporters of the volunteer soldiers who have fought for Ukraine. Instagram “He was a valued member of the battalion’s heavy weapons platoon, affectionately known as the ‘Fatboys’, and earned the respect of all who served alongside him,” he said in a statement.



“After leaving the Australian Army, Mozzie travelled to Ukraine where he saw significant combat and later joined Med Team Alpha, serving as a combat medic and support specialist with the 1st Foreign Legion Squadron. “Through his courage, skill and selfless commitment to others, Mozzie saved countless lives on the battlefield. He was the kind of bloke who never hesitated to put others before himself. Loading “He was a good man, a great soldier, and someone his mates could always rely on when it mattered most.” The news drew emotional reactions from supporters of the volunteer soldiers who have fought for Ukraine, including the Protect a Volunteer (PAV) group.



“Mozzie was a legend,” one group member posted on social media site Reddit. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war Government has abandoned Oscar Jenkins in Russian prison: Australian interviewer “The stories about him are crazy but true. He once transfused his own blood, several times over several days, to stabilise a guy and make him able to get evacuated. “Another time he [exfiltrated] himself due to injury then went BACK and saved Fifty. “I never actually met him myself. I only met his teammates because Mozzie was always out in the field. But he holds the all-time record for people contacting PAV just to say good things about him.”



The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has not made any public comment on his death. Mozzie’s full name was not released due to a request from his family for privacy. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war ‘Your typical Aussie cricket boy’: Why Oscar Jenkins went to fight in Ukraine Another former Australian Army soldier, Samuel Pedrazzini, died in June in the Donetsk region of Ukraine. Pedrazzini, 26, had trained Ukrainian soldiers in the United Kingdom, as part of a longstanding NATO project, before resigning from the ADF and travelling to Ukraine to volunteer as a soldier last year. A funeral service for Pedrazzini was held in the western Ukrainian town of Chukalivka, near Ivano-Frankivsk, early in July.



His commander, whose call sign is Alex, praised the Australian for his military skill, according to a report in The New Voice of Ukraine. “Sam was an excellent machine gunner, a great marksman and a skilled medic. He was a person who could do absolutely everything,” Alex said. Loading “Prior to enlisting, he volunteered at stabilisation points to save wounded soldiers. Samuel deeply loved Ukraine and wanted to stay here. “At some point, he realised that he wanted to fight for Ukraine, defend its freedom and independence, and become a part of this society.”



The news follows the emergence of a video interview with another Australian volunteer fighter, Oscar Jenkins, who was captured by Russian forces in December 2024 and is now in prison. Jenkins was sentenced by a Russian court to 13 years in a penal colony, in a decision that Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described as an outrage. In the interview, Jenkins told Australian interviewer Mark Lowe, a teacher and amateur journalist based in Vladivostok, that he had offered to fight for Russia but had been turned down. World.title: One Nation is not conservative, it’s reckless
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters One Nation is not conservative, it’s reckless September 1, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. NET ZERO As we watch the ongoing horror and human tragedy of Nepal, face our own record El Niño and see Europe on fire we are treated to a total reversal of what it means to be conservative on climate action.

Barnaby Joyce claims that One Nation is “the most conservative party in Australia (‴⁣⁣You just can’t’ say we are evil’, Joyce backs Hanson on claim PM inciting violence”, 1/9) as the party symbolically bury the coffin of net zero by 2050. Nothing could be further from the truth.

The parties on the right side of politics have lost sight of what it means to be conservative. Its definition of being careful and cautious, eschewing risk and valuing stability is upended in their rush to gamble ever more recklessly with the future of life on Earth.

Denying the science and evidence of a heating planet, going against the decades of research and work of the vast majority of climate scientists is risky in the extreme. Climate science and the action required to stabilise our planetary future should be a bipartisan policy. It is neither a right or left side issue, but is to be conservative with our future and that of all future generations.

Mary-Jane Walker, Geelong Little time to address climate change effects

Pauline Hanson wants to develop fossil fuels and to get rid of Australia’s goal of reaching net zero carbon emissions. Oh, and she also wants to use nuclear energy. That creates radioactive waste that has to be stored safely for thousands of years, and it would take a long time to develop it.

We don’t have time to wait before climate change becomes irreversible. The devastating Nepalese floods and bushfires in France and Spain demonstrate the tragedy that climate change is bringing the world, unless we work very hard to prevent it.

Although Australia has a small population, we have massive resources of sun and wind, which we can share with other countries. For instance, we are now planning to construct Australia-Asia Powerlink, a subsea cable to export solar energy to Singapore.

Marguerite Marshall, Eltham



Inhumanity appears to be on the rise

I am incredulous. Just three days after the catastrophic landslide and flood in Nepal, which according to scientific experts has been caused by global warming, Pauline Hanson thinks it appropriate to hammer a nail into a coffin marked ‘net zero’. Do her supporters have no compassion?

People who are against renewable energy often cite its cost. Do they ever count the cost of these disasters in economic terms (never mind the trauma and emotional cost to those affected).

When we consider Nepal, the recent wildfires in Canada, USA and Europe, more frequent and severe cyclones/typhoons, the cost of recovering from these disasters needs to be factored in.

I write not because I solely support this economic argument, there are far more existential concerns. I just despair at the inhumanity that surrounds us and appears to be on the rise. Is this what we want for Australia?

Susan Humphreys, Strathdale Joyce distorts Albanese’s words

Barnaby Joyce has put his foot in it again, this time misquoting the prime minster and using words like ″⁣malfeasance″⁣ just to make sure we all understand (1/9).

Albanese didn’t actually use the polarising label ″⁣evil″⁣ in relation to One Nation, he simply highlighted its divisive influence in the Australian community.

Although trying to present himself as the more reasonable, intellectual face of One Nation, Joyce ended up distorting what Albanese said via the lens of his own projections.

The more diplomatic PM had no need to go as far as identifying a ″⁣fundamental character malfeasance″⁣ of One Nation, as it appears they can always manage that very capably themselves.

Bruce Watson, Belgrave THE FORUM First world gripes

It has been suggested that some will be ″⁣punishing″⁣ the major parties by voting for One Nation. That’s a really, really dumb strategy. A bit like chickens voting for KFC. For all their faults, the major parties have us living in one of the world’s most stable and affluent democracies.

Terry Kelly, Coburg Unhappy Vegemites

The cost of living is always trotted out by disgruntled voters wanting change, and especially One Nation voters. They mostly think about the cost of food, insurance etc. which is controlled by huge corporations in it to make a profit.

Voting for One Nation won’t bring down the price of Vegemite or your car insurance.

Polly Mish, Hawthorn



Too little too late

The massive mandate for reform given to Anthony Albanese’s government has been squandered, with the many recommended and needed policies and reforms dismissed as ″⁣populist″⁣, while they continued to govern for big business interests.

Just like the much-needed and supported gas extraction tax, the chance to fix the population issue is now probably a little too late.

John Marks, Werribee Younger MPs needed

Your correspondent urges a reduction in the voting age so that young people can vote in the interests of the planet they will inherit (Letters, 1/9). Indeed, but without a youthful parliament, they will still struggle to bring their issues to the fore. There’s a powerful argument to be made for young people to mobilise and nominate as MPs or to be elevated for preselection by ordinary members of the major parties.

Too often, the preselection process favours factional players who have spent decades cultivating their relationships in order to win the prize and their youth has been left behind. The present parliament, swollen with property investors on both sides, is highly unlikely to favour affordable housing initiatives.

Pat Hockey, Clunes Federalism’s fault

Incompetent and parochial state governments are blocking urgently needed solutions to growing social division and the cost-of-living crisis afflicting many Australians today.

Australia’s federal system of government reached its use-by date long ago.

It’s time for the states to hand over to the Commonwealth a wide range of their jealously guarded powers – especially health, education, aged care and childcare, and infrastructure (particularly roads).

The airport rail link to Tullamarine, for example, is clearly a national issue. Tullamarine is an international gateway serving all of Australia, not just Melbourne or Victoria.

The airport rail link should be the Commonwealth’s responsibility. Over decades, Victoria’s state governments have shown they are incapable of getting it done. There are far too many bureaucratic and political hurdles that have to be negotiated to get things done on time and properly.

Ridiculous duplications and entrenched local interests, aggravated by a lack of financial and technological resources and expertise, are the symptoms of a backward 19th century federal system.

Allan Patience, Newport Future shock

Almost every day, we read or hear commentators on diverse fields of human activity blithely talking about trends and conditions that are likely to play out in the future.

The article, “Melbourne on track for megacity status: How will it cope?” (28/8), examined population growth in Victoria and concluded that after factoring in births, deaths, international and interstate migration, Melbourne “is well on the way to becoming a megacity of more than 10 million people by 2101″. Astonishingly, there is no mention of climate change, and for this reason, it is not too harsh to label its projections as absurd because at the current rate of global heating, some parts of planet Earth will be uninhabitable by the human species by 2101.

Even if this dire situation is avoided, global heating will decimate human populations worldwide in forthcoming decades and render the growth rates assumed in this article as overestimated.

Ian Bayly, Upwey Fast track where?

Melbourne’s growth is not being handled well (″⁣Councils want billion-dollar payout for state growth plan″⁣, 31/8) Developers have had a dream run for the past 20 years with their ″⁣knock down and rebuild″⁣ approach in the inner city, largely without concern for local values or need for green space.

Now, under the guise of meeting housing needs, the Victorian planning minister is fast-tracking development behind closed doors. Arbitrary decisions are made about ″⁣great design with a social housing component″⁣. But we find developers can opt out of any commitments and instead pay a fee towards social housing ″⁣somewhere else″⁣. Where?

I do not know of any social or genuinely affordable housing built in the City of Yarra since the planning minister introduced ″⁣fast tracking″⁣.

This lack of transparency is a recipe for disaster. If a Labor government can break the trust of communities who elected them, how can we hope for density done well as our population escalates?

Susan Mahar, Fitzroy North



Help starts here

The extreme flash flooding in Nepal and Tibet had an underlying cause of global heating due to fossil-fuel burning.

Rather than sending a few million dollars to Nepal, a better federal government response would be to address this by stopping the subsidisation of diesel fuel by $10 billion each year and banning the sale of obsolescent petrol and diesel vehicles in Australia.

Tom Maher, Aspendale Property ups, downs

The fall in property prices may hurt sellers but is a gain for buyers, yet it’s often framed as a crisis (″⁣Property market crunch″⁣, 1/9).

There is a long way to go before reasonable ″⁣affordability″⁣ returns for first home buyers. I purchased my home in 1990 at a multiple of three times my annual salary. To buy an equivalent home in my street now is about seven times the average annual salary.

It remains tough for new entrants, even with fairly small decreases in property prices.

Geoffrey Conaghan, St Kilda Community service

Your correspondents (Letters, 1/9) appear to be unaware that prisoners in Victoria are already put to work on tasks such as manufacturing number plates, furniture, metal goods and agricultural equipment.

While the pay is minimal, the considerable expense of housing prisoners is already fully covered by taxpayers. The government’s proposal is for low-risk prisoners to carry out tasks such as mowing grass, weeding, graffiti removal and rubbish collection to free up road crews for repair work. Nobody is proposing ″⁣chain gangs″⁣.

And this no more amounts to ″⁣slavery″⁣ than the unpaid work routinely required by community service orders.

Mark Summerfield, Northcote Good deeds done cheap

I was very surprised to read that Premier Ben Carroll has proposed low-risk prisoners do road maintenance work around the state. Readers will be surprised that this is not a new idea at all.

Almost 40 years ago, I was the manager of Brunswick Citymission Family Centre. A small group of prisoners worked one day a week weeding the laneway behind our buildings as part of a public works program. The men were certainly not worked hard. They spent time chatting together and with passers-by and enjoying time outdoors.

I wasn’t offended or upset by the program. To me, it looked more productive than being behind bars.

Pamela Bores, Eltham North Restorative justice

“Chain gangs” is surely an exaggeration as is actually fixing potholes, but the idea of low-risk prisoners rehabilitating roadsides, of which we all complain about so vociferously, seems like a reasonable idea, and restorative justice can’t be a bad thing either.

Fiona White, Alfredton



Model masculinity

As a non-binary lesbian, you might think I have non-traditional views on masculinity. But when I read about a hero racing to help a woman (1/9), I feel admiration,

and just want to say “good on you mate”.

And I feel sad if any men feel despair about their masculinity. You’re important, we need you to step up, be a hero in the everyday. Call out misogyny. Stand up for your mates, male or female.

Ange Mackie, Coburg Sky police

Lee Tulloch daringly suggests in her article to speak up ″⁣When passengers behave badly on planes, I speak up″⁣ 1/9). As a frequent traveller, I have also often wondered whether fellow travellers are aware of good travel etiquette.

Yes, instinct does enter into the situation of being crammed into a cylinder for hours on end and a smile can work wonders. We who travel often do not need to act as police in the sky, but to demonstrate good seat-neighbourliness and speak up politely where necessary.

Judith Hudson, Elwood Prince Harry’s move

I don’t understand how this bloke and the wife think (1/9). He resigned his job a few years ago and moved to what he thought were greener pastures. When he did that, he relinquished all rights and perks the old job delivered. Now, he wants what he gave away back.

Many years ago, I retired from a large public company, where I trust my contribution over many years was respected. On the day I retired, I lost my company car, my expense account, and the right to get paid. Why does Prince Harry think his resignation should be treated differently from mine?

Bill Howard, Essendon AND ANOTHER THING Matt Golding



One Nation

One Nation is being allowed to make announcements without being questioned. Coal and nuclear power – who will pay for the building of these power stations?

Michael Brinkman, Ventnor Pauline Hanson wants to help Australia and Australians. Well, her policies for use of gas and nuclear energy will destroy it.

Katriona Fahey, Alphington The only political landscape that terrifies me more than an America dominated by Donald Trump is an Australian one presided over by Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce.

Edward Combes, Wheelers Hill Dan Andrews

A Dan Andrews statue is preferable to one of Pauline Hanson’s party in the future. Since $60,000 of $134,000 is completed, we may as well finish the job as a memorial without spite.

Malcolm Cameron, Camberwell Stop blaming Andrews for all the improved rail crossings and stations.

Bruce Dudon, Woodend



Furthermore

Your headline (1/9) on falling house values should have been ″⁣Great news for first home buyers. Property prices are falling″⁣.

Grant Nichol, Ringwood North A simple solution for under 18 voting (Letters, 1/9) would be to give 16 and 17-year-olds the right to vote, but to not make it compulsory.

Neale Woods, Wattle Glen Re AI glasses and privacy (1/9). ″⁣Men seldom make passes, Without wearing glasses″⁣. (With apologies to Dorothy Parker, and the majority of men).

Pamela Lloyd, West Brunswick Finally

First Tony Wright, now Cathy Wilcox. Matt Golding, you had better not be going anywhere! I take my hat off to all the journos and cartoonists that make my day, whether it be for a laugh, or something more insightful. We still have Cathy’s GST cartoon on our fridge. For me, that was the one that started it all.

Catherine Gerardson, Tawonga South The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: The ‘lush oasis’ being built next to Sydney’s busiest motorway
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life The ‘lush oasis’ being built next to Sydney’s busiest motorway Cindy Yin September 1, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After spending years as a construction site for one of Sydney’s biggest transport projects, 2.5 hectares on the edge of Warringah Freeway will be transformed into parkland – but residents will have to wait at least another two years before they can access the space. The NSW government has unveiled draft designs for Cammeray Parklands on the lower north shore, with plans to build a synthetic-turf sporting area and courts suitable for basketball or pickleball, as well as open lawns, gardens, shared paths and an outdoor fitness station. An artist’s impression of the new Cammeray Parklands. NSW Government An artist’s impression of the new Cammeray Parklands. NSW Government Roads Minister Jenny Aitchison said the parkland would be a “lush oasis” next to one of Australia’s busiest roads, the Warringah Freeway, and open at the same time as the $7.6 billion Western Harbour Tunnel project.



But North Sydney Council’s independent mayor Zoe Baker said the two road projects had created “scarring” impacts on residents and motorists who have endured years-long disruptions. Once construction finishes in late 2028, the three-lane tunnels in the 6.5-kilometre Western Harbour Tunnel motorway will link the Warringah Freeway on the north shore to the WestConnex toll road at Rozelle in the south, providing motorists an alternative to the Harbour Bridge and Harbour Tunnel in the CBD. Aitchison said the new parkland would act as a “connecting piece of landscape” linking existing green space, Cammeray golf course and the nearby Anzac Park. An aerial view of the current Western Harbour Tunnel construction site near the Warringah Freeway. NSW Government The 2.5 hectares of open space will have open lawns, gardens, shared paths, a multi-use half court for pickleball and basketball, a synthetic-turf sports area and an outdoor fitness station. NSW Government



“What this is designed to do is to really give back to the community a green space where they can enjoy their time,” she said. The government was “getting on with delivering the Western Harbour Tunnel but we are also making sure the communities hosting this major construction work see a lasting benefit”, Aitchison added. Related Article Roads ‘Every millimetre counts’: Inside the beast tunnelling under Sydney Harbour Baker welcomed the plans and said every bit of green space that facilitated passive and active recreation was “vital” in North Sydney, but stressed the new parkland did not represent a real increase in open space because it was previously green space and a golf course before it became a construction site. “Overall it’s a net loss but it is better than what we were fearing,” she said. “The Warringah Freeway upgrade meant the loss of 3000 mature trees … When those trees went, there was a loss of biodiversity, and there was a very emotional – rightly so – response from our community. I hope this project will be part of the repair.”



The government is replanting 6000 trees to offset the 3000 lost to road upgrades but workers have discovered there is not enough room to plant them, due to a shortage of land. The Cammeray Parklands are also right next to the golf course that the Minister for Lands Steve Kamper signalled his intent, in March, to hand to Golf NSW, sparking backlash from the council who wanted the land to remain in the club’s hands. Western Harbour Tunnel project operations director Tariq Macan-Markar said Cammeray Park would have a similar feel to a park above the Rozelle Interchange. World.title: Messages of hate strike wrong note at Sydney Marathon
World.content:
NationalNSWAntisemitism Opinion Messages of hate strike wrong note at Sydney Marathon Orly Lavee Doctor September 1, 2026 — 7:30pm

September 1, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I was one of 40,000 people who ran the Sydney Marathon on Sunday. For one morning, a city of more than 5 million people becomes unusually intimate. Nobody cares what you earn, where you were born, which god you believe in or which language your grandmother spoke. It is communal joy in its purest form. Competitors in the 2026 Sydney Marathon. George Chan So perhaps that is why what happened next felt so discordant. Among all of that, I saw accusatory messages of hate directed against Israelis. I cannot know precisely who every person holding those signs intended to address. But in the current social climate, it was difficult not to understand them as being directed at Israelis participating in the Marathon, or at people perceived to be affiliated with Israel.



And for Jewish runners, particularly at a time when the distinction between criticism of Israel and hostility towards Jews is considered by many in the Jewish community as opaque, it was difficult simply to run past that language as though it existed in a vacuum. Related Article Sydney Marathon Sydney Marathon results 2026: Gobena and Jepchirchir crowned champions as thousands participate in Sydney Marathon What struck me most was not simply the politics of the signs. It was their spirit. It was inserted into an event whose entire character was the opposite of conflict: tens of thousands of ordinary people running the same course, drinking from the same cups, being cheered by the same strangers. It was immediately dispiriting not because politics should be confined to parliament, or because protest should always be polite. Some of the most important protest movements in history have been disruptive and uncomfortable. But protest is supposed to communicate something. At its best, it persuades, illuminates, demands, challenges or mobilises. It identifies an injustice and asks other people to see it. These signs seemed to ask nothing. Does telling a stranger they are hated move anyone closer to a solution?



Does importing the language of collective guilt into a community sporting event create empathy for Palestinians – or does it simply create another person who feels frightened, humiliated or despised? Political movements can become so enclosed within their own language and moral certainty that they stop noticing how they sound to everyone outside them. Slogans become articles of faith. The same ideas circulate among people who already agree with one another until expression itself becomes confused with achievement. Related Article Analysis

Antisemitism royal commission Liberals wanted to extend the royal commission. But Jewish groups did not join the call If they were protesting against the Israeli runners – most of whom would be ex-service people given Israel’s policy of conscription – who were raising money for Shalva, a disability NGO that serves Jewish, Muslim, Christian and Druze Israelis, then it highlights the futility in protest that no longer seems interested in persuasion or nuance. If the person passing you is not someone whose mind you hope to change, and not someone with power to implement the change you seek, then what precisely is the purpose of confronting them? Perhaps the answer is simply to make them feel unwelcome. If so, we should call that what it is.



It has been widely explored that criticism of the Israeli government and the Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) is not inherently antisemitic but neither is there an impermeable wall separating anti-Zionism from antisemitism. There are circumstances in which the distance between them becomes for some of us very small indeed. Perhaps the most useful test is a simple one: would we apply the same principle to anybody else? Is this a world in which ordinary people may be publicly confronted with the actions of governments, leaders or countries with which they are associated? Russians for Putin. Iranians for the Islamic Republic. Americans for American wars. Chinese Australians for Beijing. Palestinians for Hamas. Israelis for Netanyahu. Australia works, imperfectly but remarkably, because people can arrive carrying different histories, religions, languages, loyalties and inherited griefs and nevertheless meet one another in a public space without demanding that every person answer for everything done by someone who shares their ethnicity, nationality or faith. That social contract is fragile. None of this diminishes the suffering of Palestinians. None of it makes criticism of Israel antisemitic. Those are lazy binaries, and this subject deserves better than lazy binaries.



In our determination to make every public space another battlefield, I wonder whether we understand what we are giving up. Orly Lavee is a doctor who lives in Sydney. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Seddon residents asked to conserve water after major leak discovered
World.content:
Residents in the Marlborough town of Seddon have been asked to conserve water immediately after a major leak was found on the Awatere rural water main.

Council engineers are working to find and fix the leak on the main which supplies Seddon and surrounding areas - including Seaview, Grassmere and rural Awatere south of the river.

Marlborough Waters establishment chief executive Richard Coningham said residents should conserve water for the next 48 hours.

"Unfortunately it appears the leak may be in the pipe where it travels underneath the river bed. This means it may be challenging to fix," he said.

"We expect the fix is going to take at least 48 hours. However we don't know exactly what the problem is at this stage - it will take a bit of time to pinpoint the problem."

Council engineers were in touch with contractors for an early start on Wednesday morning, Coningham said.

"It's quite likely water will need to be tankered in to supply Seddon township if we can't fix the leak quickly. Residents are strongly encouraged to conserve water as much as possible for at least the next 48 hours."

World.title: Will spring cleaning help your wellbeing? The psychology of decluttering
World.content: "If you think about your living room, its natural intention is to be able to relax. So, if you can't sit on the sofa, read a book, watch TV comfortably, because there is so much stuff that you're unable to sit on that sofa or even see your TV, then you might meet criteria for hoarding disorder," she says.

World.title: SuperGold card holders missing out on discounts
World.content:
Superannuitants are being encouraged to be more assertive in asking for SuperGold Card discounts they are entitled to, as many are missing out.

A SuperGold Card discount was offered by hundreds of small and big name businesses in New Zealand, but a lack of promotion meant many older people were unaware of the details.

The Warehouse Red Sheds offered a 5 percent SuperGold Card discount on the first Tuesday of the month, but an older couple with a trolly full of goods left the retailer's St. Lukes store this morning without their discount.

"Oh well. Next time," The Red Sheds customer Marcia said, as she loaded up her boot.

Still, she was persuaded to go back to the store and ask for the discount, and returned a few minutes later $18 better off.

"We got $18 out of the SuperGold discount," she said with a broad smile and an armful of canned food items. "So we've just bought . . some extra bully beef, spaghetti, and ... a bit of fruit salad."

She said The Warehouse apologised, which was followed up with a response from the head office.

"We really appreciate this being brought to our attention and we're sorry the couple didn't get the discount they were entitled to the first time around. It's highlighted a gap in how we provide value to our customers - and we're looking at how we can make our offers more visible," a spokesperson from The Warehouse said in a statement to RNZ.

One shopper was unaware that she would get a SuperGold discount at the New World Supermarket at Point Chevalier. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

The promotion of the SuperGold Card was something concerning to other shoppers.

A shopper outside the Point Chevalier Woolworths Frances Marychurch also raised concerns about the lack of awareness.

Marychurch said she only used her SuperGold at Woolworths and was unaware she could use it across the street at the New World supermarket.

"So I find it's very difficult to find ways to use your gold card. The ones that are supposed to do it, don't ask you for it," Marychurch said.

New World shopper Ross Horne said: "Personally, I think it is not actually publicised enough. Occasionally you'll see a store with the sticker on the door, with the gold card."

Mike Matthews, general manager of Communicare, which offers community support for seniors, said businesses should do more to promote the SuperGold Card discount, though superannuitants also had a role to play.

World.title: Opponents miss vote as rates cap bill passes first reading
World.content:
The government has progressed legislation for its cap on council rates increases through a first reading in Parliament.

The bill initially sailed through the first reading unopposed, as those disagreeing with it missed their window for voting.

The legislation, which would require councils to increase rates by at least 2 percent and at most 4 percent a year, is not expected to progress further before Parliament rises this month ahead of the election if passed.

Local Government Minister Simon Watts said it was aimed at keeping rates stable and affordable.

Labour last week indicated it would give its backing, though spokesperson Tangi Utikere said the party still had concerns including that the government had not pushed ahead with giving councils other options for raising revenue.

He said sending the bill to select committee would provide needed transparency and scrutiny.

The Greens, Te Pāti Māori, and former Te Pāti Māori MPs Tākuta Ferris and Mariameno Kapa-King opposed the legislation, saying it would only mean fees for council services rise; and council rates were going up because their costs were too.

World.title: More safe and affordable housing needed for older people, charity says
World.content:
Older NZers worried about safe and affordable housing Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

A charity says New Zealand could be in "serious trouble" if it doesn't act to address the shortage of social housing for older people - with the population of renters over 65 set to triple by 2050.

Christchurch Methodist Mission executive director Jill Hawkey told Checkpoint some seniors are finding themselves homeless, amidst the shortage of affordable and secure social housing, and others are left with little money for food and medicine after paying rent.

On Tuesday, the group handed a petition to Parliament signed by more than 3000 people, calling for increased targeted investment in housing for seniors.

Data from the Ministry of Social Development shows that over 55s are the largest demographic on the social housing waitlist, and the number of over 65s on the waitlist has climbed 34 percent in four years.

Hawkey told Checkpoint that New Zealand was going to have a problem if it did not invest in suitable housing for older people now.

"Within 20 years, the number of older renters that's over 65 years of age, is going to triple.

"At the moment we've got about 138,000 renters aged over 65, and that's going to be 400,000 renters over the next 25 years, so if we don't start doing something about it now, we're going to find ourselves in serious trouble."

There is also the wider issue of the lack of social housing across the board in New Zealand, with social housing making up just 3.8 percent of all housing stock, compared with the OECD average of about 7 percent, she said.

Hawkey said the human impact was showing up as homelessness among older people.

She said that the first person their homeless outreach team housed last year was a woman in her eighties.

"It's not just Christchurch that we're seeing this, we're hearing similar stories from towns and cities throughout the country" she added, noting that they were finding people over 65 on the streets.

In Christchurch, the waitlist for the Wesley Village just kept growing, and the rent pressure was also growing - with the price of a single bedroom unit costing more than $500 for Papanui, she said.

Hawkey said for seniors who were light on supperannuation, the rents could take up all of their pension and there was little money left for food and medical supplies.

She said there was also concern with the lack of suitable, age-friendly housing, pointing to the fact that a lot of new homes built in Christchurch at the moment had a living room downstairs and bedrooms upstairs, which was unsuitable for older people.

The Christchurch Methodist Mission met with the minister for seniors Casey Costello on Tuesday, and Hawkey said that while there was no commitment yet, there was "lots of interest".

World.title: Kākāpō population soars to 325
World.content:
Biggest kakapo breeding season on record comes to an end Morning Report Download MP3 3m

The 2026 kākāpō breeding season, the biggest on record, has come to an end with a bumper number of kākāpō chicks produced. The youngest chick has just passed 150 days old, a milestone that marks its independence.

"We had 90 chicks reach that milestone," reports Deidre Vercoe, operations manager for the Department of Conservation's Kākāpō Recovery Programme, who is delighted with the success.

Kākāpō Files II 20 | Kākāpō Numbers Soar Wild Sounds: Kākāpō Files II S7 / E20 Season 7 / Episode 20 Download MP3 30m

Those 90 chicks are officially added to the kākāpō population on Monday, taking the critically endangered night parrot from 235 birds to 325.

Vercoe told RNZ's Kākāpō Files podcast that "to blow through that 300 population mark just knocks my socks off. Even as I say it now I think 'really? 325 - has that actually happened?' But it is true, it is fantastic."

When the Kākāpō Recovery Programme began in 1995 there were just 51 living kākāpō. Kākāpō only breed every two to four years, so it's taken a while to get to the point where the population can increase by a third in just a single breeding season.

Awarua-A3 is now old enough to be added to the population. Mahina Walle DOC

"It took about 16 years to make 90 chicks in the early days of the recovery programme," Vercoe says. "And we've just done that in one season."

2026 Kākāpō breeding season by the numbers:

79 female kākāpō nested

258 eggs laid

106 chicks hatched

48 females produced living chicks

32 dads fathered chicks

90 chicks made it to 150 days

Kākāpō breeding is triggered by the intermittent mass, or mast, fruiting of forest trees such as rimu. In autumn, the ripening fruit is also a great food source for kākāpō mums to feed their hungry chicks, which grow from just 25 grams at hatching to about 1.5-2 kilos in weight at independence.

Intensive management, such as extra food for breeding mums in years when the fruit fails to ripen, has been a feature of kākāpō conservation. This year a very abundant rimu crop ripened on the kākāpō's two breeding islands in Fiordland, meaning mums on those islands did not require any extra food.

However, on Whenua Hou / Codfish Island, near Rakiura / Stewart Island, the rimu failed to ripen and the female kākāpō there still needed supplementary food to raise chicks.

In the past three decades, hand-rearing has also been an important tool, but this season only two chicks that had required medical treatment ended up being hand-reared. The rest were fully raised by kākāpō mums.

DOC Kākāpō Ranger Maddy Whittaker with 2026 chick Matilda-A1 Sarah Manktelow DOC

Stepping back from intensive management, like feeding and hand-rearing, has been a deliberate move. It is an important and necessary change, says Kākāpō Recovery science advisor Andrew Digby.

"It's been a really significant breeding season for us," Digby says. "Obviously it's the biggest one we've ever had, so that's very significant. But I think just as important are the methods that we've employed and some of the things that we've changed this breeding season. And in particular that's that real emphasis on trying to step back and do a little less of the intensive management that we've done in the past, and let kākāpō do things on their own."

Technology has been key to the evolving management regime for kākāpō. Every bird wears a smart transmitter and its activity can be remotely monitored.

Deidre Vercoe says "we were able to put a lot more faith in our remote technology data, and really carefully monitor that data, and make decisions about when we would step in and interfere at a nest, to move an egg or to help a chick, or when we were okay to stay hands off".

2026 kākāpō chick Hananui-A2 is living independently, but still gets regular ranger checks. Sarah Manktelow/DOC

All existing adult kākāpō have names, but Vercoe says this tradition is about to change.

"Not all the chicks will be named this year - some will remain unnamed. That's a bit of a symbol of heading towards a more natural state for kākāpō where they're not all individually managed and individually known."

The last two kākāpō breeding seasons were four years apart, but we won't have such a long wait until next time, Digby says. The key is a pattern of summer temperatures that triggers rimu fruiting.

"We look at temperature differences and that gives us a two-year heads-up. And there's an indication from those differences that 2028 will be another kākāpō breeding season."

While it's exciting news that there'll be more kākāpō chicks in two years time, the rapidly growing kākāpō population faces a challenge - the existing kākāpō islands are already full and we need more safe predator-free places for kākāpō to call home.

Pakiki-A1 is one of 90 chicks that successfully made it to independence in the record 2026 kākāpō breeding season. Sarah Manktelow/DOC

"After this next breeding season we desperately need another breeding site," Digby says. The search is on.

Among the highlights of the 2026 kākāpō breeding season were three four-year-old females that bred for the first time, the youngest females to ever breed.

Ten chicks were conceived through artificial insemination, a technique which is used to boost egg fertility and match-make good genetic matches. Ralph, an original male from Rakiura / Stewart, became a father for the first time as a result of artificial insemination.

The 'dad of the year' was ten-year-old Tūterangi. A first-time breeder, he mated with six females and fathered 10 living chicks.

World.title: Government says cervical screening will be free from March next year
World.content:
The government says screening for cervical cancer will be free from March next year.

Health Minister Simeon Brown and Women's Minister Nicola Grigg made the announcement on Tuesday.

Brown said from 1 March, 2027, all eligible women aged 25 to 69 would have free screenings - implementing a recommendation from successive Parliamentary Reviews since 2018.

He said cervical cancer was one of the most preventable diseases, but cost could be a barrier to screening, with around 55 percent of eligible women now paying anywhere from $35 to more than $100 for appointments.

The policy would make screenings free for an estimated additional 786,000 women, Brown said.

Screening is currently free for Māori and Pacific women aged 25 to 69, Community Services Card holders, and women who have never been screened or are overdue.

Grigg also released the Government's Cervical Cancer Elimination Plan 2026 to 2040.

She said the plan set out the goal to eliminate the cancer, reducing it to fewer than four cases per 100,000 women a year, across every population group, by 2040.

Grigg said the country already had the tools to do it.

"A vaccine that prevents the virus behind almost every case, a test that picks it up early, and treatment that works when it is caught in time.

"Making screening free is part of that."

Grigg said 69 percent of young people had their first HPV vaccine by age 15. She said the plan sought to raise that to 90 percent by 2035.

"Today is a good day for women, but screening only saves lives if it's taken up. So my message to every woman who is overdue is simple. Please don't delay - talk to your healthcare provider today," she said.

World.title: Nature Baby recalls baby onesies over choking hazard
World.content:
Nature Baby is recalling a baby onesie after a dome fastening was found to potentially detach and pose a choking hazard to infants and young children.

The recall affects the Merino Kimono Pointelle Stretch and Grow, product number NB2206, in Lilac, Natural and Thyme.

The affected garments were sold in Newborn, 0-3 months and 3-6 months sizes between 27 February and 27 August, 2026, through Nature Baby stores and online.

Nature Baby said a detached dome fastening may present a choking hazard.

Customers who have the affected garment are advised to stop using it and return it to their nearest Nature Baby store or through the company's online returns process for a full refund.

The garment was previously listed on Nature Baby's website at NZ$44.95.

World.title: Beach sprinting was just the start of Damien Cook's NRL story
World.content:
With a bit of luck, they'll tell the old Damien Cook story one more time.

This weekend, the 35-year-old St George Illawarra skipper will play his final NRL match before heading to Super League side Castleford next year.

His farewell will be at Wollongong Showground, the closest ground in the league to the ocean. When the swell's big, you can almost hear the waves crashing on City Beach from the hill.

Maybe it will be when Cook runs out for the 263rd and last time, or perhaps he'll dart out from dummy half to take on the Parramatta defence with a glimpse of the old quickness.

Maybe it'll be the commentators who say it, maybe it'll just be fans in the stands, but someone, somewhere will almost certainly tell somebody else "you know, he used to be a champion beach sprinter."

It's a story nobody seems to tire of telling — Cook himself still hears about it all the time.

"It's the great Dane Gagai's fault. He mentioned it one day when I was doing media — a few people knew about it, but he said it real loud, the journo I was speaking to did a story on it and it got out from there," Cook said.

"It's never stopped; I still get it every day. Commentators say it, I get it in comments, DMs, Instagram stories; if people see a post about a beach sprinter they tag me in it. You have to laugh."

The yarn got its greatest play during Cook's ascent to becoming one of the best hookers in rugby league, which came almost 10 years ago now, and it's worth breaking it out one more time to celebrate the end of an NRL career with an extraordinarily long tail.

It took a while to get going. Cook spent plenty of time as a second-stringer on second-rate teams.

Cook's NRL career took a while to get going. (Getty Images: Brett Hemmings)

He did not make the run on side for an NRL match until he was almost 23 and wasn't a full-time starter at hooker until the year he turned 27.

But after taking the long way, he made up for lost time immediately, and once the beach sprinting tale got used up, we started to tell others.

Cook can't pick his favourite himself. He is overwhelmed by the memories he's made because there are so many.

This late starter has now played the seventh-most matches of any dummy half in the history of the game, so when you ask him about his favourite match there's so much to choose from.

There's the first grade debut back in 2013, of course, which came for St George Illawarra against Wests Tigers at the Sydney Cricket Ground in Heritage Round. The retro jerseys and brown football made it feel like history even while it was happening.

There was the first game at Wollongong a week later. Cook is proud to finish his NRL journey there, given it's where he grew up watching football and where he played his junior grand finals for Helensburgh.
