In a nice full-circle moment, his first match there in the top grade came against the Eels, just like his last will.

"The big one that day was when I got under Fuifui Moi Moi — it wasn't me being brave, he was coming straight at me," Cook said.

"I didn't have much of a choice."

Cook is one of the best dummy halves in New South Wales Origin history. (Getty Images)

There's the late-season cameo for Canterbury in 2015, which first made Cook's name and proved he could ride the lightning, and his debut at South Sydney, where he played more than 200 games and spent his most glorious times.

There's his first State of Origin match in front of 90,000 at the MCG in 2018, when he was one of 11 New South Wales debutants alongside players like Nathan Cleary, Tom Trbojevic, Latrell Mitchell and Cameron Murray.

Cook was the best of them that night in a magnificent beginning, and he always seemed to find something extra for the Blues — among dummy halves, only Ben Elias and Danny Buderus have worn the jersey more.

The 2019 decider, when he scored a scorching try right through the heart of the Queensland defence, was perhaps his single greatest highlight in rep football, but playing for Australia against Tonga in Auckland later that season was another special night.

As the Tongan anthem rang out through the night, Cook thought he'd be crushed by the noise.

"All the Tongans were singing their anthem, just this sea of red. I thought 'bloody hell, nobody is going to sing our anthem; we're up against it here'," Cook said.

"But then all the Tongans sang our anthem as well. The sound of it, I'll never forget it."

The pandemic ravaging international football and the eventual emergence of Harry Grant kept Cook to just four Tests, but he did get the special honour of playing one in Wollongong the following season and duly marked it by scoring a try.

It was no barge-over from close range though — it was an intercept that Cook took 70 metres all the way home.

He could have run along Lawrence Hargrave Drive, across the Sea Cliff Bridge, and up the hill all the way back to Helensburgh and the Kiwis wouldn't have caught him.

Cook ran all the way into an Australian jersey. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Then there's all the club wars as well, because once Cook became one of the best he liked nothing more than testing himself against the top sides.

He says he relished the days where South Sydney had a real shot at being pride of the league again and had it out with the likes of Melbourne, Penrith and the Sydney Roosters with everything to play for and no quarter asked for or given.

All told, when asked to pick a single favourite game, Cook named almost a dozen. He just couldn't leave anything out.

"I know you asked for one, but rugby league has given me so much," Cook said.

"The mates, the moments, the memories, it's why you do it."

Cook himself gave plenty of people similarly glorious memories.

He was fast enough that a dart from dummy half would make the crowd rise, fast enough that he could break into space and round the fullback from anywhere, fast enough that when Wayne Bennett came out favouring the NRL's proposed set restart rules in 2020 some said the wily old coach was doing it just to suit Cook.

But there was more to Cook's game than raw pace. He's a cannier playmaker than some might think — in 2019 he accumulated 18 try assists, more than Grant has ever managed in a single season and equal to Cameron Smith's career high.

Cook was also among the top four players in the league for tackles made in seven of his first eight seasons.

If he gets through 25 tackles on Sunday, which is light work so long as he plays big minutes, he'll pass 10,500 of them for his career, and given the middle of the field is where the giants live, he'll have given up size and weight on just about every one of them.

Cook has never shirked the tough stuff through his long NRL career. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Somehow, he has gotten through those 10,000 blows without ever being seriously broken — this year marks the 10th season in a row Cook will manage at least 23 games.

That's a point of pride for Cook. Once he got a taste of his dream coming true, it became a prize beyond value.

"It took a while to get there, so once I did I never wanted to let it go. I'm very proud of that because I put a lot of time into recovery and working hard and staying fit and being ready for every pre-season so I can get the most out of it," Cook said.

"I've set high standards for myself, which is why I've been able to play consistently. Even in NSW Cup I tried to do that.

"Touch wood, I haven't had a bad injury since I was at the Dogs when I broke my thumb — the other games that ruin my record were getting rested or COVID protocols, and I wish we could take those off.

"Longevity and consistency are something I'm really proud of."

Both Damien Cook and his club have done it tough in 2026. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

In the end, being there all day every day has taken its toll on Cook. It has slowed him down, and the ravages of age have finally overtaken whatever benefits he gained from his late start.

He has just two try assists and one line break for the season and has spent time on the bench and as 18th man. It feels like this change has come at the right time for him.

The wins have not come as Cook or St George Illawarra would have liked in the two seasons since he joined, but that doesn't mean he won't leave a legacy.

The Dragons have a host of young players who hold the future in their hands, perhaps none more than 23-year-old backrower Hamish Stewart.

Despite recent struggles, Cook's efforts have never wavered. (Getty Images: Brett Hemmings)

"It's me, Gutho [Clint Gutherson] and Cooky in the gym. You see him, day in and day out, and he has the most energy of anyone. He never skips a rep," Stewart said.

"He's been massive for all us young blokes, showing us how to run a team and how a club really works.

"I love how he goes about life off the field as well — I feel like I can go to him about anything."

Stewart has played every game this season and earned plenty of plaudits despite the Red V's struggles.

Along with the Couchman brothers, Dylan Egan and Loko Pasifiki Tonga, Stewart is part of the sun that can break through the clouds and of all those players, his tomorrows may be the brightest.

The Dragons have found wins hard to come by during Cook's time with the club. (AAP: Mark Evans)

If Stewart does go on and makes the most of it, Cook will play a role even if they're not packing down together.

The veteran is the kind of guy who can hold a beaten-down town together, and even if the team hasn't been winning, that doesn't mean Cook hasn't been teaching.

In trying to impart the hard-won wisdom of his rise, Cook is leaving behind something that will last once he's gone. His lessons will remain, like footsteps in the sand.

"You have to make sure you're doing the right things all the time, to lead by example. You have to push right along to the end of the season, even if it's a tough one," Cook said.

"It's easy to tick the boxes when you're winning games, but when you're up against it you still have to push hard every day.

"That's a good value to have, and a lot of the players here have that."

If he's right, that could be the longest tail of all for Cook, who leaves the club in a far better place than he found it.

He has shown these boys how to live, but now they must become men without him.

"He's always got a smile on his face every day. You see him when you walk through the doors and you know you're gonna have a good day," Stewart said.

"That's what I'll miss the most."

Cook's ultimate legacy is the players he leaves behind at St George Illawarra. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

For Cook himself, this is an end but not the end.

He's excited about playing for Castleford next year, to have a new challenge in a new place, to have something to prove again, to do the work and love it and to give it everything he's got, which Cook says is all he's ever done.

He's excited for Sunday, to see family and friends in the crowd and, one last time, to live that dream he would not surrender during the hard times.

There's no beach, but it'll be a fine day to get a sprint in.

"If I told my younger self what would happen over the past 14 or 15 years, I don't think he'd believe me," Cook said.

"Definitely after the season it will [sink in], especially when I'm packing up the house and going through some jerseys. That'll bring back the memories.

"But there's still more to do."

World.title: Is Marnus Labuschagne finally out of luck?
World.content:
For a period of 23 Tests, Marnus Labuschagne was statistically the luckiest batter in Test cricket.

He had more genuine chances dropped or missed than any other batter from his debut up until the end of the 2021/22 Ashes series. He was more often than not able to turn those reprieves into significant scores.

In more recent times, it's been slim pickings. In fact, it's been 23 Tests since his last century, dating back to the fourth Ashes Test at Old Trafford in 2023.

He's been left out of the ODI squad travelling to take on Zimbabwe and South Africa later this month. The right-hander has only missed five of Australia's last 56 ODIs, raising questions about his future in the Test side.

"We're still very much working through what that Test squad looks like, but I can say we separate out those formats," chair of selectors George Bailey told reporters when unveiling the ODI squad.

"He has played some really important one-day cricket for us; at his best that looks a certain way, but the way that squad and team is structuring up there just wasn't space for him."

If you break down Labuschagne's career into the period before his last Test ton and the period since, there is somewhat of a trend: his luck has seemingly run out.

The 2023 Ashes series in England was the last time Marnus Labuschagne made a Test century. (Getty Images: Richard Heathcote)

Looking at only genuine chances missed by opposition teams — dropped catches, missed stumpings, opposition teams not reviewing a decision that would have seen him dismissed, or wickets on a no ball — he was given a reprieve 25 times from 75 innings where he faced at least one ball.

That's a chance every three innings from his Test debut in 2018 to his most recent hundred back in 2023.

Across his first 20 Tests he scored six centuries and 12 fifties, earning him a batting average of 62.15. If, in that time, he had been taken at the first opportunity, that average drops to 46.50.

In the 2019-2021 World Test Championship cycle, Labuschagne played 13 Tests and scored the most runs of any other batter in the world. He finished that period with 1,675 runs at an average of 72.82. Across the 23 innings he was required to bat in, he was afforded 12 chances, or one every 1.92 innings.

When you compare that with Steve Smith in the same period, he was given a reprieve four times, which equates to one every 5.5 innings. Smith was still able to score 1,341 runs in that WTC cycle, which highlights Labuschagne's ability to capitalise when given the opportunity.

In fact, his entire Test career has been based on it.

Labuschagne's luck was a key feature of his game in his early Tests, with his ability to capitalise on opportunities given to him by opposition mistakes. (AP: Rick Rycroft)

Labuschagne made his Test debut in 2018 due to the bans handed down to Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft after the sandpaper incident the last time Australia's Test team toured South Africa.

That put him in the frame for the 2019 Ashes squad and, after a red-hot Smith was hit in the neck by a Jofra Archer bouncer at Lord's, Labuschagne got his next chance as the first concussion substitute in the history of international cricket, courtesy of a rule introduced the month before the series started.

In the next Test in Leeds, Labuschagne was dropped on 14, 42 and 60, and England failed to review an edge that would have been given out when he was on 35. He went on to make 80.

That series, including that fortunate knock of 80 at Headingley, cemented his spot in the side, with Usman Khawaja the unfortunate one to make way when Smith returned, a decision that left Khawaja on the outer for three years.

His ability to turn a reprieve into a significant score was a hallmark of his early Test career. Labuschagne's maiden Test century came against Pakistan at the Gabba in 2019 when he scored an impressive 185 off 279 balls. Pakistan fans might still be ruing the fact he was dropped by Asad Shafiq on 33 that same innings.

Labuschagne made a habit of scoring big runs when given a reprieve by the opposition. (AAP: David Mariuz)

In that WTC cycle alone, if he had been taken at the first opportunity, his batting average would drop to 55.68, which would have had him ranked 11th in the world.

It's not just his luck that's seemingly run out; it's his ability to capitalise on it.

From that first Ashes series to his last Test century, Labuschagne was able to turn missed opportunities into scores of 50 or more on nine occasions, including five hundreds.

Since that last century, he has been afforded only four reprieves, and the most he's added to his total is 18 runs.

Loading...

He was briefly dropped from the side after failing to impress as a makeshift opener in last year's World Test Championship final, missing Australia's tour of the West Indies. But, after only three Tests out of the side, he came back in for the 2025/26 Ashes and has remained in the team since.

When you compare that to the likes of Jake Weatherald, who has been in and out of the Test squad with questions around his form, Labuschagne has not just been given chances by opposition fielders; he's also been given them by the Australian selectors.

With an important series against South Africa on the horizon and his omission from the ODI squad, all eyes now look to see if his luck really has run out.

World.title: Dockers 'know what's on the line' ahead of Hawthorn showdown: Longmuir
World.content:
The Fremantle Dockers may be just three wins from claiming the club's first-ever AFL premiership, but coach Justin Longmuir has dismissed suggestions he will be using that as motivation heading into the finals.

The 2026 version of the Dockers is comfortably the best-performed team in the club's history when it comes to the home-and away season.

Fremantle won 19 of its 23 games to race away with the minor premiership, earning the right to host Hawthorn in a qualifying final at Perth Stadium on Thursday night.

Murphy Reid (left) will return for the Dockers against the Hawks after recovering from a groin knock. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos )

It has seen excitement build among the Freo faithful, who are hopeful this could be their year, having made just one grand final since the club entered the AFL in the 1995 season, losing to the Hawks in 2013.

But throughout this year's campaign, Longmuir has urged his players to stay in the moment and focus on more immediate tasks, and he insisted thinking about the ultimate goal is not what would get the job done.

'I'm only human': Fremantle star Jackson dreaming of Dockers' maiden flag Luke Jackson has already been to the top of the AFL mountain and now, with Fremantle just three wins from a maiden premiership, the man known as 'Dogga' is desperate to get there again.

"I just don't feel like we need to [lean into it]. If there's someone at the footy club that doesn't see that carrot, well then you're probably in the wrong game, right?" he said.

"All our players know what's on the line, and we just need to make sure that we use whatever motivation that gives us to give it all to your next moment.

"Everyone feels it in different ways … some players will see it as a stimulus and some players will maybe see it as a distraction, and we'll work through that.

"Everyone sees pressure as different things and we've done some work on that, and it's all about staying in the moment.

Hawks forward Nick Watson will be one man the Dockers are keen to keep a close eye on. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

"The way to win premierships is to win games of footy, and you win games of footy by winning more moments than the opposition.

"We've just got to make sure that we give our best to each moment, and the next moment is the most important one."

Fast start wanted

Much of the talk in the build-up to Thursday's game has focused on the Dockers' home-crowd advantage, after they rode the Wharfie Time rallying cry to come from behind to win their last clash against Hawthorn at Perth Stadium.

But Longmuir is hopeful they will not have to rely on the fans to overcome another slow start.

Fremantle got up in Wharfie Time against the Hawks in round nine, but hope they will not need it this week. (Getty Images: Daniel Carson)

"They're not going to get us over the line if we're not playing good footy, so we've got to give them something to cheer for, and it needs to be from the start," he said.

Key defender Brennan Cox will miss Thursday's match through injury, but Fremantle is set to welcome back the likes of Murphy Reid, Jye Amiss, Heath Chapman and the retiring Sam Switkowski.

Hawthorn is at virtually full strength for the clash, with only two players unavailable on its most recent injury list.

The Hawks enjoyed a comfortable win over West Coast at Perth Stadium in their final game of the home-and-away season.

World.title: Cats coach speaks for first time since club's concussion fine
World.content:
Geelong coach Chris Scott insists he is unsure if Jake Kolodjashnij will play for the Cats again following the club's concussion saga.

Speaking for the first time since Geelong was fined $140,000 for failing to officially let the AFL know about the concussion waiver in Kolodjashnij's contract, Scott kept it brief.

The dual premiership coach referred back to the club's response and was adamant he had stayed out of dealings about Kolodjashnij's future.

Geelong fined over concussion scandal The AFL hands down its penalty after a meeting between the commission and Geelong regarding Jake Kolodjashnij's now-controversial contract.

Kolodjashnij, who came forward as the player involved shortly after the story broke and has not played at any level since, returned to the club last week ahead of the finals.

If the defender does play it will almost certainly be at VFL level, with the club premiership favourites to win the second-tier competition.

"I've been really conscious to separate myself from this," Scott said about Kolodjashnij.

"This is one of those situations [where] if I could help, I would.

"But I'm told, and I believe independently, that I just wouldn't be any assistance, so I just don't get in the way."

The penalty was $100,000, plus a suspended sanction of $40,000, which stems from the league fining Geelong last October after an investigation into the club's third-party agreements.

"Hand on heart, I don't really even know the facts, so I'm certainly not going to be swayed by people who understand the facts less than I do," Scott said.

"So my go-to is that I just support the club's position … whether some people accept that wholeheartedly, that's something you can ask them privately.

"But the club's position is, it's best for us to say, 'OK we acknowledge certain aspects, and we're keen to move forward.'"

After having the pre-finals bye, Geelong will face red-hot Carlton in an elimination final at the MCG on Friday night.

Speaking on Monday, experienced midfielder Tom Atkins denied the saga was a distraction for the Cats as they aimed to win their fifth premiership this century.

AAP

World.title: Sharks want to play their home NRL finals match at their home ground
World.content:
Cameron McInnes would not be surprised to see the NRL deny Cronulla a home final at Shark Park, warning players were now used to head office making rule changes "at the drop of a hat".

Out of form on the eve of finals, the fifth-placed Sharks are nevertheless guaranteed to host a week-one elimination match against one of South Sydney, North Queensland or Newcastle.

But the finals suitability of dilapidated Shark Park, the NRL's lowest-capacity regular venue at 15,000 seats, has been a discussion point in recent years.

ABC NRL Daily podcast Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

The NRL pockets ticket sales from finals games so would take a financial hit from hosting in the shire rather than the Sydney Football Stadium or Stadium Australia, which each have more than twice the capacity.

Shark Park has been deemed unfit for use in week two or three of the finals, but hosted week-one finals matches in 2022, 2023 and 2025.

The NRL is unlikely to publicly confirm venues until after round 27 finishes this Sunday, and told clubs in the pre-season it had the discretion to determine where finals games were played.

The possibility of playing elsewhere did not sit well with England-bound McInnes, who could be playing his last game at Shark Park against Melbourne this Saturday.

"I was under the impression the rule was if you earn a home semi, whether you're first or second, or fifth or sixth, you get to play it at your home. Our home is Shark Park," he said.

"I don't know if that was a rule change that they can just put in, but then again, the NRL changes rules all the time.

"Rule changes just happen at the drop of a hat now, don't they? So as a player, you just have to adapt."

The league most recently trialled a change to the kick-off rule in Melbourne's defeat of Brisbane last week, having introduced six-agains, 20/40 kicks, two-point field goals and captain's challenges since the start of the decade.

The NRL has also made less prominent changes to its trainer and interchange policies in that time, as well as reverting to one on-field referee per game.

"How much do you need to change? I understand at the end of the day, it's entertainment, I get it," McInnes said.

"But it's like someone's constantly sitting there going, 'The game's going really well, but now let's change something else'."

Inconsistency around ruck infringements was most dismaying to veteran McInnes, who sympathised with the league's match officials.

"When you bring that [six-again rule] in, I get it, to speed the game up and have the speeds to score long-range tries with fatigue, but it also creates an inconsistency in the game," he said.

"[It's] hard for the refs, isn't it? Because it's so subjective.

"If someone gets hit in the face and is offside, that's clear as day, but with the six-agains, it's just sort of a lottery."

AAP

World.title: Former rival says Nick Kyrgios's drug ban 'pretty much expected'
World.content:
Stefanos Tsitsipas says he was not surprised when Nick Kyrgios was suspended from tennis for drug use.

Kyrgios was banned earlier this month after he revealed he tested positive for cocaine in June when he was in Spain to play at an event.

The Australian could be suspended for four years, though a lighter punishment is expected.

Tsitsipas was asked about Kyrgios on Monday after upsetting 10th-seeded Arthur Fils in the first round of the US Open.

The former world number three, who had a famously contentious relationship with Kyrgios, said he was surprised the suspension did not come sooner.

"I mean, to be entirely honest with you, I knew about this before the announcement. Myself, I knew about it," Tsitsipas said.

"So, what can I tell you? I will just tell you the truth. I knew about all of this before any announcement was made, and when I saw it on social media, I was, like, 'Here we go'. I kind of expected it, to be honest."

Tsitsipas and Kyrgios played a fiery match at Wimbledon in 2022 , when Kyrgios reached his only Grand Slam final. Tsitsipas blasted a couple of shots directly at Kyrgios, intentionally hit a ball into the crowd, and afterward called Kyrgios a "bully".

Kyrgios has largely battled injuries since and said when he was suspended that he had felt "helpless and alone", though added that "none of that excuses what I did".

Nor did it come as a shock to Tsitsipas.

"I knew that those were things that were happening away from the tennis courts. I will tell you that," he said.

"I'm not going to try and cover up someone that I know the truth for. I'll consider myself a nice person with everyone, but these were behaviours that I personally heard on the tour and heard other people in that same environment saying those sort of things to me.

"So, when I saw it, I was like, 'Well, pretty much expected, to be honest'. I am surprised it came so late, though."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AP

World.title: Messi's legendary run for Argentina almost never happened after heartbreak
World.content:
Lionel Messi's retirement from the Argentina national side brings down the curtain on one of world football's most storied international careers.

The records and achievements of Messi are stuff of legend, and his status in international sport is reserved for only the very greatest of their craft.

Messi was denied the perfect finish to his Argentina career in July, defeated in a thrilling FIFA World Cup final by Spain that went to extra time.

But the loss in New Jersey only denied the fairytale finish, and did not diminish the legend that Messi created for himself, or the legacy that he has left among his people.

But the love and admiration of his people, the two Copa America wins, and the 2022 FIFA World Cup triumph, which brought Argentina back to the pinnacle of world football and raised Messi to the legendary status of fellow countryman Diego Maradona, almost never happened.

Legend at Barca, struggles with Argentina

Messi has been on top of world football for two decades, winning the coveted Ballon d'Or as the world's best player a staggering eight times.

From 2004 to 2021, he won 10 La Liga titles, seven Spanish Cups, seven Spanish Super Cups, four Champions Leagues, three UEFA Super Cups and three FIFA Club World Cups with Barcelona.

Football great Lionel Messi announces retirement from Argentina team The announcement comes just weeks after the death of his father Jorge.

In a legendary 2012, he scored 91 goals in all competitions, a record haul for a calendar year, and slotted 50 goals in the 2011-12 La Liga season.

Trophies, accolades, love and admiration grew and grew for the Barcelona great, but success for Argentina was not forthcoming.

Coming through the ranks, Messi led Argentina to a Youth World Championship in 2005 and the Olympic medal at the Beijing Games in 2008.

But in the very big tournaments, trophies were harder to come by.

When Messi made his senior debut for Argentina in 2005 against Hungary, the South American giants had not won a trophy since the 1993 Copa America.

Messi's final tears As the champion wept on the pitch after the World Cup final defeat, Argentina may well have wondered with trepidation what life will look like in the post-Messi era.

Messi's Argentina senior debut was nothing to write home about either, sent off after less than a minute on the pitch for elbowing an opponent.

But Messi overcame that infamous beginning to establish himself as a star, and the hope of a nation that Argentina could return to the top of South America, and the world.

What followed was a string of bitter disappointments.

Argentina made the final of the Copa America in 2007, but was soundly beaten 3-0 by arch rival Brazil.

At the 2010 FIFA World Cup in South Africa, Messi failed to score at the tournament as Argentina exited at the quarterfinal stage.

Argentina was then knocked out again at the quarterfinal stage, this time at the 2011 Copa America, by eventual winner Uruguay.

These were bitter disappointments for Argentina and Messi, but the pain was about to increase, and it led to the great man announcing he did not want to be part of it anymore.

Three years, three finals, three painful defeats

Heading into the 2014 FIFA World Cup in Brazil, it had been 21 years since Argentina's last major trophy.

But the blue and whites marched into enemy territory intending to claim international football's greatest prize, and doing it in the backyard of their greatest rival.

Loading...

Argentina won all three group games — over Bosnia and Herzegovina, Iran, and Nigeria — to top the group, beat Switzerland 1-0 in extra time, and finally won a quarterfinal by defeating Belgium 1-0.

A scoreless semifinal against the Netherlands, finalists in 2010, went to penalties, where Argentina won 4-2, including a successful spot kick from Messi.

But the joy ended there.

In a major final for the first time in seven years, Argentina faced a German side that had just humiliated Brazil 7-1 in the semifinal.

Like all of Argentina's games to that point, the game was tight and tense. It went to extra time, but the strike of German Mario Götze sealed Germany's triumph.

A photograph of Messi looking at the World Cup trophy after the defeat, captured by Bao Tailiang for Chengdu Economic Daily in China, became the defining image of Messi for years.

Lionel Messi walking past the FIFA World Cup trophy after defeat in the 2014 final. (Supplied: Bao Tailiang for Chengdu Economic Daily via X)

The heartbreak only continued for Messi and Argentina.

The Copa America was held in 2015 and 2016, with Argentina reaching the final both times and losing to Chile each time.

Both finals ended scoreless and went to penalties. Messi converted his penalty, the only Argentinian player to do so, in the 2015 defeat, but the great man missed his spot kick in 2016.

The pain of the 2016 final defeat was too much for Messi, who announced he was retiring from Argentina.

"For me, the national team is over," he said after the loss to Chile in 2016. "I've done all I can. It hurts not to be a champion."

"It's been four finals, I tried.

"It was the thing I wanted the most, but I couldn't get it, so I think it's over.

"I think this is best for everyone. First of all for me, then for everyone.

"I think there's a lot of people who want this, who obviously are not satisfied, as we are not satisfied reaching a final and not winning it."

World football was that close to never seeing Messi reach the heights he would achieve.

Six-week retirement, 10 years of legacy building

When Messi announced on Sunday, June 26, 2016, that he would no longer play for Argentina, he ended what was by any other measure a magnificent international career.

He had made 113 appearances, scored 55 goals and led his country to four major finals.

But the absence of a trophy was not good enough — not for someone as great as Messi.

On July 10, the world watched Cristiano Ronaldo lift an international major trophy as Portugal won the 2016 Euros.

On August 12, Messi announced that he was back.

What followed after his six-week retirement is, on its own, one of the greatest international careers ever forged.

Messi would add another 94 caps to his name, score another 70 goals, and more importantly, end Argentina's trophy drought.

And Messi didn't just win one major trophy for Argentina; he won four.

The 2018 FIFA World Cup in Russia was another familiar quarterfinal exit for Argentina, but it was the precursor to an era of success.

Argentina finally broke through to win the Copa America in 2021, and they did it against Brazil, in Brazil.

Lionel Messi was thrown into the air in celebatrion after Argentina ended a 28-year trophy drought. (Getty Images: MB Media)

With the COVID-19 pandemic keeping many fans away from the famed Maracanã Stadium in Rio, Argentina ground out a 1-0 win to claim the nation's first major trophy in 28 years.

Messi was hoisted in the air by teammates in images that went around the world.

The drought was over, and the rain was here to stay. Argentina won a second trophy in 2022 when they defeated European champions Italy in the relaunched Finalissima, but greater prizes were to come.

By this stage, Messi had surpassed everything achieved by Maradona, except one.

Maradona almost single-handedly won the World Cup for Argentina in 1986, and gave him a legendary status that was near God-like.

Now, it was Messi's time to do the same.

He did it in Qatar at the 2022 World Cup, leading the blue and whites back to the top of world football.

The final against France, the defending world champions, was anything but ordinary. Those who were accustomed to Argentina grinding out 1-0 wins got the shock of their lives when they traded blows with France in one of the greatest finals ever played.

Messi scored two goals, including in extra time, while Ángel Di María also scored for Argentina. But the South Americans met their match in France, or more specifically, Kylian Mbappé, who scored a hat-trick, including a 118th-minute penalty to send the final to spot kicks.

In the penalty shootout, Messi converted, Mbappé converted.

Argentina was perfect. France was not.

When Gonzalo Montiel's shot hit the back of the net, Argentina was world champion and Messi had reached the God-like status that had only been reserved for Maradona.

The image of Messi kissing the World Cup became the defining image of his illustrious career.

Lionel Messi finally got his hands on the FIFA World Cup trophy, which had eluded him for so long. (Getty Images: China News Service/VCG/Cui Nan)

One more trophy would follow for Argentina, another Copa America in 2024 to make it three major trophies in four years.

That trophy was icing on the cake for Messi's legacy, which by now was in uncharted territory.

Messi's international career by numbers

1

Lionel Messi led Argentina to the FIFA World Cup title in 2022. He also led his country to two more finals, 2014 and 2026, which both resulted in 1-0 defeats in extra time.

2

Lionel Messi led Argentina to two Copa America titles in 2021 and 2024. Before then, the last time Argentina was champion in the Copa America was in 1993.

6

Lionel Messi has played in a record six FIFA World Cups — 2006, 2010, 2014, 2018, 2022 and 2026. Only Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo has also managed that feat.

21

Lionel Messi scored 21 goals at the FIFA World Cup finals. He is second on the all-time list behind French star Kylian Mbappé, who has scored 22 from just three tournaments.

34

Lionel Messi holds the record for the most FIFA World Cup finals matches played. He was on the field 34 times for Argentina in a FIFA World Cup tournament. Ronaldo is second on the list with 27 appearances for Portugal.

125

Lionel Messi holds the Argentina goal-scoring record, netting 125 times for his country. That is more than double the previous record holder, Gabriel Batistuta, who scored 54 times for his country.

207

Lionel Messi made 207 appearances for Argentina, a national record. He made his debut in 2005 against Hungary, and played his final match against Spain in the 2026 FIFA World Cup final. Ronaldo holds the world record for international appearances, playing 233 times for Portugal.

World.title: Labuschagne dropped as Australia names ODI squad for African series
World.content:
Australia has named its ODI squad for its back-to-back series in Zimbabwe and South Africa later this month, with World Cup winner Marnus Labuschagne among five players dropped.

Australia are reigning ODI world champions, after a stunning final win over India in Ahmedabad in 2023.

Labuschagne scored a half-century in that final, but his struggles since then have led to him being dropped from the ODI squad that will play in Africa, almost a year out from the next World Cup, which will be held in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia.

Labuschagne has missed five of Australia's previous 56 ODIs, but the 32-year-old has been dropped, along with Matt Short, Ben Dwarshuis, Todd Murphy and Liam Scott, from the squad picked to play in Pakistan and Bangladesh in May and June.

Pat Cummins and Mitch Starc will play in the ODIs against South Africa, while Mitch Marsh and Travis Head return after not playing in Pakistan or Bangladesh.

Emerging stars Cooper Connolly, Oliver Peake and Joel Davies have been added to the Australian ODI squad.

Australia ODI squad: Mitchell Marsh, Pat Cummins (SA only), Xavier Bartlett, Alex Carey, Cooper Connolly, Joel Davies, Nathan Ellis, Cameron Green, Josh Hazlewood, Travis Head, Josh Inglis, Spencer Johnson, Oliver Peake, Matthew Renshaw, Billy Stanlake, Mitchell Starc (SA only), Adam Zampa

Tech.title: Sonos introduces new headphones, soundbar, and software in its biggest announcement in years
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer covering TVs and audio. He has over 20 years experience in AV, and has previously been on staff at Digital Trends and Reviewed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

At an event in New York City, Sonos announced two new audio products — the Sonos Beam Ultra soundbar and Sonos Ace Ultra headphones, details of which were found in an FCC filing in early August — and a major update to its audio operating system dubbed Sonos 27. It’s the biggest single Sonos announcement since 2024, when a new app rollout upset its customers and sent it into damage control mode.

Software changes are core to Sonos’ announcements, with the company leaning heavily into AI integration with Sonos 27. This includes the company’s own Sonos 27voice assistant that it built in-house for music and system control. It’s coming as an early access, opt-in feature this fall. There’s also Sonos 27mcp, which gives the ability to connect any existing AI models such as ChatGPT or Google Gemini — although for some reason Google Assistant is still not natively supported. Sonos 27mcp launches in early access on September 8th.

In addition, users will be able to create up to 10 of their own agents through Sonos 27 to run, with whichever model they choose. These custom agents can be given different voices and roles. Brandon Holley, senior director of product development, gave examples of having a moody detective give you the morning news or a motivational coach whisper motivational aspirations when you wake up. Custom agents won’t be available until sometime in 2027.

Both Sonos 27mcp and the custom agents seem to expand the customization and control of a Sonos system beyond what the app and Sonos 27voice is capable of.

Features like a new 8-band EQ for the Sonos Ace Ultra have been added to the app. Image: Sonos

All products compatible with the current Sonos app can be controlled with Sonos 27mcp, and everything with a microphone works with Sonos 27voice. When the Sonos custom agents are available, they’ll work everywhere Sonos 27voice is enabled.

There are two new features being added to Sonos Fabric, which is the name given to its whole-home connected system. The wireless Play and Move 2 portable speakers can be used as surround sound speakers in a home theater system. Once in place, the speakers will automatically configure to their new positions and roles as surround speakers without needing to initiate setup in the Sonos app. It’s not possible to use this feature with a single Play or Move 2.

Compatible Sonos headphones will now be included in a Sonos home system and support moving sound between speakers and headphones — the system senses the closest speaker and will pass the audio from it to the headphones. Headphone linking, as Sonos calls it, will roll out as an early access feature on September 29th. Sonos hints that this is just the beginning of added features, but no further details about possible future options were given.

Improvements continue to come to the app, as well, again with feedback from the community, including the Sonos subreddit. Home, system, and search tabs will be added across the bottom of the screen, and a room sort option can be pinned to the top for easier access to a customizable list. There’s a cool feature that calls back to physical audio components: a virtual volume knob, you control with two fingers like you would in the real world. It’s not a major quality of life improvement, but it’s something that adds character and fun, and something I’ll probably use regularly. The new navigation, room sorts, and virtual volume knob starts rolling out on September 8 (although the volume knob will only launch on iOS at that time).

Lockscreen controls for volume and play/pause are also returning to the app, and started rolling out on August 17th. System health views to help troubleshoot issues and presets will roll out at some point later this fall.

It’s not just software announcements, though, as Sonos has two new products coming — the long-rumored Ace Ultra headphones and Beam Ultra soundbar.

If the Ace Ultra add to what was already great about the Ace, they could compete with Sony and Apple. Image: Sonos

The Sonos Ace Ultra are what the original Sonos Ace should have been from the beginning — an integrated part of the Sonos ecosystem. They are built upon Sonos’ Headphone Engine 2, which allows them to use the headphone linking feature rolling out at the same time as the headphones release on September 29th. A button on the headphones allows audio to be passed between a speaker and the headphones. No phone is necessary if it’s out of reach.

They look very similar to the Ace, with what appears to be slightly different button placement on the left ear cup. The Ace Ultra are also a little bigger, with a little more space in the ear cup, and 10 grams heavier. They have newly custom-designed 40mm drivers and 10 microphones for noise control (two more than the Ace) which Sonos claims makes their ANC twice as effective at noise cancellation than the Ace with “the frequencies that really matter,” as Brandon Holley told me. Those frequencies happen to be 65Hz (the general frequency of an HVAC) where the Sonos Ace Ultra are 2.2 times more effective, and 120Hz — the airplane drone range — where they’re 1.8 times better. No information is provided for performance with the chatter you might encounter at the coffee shop, for example.

An adaptive EQ adjusts the sound, compensating for any air leaks in the headphones’ fit due to glasses, jewelry, or hair. It includes both a 3-band and 8-band EQ to customize the sound for your taste. In addition to SBC and AAC codecs, the Ace Ultra supports aptX Adaptive Lossless over Bluetooth, and 16-bit/48kHz high resolution when connected with USB-C.

Battery life has improved by five hours, with the Sonos Ace Ultra offering up to 35 hours of listening with ANC on. A fast charge of three minutes gets an additional three hours of listening time.

Instead of just black and white, the Ace Ultra are also available in a muted blue agave and beige sand color. The headphones release on September 29th for $449.

The Beam Ultra adds up-firing speakers to its compact size, making it a true Atmos soundbar. Image: Sonos

The Beam Ultra is a completely redesigned 7.1.2 compact soundbar (as opposed to the 5.0 configuration of its predecessor), including two up-firing drivers to support Dolby Atmos spatial audio. The center channel mid-tweeter features a new waveguide, mechanic and acoustic design, and DSP, which includes four levels of AI speech enhancement for clarity.

While the Beam Ultra still has a compact design, to accommodate the additional speakers it is just under four inches longer than the Beam Gen 2. It comes in a black or white matte finish, and will be available for purchase on September 29th for $699.

With the headphones’ deeper integration into the Sonos ecosystem and the addition of up-firing drivers to the Beam Ultra, it looks like Sonos has made some great improvements to already solid products. But I won’t know for sure until I can dig into them for reviews. The app updates — particularly the AI integration — I’m a bit more cautious about. But Sonos is making the right move by rolling out the updates over time, allowing its users to opt in to early access instead of dumping it on everyone at once. This more measured approach could be what wins back the masses.

Tech.title: Tim Cook’s legacy isn’t just phones, it’s politics
Tech.content:
As much as any Apple product released during his time as CEO, Tim Cook’s tenure will be remembered for its ruthlessly efficient tight-rope walk between an autocrat in China and a would-be autocrat in the US.

During his 15 years as CEO, Cook steered Apple through relations with both Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump, including escalating conflicts between the two. As Apple’s enmeshment in China raised serious questions about reports of forced labor and censorship, Cook managed to appease Xi while maneuvering around political blowback in the US. And when Trump launched a trade war against China, Cook managed to soften the blow through his White House diplomacy. Cook’s ability to thread the needle between two superpowers helped expand Apple into a multi-trillion-dollar company, while downplaying concerns about civil rights, working conditions, and other serious issues.

In 2014, Apple departed from tech peers like Google by choosing to store some Chinese users’ personal data on servers in mainland China, saying at the time it was meant to improve its services for those users. But the move raised significant concerns that data could be at risk and subject to government censorship, though Apple reportedly stored the encryption keys outside of China. While Apple said an audit of labor conditions at its contractors found no forced labor, it also reportedly lobbied to weaken a US bill that sought to put a stronger onus on American companies to guarantee they weren’t using such a workforce. It’s submitted to Chinese regulations that required it to lower in-app purchase fees but also removed apps from its app store that the government objected to.

Cook knew how to pick his battles

Beginning in Trump’s first term, Cook also deftly navigated the US president’s whims, and appealed to him with showy displays that cost Apple relatively little. At one memorable tour of a contractor’s Mac Pro manufacturing plant, Cook stood beside Trump as the president falsely claimed that Apple was “building plants in the United States.” (The Texas plant had manufactured Mac Pros for years, and while Apple was building something in Austin at the time, it was a new campus, not a manufacturing facility.) Cook knew how to pick his battles, balancing his relationship with Trump with maintaining confidence from staff and customers. After Trump imposed immigration restrictions on seven Muslim-majority countries in 2017, for instance, Cook told employees it was “not a policy we support.”

Trump kicked off the initial trade war with China in his first term, leading China to impose its own tariffs on US goods in response. Eventually, Cook was able to win Apple a reprieve from some of the high tariffs imposed by the US on goods from China, such as the Apple Watch.

In Trump’s second term, Cook’s support became more visible and his pushback more muted. Cook attended Trump’s second inauguration alongside many other tech CEOs, and donated $1 million to his inauguration committee. After Cook and other CEOs attended a film screening of Amazon’s documentary on Melania Trump hours after federal agents shot and killed protester Alex Pretti in Minneapolis, Cook assured employees he was “heartbroken” by the situation and “had a good conversation with the president this week where I shared my views.” But similar to the stunt at the Texas manufacturing plant, Cook continued to present Trump with useful trophies to tout his policies — in August 2025, that came in the form of a gold and glass statue, awarded to the president as a symbol of Apple’s “Made in the USA” efforts. And to stave off more costly tariffs, he cut deals to bring more manufacturing to the US.

Walking that line let Cook and Apple do what they do best: pumping out a new version of the iPhone year after year, with the supply chain and trade conditions in place to make it happen. It’s only now that the AI-fueled RAM shortage is forcing Apple’s hand to raise prices, according to Cook. But even as Cook’s time as CEO has come to an end, it seems he won’t soon shake his role as Apple’s geopolitical negotiator-in-chief. In announcing Cook’s ascension to executive chairman, Apple wrote, Cook would continue “engaging with policymakers around the world.”

Tech.title: John Ternus takes over as Apple’s new CEO
Tech.content: The multitrillion-dollar home of the iPhone, Mac, and so many other tech gadgets has a new leaader, as Tim Cook has been replaced as CEO as of September 1st by former hardware boss John Ternus. How will we look back on Cook’s legacy, and what will Apple look like under the leadership of Ternus and new chief hardware officer Johny Srouji?

Tech.title: Florida blocks Flock cams on state highways
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Florida is banning Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers across state highways, as reported earlier by NBC News and local news outlet WUSF. In a memo on Monday, Florida’s Department of Transportation says it’s revoking permits for all license plate readers, adding that they must be removed from state highways within 30 days.

As noted in the memo, Florida’s DOT says it’s issuing the order in response to the “recent exponential increase in deployments” of license plate readers, “coupled with concerning reports of misuse, data privacy concerns, and surveillance schemes.” The agency is also halting future requests for license plate reader placements on state roadways.

Tech.title: Get ready for a really busy month of smartphones
Tech.content:
We’re not even half a day into September, and two new smartphones have already launched: the Poco F9 Pro and F9 Ultra. We’re expecting more this week, as the IFA trade show kicks off in Berlin, before we get new iPhones a week after that. And that’s only the beginning of what promises to be an exceptionally busy month for smartphone launches.

For the decade I’ve worked in the industry, tech journalists have always spoken in hushed tones about the dreaded “Techtember,” when just about every tech company on the planet seems to be in unspoken agreement that it’s time to launch new products in time for the holiday buying season. (It’s followed, in particularly packed years, by Techtober too). In the last few years the pressure has lessened a little, the release calendar stretching out into neighboring months. But in 2026 Techtember is back with a vengeance, especially when it comes to phones.

It always starts with IFA. Europe’s biggest tech trade show attracts over 200,000 visitors and global manufacturers from across tech. IFA doesn’t have as many phone launches as it did a decade ago, when the likes of Sony, Samsung, and LG would routinely launch flagships at the show, but there’s still plenty on the way this week.

Tecno has teased a bezelless concept phone, which it says it’ll be bringing to the show. TCL usually brings an array of E Ink-esque Nxtpaper phones to show, so I’d hope to see some at its press conference. There’s even an outside chance of a whole new foldable: Xiaomi is attending IFA for the first time ever, just a week after it teased the upcoming Xiaomi 18 Fold and promised the phone a launch in early September. Its September 3rd press conference would certainly make sense for that.

Then there’s Apple. The company won’t be at IFA, but it has already announced a September 9th event, where we expect it to launch new iPhones. Rumor has it that it’s splitting its launch up in an act of solidarity with overworked phone reviewers (I wish), delaying the regular iPhone 18 to next spring and sticking to the Pros this month. Still, the long-awaited arrival of the first foldable iPhone should be enough to keep us busy.

But that’s far from all that’s coming. Android Headlines reckons at least 20 phones will launch this month, and that might be a conservative estimate.

Huawei will launch its latest trifold, the Mate XT 2, in China on September 7th, and perhaps the Mate 90 lineup too. Xiaomi will follow up the 18 Fold with the 18 Pro lineup later in the month. Vivo has confirmed its flagship X500 series will also arrive in September, and Honor has done the same for its Magic 9 flagships. Oppo’s Find X10 line has been heavily tipped to arrive in September too, though thankfully some suggest it might slip to the following month. Even OnePlus is expected to get in on the action: its OnePlus 16 rumored to release in September too — though not in the US or Europe.

Why the sudden glut? I blame Qualcomm. It used to launch its flagship Snapdragon chips in December, but that launch date has steadily moved forward, in part to give manufacturers time to ship new products ahead of lucrative holiday sales seasons, both in China and abroad. So this year it’s holding its annual Snapdragon Summit from September 22nd to 24th, when it’s likely to reveal the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6. Promptly after that, we can expect a rush of Android manufacturers announcing phones powered by the new silicon.

With RAMageddon in full swing, the jury’s still out on how appealing these launches will be. Outside of Samsung’s fun Galaxy Z Fold 8, a lot of this year’s biggest phones have been rehashes of 2025 models with a price hike and a chipset bump — and occasionally not even that. At least we’ll have more foldables to be excited about, and hopefully a couple of manufacturers have another surprise or two in store.

A month chock-full of phones, that I can do. But if we’re about to get a Techtember full of iterative updates that cost more, without delivering anything special? Wake me up when it’s Techtober.

Tech.title: Nvidia’s controversial DLSS 5 arrives September 3rd and requires serious GPU horsepower
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Nvidia is officially launching DLSS 5 this week, following a divisive announcement in March where we likened the AI upscaling tech to a “real-time generative AI filter for video games” and “motion smoothing for video games, but worse.” DLSS 5 will officially be available on RTX 50-series desktop and laptop GPUs and through GeForce Now cloud gaming, though the only game with the tech so far is NBA 2K27 — which is launching September 3rd at 9PM PT on PC.

When it was announced, Nvidia lauded DLSS 5 as “the company’s most significant breakthrough in computer graphics since the debut of real-time ray tracing in 2018,” and highlighted how the tech uses AI to make games look more realistic by enhancing a game based on its source content. Nvidia also stressed that DLSS 5 gave developers controls that let them decide how changes from DLSS 5 appeared in their games.

Image compare: drag the handle to see the difference Nvidia says it can provide in NBA 2K27. Tap here for full-res with DLSS 5 off, and with DLSS 5 on.

But accompanying examples shared by Nvidia were widely criticized and meme’d on for significantly changing how characters looked, such as the “yassification” of Resident Evil Requiem protagonist Grace Ashcroft. With the official launch, Requiem still doesn’t support DLSS 5, and neither do other games shown in the March reveal, including EA Sports FC, Starfield, and Hogwarts Legacy, so we don’t know how the final version of the tech might now appear in those titles.

Nvidia did not answer our questions about when DLSS 5 might come to any game beyond NBA 2K27, nor reconfirm that previously confirmed titles will still include the tech.

Tap, twice, for higher res versions. Image: Nvidia

Tap, twice, for higher res versions. Image: Nvidia

In examples from NBA 2K27 we saw in a press briefing, though, changes from DLSS 5 don’t appear to be quite as dramatic as the types of adjustments shown in the initial reveal. The shadows and textures added by DLSS 5 generally made the players in the game look more realistic instead of turning them into AI caricatures. You can see more in our deeper dive here.

In briefings, Nvidia showed how developers will have many sliders at their disposal to determine exactly how much DLSS 5 changes things, and that developers can choose to amp up whichever parts of the scene they prefer. They can even leave characters’ faces alone and just enhance silverware or food or foliage, Nvidia says.

Image slider: drag the handle to make bacon look more real by giving it shadows.

While Nvidia’s original DLSS 5 demos required a pair of RTX 5090 gaming graphics cards, the company claims even a single midrange RTX 5060 can manage to play NBA 2K27 at 1080p with ray tracing and DLSS 5 at ultra spec — if you have one of he fastest gaming CPUs and enable 6x frame generation (meaning the game is only producing one “real” frame for every six frames you see).

DLSS 5 is still a huge performance hit. Nvidia estimates it at 50 to 60 percent, and we saw performance cut in half when we tried an unofficial DLSS5 mod in Shadow of the Tomb Raider.

Image: Nvidia

So far, Nvidia has shown us examples that demonstrate the ideal version of what’s possible with DLSS 5 (and promote NBA 2K27). We haven’t yet tested an official build of DLSS 5 ourselves to get an idea of how the tech might look, but we have tried the unofficial version that modders are using to mess with older games like Control and Skyrim. With older games, it seems, a little sprinkle of DLSS 5 goes a long way.

Tech.title: Nvidia’s DLSS 5, explained
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Nvidia knows that DLSS 5 left a bad first impression. In March, many gamers took one look at Resident Evil Requiem protagonist Grace Ashcroft’s DLSS 5-ified face and declared it AI slop. So this week, the company’s re-introducing its controversial “neural rendering” with firm messaging about how it “preserves artistic intent,” “respects the rendered frame,” and gives game developers full control.

Now, ahead of its September 3rd launch, with an official Nvidia briefing under our belt and some hands-on time with the version that leaked onto the web, we think we finally get the picture. Here’s what’s going on.

Is DLSS 5 AI slop?

The critics weren’t wrong: DLSS 5 largely is a generative AI filter for video games. Kind of like a camera filter on your phone, DLSS 5 analyzes and modifies a real-time stream of 2D images after your 3D game engine is done spitting them out. It can indeed make game characters look terrible if applied poorly, like they’ve aged 20 years in a split-second. It uses a lot of GPU power, and can easily cut framerate in half — even applied well, you could argue that existing games look better without it.

But DLSS 5 isn’t what we typically think of when we think of generative AI. It doesn’t change shapes, or hallucinate words on a sign, or place brand-new fake objects in view. Instead, it imagines light, shadow, color, and detail that make the same shapes appear differently.

Image: Nvidia

DLSS 5 can make dull, pasty characters look far more photorealistic. It can fill their hair and clothing and nearby foliage with signs of realistic light. It can ground characters and objects and clothing so they don’t look like they’re floating above video game surfaces.

Here’s an example I captured myself in Yakuza Kiwami: with DLSS on, see how contact shadows underneath each character make them seem like they’re actually standing on the ground?

DLSS 5 off. Screenshot by Sean Hollister / The Verge DLSS 5 on. Screenshot by Sean Hollister / The Verge

(Later in this story, you should really check out how Cade Cunningham’s jersey casts shadows on his video game body, so it looks more like he’s wearing it.)

And unlike AI-generated photos and videos, that usually produce different results with the same prompt, Nvidia claims DLSS 5 is deterministic, so games should look the same every time.

DLSS 5 is also not one-size-fits-all. Despite what it sounds like, “DLSS 5 On” and “DLSS 5 Off” isn’t just an on-off switch. Developers (and apparently modders) can drag various sliders to change how DLSS 5 plays with color and light, and they have three different AI models to work with at launch, giving your graphics “default,” “natural” or “cinematic” looks.

Plus, developers can decide whether to apply DLSS 5 everything in a scene, just a character’s face and skin, just foliage, just silverware or furniture or even just food.

You’re saying game studios could leave character faces alone?

Yep. The toolset can automatically cut out a mask, like in Photoshop, to isolate a character’s face and skin from everything else:

The automated mask precisely selects this character’s face, so game developers can enhance it — or make sure it’s left alone. Image: Nvidia

If they don’t like the automated mask, devs can cut one out themselves. That’s the little “Developer Masking” checkbox in the image above. “There’s no limit to how many masks, how many groups, they could implement,” says Nvidia’s director of real-time content technology Gabriele Leone.

Would game studios actually leave the faces alone?

Probably not! The first game brave enough to ship with the tech is NBA 2K27, and I suspect that’s because Cade Cunningham actually looks a bit better with detailed skin, a uniform that doesn’t seem glued to his body, and a bit more glint in his eye. Take a look at Nvidia’s images for yourself:

That basketball, too — doesn’t it feel a bit more lifelike now most of its detail is in shadow?

But what about DLSStelle and all the other horrific AI faces I’ve seen since modders got hold of the tech?

Truly deranged. But these games are supposed to look like animation, and surely their creators would never do anything like this to them, right? Right??

“The soul and goal of GeForce is to achieve photorealism in real-time rendering,” Nvidia’s director of applied deep learning Edward Liu told journalists. And games with more realistic art styles don’t look anywhere near this bad. But even realistic games can look wrong if the sliders are set too aggressively.

What do you mean by “too aggressively?”

I’m willing to bet that if you’ve seen the leaked DLSS 5 modifying an existing game, the unofficial DLSS 5 mod was set to its default level of around 80 percent intensity or even higher. Some creators will even pump it up to 200 percent to make the difference between “DLSS on” and “DLSS off” especially clear.

But I believe even 80 percent is far too aggressive for many existing games. It can feel like you’re artificially aging a character by weathering their skin and deepening the wrinkles and creases in their face.

To show you, I fired up Shadow of the Tomb Raider. Here’s what Lara Croft looks like with DLSS 5 at 0 percent, 80 percent, and 200 percent intensity:

0 percent intensity (DLSS 5 off). Tap to enlarge; use arrows to compare. Screenshot by Sean Hollister / The Verge 80 percent intensity. Screenshot by Sean Hollister / The Verge 200 percent intensity. Screenshot by Sean Hollister / The Verge

She seems… weathered, no? But at 40 percent intensity, she still looks like the same video game character to me, only with a bit more life in her eyes:

0 percent intensity (DLSS 5 off). Tap to enlarge; use arrows to compare. Screenshot by Sean Hollister / The Verge 40 percent intensity. Screenshot by Sean Hollister / The Verge

Similarly, here’s Kazuma Kiryu from Yakuza Kiwami once more. In this part of the game, he’s supposed to be 27 years old, and nowhere near the grizzled veteran he is by Yakuza 6. But as I ramp up the intensity from 0 to 40 to 85 percent, you can see his furrowed brow gets more furrowed, his hair lightens, and the increased shadow across his cheeks makes his face appear slightly gaunt.

0 percent intensity (DLSS 5 off). Tap to enlarge; use arrows to compare. 40 percent intensity. 85 percent intensity.

He looks older — even if the underlying geometry of his face hasn’t actually changed. In a cutscene at 85 percent, it even looks like his hair might be tinged with grey:

Does this look like a 27-year-old man to you? Screenshot by Sean Hollister / The Verge

But again, it’s something developers and modders can control with some granularity. I’d probably enjoy a version of DLSS 5 for older games that ignores the faces but enhances a character’s gear. Kiryu’s sworn brother and antagonist Majima, below, doesn’t quite look right to me — but his eyepatch and necklace look excellent.

DLSS 5 off. Screenshot by Sean Hollister / The Verge DLSS 5 on. Screenshot by Sean Hollister / The Verge

By the way, these are just me playing with the overarching DLSS 5 slider when set to its “default” model. There are actually three different AI models, each with a slightly different look, and two different sliders, one for “tone” and one for “structure.”

What’s the difference?

I’m telling myself that “tone” is about light and color, while “structure” is about shadows and definition. But it’s probably easier to show you by isolating each:

Tone intensity 0, structure intensity 0. Screenshot by Sean Hollister / The Verge Tone intensity 100, structure intensity 0. Screenshot by Sean Hollister / The Verge Tone intensity 0, structure intensity 100. Screenshot by Sean Hollister / The Verge

Officially, Nvidia says that “structure intensity” controls a mix of ambient occlusion, contact shadows, reflections and subsurface scattering (read: how light scatters through materials like hair, skin, and leaves), while “tone intensity” controls color and “broader lighting” details.

What about the three different AI models?

Nvidia only called them Model A, Model B and Model C in my briefing, but the DLSS 5 mod I used describes them as “default,” “cinematic” and “natural.” Here’s the image Nvidia provided to show the difference:

Nvidia’s three AI looks. Image: Nvidia

And here’s my own comparison in Shadow of the Tomb Raider — you may need to blow these up and cycle through to spot the differences.

DLSS 5 off. Screenshot by Sean Hollister / The Verge “Default,“ 80 percent intensity. Screenshot by Sean Hollister / The Verge “Cinematic,“ 80 percent intensity. Screenshot by Sean Hollister / The Verge “Natural,“ 80 percent intensity. Screenshot by Sean Hollister / The Verge

Is this really an AI filter? It doesn’t use the game engine at all?

Nvidia says that DLSS 5 can take some cues from game engines. But it’s based on the colors and motion vectors that it sees in the flat 2D frames, after they’re rendered and after other techniques like DLSS Super Resolution are applied.

When we asked how DLSS 5 knows the difference between a character model, an object, and a piece of foliage, Liu replied that the model was trained to recognize what it sees. “Just like a person, if you look at anything, you know where things are.”

You can even technically run DLSS 5 on video capture from a Nintendo Switch 2, and modders have already found ways to inject it into earlier games that used OpenGL and DirectX 9.

Will game developers actually buy into DLSS 5? Will they use it well?

That’s one of the big remaining questions — and one that Nvidia left unanswered during and after our briefing.

While Nvidia said in March that DLSS 5 would come to at least 16 different games including Assassin’s Creed Shadows, Hogwarts Legacy, Starfield, and Resident Evil Requiem, the company did not answer questions about when DLSS 5 might come to any game beyond NBA 2K27, nor did it confirm that other titles are still coming following the original backlash. Perhaps Nvidia and its partners will wait and see how reviewers and gamers react first.

It’s worth noting that this may be a niche technology to start: while it no longer requires two RTX 5090 GPUs to function, it still uses a lot of horsepower. Officially, DLSS 5 is only coming to the latest RTX 50 series GPUs, which have become quite expensive: even a lower-mid-range RTX 5060 retailers for around $470 these days.

Nvidia claims that an RTX 5060 is enough to play NBA 2K27 at 1080p with ultra settings, ray tracing, and DLSS 5 enabled — assuming you’re pairing it with a fast gaming CPU and a whole heap of RAM.

These framerates are with 6x frame-gen enabled, so divide by six to get a better idea of how responsive the game might feel.

Just how much of a performance hit are we talking?

With NBA 2K27, Nvidia claims the performance hit is 50 to 60 percent on average across all Nvidia RTX 50-series GPUs. When I ran the Shadow of the Tomb Raider benchmark at 1440p with on an RTX 5090 at Highest spec, DLSS Quality and an unofficial DLSS 5 mod, I saw framerate exactly cut in half — 312fps with DLSS 5 off, 156fps with it on.

Will gamers be able to tweak DLSS 5 the way they like?

The DLSS 5 mods are so easy to apply, it seems like the cat is out of the bag. But Nvidia’s message is that the developer has full control, and it didn’t answer questions about whether it’ll provide controls to gamers, too.

Which mod should I install?

I don’t yet feel comfortable recommending one — there’s been a feeding frenzy for DLSS 5 mods ever since the leak and we haven’t been able to properly vet. I installed one on a completely fresh system, just in case something went wrong.

How have gamers reacted to Nvidia’s re-introduction of DLSS 5 so far?

The reactions have been all over the place since DLSS 5 leaked and modders began posting their work. I’ve seen people say that DLSS 5 looks like a free next-gen remaster of any game you like, and I’ve seen people say it looks as terrible as it did before. I’ve seen people suggest that even if it looks good, it’ll make every game look too similar once developers start using it as a crutch.

But many of those impressions were based on images and videos of the tech at its extremes. Once people realize there’s granular control, perhaps reactions will become more measured.

Correction: An earlier version of this article misidentified characters in screenshots; they are NBA player Cade Cunningham and Majima Goro from Yakuza.

Tech.title: Roku’s first OLED TVs undercut the midrange competition
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer covering TVs and audio. He has over 20 years experience in AV, and has previously been on staff at Digital Trends and Reviewed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Just a few weeks ago the only midrange OLED options available were from LG and Samsung. But after Sony officially announced the Bravia 6 last week, Roku has now launched its first-ever OLED TV — the Roku Pro Series — which will be followed by the step-up Pro Series LX next month.

The Roku Pro Series has a 120Hz panel, four HDMI 2.1 ports, and supports Dolby Vision and HDR10 Plus. It also has auto low latency mode, FreeSync Premium, and VRR for gaming. A backlit Roku remote is included, and a remote finder button on the TV helps locate it when misplaced. The Pro Series LX is about twice as bright as the regular Pro Series, supports 144Hz VRR, and has a polarizer to reduce reflections. And of course both TV series use the Roku operating system.

The Pro Series is exclusive to Amazon for 2026, available now, and comes in 55- and 65-inch sizes starting at $999. The Pro Series LX will be available in October in 55 inches for $1,299 and 65 inches for $1,599.

Tech.title: Florida and Texas move to block Flock cameras over privacy concerns
Tech.content:
The states of Florida and Texas are moving to end their relationship with surveillance giant Flock, as the company faces increasing backlash over privacy concerns and misuse of its tracking technology.

Florida’s Department of Transportation said in a memo on Monday that it will cease using license plate readers across the state’s highways, such as Flock’s cameras, citing “concerning reports of misuse, data privacy concerns, and surveillance schemes.” The state now has 30 days to remove the cameras.

The decision comes days after Florida governor Ron DeSantis called the license plate reading technology “out of control” in remarks during a press conference last Wednesday.

Florida follows similar action by Texas, which last week ordered state agencies to stop funding Flock cameras. Texas governor Greg Abbott’s office cited abuse of the surveillance system, including the recent indictment of a Lufkin, Texas police officer with 100 felony counts related to allegedly searching Flock’s database to track people without authorization.

Abbott’s office did not say which agencies would be affected, but local media reports that Dallas could be broadly affected, as officials say there are hundreds of Flock cameras operating throughout the city.

The move comes amid rising bipartisan concerns over privacy and civil liberties concerns, following reports of cybersecurity issues, police abusing their access to Flock’s database to stalk their ex-partners, and accuracy issues that have led to police stops and wrongful arrests. Recent reporting shows that Flock cameras are moving away from scanning license plates and are also working to identify and track people.

Flock currently has around 130,000 license plate readers across the United States. The company has faced pushback from communities whose residents say they do not want Flock in their neighborhoods. Several towns, including Evanston, Ill., Cambridge, Mass., and Eugene, Ore., reported that Flock reinstalled or reactivated their cameras, despite local officials terminating their contracts with the company.

TechCrunch contacted Flock to ask if the company plans to allow Florida and Texas to remove their cameras, or if Flock plans to reinstall or reactivate them. A Flock spokesperson did not respond to our request for comment.

Tech.title: This startup is fuel-injecting hydrogen to make cargo ships more efficient
Tech.content:
It’s one the most iconic scenes in the Fast & Furious film franchise: Paul Walker’s thumb comes off the steering wheel and smashes a small red button, pumping nitrous oxide into the engine of his Mitsubishi Eclipse and giving the car an explosive boost.

This is not exactly how the hydrogen-injection system developed by a startup called Newlight works on cargo ships. In fact, the company’s system uses compressed hydrogen fuel to boost efficiency — not to beat Vin Diesel. But it’s an analogy that’s proved to be useful for co-founder Evyatar Cohen.

“Instead of getting power, we actually say to the engine: ‘Hey, reduce the fuel [flow] to the engine, we don’t need as much because we have some nitrous. It’s [just] called hydrogen,’” he told TechCrunch in an exclusive interview.

The small team based in the San Francisco Bay Area has developed this hydrogen injection system as a retrofit, which it claims can be installed in less than two weeks without needing a dry dock. It cuts fuel use and emissions by more than 20%, and can save some vessels as much as $500,000 in annual costs, according to the startup.

Newlight does this by constantly monitoring the diesel engine and finding optimal moments, down to the millisecond level, to inject the hydrogen fuel. That includes measuring exhaust temperature, combustion pressure, and air intake pressure, and increasing or decreasing the hydrogen flow every time a piston moves inside the engine’s cylinders.

The startup says this hybrid system has completed its first long-range commercial voyage: an 8,500-nautical mile trip from Singapore to Ghana. Newlight installed its tech on a 650-foot-long Lomar Shipping bulk carrier ship for the test. The startup said its system reduced fuel consumption by 24% and carbon dioxide emissions by 28%.

“It was amazing,” Haran Cohen Hillel, Cohen’s co-founder and the CEO of Newlight, said of the month-long voyage. “Being onboard and seeing the system operate in real conditions was a completely different experience from anything we had done in the lab.”

Turning the system on with his co-founder for the first time, he said, was an “emotional moment for both of us.”

“We spent a lot of time monitoring the system, the engine behavior, and the performance, and what impressed us most was how smoothly everything worked,” he told TechCrunch. “Seeing the system integrate with the vessel, operate reliably, and deliver the results we had been working toward was a huge milestone for us and for the entire Newlight team.”

The combination of those projections, the clever pitch, and the years Cohen and Hillel spent working in the Israeli Navy has helped the duo secure a $9 million seed round. The fundraise included investment from lomarlabs, the venture arm of Lomar Shipping, BIRD Energy, a joint venture between the U.S. Department of Energy and the Israel Ministry of Energy, deep tech funds Undeterred Capital and CiRi Ventures, and Fusion VC, an accelerator for Israeli startups in the U.S.

Newlight also says it’s attracting commercial interest. The company claims it has signed agreements to put the hydrogen injection system on 12 vessels across multiple companies with “broader fleet rollouts planned for next year.”

There are other companies working to use fuel injection methods to cut emissions and boost efficiency, including with ammonia or methanol. But Newlight argues its hydrogen setup is leaner and requires fewer changes to the diesel engines typically used on cargo ships.

The two co-founders also told TechCrunch they see opportunities beyond the marine industry, too — though they expect to stay focused on the sea for now.

“We’re an energy company, right? So we look at the whole energy situation that is happening around the world, with transportation, and data centers, and we have some investors that even have trains,” Hillel said. “But we’re gonna try to be focused on shipping right now, and to get on a scale there, and then we can probably expand.”

Tech.title: Waymo accelerates robotaxi expansion with launches in Denver, San Diego and Tampa
Tech.content:
Waymo has started to offer its robotaxi service to the public in Denver, San Diego, and Tampa, extending the Alphabet-owned company’s commercial operations to 14 U.S. cities.

The company said on Tuesday that it will begin inviting riders on a rolling basis and slowly ramp up access in the three cities, following its usual commercial playbook. The expansion has increased its fleet of self-driving Jaguar I-Pace hatchbacks and a new minivan called the Ojai to more than 4,000 vehicles.

The launch in these three cities comes as Tesla is striving to close the gap in the robotaxi market. Tesla now charges for rides in its driverless Tesla Model Y vehicles in Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando and Tampa. Service in some of these markets is limited, but the company continues to expand within these cities and add vehicles to its fleet. The company is also banking on its Cybercab, a custom-built two-seater with no steering wheel or pedals, to speed up its efforts.

Waymo’s announcement highlights a relentless expansion push that kicked into gear 18 months ago, and helped cement its position as U.S. robotaxi market leader.
