Tech.title: People’s Picks ISP Winners: Is Your Internet Service Provider a Flop or Favorite?
Tech.content:
Your internet service provider choice will depend on what’s available in your area, but CNET readers’ survey responses can help narrow down your choice if you have several options. Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

The internet service provider you choose hinges on a lot. We rely on the internet for many daily tasks, streaming, shopping, work and social media. Several factors that go into choosing the right one, like cost effectiveness, satisfaction, speed and customer support are important. But Joe Supan, CNET’s broadband principal writer, says a reliable connection is paramount.

We asked CNET readers what they like (and don’t) about their ISP for People’s Picks, CNET’s community awards program. Did your provider make the cut? Here’s what they said and what we didn’t expect to find out.

CNET’s People’s Picks ISP Winners

J. Hazelwood/CNET GFiber GFiber, previously known as Google Fiber, is a household name among internet service providers and a popular fiber internet option. CNET readers give it high scores, making it the overall top pick among ISPs. GFiber has an overall satisfaction score of 4.72 out of 5, and scores highly for reliability (4.70) and plan speed (4.82). GFiber also scores 4.28 out of 5 for price, Verizon Fios and AT&T Fiber are close runners-up to GFiber. Both score highly for reliability (4.39 and 4.48, respectively) and plan speed (4.41 and 4.49, respectively). But GFiber wins by a landslide for its customer support. Most CNET readers who have contacted customer support within the past year rate their experience as “Excellent,” while other GFiber customers say customer service was “Good” and don’t have any negative ratings for the fiber-optic ISP. Winner for: Fiber internet, customer service, price, reliability and speed See at GFiber

J. Hazelwood/CNET T-Mobile Home Internet (5G) T-Mobile is often known as a popular cellphone provider, but it wins CNET’s People’s picks for 5G internet. T-Mobile scores 4.20 out of 5 for customer satisfaction, the highest among 5G internet providers. CNET readers say their T-Mobile internet connection rarely drops, noting only a few times a year. And there’s no noticeable difference in speed during peak hours. T-Mobile readers haven’t experienced unexpected price hikes within the past year and many wouldn’t change providers if a new one moved into their neighborhood. T-Mobile’s 5G internet is a close runner-up to GFiber in terms of price. Verizon’s 5G internet is just behind T-Mobile, with a price score of 4.10 out of 5. T-Mobile won 5G internet by narrowly beating Verizon in speed and reliability. Wins for: 5G internet See at T-mobile

J. Hazelwood/CNET Starlink Starlink wins among major internet companies with a high overall satisfaction rating of 4.47 out of 5, compared to Verizon Fios and T-Mobile, which score 4.16 and 4.20, respectively. And it has the second-highest reliability score among major winners. Starlink scores 4.59 in reliability while GFiber scores 4.70. “A few years ago, it would have been unfathomable that a satellite company would be considered this reliable. This really speaks to how massive Starlink’s technical improvements have been,” said Supan. Satellite internet also scores fairly highly for plan speed (4.41 out of 5), with no noticeable changes during peak hours. However, Starlink falls short on price satisfaction compared to other major internet providers because it has traditionally required an upfront $349 charge for a satellite dish. However, it recently switched to a $10 monthly charge. “Starlink isn’t particularly fast or affordable, but it serves customers who essentially had no modern internet options before it came along,” said Supan. Wins for: Rural satellite internet, overall satisfaction for satellite, reliability for satellite and speed for satellite See at Starlink

CNET’s People’s Picks regional ISP winners

We pored through our readers’ responses to find the best ISP in each region based on the internet service features you rely on every day. Here’s how each regional winner compares to other ISPs in your area and what to know before choosing one.

West: Sonic

Wins for: Customer service, overall satisfaction, price, reliability and speed

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Sonic is a California-based fiber optic ISP that wins in several of CNET’s categories compared to other Western providers. It earns high marks for price (4.65 out of 5), speed (4.80 out of 5) and overall satisfaction (4.85 out of 5) — the highest among other Western providers. It even beats out national ISPs GFiber and Verizon FiOS for its reliability.

Sonic received nearly flawless feedback from CNET readers. Many readers never experience internet drops or need to reset their router. They also report no noticeable speed differences during peak hours. And when it comes to customer service, no readers report poor or fair customer service.

South: EPB (Electric Power Board)

Wins for: Customer service, overall satisfaction, price, reliability and speed

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Electric Power Board is a fiber optic ISP based in Chattanooga, Tennessee that scores highly compared to other southern ISPs. It scores 5 out of 5 for overall satisfaction, speed and reliability, and 4.5 out of 5 for price satisfaction, beating out national ISPs AT&T Fiber, GFiber, Comcast Xfinity and Spectrum.

CNET readers also give EPB an “Excellent” customer satisfaction rating with no lower ratings. They don’t experience connection drops or speed lags, and wouldn’t change providers if another ISP came to their area.

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Northeast: T-Mobile Home Internet 5G

Wins for: Overall satisfaction and price

T-Mobile Home Internet 5G scores the highest overall satisfaction score in the northeast — earning a 4.40 out of 5. Verizon Fios comes as a close contender with a 4.19. CNET readers also give T-Mobile’s 5G home internet 4.60 out of 5. T-Mobile still has solid customer satisfaction scores (4.20), with many readers noting no noticeable difference in speed during peak hours and no unexpected price hikes.

Midwest: Quantum

Wins for: Overall satisfaction, reliability and speed

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Quantum Fiber wins among Midwest ISPs with a satisfaction score of 4.67 out of 5. Quantum has a flawless 5 out of 5 for reliability. CNET readers say the connection rarely drops — only a few times a year and they don’t experience speed lags during peak hours, which earns Quantum another 5 out of 5 score for speed.

Quantum Fiber was acquired by AT&T earlier this year. Even though customers still see Quantum on their bills, they now have some AT&T perks and benefits like bundling wireless discounts.

GFiber is a close second to Quantum with an overall satisfaction score of 4.64. It falls short on reliability, plan speed and price.

These top 4 ISP features matter most

Speed of plan

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Speed and price are the two most important factors when shopping for internet. “The more people and connected devices in your home, the more speed you’ll need,” Supan says.

Supan adds that even though ISPs generally highlight their download speeds, upload speeds are arguably just as important, especially if you work from home or play games online. CNET has an internet speed guide to help you determine whether you’re getting the right amount of speed for your home.

GFiber scores a 4.82 out of 5 for speed, and most users don’t have any speed issues during peak hours. Regionally, Ting scores the highest 5 out of 5 score for speed compared to other regional providers. Your home internet speed will vary depending on your needs and usage.

Price of plan

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Choosing an internet service provider at a reasonable price can be tough, as prices continue to rise due to improvements in internet technology and equipment. How much you can expect to pay depends on your plan’s speed, connection type and which providers are available in your area.

Supan says that pricing isn’t always straightforward because many ISPs, especially cable providers, will hike your price after a year or two. However, providers are required to list increases in a broadband label so you can see exactly how much your bill will increase and when, he says. It’s also worth noting that some providers charge a fee if you exceed your plan’s data cap. And your price may change if an introductory promotional period ends.

T-Mobile Home Internet scores highly with a 4.24 out of 5. It doesn’t have equipment fees, data caps or contracts, which makes its home internet service a more flexible and cost-effective option. Pricing starts at $50 per month, or $35 per month if you bundle with any T-Mobile voice line and 

Reliability

J. Hazelwood/CNET

Earlier this year, CNET found that 86% of US adults experience wonky Wi-Fi connections or drops. And 1 in 5 (19%) regularly have Wi-Fi problems. Internet reliability can depend on a number of factors that may or may not be your ISP’s fault.

Supan says some internet connection types can be more susceptible to drops or disconnections, but your ISP may still be able to help. You may be able to get your router replaced or switch your internet channel from 2.4 to 5GHz. Your connection reliability may also depend on where your router is placed in your home or on the type of router you’re using. Bigger homes can usually benefit from a mesh router system to extend your connection and reduce dead zones.

CNET readers highly recommend GFiber for reliability and give it a 4.70 out of 5. It offers mesh networking and Wi-Fi 7, the newest and fastest router generation, without data caps or throttling. Sonic scores even higher as a regional provider with 4.90 out of 5. Most don’t experience random connection drops, while others say only a few times a year. Sonic also offers a free Wi-Fi check when installing your internet to double-check your connection and Wi-Fi, which could speak to its high reliability score.

Customer service

J. Hazelwood

Trying to troubleshoot your internet troubles on your own can be tough. The right customer support can help — whether it’s extended live assistance hours, online assistance or text message notifications of outages. Some providers even let you schedule in-person appointments online and provide up-to-date articles.

When choosing a provider, review the support options to ensure you’re comfortable with the availability and resources in case you need them. CNET readers give GFiber high marks for its fast, helpful customer support.

GFiber scores a 4.72 out of 5 for CNET readers. It offers a customer support page and several ways to get help, including scheduling a call or an online chat. There’s also a list of FAQs covering topics such as billing, internet support and self-installation. EPB scores a flawless 5 out of 5 for excellent customer service ratings. It offers a comprehensive FAQ page with troubleshooting assistance, live online chat, short videos and phone assistance.

Did you agree with these findings? CNET’s People’s Picks is community-driven and helps us spread the word about the tech and services you love. Take our ongoing TV survey to tell us what you love about yours.

Correction, July 10: An earlier version of this story gave an incorrect starting price for T-Mobile Home Internet.

Tech.title: Brave’s Browser Hides Your Real Email When You’re Signing Up for Websites
Tech.content:
Have you ever received the dreadful notification that your go-to email address was exposed during a data breach? Me, too — but one browser touting itself as an alternative to Google Chrome just might have the solution.

Brave announced last Thursday that it has launched a new “email aliases” feature for its browser, allowing you to create several managed dummy email addresses that contain no personal information and will forward all relevant mail to your main email account.

There are multiple problems with sharing your email during a website sign-up. Aside from the obvious threat of bad actors trying to scrape your sensitive information during a data leak or the nuisance of your main account being targeted by repeated phishing scams, your email address can be used to track you across the web.

According to Brave, “ad tech companies like Google, Meta and LinkedIn publicly promote how businesses can upload email addresses to match customers against their own user profiles.” These companies have been known to trade information to find out what you buy and where you buy it, and continue to accumulate information about you. Brave writes that its email aliases were built to “plug this privacy hole.”

“What’s so powerful about this is that we’re extending privacy beyond the browser: Websites no longer get your persistent email address identifier to track you across the web,” Brave vice president of privacy and security, Shivan Sahib, wrote over email. “We’re one of the first few companies deploying Opaque in production at scale, thanks to which even Brave doesn’t learn your Brave Account password.”

How to use Brave’s email aliases feature

The new email aliases feature isn’t automatically turned on, even if you’re already using Brave’s browser. There are a few easy steps you can follow to 

Navigate to the Brave login page (located at brave://settings/email-aliases) during your Brave desktop browsing session. Sign up and verify your main email address. While using the Brave browser, right-click on any website’s email address field in order to create and use a new email alias. To manage email aliases, navigate to the “autofill & passwords” page located within the Brave browser settings. All email alias mail will be forwarded to the email address used to 

But wait, doesn’t that mean Brave has my main email address?

Yes, you need to use your main email address to 

Brave has also made several security assurances that make it seem less likely that your sensitive information is in jeopardy when using the email aliases service.

According to Brave’s blog post, all data associated with the alias emails is encrypted at rest, meaning it’s cryptographically scrambled up for the little time it remains on the company’s servers.

“Brave doesn’t read the contents of emails sent to an alias,” the post reads. “We only process emails to perform standard spam and virus filtering (we need to do this to maintain our status as a reputable email provider). Once an email is delivered, it is deleted from our servers within seconds.”

Brave also promises that any notes you might add to your email aliases are stored locally on your computer, and not on Brave servers. If you use Brave’s online syncing service, the company promises those notes “will be encrypted end-to-end between devices on the same sync chain.”

The new feature is available for free, but you’re currently limited to five aliases. Sahib told CNET that Brave might eventually increase the number of free aliases, dependent on operating costs. For most people, this will be more than enough to avoid having to drop your main email address anywhere on the web — but Brave plans to add more email alias features to its Premium plan in the future.

“We’re generally thinking about how we can integrate Brave Accounts better with Premium services to improve the user experience, while keeping our privacy and security guarantees,” wrote Sahib. “We’d also like to add custom vanity email aliases in the future.”

A Google representative did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Tech.title: New JBL Cove Wireless Speakers Seem Like a Worthy Sonos Alternative
Tech.content:
Sonos is the big name in whole-home wirelesss audio, but JBL is taking another crack at it with its new Cove Wi-Fi speaker line. There are three models at launch: the Cove M1 ($229), Cove P1 ($399) and Cove X1 ($449). The Cove P1 is the only model that’s portable and has a built-in rechargeable battery, though all three speakers have both Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. They’re available for preorder now and ship Sept. 13.

While I haven’t tried the speakers in my own home, I got a taste of them in action at a JBL demo in a swanky loft in New York, and I was impressed by what I saw and heard. As part of the demo, JBL played each speaker on its own and then linked them together with other Cove speakers. It also created a stereo pair using two Cove M1 speakers, which can be used as rear channels when linked with JBL’s Bar Series MK2 soundbars.

The Cove P1 in white. David Carnoy/CNET

The system works a lot like a Sonos system, with speakers grouped by room (or on their own) using the JBL One app for iOS and Android. There’s an automatic self-tuning option, as well as AI Sound Boost technologies that “work to optimize performance based on where and how you listen.” They also have built-in microphones and are Alexa-enabled.

Needless to say, the X1, which has four tweeters and dual woofers, delivers the biggest, richest sound with the strongest bass performance (it’s comparable to Sonos’ $470 Era 300 speaker). But the M1 and P1 deliver big sound for their size, too, and seem to stack up well against their Sonos counterparts. They’re also priced similarly, though the Sonos speakers cost a little more (for example, the Sonos Move 2 portable speaker costs $499 while the P1 is $399).

The Cove X1 is the current flagship speaker David Carnoy/CNET

Back in the day, I liked JBL’s now-discontinued Link Series Wi-Fi speakers, which were released in 2017. They were fairly affordable and sounded decent, but just weren’t as well-designed as Sonos speakers, nor did they have the most user-friendly setup or as polished an app as Sonos’.

At first listen, its new Cove platform seems like a worthy alternative to Sonos, but I’ll have to A/B test those Cove speakers side by side with Sonos’ offerings to really get a sense of how their audio quality measures up. It’ll also be interesting to see where street prices for the Cove speakers land, and whether JBL will offer any discounts on speaker bundles. If they sound as good or even slightly better than their Sonos counterparts and cost less, that would certainly help them find a foothold in the whole-home audio marketplace.

Tech.title: Which Laptop Do You Rely on the Most? Help Us Find the Top Picks
Tech.content:
Your laptop is like your personal command center. Whether you’re working from a coffee shop, hopping on a video call or working on creative projects, your laptop shapes how you get things done. You probably use a laptop every day, so we want to know your opinions about its performance, battery life and if the features are worth the price tag.

Every month, we ask our readers about the tech and gadgets they use and swear by. This time, we want to know which laptop you rely on. You can take our 2-minute survey to share your experience with your device’s battery life, software, hardware and value. The top picks will make it into our roundup, so be sure to check back in a few weeks to see if your favorite made the list.

Why we want to hear from you

Anyone can visit a retailer’s website and check out a device’s specs, but that rarely tells the full story. How well it performs under your workload, how long the battery lasts and whether the build is solid enough to last over the years are invaluable pieces of information that only real-world users like you can provide.

“I test a lot of laptops and try to provide as much detail as I can about my hands-on experience in my reviews because actually using a laptop helps you get to the truth about a product much more quickly than relying on specs lists and marketing fluff,” says CNET Senior Editor Matt Elliott. “I am very curious to learn which types of laptops are the favorites and those that are failing to live up to expectations from CNET readers’ lived-in, real-world experiences.”

Whether you’re working with a budget laptop or a high-end model, you can help other CNET readers find a laptop that’s actually worth it by sharing your thoughts.

How to make your voice heard

The survey is open through September and takes only a few minutes to complete. After we gather enough information, we’ll crunch the numbers and publish the winners.

Need a refresher? Check out our list of best laptops to see which ones CNET editors recommend.

Tech.title: I’ve Run the Numbers and Read the Tea Leaves. Here’s When I Expect Apple to Release iOS 27
Tech.content:
Apple announced iOS 27 at its Worldwide Developers Conference in June, and the tech giant has since released multiple beta versions of the software. The betas have brought Siri AI and a handful of other features to the iPhones of developers and beta testers, and you can expect many of those capabilities to land on your iPhone soon.

Perhaps sooner than you expect.

So far, Apple has only said that it will release the update to the general public this fall, which isn’t the most helpful timeframe. If we look at past Apple events in September and earlier iOS releases, though, we can see a release pattern. Apple usually releases iOS versions a few days after the company’s September event, and I expect that trend to hold this year.

Based on those trends and a little psychic peering, I believe Apple will release iOS 27 on Monday, Sept. 14.

I was right about iOS 26’s release in 2025, iOS 18’s release in 2024 and iOS 17’s release in 2023, so I’m sure I can keep this streak going. But if you want the full breakdown of how I arrived at that date, here’s how.

How my iOS 27 release date math works

Usually Apple releases the next iOS update soon after the September event and the company is set to hold its “Surprise and shine” event on Wednesday, Sept. 9. While Apple doesn’t usually announce the release of iOS versions, the company has been pretty consistent with its release schedule over the years.

After most of Apple’s September events, the company releases the next iOS within a week. In 2025, for example, Apple’s event was held on Sept. 9 and the company released iOS 26 on Sept. 15. And in 2024 Apple’s event was held on Sept. 9 and iOS 18 was released seven days later on Sept. 16.

There’s only been one year over the past decade where it took longer than a week for Apple to release the next iOS version – 2019. That year, Apple released the next iOS version nine days after its September event.

In that same timeframe, most of the iOS releases were either five, six or seven days after the September event. Apple has also released the past five iOS versions on the Monday following its September events. This could be the new norm, with Apple releasing future iOS versions on the Monday after its September events moving forward.

So it’s most likely that Apple will release iOS 27 on the following Monday, Sept. 14.

For more on iOS 27, here are my first impressions of the beta and what to know about iOS 27 before Apple brings it to your device later this year.

Tech.title: Yearn for the Tern: Apple Has a New Daddy
Tech.content:
John Ternus took over as Apple CEO on Tuesday, succeeding Tim Cook after serving as the company’s senior vice president of hardware engineering. His first day comes just over a week before the annual iPhone launch event on Sept. 9.

Under Cook, Apple became a $4 trillion company with an impressive, world-changing lineup of tech products, including every iPhone from 2012’s iPhone 5 onward, the Apple Watch, the AirPods, the Vision Pro and the HomePod, and services including Apple Music, Apple TV Plus and Apple Fitness Plus.

But what exactly is Ternus walking into? There are major challenges ahead, driven by the global RAM shortage, increasing smartphone competition and Apple’s struggles to keep up with the artificial intelligence race.

Farewell to Tim Cook

Cook, who took over as CEO two months before Apple co-founder Steve Jobs passed away in 2011, reportedly held a farewell party at Apple Park last weekend to cap off his 15 years at the helm of the company. Around 200 people — mostly Apple employees, but also Cook’s partner and the band OneRepublic — attended the party, according to The Information, citing unnamed sources.

Ternus reportedly spoke at the event, along with Steve Jobs’ widow, Laurene Powell Jobs; Apple’s former COO, Jeff Williams; and head of Apple Services and Health, Eddy Cue.

According to that report, anonymous sources have said the transition from Cook to Ternus should be one of continuity rather than upheaval, with many things expected to stay the same.

During his final earnings call as CEO in July, Cook praised Ternus, saying, “There is no better person to take the helm of the company.” He also called Ternus “brilliant and wonderful and capable” in his farewell note as Apple CEO on Monday.

“Few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does, and I could not be more excited for his leadership,” Cook wrote this week.

With Ternus as CEO, Cook now serves as executive chair of Apple. Keeping him on in a senior role means Cook will still have influence over where Ternus decides to take Apple, and he could continue to be particularly influential with the current presidential administration, with which he’s fostered a good working relationship.

The Ternus takeover: Who is the new Apple CEO?

Ternus joined the tech giant back in 2001 as part of the product design team, having earned a bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering from the University of Pennsylvania and working as a mechanical engineer at Virtual Research Systems.

Rising through the ranks at Apple over 25 years, he became a VP of hardware engineering in 2013 and SVP in 2021. Ternus worked across many flagship devices, including the iPad, AirPods, iPhone, Apple Watch and, most recently, the MacBook Neo. Apple also credits Ternus with improving device durability by incorporting 3D-printed titanium in the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and creating a recycled aluminum compound.

Ternus was last year tipped to be the frontrunner in the race to succeed Cook, and at 51, he’s around the same age Cook was when he took over as Apple CEO.

The September launch will be an important first test for John Ternus as CEO. Counterpoint Research principal analyst Yang Wang

In Apple’s April announcement, Cook said Ternus “has the mind of an engineer, the soul of an innovator and the heart to lead with integrity and with honor.”

“Having spent almost my entire career at Apple, I have been lucky to have worked under Steve Jobs and to have had Tim Cook as my mentor,” Ternus said at the time.

IDC Worldwide Device Trackers senior research director Nabila Popal told CNET that she is “genuinely excited for Apple to go full circle and bring a products guy to lead Apple in this next phase, with an innovative lineup of interesting devices rumored to launch in the first few years of his leadership.”

The first two CEOs of Apple were likewise “products guys” — Michael Scott ran a semiconductor company, and Mike Markkula was an electrical engineer — so the choice of Ternus is a return to Apple’s roots.

The state of Apple in 2026: What is Ternus inheriting?

Bloomberg/Getty Images

His takeover comes just over a week before Apple unveils its next set of products, likely including the long-rumored foldable iPhone and the iPhone 18 lineup — but there are challenges ahead, even with a highly anticipated product launch.

One major test for Ternus will be the prices for the next iPhone, which are likely to have a higher price tag due to the ongoing global RAM shortage caused by the rapid expansion of AI tools. In June, Apple raised prices on over a dozen products across iPads, Macs and home devices.

“The September launch will be an important first test for John Ternus as CEO,” Counterpoint Research principal analyst Yang Wang told CNET. “A premium-focused lineup could strengthen Apple’s product mix, but it also increases the risk if pricing moves too far ahead of consumer demand.”

Most phones released this year have seen $100 bumps, including the Samsung Galaxy S26 line, while a few higher-end models have gone up $200 over their predecessors. Counterpoint projects the iPhone 18 lineup to see a price increase of $200-$250 per phone compared to the iPhone 17 lineup, “with high-spec models potentially seeing price hikes even beyond the range.”

The components that make AI possible are the same ones in short supply, and their cost is being passed straight through to the shelf. IDC vice president for worldwide client devices Francisco Jeronimo

Rumors suggest a standard iPhone 18 won’t be part of the lineup next week, instead launching in the spring alongside a potential iPhone 18E. This could extend the shelf life of the current iPhone 17, which is still seeing “strong demand” in 2026, according to Counterpoint Research. Typically, Apple discounts its previous model by $100 when a new iPhone is announced; if there’s no new base model, Apple can keep the iPhone 17 at its full price.

“Ternus knows the hardware organization very well, but the challenge will be balancing product ambition with affordability and launch execution,” Wang said, adding that he expects Samsung to overtake Apple for the global smartphone lead by the end of 2026.

The chip shortage across DRAM and NAND flash, which are needed for phones but are being gobbled up by AI data centers, is real. But there has been some criticism that tech giants are not shielding customers from chipflation despite seeing record sales; Apple, for instance, raked in roughly $109 billion in net sales and reported almost $30 billion in net income during the previous quarter.

At the end of August, analyst firm IDC said smartphone shipments are set for a record 17% drop this year due to the memory crisis, with NAND and DRAM costs up 300% compared to last year.

“The components that make AI possible are the same ones in short supply, and their cost is being passed straight through to the shelf,” IDC vice president for worldwide client devices Francisco Jeronimo wrote on Aug. 26. “Average selling prices are up 27.6% this year and will keep rising well into 2027. The era of the cheap smartphone has ended.”

According to IDC, “foldables remain the only silver lining.”

Could a foldable revitalize the iPhone?

Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

Apple is late to the foldable phone game, assuming it finally launches one next week. Samsung is now on its eighth generation of foldable phones, with the recent launch of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Galaxy Z Flip 8, which follow the company’s first foldable phone in 2019. There are also competitor folding phones such as Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold, Motorola’s Razr Fold and other Chinese options from Oppo, OnePlus and Huawei.

IDC is predicting “rapid growth” in the foldable phones market thanks to Apple’s expected entry into the sector. It forecasts Apple will ship more than 17 million foldable iPhones by next year, snatching 40% of the folding phone market share, potentially making it the dominant force over Samsung, Google and Huawei.

Counterpoint Research has a little less glaze on its folding iPhone predictions, saying that with an expected price tag of $2,200 — IDC predicts $2,550 — its customer base will be limited and shipments will account for just 3% of all iPhones.

“The device is likely to target affluent early adopters and existing Pro Max users looking for something between an iPhone and an iPad,” Wang told CNET. “This is less about competing directly with Samsung or Google and more about creating a new top tier within Apple’s own portfolio.”

Ternus knows the hardware organization very well, but the challenge will be balancing product ambition with affordability. Counterpoint Research principal analyst Yang Wang

Wang said Apple’s late entry into the foldable market is unlikely to be a disadvantage, though, given the supply chain is now more mature and there have been technological improvements in hinge design, display creases and durability.

It’s important to remember that a foldable isn’t guaranteed success, however. CNET’s survey of more than 2,600 adults last month found that 75% were not interested in a foldable iPhone, and that most would only want to spend around $781 on an Apple foldable phone — which is $48 less than a base-model iPhone 17.

Under Cook, Apple expanded from two iPhone models a year to five; the addition of a foldable phone would bring the total to six iPhone models just a week into Ternus’ new role. It wouldn’t necessarily matter whether the iPhone Fold is a hit if it does the job of expanding the iPhone price range well beyond $2,000 to appeal to higher-end buyers.

Regardless of how much work was put into the folding iPhone before he took over, Ternus will own the success or failure of Apple’s purported foldable. But it’s not the only area he’s tasked with bringing Apple back into the lead.

Where does AI fit into Apple’s future?

Apple is also behind on AI, even settling a lawsuit over the lack of AI features in its previous iPhones after overpromising and underdelivering. While Siri AI remained under development, Apple inked deals with OpenAI to use ChatGPT on iPhones and with Google to leverage Gemini to expand Siri.

After years of delays, Apple finally unveiled Siri AI and improved Apple Intelligence during its annual software conference, WWDC, in June. It now has its own app, a fresh design, customized voice options, more accurate dictation, better context for improved suggestions, integrated writing tools, the ability to pull info from your messages, emails and other apps and what Apple calls “broad world knowledge.”

Visual Intelligence has been rolled into a new Siri mode in the camera app, including the ability to identify family and friends in photos by name and to search screenshots for products online.

Siri AI is expected to launch later this year in beta, possibly timed with the release of the new iPhones, so for now, it remains to be seen whether Apple can truly compete with AI giants such as Google and OpenAI.

The biggest challenge for Apple as Ternus takes over is how to keep the company relevant in the age of AI. IDC Worldwide Device Trackers senior research director Nabila Popal

One of the biggest industry pressures facing Ternus will be remedying this and ensuring a smooth rollout of AI features in Apple’s phones and Macs to match its competitors. However, a CNET survey found that AI isn’t a major motivator for people to upgrade their phones, and there are also rising concerns from consumers about how much water and power AI data centers are sucking up and what kind of privacy implications there are when AI is integrated into everything.

By choosing a hardware-focused CEO, however, Apple may be signaling that it wants to focus on devices over AI — unless a move into physical AI is imminent for the tech giant.

“The biggest challenge for Apple as Ternus takes over is how to keep the company relevant in the age of AI,” Popal told CNET. “But what will be crucial is whether the level of innovation can keep up with consumer expectations as the world is rapidly shifting into an unknown AI era, where how we interact with our devices is changing, and for the moment, it is increasingly looking like we are moving towards a more voice-powered interface than touch.”

While a smart glasses announcement next week is unlikely, we’re expecting a refresh of Apple’s AirPods, and rumors are swirling around AirPods with AI-powered cameras that can use Visual Intelligence to improve Siri’s context about your surroundings and give better suggestions and answers. It’s part of a slate of unreleased products that are powered by Siri AI.

But there are privacy implications in being tracked and monitored by tiny, hidden cameras embedded in earbuds, too.

“It’s hard not to see this upcoming product launch as Apple simply chasing the AI arms race rather than genuinely listening to customer needs,” said Lee Elliott, chief product officer at Compare and Recycle, a tech recycling comparison site, in a statement last week. “Camera-equipped earphones will certainly be storing far more personal data, including images, locations and environmental data.”

Announcing new products always comes with an air of excitement, but in the age of AI everywhere and RAM shortages driving global price hikes, the main challenge for Ternus as he steps into the CEO role will likely be balancing privacy, AI hesitancy and pricing against launching one more thing.

Tech.title: Dyson Blasts Into Dental Care With a $499 Camera-Equipped Toothbrush
Tech.content:
Taking care of our teeth is a straightforward process: brush, floss, rinse, done. But with its new CameraJet toothbrush, launched on Tuesday, Dyson wants to simplify the process. The toothbursh has an AI-powered camera that detects gaps between teeth so it can floss while you brush.

“Our research has shown that people consistently miss the areas where plaque forms: the gaps between teeth,” Founder and Chief Engineer James Dyson said in a press release. “We wanted to solve three fundamental problems: how to see those gaps, remove plaque and how to improve cleaning performance while brushing.”

The Dyson CameraJet was developed by 661 Dyson engineers and 30 dental professionals over six years. Dyson

A camera for capturing your pearly whites

The toothbrush’s camera uses a 100,000-pixel macro lens with a light. It’s powered by the company’s trademarked AI machine-learning algorithm, Gap Optical Targeting, which was trained on 470,000 dental images collected by Dyson during development.

Gap Optical Targeting analyzes 28 live images per second to detect gaps between teeth within 100 milliseconds. The CameraJet’s jet then shoots a burst of mouthrinse at the gap to floss it.

Since the CameraJet also connects to 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, you can use the camera as an endoscope to see a live view in the brush’s live-viewing or auto-jetting modes. In the app, you can also see coverage maps, guided cleaning, brushing and flossing insights and feedback.

According to the press release, no images are recorded or stored on the product or in the cloud. All images remain private to the CameraJet user.

Dyson CameraJet See at Dyson

How the CameraJet’s jet differs

In collaboration with the National University of Singapore’s Faculty of Dentistry for over five years, Dyson created its own proxy plaque to test its flossing jet. Researchers found that traditional water flossers tend to use a needle-like jet that pierces a hole in plaque but doesn’t remove it entirely.

In contrast, the CameraJet uses a conical jet that provides wider coverage while operating at a lower pressure to remain gentle.

You’ve got a camera, light and mouthrinse jet all in one toothbrush. Dyson

Built with an anti-gravity tank

To contain the recommended amount of mouthrinse for its jet, the CameraJet has a built-in 12.5-ml tank that delivers mouthrinse in any orientation.

Unlike other water flossers that use what Dyson described in its press release as a “straw in a cup” design, this anti-gravity tank was designed to minimize air pockets that could prevent the jet from firing, especially when the device is horizontal while cleaning the back of the teeth.

Baroque brush heads

Every dual-bristle brush head comes with its own RFID (radio-frequency identification) tag that allows the CameraJet to detect when a brush head is connected and how many times it has been used. This helps users know when it’s time to replace the brush head with a fresh one.

For less noise, each brush head was also created with a sonic dampener.

To keep the bristles in constant motion and prevent stalling, the CameraJet uses variable sonic oscillation, which varies the oscillation angle as you brush. This is particularly useful in areas of your mouth that are tough to access, as external lab testing found that the CameraJet’s variable mode removes up to 69% more plaque than market-leading premium electric toothbrushes in hard-to-reach areas.

On the toothbrush, you can choose between auto-detect and manual jetting modes, and adjust the brushing intensity.

For sensitive teeth and gums, a sensitive-bristled brush head is also available.

Below the power button, you can switch between auto-detect and manual jetting modes and change the brushing intensity. Dyson

The price is on the higher side

Now available on the Dyson website in ceramic ultra blue and ceramic pink, the $499 CameraJet comes with two regular brush heads, a charging dock, a charging cable and a travel case.

In addition to charging the toothbrush, the dock can also refill its mouthrinse tank in three seconds.

It’s recommended that you use a clear, SLS-free mouth rinse and an SLS-free toothpaste with the CameraJet to prevent foam from interfering with the camera. SLS is a common foaming agent in toothpaste, shampoo and soaps.

However, if you’re looking for a smart toothbrush with a cleaning coach that’s under $499, CNET recommends the $100 Oral-B iO Series 5 on our list of the best electric toothbrushes.

The charging station refills the CameraJet with mouthrinse in three seconds. Dyson

Coming soon

Dyson developed a proprietary non-foaming toothpaste without SLS and a low-foaming mouthrinse specifically designed for the CameraJet’s jet. While no specific release date is available, Dyson said both are coming soon.

The CameraJet is currently on its way to my home for testing, so I’ll post a review once I find out if it’s worth the price.

Tech.title: The Wickedly Easy Ways Smart Thermostats Tackle Home Humidity Problems
Tech.content:
I wouldn’t wish humidity problems on anyone’s home. On the dry side, low humidity can cause everything from nosebleeds to cracks in dried-out wood flooring. And high humidity can encourage mold, warp wood or damage paint. Depending on how delicate your houseplants are, both extremes could also threaten their health.

But the smart thermostat, that unsung hero of the modern home, has hidden potential to fix this problem. These thermostats not only help gauge humidity, but they can automatically take action to prevent issues or alert you so you can maintain just the right indoor air quality. Here’s how to get started.

Yes, the right thermostat really can sense humidity

Today’s smart thermostats, including the Google Nest, have humidity sensors. Google

Quick, what’s the humidity in your house right now? Most households don’t know, certainly not by checking traditional thermostats and definitely not when they’re away from home. Smart thermostats are different.

Today’s smart thermostats, including some of our favorite models like the Ecobee Premium and Google Nest thermostats, have built-in humidity sensors that are always detecting moisture in the air of your home. With the app on your phone, including popular platforms like Google Home and Alexa, you can check on humidity levels at any time, no matter where you are, before problems begin emerging.

With a smart thermostat, you can check humidity and get alerts from anywhere. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Some thermostats even allow you to set alerts when humidity levels reach certain thresholds, so your phone will tell you when you need to take action. Humidity isn’t always related to temperature, either. When I asked Dan Bereiter, senior product manager of Honeywell Home Solutions at Residio, about these features, he advised a combo approach. “If the temperature looks comfortable, but the home still feels stuffy, clammy, or dry, humidity may be part of the issue. Watching both temperature and humidity can help homeowners make more informed adjustments.”

What if your smart thermostat doesn’t have a humidity sensor? That’s easy to address.

You can hook up a humidity sensor to nearly any smart thermostat

Thermostat satellite sensors are one of the best inventions for home heating. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

I’ve experimented with an array of sensors that can measure humidity, from all-purpose versions from SwitchBot to the Wyze room sensor, the capable Aqara sensor and even an affordable humidity sensor from Ikea.

All these sensors can provide humidity readings to your thermostat, or independently to their own apps, which can still supply alerts to your phone about certain humidity levels. Many can also work with broader smart home platforms that can combine multiple devices like Google Home, Apple Home and Alexa, which can make it even easier to connect to thermostats and other devices.

With a press of this Ikea button, you can see the nearby temperature and humidity. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

In some ways these smaller devices are even more useful than built-in humidity sensors, because you can move them to whichever room has the worst humidity problems, or the most delicate plants, etc., to get more accurate readings.

Then humidity levels can automatically turn on appliances

Humidifiers are easy to find at major retailers and are sold at a variety of price points. MistAire via Amazon

With a smart humidity sensor, it’s now easy to set up a routine to let your house automatically tackle humidity problems. One of the best ways to do this is with a smart humidifier or dehumidifier. These include features that can connect to smart home platforms, too, which means you can set up an easy rule: “If the humidity reaches a certain level, turn on the humidifier/dehumidifier.”

What indoor humidity levels are best? Bereiter told me: “The EPA recommends maintaining indoor relative humidity (RH) between 30% and 50% because balanced humidity can help improve comfort, support HVAC system efficiency, and help protect building materials from excess moisture.”

You can set up a rule like this in just a couple of minutes, usually under the “Automations” section. The hardest part is connected sensors and appliances to Wi-Fi and adding them to apps, but as long as you have a reliable Wi-Fi router nearby, this shouldn’t be a problem.

These automations works best for larger models that can quickly adjust humidity, but of course the biggest will need to be refilled with water, or need a way to empty the water they’ve collected from the air (some use window units with a hose going outside). There are also whole-house dehumidifiers with smart capabilities by companies like AprilAire and TCL, as well as ways to connect to whole-house units with thermostats like Ecobee’s.

Of course, these smart appliances can get pricey. If you want to save money or already have a humidity device, you can usually make it smart by connecting it to a smart plug. These smart plugs can turn humidifiers/dehumidifiers on or off based on schedules and rules you set up in apps. Smart plugs are only around $10 to $15, so it’s a very cheap way to add smart features to an appliance you already have.

If you do want to add a smart plug to your appliance, double-check it can function with basic on/off commands. Not all humidifiers, for example, turn on correctly when controlled by a smart plug. I suggest scanning reviews online to see if anyone has tried using the appliance or a model from the same brand with a smart plug to make sure it works before you buy.

Some thermostats can even tap directly into AC and heat pumps

Cooling and humidity settings are more advanced then ever and can connect to current home systems. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Setting up rules to automatically turn on humidifiers or dehumidifiers is an excellent use of the smart home, and your plants, pets, family and lungs will benefit. But many smart thermostats can do even more.

Thermostat models also have the ability to connect to supported air conditioner systems and heat pumps (they don’t even have to be smart). These systems can act as natural dehumidifiers when they turn on, so it’s an easy way to lower humidity and heat in a home when they become problematic.

One of my favorite versions is Google Nest’s Cool to Dry, because it’s nearly effortless to turn on and can work with any AC or heat pump as long as you have the right wiring – follow the link to learn more about the details. Nest even takes it a step further with its new thermostat capability Humidity Helper, which taps into existing humidifiers/dehumidifiers to automatically set up rules for you.

Honeywell Home smart thermostats can also connect to AC and humidity features, particularly Resideo systems. AprilAire also offers a whole home setup that allows smart thermostats to control AC, air purifiers and more. Remember, if these setups get too complicated for you, you can always contact an HVAC professional to connect everything for you or find out what your home supports.

Even without automations set up, you can still take action

Do all these smart connections and automations feel like too much? Don’t want to spend any more money on appliances? You don’t have to use them to improve humidity levels. Take manual action and use your thermostat’s humidity readings to make decisions about when to open windows, turn on your AC, flip on a humidifier and so on. More information from your thermostat means better decisions for your home, no matter how you go about it.

Humidity changes can even help you save money

Humidity management could even lead to savings. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Humidity has such a big influence on how we feel at home, dealing with it may mean running your heating or cooling system less and potentially saving money.

“High humidity can make a home feel warmer than it actually is, often leading homeowners to lower the thermostat and forcing the AC system to work harder,” Bereiter warned me.

A combination of smart thermostat suggestions and eco modes, plus taking care of humidity, may be able to make your home feel cooler while also saving on your energy bills. However, be careful. Constantly using your AC or humidifier to control humidity can have the opposite effect and cost more energy, so work on hitting the sweet spot for savings.

Final note: Humidity can change significantly between seasons in some climates. Certain setups may work best in winter if your cold season is especially dry, or you may only need a humidifier setup in sweltering summers. Either way, smart thermostats and sensors can help out.
